The characteristic angular size of the hot and cold spots in the CMB (the acoustic peak scale, near 1 degree) acts as a standard ruler laid down at redshift z ≈ 1100; how big it looks today depends on the curvature the light travelled through. WMAP and then the Planck satellite (2018 results) measured the curvature density Ω_k = −kc²/(a₀²H0²) to be 0.0007 ± 0.0019 — consistent with exactly zero. In plain terms, Ω_total = 1.000 to better than half a percent, so the universe is flat as far as we can measure. This is a striking result, because a flat universe requires the components to sum to critical density: Ω_m + Ω_Λ + Ω_r ≈ 1. Visible matter accounts for only about 5% of that, dark matter about 27%, and dark energy about 68% — the "energy budget" the rest of this unit unpacks.

lessons.workedExample: Compute the critical density and turn a measured mass density into Ω_m. Using ρ_c = 3H0²/(8πG) with H0 = 2.27×10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹ (that is 70 km/s/Mpc in SI, from the previous lesson): ρ_c = 3(2.27×10⁻¹⁸)² / (8π × 6.674×10⁻¹¹) = 3(5.15×10⁻³⁶) / (1.677×10⁻⁹) ≈ 9.2×10⁻²⁷ kg/m³. Divide by the proton mass 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg to express it as particles: 9.2×10⁻²⁷ / 1.67×10⁻²⁷ ≈ 5.5 protons per cubic metre. Now suppose a survey infers a total matter density (dark plus baryonic) of ρ_m ≈ 2.9×10⁻²⁷ kg/m³. Then Ω_m = ρ_m/ρ_c = 2.9×10⁻²⁷ / 9.2×10⁻²⁷ ≈ 0.31 — the standard value. Since 0.31 is well below 1, matter alone leaves the universe open; only by adding Ω_Λ ≈ 0.69 does the total reach 1 and match the flat geometry the CMB independently demands.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often push on "how do you know the universe is flat, and what does that even mean?" — because students routinely confuse "flat" (zero spatial curvature, Ω_total = 1) with "two-dimensional" or "not expanding." The concept that scores is recognising that flatness is a statement about Ω_total relative to 1, that it is measured geometrically from the CMB acoustic-peak angular scale (a standard ruler), and that flatness plus a below-critical matter density is precisely what forces dark energy into the budget. A student who says "flat means Ω = 1, matter only gives 0.3, so something else supplies the missing 0.7" has connected geometry to the energy inventory.

questions.prompt: The critical density ρ_c is best described as:

options.text: The density of an average galaxy
The density that makes the universe spatially flat at a given expansion rate H
A fixed universal constant, the same at all times
The density of dark energy specifically

explanations.a: Galaxies are enormously denser than critical; ρ_c is a space-averaged threshold, about 5–6 hydrogen atoms per cubic metre, not the density of any object.
explanations.b: Correct — ρ_c = 3H²/(8πG) is the density that zeroes the curvature term, making Ω_total = 1 and the geometry flat, at whatever H holds at that epoch.
explanations.c: Because ρ_c depends on H, and H changes over cosmic time, the critical density was far higher in the early universe; it is not constant.
explanations.d: ρ_c is the yardstick for all components combined; dark energy is one contributor (Ω_Λ ≈ 0.69), not the definition of critical density.

questions.prompt: If measurements gave Ω_total = 1.4, what would that imply about the geometry and fate (matter-dominated intuition)?

options.text: Flat and infinite, expanding forever at a constant rate
Open, negatively curved, expanding forever
Closed, positively curved (k = +1), finite volume
Geometry is undefined because Ω cannot exceed 1

explanations.a: Flat requires Ω_total = 1 exactly; 1.4 is above critical and therefore not flat.
explanations.b: Open geometry corresponds to Ω_total < 1 (below critical), the opposite of 1.4.
explanations.c: Correct — Ω_total > 1 means density exceeds critical, so k = +1: space is positively curved and closed with finite volume (in a matter-only universe it would eventually recollapse).
explanations.d: Ω can certainly exceed 1; that is exactly the closed case. Nothing forbids Ω_total > 1.

questions.prompt: Match each value of the total density parameter to the curvature and geometry it implies.

right.text: k = +1: closed, positively curved, finite
k = 0: flat, Euclidean, infinite
k = −1: open, negatively (saddle) curved, infinite

questions.explanation: From Ω_total − 1 = kc²/(a²H²), the sign of (Ω_total − 1) equals the sign of k: above critical (Ω > 1) is closed/positive curvature, exactly critical (Ω = 1) is flat, below critical (Ω < 1) is open/negative curvature.

questions.prompt: The tightest evidence that the universe is spatially flat (Ω_total ≈ 1.00) comes from:

options.text: Weighing all the galaxies with a scale
The angular size of the acoustic peaks in the cosmic microwave background (a standard ruler) as measured by WMAP and Planck
The rotation curves of spiral galaxies
The Chandrasekhar mass of white dwarfs

explanations.a: Summing galaxy masses gives a matter density (Ω_m ≈ 0.31), which alone is below critical; it does not directly measure total curvature.
explanations.b: Correct — the ~1° acoustic-peak scale at z ≈ 1100 is a standard ruler; its observed angular size depends on curvature, and Planck measured Ω_k = 0.0007 ± 0.0019, i.e. flat to sub-percent.
explanations.c: Rotation curves reveal dark matter within galaxies but do not measure the global spatial curvature of the universe.
explanations.d: The Chandrasekhar mass (~1.4 M_sun) underpins Type Ia supernova standard candles for the expansion history, not the direct curvature measurement.

lessons.label: The Cosmic Inventory: How Radiation, Matter, and Dark Energy Densities Scale with a(t)

sections.heading: Each component dilutes differently as space stretches
sections.body: The Friedmann equation is only useful once you know how ρ behaves as the universe expands, and the answer is different for each component — that difference is the engine of cosmic history. Matter (both ordinary baryons and dark matter) is a fixed number of particles spread through an expanding volume. Volume scales as a³, so the number density and hence the mass density fall as ρ_m ∝ a⁻³. Radiation — photons and other relativistic particles — dilutes the same way by volume (a⁻³) but suffers an extra effect: every photon's wavelength is stretched by the expansion, so its energy E = hc/λ redshifts down by an additional factor of a. That gives ρ_r ∝ a⁻⁴, one power steeper than matter. Dark energy, if it is a cosmological constant, is a property of space itself: its density stays fixed as space expands, ρ_Λ ∝ a⁰ = constant. So as a grows, radiation thins fastest, matter next, and dark energy not at all.

sections.heading: Redshift is the clock: 1 + z = 1/a
sections.body: To connect these scalings to observations, use the exact relation between scale factor and redshift. Light emitted when the scale factor was a arrives today (a₀ = 1) stretched by exactly the factor by which space grew: 1 + z = a₀/a = 1/a. So a redshift of z = 1 means light left when the universe was half its present size (a = 1/2); z = 9 means a = 0.1, one-tenth today's size. Substituting a = 1/(1+z), the density histories become ρ_m ∝ (1+z)³, ρ_r ∝ (1+z)⁴, and ρ_Λ = constant. Reading right to left toward the past (increasing z), radiation climbs fastest. This is why the early universe was radiation-dominated even though radiation is utterly negligible today (Ω_r ≈ 9×10⁻⁵): run the clock back far enough and the steepest-rising term must win.

sections.heading: The three eras and their handover points
sections.body: Because the components rise at different rates going back in time, cosmic history splits into three eras, each ruled by whichever density is largest. Earliest is the radiation era, when ρ_r ∝ a⁻⁴ dominated. Matter-radiation equality — where ρ_m first overtook ρ_r — occurred at z_eq ≈ 3400, a few tens of thousands of years after the Big Bang; after it, the matter era set in and structure could begin to grow. Much later, as matter kept thinning as a⁻³ while dark energy held constant, ρ_Λ overtook ρ_m at a redshift of about z ≈ 0.3 (scale factor a ≈ 0.75), only a few billion years ago, beginning the present dark-energy era. Today's inventory, pinned down by Planck combined with supernova and galaxy-survey data, is roughly Ω_m ≈ 0.31 (of which baryons are only ~0.05 and dark matter ~0.26), Ω_Λ ≈ 0.69, and Ω_r ≈ 9×10⁻⁵. The order of eras — radiation, then matter, then dark energy — is a direct consequence of the exponents −4, −3, and 0.

lessons.workedExample: Locate matter-radiation equality from the present densities. Equality is where ρ_m(z) = ρ_r(z). Using ρ_m = ρ_m,0(1+z)³ and ρ_r = ρ_r,0(1+z)⁴, set them equal: ρ_m,0(1+z)³ = ρ_r,0(1+z)⁴. Cancel (1+z)³ from both sides: ρ_m,0 = ρ_r,0(1+z), so 1 + z_eq = ρ_m,0/ρ_r,0 = Ω_m/Ω_r. Plug in today's values Ω_m ≈ 0.315 and Ω_r ≈ 9.1×10⁻⁵: 1 + z_eq = 0.315 / 9.1×10⁻⁵ ≈ 3460, so z_eq ≈ 3460. That matches the standard result (~3400). The single extra power of (1+z) in radiation's scaling — the photon redshift on top of volume dilution — is entirely responsible for radiation winning at high z: without it, radiation and matter would dilute in lockstep and there would be no radiation era.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe "why did radiation dominate the early universe if it is negligible now?" because it directly tests whether a student understands the a⁻⁴ versus a⁻³ scaling rather than just naming eras. The winning answer names the extra factor of a for radiation — photons dilute by volume like matter but additionally lose energy as their wavelength redshifts — so its density rises one power faster toward the past and inevitably overtakes matter at high redshift. A student who can also state that dark energy stays constant (a⁰) and therefore only ever dominates late explains the whole radiation→matter→dark-energy sequence from three exponents.

questions.prompt: Order these components from the steepest (fastest-diluting as the universe expands) to the shallowest density scaling with the scale factor a.

items.text: Radiation (ρ ∝ a⁻⁴)
Matter (ρ ∝ a⁻³)
Dark energy / cosmological constant (ρ ∝ a⁰ = constant)

questions.explanation: Radiation falls fastest (a⁻⁴: volume dilution a⁻³ plus an extra a⁻¹ from photon redshift), matter next (a⁻³, pure volume dilution), and dark energy not at all (a⁰). This ordering of exponents is exactly why the eras run radiation → matter → dark energy.

questions.prompt: Why does radiation density scale as a⁻⁴ while matter scales as a⁻³?

options.text: Photons are created continuously, adding density over time
Radiation dilutes by volume (a⁻³) like matter, plus each photon’s energy redshifts down by an extra factor of a
Radiation is affected by gravity but matter is not
Matter is created as the universe expands, offsetting its dilution

explanations.a: Photon number is (to excellent approximation) conserved after the early universe; the steeper scaling is not from creating photons.
explanations.b: Correct — both dilute as a⁻³ by expanding volume, but a photon’s wavelength stretches with a, so its energy hc/λ drops by an extra factor of a, giving radiation a⁻⁴ overall.
explanations.c: Both matter and radiation gravitate; that is not the origin of the different exponents.
explanations.d: Matter particle number is conserved; matter simply dilutes as a⁻³ with volume, and nothing offsets it.

questions.prompt: A galaxy is observed at redshift z = 3. What was the scale factor of the universe when its light was emitted?

explanations.a: The scale factor in the past is always less than 1 (the universe was smaller); a = 3 would mean it was larger then, which is backwards.
explanations.b: This uses a = 1/z, but the correct relation is a = 1/(1+z), so the +1 must be included.
explanations.c: Correct — 1 + z = 1/a gives a = 1/(1+z) = 1/(1+3) = 1/4, so space was one-quarter its present size when the light left.
explanations.d: a = 1/2 corresponds to z = 1, not z = 3.

questions.prompt: Approximately what is the present-day cosmic energy budget (density parameters)?

options.text: Ω_m ≈ 0.31 (matter), Ω_Λ ≈ 0.69 (dark energy), Ω_r ≈ 9×10⁻⁵ (radiation)
Ω_m ≈ 0.05 (all baryons), Ω_Λ ≈ 0.5, Ω_r ≈ 0.45

explanations.a: Correct — Planck plus supernova and galaxy-survey data give roughly Ω_m ≈ 0.31 (baryons ~0.05, dark matter ~0.26), Ω_Λ ≈ 0.69, and a tiny Ω_r ≈ 9×10⁻⁵ today.
explanations.b: The matter and dark-energy values are swapped; dark energy dominates today, not matter.
explanations.c: An Einstein–de Sitter (matter-only) universe with Ω_m = 1 is ruled out; supernovae show acceleration requiring Ω_Λ ≈ 0.7.
explanations.d: Matter is ~0.31, not 0.05 (0.05 is baryons alone), and radiation is negligible today, not 0.45.

lessons.label: Equation of State w: Why Matter Decelerates and Dark Energy (w = −1) Accelerates

sections.heading: One number encodes each component: p = w·ρc²
sections.body: The reason the components in the last lesson scale with those particular exponents is a single parameter: the equation-of-state parameter w, defined by the ratio of a component's pressure to its energy density, p = w·ρc². It captures how "springy" a fluid is. Pressureless matter (galaxies and dark matter, moving slowly, exerting negligible pressure) has w = 0. Radiation — a relativistic gas of photons — has w = +1/3, a standard result of kinetic theory for an ultra-relativistic gas. A cosmological constant, remarkably, has w = −1: it exerts negative pressure (tension) equal in magnitude to its energy density. Spatial curvature can be bookkept as an effective fluid with w = −1/3. These are not arbitrary; each follows from the physics of the component, and each w fixes exactly how that component's density changes with expansion.

sections.heading: w sets the dilution rate: ρ ∝ a^(−3(1+w))
sections.body: Feed the equation of state into energy conservation for the expanding fluid and you get a master scaling law: ρ ∝ a^(−3(1+w)). Every result from the previous lesson drops out of this one formula. Matter (w = 0): a^(−3(1+0)) = a⁻³. Radiation (w = 1/3): a^(−3(4/3)) = a⁻⁴. Cosmological constant (w = −1): a^(−3(0)) = a⁰ = constant. The formula also shows the boundary that matters most: a component's density stays constant only when w = −1, and it would actually grow as space expands if w < −1 (so-called "phantom" dark energy). The more negative w is, the less a component dilutes, and the longer it will eventually dominate. w is therefore the compact way to specify what a mysterious component does without knowing what it is.

sections.heading: The acceleration threshold is w < −1/3
sections.body: Return to the acceleration equation, ä/a = −(4πG/3)(ρ + 3p/c²). Substitute p = w·ρc² and it becomes ä/a = −(4πG/3)ρ(1 + 3w). The bracket (1 + 3w) decides the sign. For matter (w = 0): 1 + 3(0) = 1 > 0, so ä < 0 — matter decelerates the expansion, exactly as Newtonian intuition demands. For radiation (w = 1/3): 1 + 1 = 2 > 0, even stronger deceleration. But for a cosmological constant (w = −1): 1 + 3(−1) = −2 < 0, so ä > 0 — the expansion accelerates. The dividing line is w = −1/3, where 1 + 3w = 0 and the component neither accelerates nor decelerates. Any component with w more negative than −1/3 drives acceleration. This is the mechanism behind cosmic acceleration: dark energy's deeply negative pressure, not any exotic new force, tips ρ + 3p/c² negative. Measuring w is thus the central goal of dark-energy surveys; combining Planck CMB data with Type Ia supernovae and baryon acoustic oscillations gives w = −1.03 ± 0.03, statistically indistinguishable from the cosmological-constant value −1. Models where w differs from −1 or evolves in time (dynamical scalar fields called quintessence, with −1 < w < −1/3) remain viable and are actively tested; the 2024 DESI galaxy survey reported hints of an evolving w, though the case for a simple constant Λ is not yet overturned.

lessons.workedExample: Predict the density scaling and the acceleration verdict for dark energy from w alone, then contrast with matter. Take a cosmological constant, w = −1. Density scaling: ρ ∝ a^(−3(1+w)) = a^(−3(1−1)) = a^0 = constant — dark energy does not dilute, confirming the a⁰ behaviour. Acceleration: ä/a = −(4πG/3)ρ(1 + 3w) = −(4πG/3)ρ(1 + 3(−1)) = −(4πG/3)ρ(−2) = +(8πG/3)ρ > 0, so ä > 0 — it accelerates. Now matter, w = 0: ρ ∝ a^(−3(1+0)) = a⁻³ (dilutes), and ä/a = −(4πG/3)ρ(1 + 0) = −(4πG/3)ρ < 0, so ä < 0 — it decelerates. The same one-line substitution of w reproduces both the dilution exponent and the sign of the acceleration for any component, which is why w is the parameter observers most want to pin down.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "what exactly makes the universe accelerate?" to see whether a student can go beyond "dark energy pushes things apart" to the actual condition. The concept that scores is that gravity's source in GR is ρ + 3p/c², and with p = wρc² acceleration requires 1 + 3w < 0, i.e. w < −1/3 — negative pressure, not a repulsive force. A student who states the threshold, notes that a cosmological constant sits at w = −1, and knows the current constraint (w ≈ −1.03 ± 0.03, consistent with −1) demonstrates they understand acceleration as an equation-of-state effect and know where the observations stand.

questions.prompt: The acceleration equation ä/a = −(4πG/3)ρ(1 + 3w) means the expansion accelerates (ä > 0) when:

explanations.a: Positive w (like matter or radiation) gives 1 + 3w > 0, so ä < 0 — deceleration, not acceleration.
explanations.b: w = 0 is pressureless matter: 1 + 3(0) = 1 > 0, giving ä < 0 (deceleration).
explanations.c: Correct — acceleration needs 1 + 3w < 0, i.e. w < −1/3. A cosmological constant (w = −1) satisfies this; the boundary is exactly w = −1/3.
explanations.d: w = +1/3 is radiation, which strongly decelerates (1 + 3(1/3) = 2 > 0).

questions.prompt: Match each component to its equation-of-state parameter w.
questions.explanation: Slow-moving matter exerts negligible pressure (w = 0); an ultra-relativistic photon gas has w = +1/3 by kinetic theory; a cosmological constant has negative pressure equal in magnitude to its energy density, w = −1.

questions.prompt: Using ρ ∝ a^(−3(1+w)), what density scaling does a cosmological constant (w = −1) have?

options.text: ρ ∝ a⁻³ (dilutes like matter)
ρ ∝ a⁻⁴ (dilutes like radiation)
ρ ∝ a⁰ = constant (does not dilute)
ρ ∝ a⁺³ (grows rapidly)

explanations.a: a⁻³ is the matter case (w = 0); the cosmological constant scales differently.
explanations.b: a⁻⁴ is radiation (w = 1/3), not a cosmological constant.
explanations.c: Correct — with w = −1, the exponent is −3(1 + (−1)) = −3(0) = 0, so ρ ∝ a⁰ = constant: dark energy density stays fixed as space expands.
explanations.d: A growing density would require w < −1 (phantom energy); a cosmological constant stays constant, not growing.

questions.prompt: What does the current best combined constraint on dark energy’s equation of state (Planck CMB + Type Ia supernovae + baryon acoustic oscillations) indicate?

options.text: w ≈ −1.03 ± 0.03, statistically consistent with a cosmological constant (w = −1)
w ≈ 0, meaning dark energy behaves like ordinary matter
w ≈ +1/3, meaning dark energy is a form of radiation
w is completely unconstrained by current data

explanations.a: Correct — combining CMB, supernova, and BAO data yields w ≈ −1.03 ± 0.03, indistinguishable from the cosmological-constant value −1, though evolving-w models remain under test (e.g. 2024 DESI hints).
explanations.b: w = 0 (matter) would decelerate the universe; the data show acceleration, requiring w near −1.
explanations.c: w = +1/3 is radiation and would decelerate strongly, contradicting the observed acceleration.
explanations.d: w is in fact constrained to within a few percent of −1 by the combined datasets, not unconstrained.

lessons.label: Fitting Omega_m and Omega_Lambda to the Redshift-Distance (Hubble) Diagram

sections.heading: Type Ia supernovae are the standardizable candles
sections.body: To fit the cosmic energy budget you need to measure distances to objects at large redshift, and the workhorse is the Type Ia supernova. A Type Ia is a white dwarf that accretes matter until it approaches the Chandrasekhar mass — about 1.4 solar masses, the ceiling above which electron degeneracy pressure can no longer support the star — and detonates in a thermonuclear runaway. Because the trigger mass is nearly universal, the peak luminosities are nearly identical, making Type Ia supernovae excellent standard candles. They are not perfectly standard, but the Phillips relation (Mark Phillips, 1993) — brighter ones fade more slowly — lets astronomers calibrate the small spread and turn them into standardizable candles good to about 0.1–0.15 magnitudes, roughly 5–7% in distance. Compare the known intrinsic luminosity to the observed brightness and you get the luminosity distance d_L; measure the host galaxy's redshift z spectroscopically, and each supernova becomes one point on a redshift-distance (Hubble) diagram out to z ≈ 1 and beyond.

sections.heading: The distance depends on the whole expansion history
sections.body: At small redshift the relation is just Hubble's law, v = H0·d, so distance rises linearly with redshift. But at large z the luminosity distance depends on the entire expansion history the light traversed — and that history is set by Ω_m and Ω_Λ through the Friedmann equation. In a flat universe the luminosity distance is d_L = (1 + z)·(c/H0)·∫₀ᶻ dz′/E(z′), where E(z) = H(z)/H0 = √(Ω_m(1+z)³ + Ω_Λ) for a matter-plus-cosmological-constant model. More matter means more deceleration in the past, a faster-expanding early universe, and therefore smaller distances at a given redshift (objects look brighter). More dark energy means the expansion was slower in the past and has accelerated, stretching the light path so objects at a given redshift are farther away and look fainter. The Hubble diagram — apparent brightness (distance modulus) versus redshift — is therefore a direct readout of the energy budget: the shape of the curve at z ≈ 0.3–1 pries Ω_m and Ω_Λ apart.

sections.heading: The 1998 discovery and why three probes are combined
sections.body: In 1998–1999 two independent teams — the High-z Supernova Search Team (Adam Riess, Brian Schmidt, and collaborators, 1998) and the Supernova Cosmology Project (Saul Perlmutter and collaborators, 1999) — measured distant Type Ia supernovae and found them systematically fainter than any decelerating universe predicted, by roughly 0.2–0.4 magnitudes near z ≈ 0.5. The only fit was a universe that had begun to accelerate, requiring Ω_Λ ≈ 0.7. This won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for Perlmutter, Schmidt, and Riess. Supernovae alone, however, mainly constrain a combination close to Ω_m − Ω_Λ, giving a long diagonal error ellipse in the Ω_m–Ω_Λ plane. To break the degeneracy, cosmologists overlay two orthogonal constraints: the CMB (which fixes Ω_m + Ω_Λ ≈ 1, the flatness line) and baryon acoustic oscillations from galaxy surveys (a standard ruler cutting across at yet another angle). The three ellipses intersect tightly at Ω_m ≈ 0.3, Ω_Λ ≈ 0.7 — a value no single probe pins down alone, which is why the concordance model rests on their agreement.

lessons.workedExample: Show how much fainter distant supernovae look in an accelerating versus a decelerating universe. Compare two flat models at z = 0.5 with H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc (Hubble distance c/H0 ≈ 4283 Mpc). Model A is Einstein–de Sitter (Ω_m = 1, Ω_Λ = 0), fully decelerating; Model B is concordance ΛCDM (Ω_m = 0.3, Ω_Λ = 0.7). Numerically integrating d_L = (1+z)(c/H0)∫₀ᶻ dz′/E(z′): Model A gives d_L ≈ 2360 Mpc, Model B gives d_L ≈ 2830 Mpc. Convert to distance modulus μ = 5·log₁₀(d_L/10 pc) = 5·log₁₀(d_L in pc) − 5. For A: μ = 5·log₁₀(2.36×10⁹) − 5 ≈ 41.86. For B: μ = 5·log₁₀(2.83×10⁹) − 5 ≈ 42.26. The accelerating model puts the supernova ~0.4 magnitudes fainter (larger μ) at the same redshift — exactly the direction and rough size of the 1998 signal. (The often-quoted ~0.25 mag figure was relative to a low-density open universe rather than Einstein–de Sitter; against a fully decelerating model the gap is larger.) A survey that measured many supernovae to ~0.15 mag precision could clearly distinguish these, which is how the acceleration was detected.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe "how do supernovae actually tell you there is dark energy?" because students often assert the 1998 result without the logic. The concept that scores is the chain: Type Ia supernovae are standardizable candles (Chandrasekhar ~1.4 M_sun trigger, Phillips-relation corrected), so they give luminosity distances; distant ones came out fainter — meaning farther — than a decelerating universe allows, forcing Ω_Λ ≈ 0.7. A strong student also explains why the answer needs the CMB and BAO layered on: supernovae alone constrain roughly Ω_m − Ω_Λ, and only the intersecting constraints nail Ω_m ≈ 0.3, Ω_Λ ≈ 0.7. Naming Riess/Schmidt (1998), Perlmutter (1999), and the 2011 Nobel accurately signals real command of the history.

questions.prompt: Why are Type Ia supernovae usable as standard(izable) candles for measuring cosmological distances?

options.text: They all have exactly the same redshift
They detonate near the Chandrasekhar mass (~1.4 M_sun), so their peak luminosities are nearly uniform and correctable via the Phillips relation
They are the brightest objects in the sky, so distance does not matter
Their brightness is independent of distance

explanations.a: Redshift varies from supernova to supernova — that is the very quantity plotted against distance; it is not fixed.
explanations.b: Correct — the near-universal Chandrasekhar trigger mass (~1.4 M_sun) makes peak luminosities nearly identical, and the Phillips relation (brighter ones fade slower) corrects the residual spread to ~0.1–0.15 mag.
explanations.c: They are luminous, but distance absolutely matters — observed brightness falls with distance, which is exactly how d_L is inferred.
explanations.d: Observed brightness depends strongly on distance (inverse-square law); that dependence is what makes them distance indicators.

questions.prompt: At a fixed redshift, how does a supernova’s inferred distance (and apparent faintness) change if the universe has more dark energy (larger Ω_Λ)?

options.text: It appears closer and brighter
It appears farther away and fainter
Distance is unaffected by Ω_Λ
It disappears entirely below z = 1

explanations.a: More matter (deceleration) makes objects appear closer/brighter; more dark energy does the opposite.
explanations.b: Correct — more Ω_Λ means slower past expansion that later accelerated, stretching the light path, so an object at a given z is farther and fainter — the observed 1998 signal.
explanations.c: The luminosity distance integral d_L = (1+z)(c/H0)∫dz′/E(z′) depends on E(z), which contains Ω_Λ, so distance certainly depends on it.
explanations.d: Supernovae remain observable well past z = 1; dark energy shifts their brightness, it does not make them vanish.

questions.prompt: Which teams and people are credited with the 1998–1999 discovery of cosmic acceleration (and the 2011 Nobel Prize)?

options.text: Penzias and Wilson, for the cosmic microwave background
The High-z Supernova Search Team (Riess, Schmidt, 1998) and the Supernova Cosmology Project (Perlmutter, 1999)
Vera Rubin and Kent Ford, for galaxy rotation curves
Mayor and Queloz, for the first exoplanet

explanations.a: Penzias and Wilson discovered the CMB in 1965 (Nobel 1978) — a different discovery entirely.
explanations.b: Correct — Riess and Schmidt (High-z team, 1998) and Perlmutter (Supernova Cosmology Project, 1999) found the acceleration from Type Ia supernovae; the three shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
explanations.c: Rubin and Ford’s 1970s rotation curves evidenced dark matter, not cosmic acceleration or dark energy.
explanations.d: Mayor and Queloz discovered 51 Pegasi b in 1995 (Nobel 2019) — exoplanets, unrelated to the acceleration result.

questions.prompt: Match each cosmological probe to the combination of parameters it most directly constrains in the Ω_m–Ω_Λ plane.

right.text: Roughly Ω_m − Ω_Λ (a long diagonal error ellipse)
Roughly Ω_m + Ω_Λ ≈ 1 (the flatness line)
A standard-ruler constraint cutting across at another angle

questions.explanation: Supernovae mainly constrain a combination close to Ω_m − Ω_Λ (a diagonal ellipse); the CMB fixes total density, giving Ω_m + Ω_Λ ≈ 1 (flatness); BAO provide an independent standard ruler at yet another angle. Their intersection nails Ω_m ≈ 0.3, Ω_Λ ≈ 0.7.

lessons.label: The Deceleration-to-Acceleration Transition and the Coincidence Problem

sections.heading: The universe braked, then hit the gas
sections.body: Cosmic history is not a story of steady acceleration — it is a two-act story of braking followed by acceleration, and the switch is a direct consequence of the different density scalings. The acceleration equation gives ä/a = −(4πG/3)(ρ + 3p/c²), and the sign depends on which component dominates. In the matter era, matter (w = 0) dominated, ρ + 3p/c² > 0, and the expansion decelerated — gravity was winning. But matter dilutes as a⁻³ while dark energy stays constant, so eventually dark energy (w = −1) overtook matter, the combined ρ + 3p/c² went negative, and ä flipped from negative to positive. The universe stopped decelerating and began to accelerate. This is captured by the deceleration parameter q ≡ −ä·a/ȧ², defined so that q > 0 means slowing and q < 0 means speeding up. Today q0 ≈ −0.55: we live in the accelerating act.

sections.heading: When did it switch? The transition redshift
sections.body: The transition happens at the moment ä = 0, i.e. ρ + 3p/c² = 0. With matter and a cosmological constant, that condition is ρ_m − 2ρ_Λ = 0, or ρ_m = 2ρ_Λ (the factor 2 comes from Λ's pressure term 3p/c² = −3ρ_Λ). Since ρ_m ∝ (1+z)³ and ρ_Λ is constant, write Ω_m(1+z)³ = 2Ω_Λ and solve: (1+z)³ = 2Ω_Λ/Ω_m. With Ω_Λ = 0.69 and Ω_m = 0.31, (1+z)³ = 2(0.69)/0.31 ≈ 4.45, so 1 + z ≈ 1.64 and the transition redshift is z_t ≈ 0.6. In cosmic time that is roughly 6 billion years ago — less than half the universe's age. Adam Riess and collaborators (2004), using Type Ia supernovae observed with the Hubble Space Telescope out to z > 1, directly detected this turnover: the most distant supernovae showed the earlier decelerating phase, confirming the universe was decelerating before it accelerated, exactly as ΛCDM predicts. Seeing both phases in one dataset was strong independent evidence that dark energy is real and not a supernova systematic.

sections.heading: Two hard problems: coincidence and the cosmological constant
sections.body: The transition being recent raises the coincidence problem: why do we happen to live so close to the crossover, when Ω_m ≈ 0.31 and Ω_Λ ≈ 0.69 are of the same order of magnitude right now? These two densities scale utterly differently — matter as a⁻³, dark energy as a⁰ — so their ratio sweeps through many tens of orders of magnitude over cosmic history and is near unity for only a brief window. In the far past matter overwhelmingly dominated; in the far future dark energy will overwhelmingly dominate. That we observe them comparable seems suspiciously special, and explaining why "now" is when they cross is the coincidence problem. Proposed responses range from anthropic selection (structure and observers can only form in the narrow era before dark energy shuts down growth) to dynamical dark-energy models (quintessence "tracker" fields engineered to track the dominant component and ease the fine-tuning). A distinct and even worse puzzle is the cosmological-constant problem: if dark energy is the quantum vacuum energy of empty space, naive quantum field theory overpredicts its density by some 120 orders of magnitude — often called the worst quantitative prediction in physics. The coincidence problem asks "why now?"; the cosmological-constant problem asks "why so absurdly small (but not zero)?" Both remain open, and they are the reason dark energy is the deepest unsolved problem in cosmology.

lessons.workedExample: Compute today's deceleration parameter and the transition redshift from the standard budget. For a flat matter-plus-Λ universe, q0 = (1/2)(Ω_m + (1 + 3w)Ω_Λ) with w = −1, so q0 = (1/2)(Ω_m − 2Ω_Λ). Plug in Ω_m = 0.31, Ω_Λ = 0.69: q0 = (1/2)(0.31 − 2(0.69)) = (1/2)(0.31 − 1.38) = (1/2)(−1.07) ≈ −0.54. The negative value confirms the present universe is accelerating. Now the switch point, where ä = 0 (q = 0): set ρ_m = 2ρ_Λ, i.e. Ω_m(1+z)³ = 2Ω_Λ. Then (1+z_t)³ = 2Ω_Λ/Ω_m = 2(0.69)/0.31 = 4.45, giving 1 + z_t = 4.45^(1/3) ≈ 1.64, so z_t ≈ 0.64. Both numbers — a present q0 ≈ −0.55 and a transition near z ≈ 0.6 — match the measured concordance cosmology and Riess et al.'s (2004) direct detection of the deceleration-to-acceleration turnover.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "if dark energy dominates, was the universe always accelerating?" to catch the common misconception that acceleration is eternal. The concept that scores is the two-phase history: matter (a⁻³) dominated and decelerated the early universe, dark energy (a⁰) took over only recently, and the switch — the transition redshift z_t ≈ 0.6 — was directly observed by Riess et al. (2004) with HST supernovae past z = 1. A student who then articulates the coincidence problem (why is now the special epoch when Ω_m and Ω_Λ are comparable, given how differently they scale?) and keeps it distinct from the cosmological-constant problem (the ~120-order-of-magnitude vacuum-energy mismatch) shows they grasp not just the model but the frontier questions it leaves open.

questions.prompt: Order these phases of cosmic dynamical history from earliest to latest.

items.text: Radiation-dominated, decelerating expansion
Matter-dominated, decelerating expansion
Deceleration-to-acceleration transition (z_t ≈ 0.6)
Dark-energy-dominated, accelerating expansion (today)

questions.explanation: Radiation (a⁻⁴) dominated first and decelerated; matter (a⁻³) took over at z ≈ 3400, still decelerating; as matter thinned and constant dark energy overtook it, the expansion switched from decelerating to accelerating at z_t ≈ 0.6; today dark energy dominates and the expansion accelerates.

questions.prompt: The deceleration-to-acceleration transition occurs at the redshift where:

options.text: The matter and radiation densities are equal
ρ_m = 2ρ_Λ, so that ρ + 3p/c² = 0 and ä = 0
The universe becomes spatially flat
The Hubble constant reaches zero

explanations.a: Matter-radiation equality is a much earlier, separate event at z ≈ 3400; it is not the acceleration turnover.
explanations.b: Correct — ä = 0 requires ρ + 3p/c² = 0, which for matter plus a cosmological constant is ρ_m − 2ρ_Λ = 0, i.e. ρ_m = 2ρ_Λ, giving z_t ≈ 0.6.
explanations.c: Spatial flatness (Ω_total = 1) holds throughout in the concordance model; it is not what defines the transition epoch.
explanations.d: H does not reach zero in an accelerating universe; the transition is where ä (not H) changes sign.

questions.prompt: What is the "cosmic coincidence problem"?

options.text: That the CMB temperature is almost exactly 2.7 K
That Ω_m and Ω_Λ are comparable today even though they scale very differently, so their near-equality lasts only a brief cosmic window — why do we observe it now?
That the universe is spatially flat
That two supernova teams found the same result in 1998

explanations.a: The CMB temperature is a separate fact; the coincidence problem is about the matter/dark-energy density ratio being of order unity now.
explanations.b: Correct — matter scales as a⁻³ and dark energy as a⁰, so their ratio is near unity only briefly; the puzzle is why our epoch happens to sit in that narrow crossover window.
explanations.c: Flatness relates to Ω_total = 1, not to the coincidence that Ω_m and Ω_Λ are comparable at the present time.
explanations.d: Two teams agreeing was a strength of the discovery, not a coincidence problem in the cosmological sense.

questions.prompt: The "cosmological-constant problem" (distinct from the coincidence problem) refers to:

options.text: Quantum field theory overpredicting the vacuum energy density by roughly 120 orders of magnitude
The difficulty of measuring H0 precisely
The fact that dark matter is invisible
The 8% tension between local and CMB values of H0

explanations.a: Correct — if dark energy is the quantum vacuum energy, naive QFT estimates exceed the observed value by ~120 orders of magnitude, the "worst prediction in physics"; this is separate from the coincidence (why-now) problem.
explanations.b: Measuring H0 is a practical/statistical challenge; the cosmological-constant problem is a theoretical mismatch in the predicted vacuum energy.
explanations.c: Dark matter’s invisibility is a different open problem; the cosmological-constant problem concerns dark energy’s vacuum-energy magnitude.
explanations.d: The Hubble tension is a real but separate discrepancy in H0 values, not the vacuum-energy magnitude problem.

units.label: The Cosmic Microwave Background and the Hot Early Universe

lessons.label: Recombination and the Surface of Last Scattering: Why the CMB Was Released at z ~ 1100

sections.heading: A universe that was once an opaque plasma
sections.body: Run cosmic expansion backwards and everything gets hotter and denser, because the temperature of the radiation scales as T ∝ (1 + z). Today the cosmic microwave background sits at 2.725 K; at redshift z = 1100 it was about 2.725 × 1101 ≈ 3000 K. Above roughly 3000–4000 K, hydrogen — by far the most abundant element — was fully ionized: free protons and free electrons everywhere. Free electrons are extremely efficient at scattering photons (Thomson scattering), so a photon in that plasma could travel only a tiny distance before being deflected. The early universe was therefore opaque, like the glowing interior of the Sun: a hot, uniform, light-trapping fog. The CMB is the moment that fog cleared. It is not light from "the Big Bang" as an explosion; it is the thermal glow of the last hot plasma, released when the universe finally became transparent.

sections.heading: Recombination: electrons and protons finally bind
sections.body: As the universe expanded and cooled, electrons and protons began to combine into neutral hydrogen — a process cosmologists call "recombination" (a historical misnomer, since they had never been combined before). Neutral atoms do not scatter the background photons efficiently, so once the free-electron density collapsed, the photons were set free to travel in straight lines essentially forever. The physics is captured by the Saha equation, which balances ionization against recombination given the temperature and density. The striking result is that recombination did NOT happen at the temperature you would naively guess from hydrogen's 13.6 eV ionization energy (that would be tens of thousands of kelvin). It happened far cooler, near 0.3 eV (~3000 K). The reason is the enormous number of photons per baryon.

sections.heading: Why so cool? The photon-to-baryon ratio
sections.body: There are roughly 1.6 billion photons for every baryon in the universe (the baryon-to-photon ratio η ≈ 6 × 10⁻¹⁰). Even after the AVERAGE photon energy drops well below 13.6 eV, the tiny high-energy tail of the blackbody distribution still contains enough >13.6 eV photons to keep re-ionizing any hydrogen that forms. Only when the temperature falls to about 0.26–0.3 eV does that energetic tail thin out enough for neutral atoms to survive. So the sheer entropy of the universe — a billion-plus photons per atom — delays recombination to z ≈ 1100, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This is a beautiful case where a big pure number (η) sets a physical epoch.

sections.heading: The surface of last scattering is a shell, not an instant
sections.body: Because recombination took a finite time (the ionization fraction fell from ~1 to ~0 over a redshift interval Δz ≈ 80–100, roughly z ≈ 1100 down to ~1010), the "surface of last scattering" is really a fuzzy shell about 40,000–80,000 light-years thick from which the last-scattered photons come. When we map the CMB, we are imaging a spherical surface centered on us at that redshift — a snapshot of the plasma as it was at 380,000 years. Every CMB photon we detect last touched matter on that shell. The theoretical framework was worked out in the 1960s (Peebles; Zeldovich; and the detailed recombination calculation by Peebles 1968 and Zeldovich, Kurt & Sunyaev 1968), predicting the delayed, non-instantaneous freeze-out we now measure precisely.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate the last-scattering temperature from the redshift, then sanity-check it against hydrogen physics. Given T₀ = 2.725 K today and z = 1100, the CMB temperature at last scattering is T = T₀(1 + z) = 2.725 × 1101 ≈ 3000 K. Converting to energy, kT = (8.617 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K) × 3000 K ≈ 0.26 eV. That is about 50× SMALLER than hydrogen's 13.6 eV binding energy — so why did atoms finally form here? Because with ~1.6 × 10⁹ photons per baryon, the fraction of photons in the blackbody tail above 13.6 eV is roughly exp(−13.6/0.26) ≈ e⁻⁵² ≈ 10⁻²³. Multiply that vanishing fraction by a billion photons per baryon (~10⁹) and you still get ~10⁻¹⁴ ionizing photons per baryon — finally few enough that neutral hydrogen survives. The huge photon-to-baryon ratio is exactly what pushes recombination down from ~13.6 eV to ~0.26 eV, and the numbers land at z ≈ 1100, t ≈ 380,000 yr.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who probes "why is the CMB at z ~ 1100 and not earlier?" is testing whether a student understands that recombination temperature is set by the photon-to-baryon ratio, not simply by hydrogen's 13.6 eV ionization energy. The tell of real understanding is naming the huge number of photons per baryon (~10⁹) and its high-energy tail as the reason atoms form near 0.3 eV rather than at tens of thousands of kelvin. A student who says "the CMB is 3000 K because that's when hydrogen ionizes at 13.6 eV" has the number roughly right but the physics wrong — and a good judge will catch the missing factor of ~50.

questions.prompt: The universe was opaque before recombination primarily because:

options.text: Neutral hydrogen atoms absorbed all the light
Free electrons Thomson-scattered photons, so light could not travel far
Dust grains blocked the radiation
The universe was too dense for any photons to exist

explanations.a: Neutral atoms are what made the universe TRANSPARENT — their formation ended the opacity. Before recombination the hydrogen was ionized, not neutral.
explanations.b: Correct — before recombination hydrogen was ionized, and the abundant free electrons scattered photons via Thomson scattering, trapping light in an opaque plasma until the electrons were bound into atoms.
explanations.c: Dust grains are made of heavy elements that did not yet exist in significant amounts, and dust is not the source of the pre-recombination opacity; free-electron scattering is.
explanations.d: Photons existed in vast numbers (a billion-plus per baryon); the issue was scattering, not the absence of photons.

questions.prompt: Why did recombination occur near kT ≈ 0.3 eV rather than at hydrogen's 13.6 eV ionization energy?

options.text: Hydrogen's real ionization energy in the early universe was only 0.3 eV
There are ~10⁹ photons per baryon, so the high-energy tail keeps re-ionizing hydrogen until the temperature falls well below 13.6 eV
Dark energy lowered the ionization threshold
The electrons were moving too slowly to recombine at higher temperatures

explanations.a: Hydrogen's ionization energy is always 13.6 eV; it did not change. The recombination temperature is lower for a statistical reason, not because the atomic physics changed.
explanations.b: Correct — with roughly a billion-plus photons per baryon, even a tiny high-energy tail above 13.6 eV contains enough ionizing photons to keep hydrogen ionized until kT drops to ~0.26–0.3 eV.
explanations.c: Dark energy is negligible at z ~ 1100 (the universe was matter/radiation dominated) and does not set atomic ionization.
explanations.d: Recombination is a thermodynamic balance governed by the Saha equation and the photon-to-baryon ratio, not by electron speed being too low.

questions.prompt: The "surface of last scattering" is best described as:

options.text: A perfectly sharp instant with zero thickness
A fuzzy shell of finite thickness (Δz ≈ 80) from which the last-scattered CMB photons originate
The present-day edge of the observable universe made of stars
The surface of the first galaxies

explanations.a: Recombination was not instantaneous — the ionization fraction fell over a redshift interval of order Δz ≈ 80, giving the shell a real thickness.
explanations.b: Correct — because recombination took finite time, last scattering happened across a shell roughly z ≈ 1100 to 1000, tens of thousands of light-years thick, not at a single instant.
explanations.c: The surface of last scattering is a plasma shell at z ~ 1100, released ~380,000 years after the Big Bang — long before any stars or galaxies formed.
explanations.d: The first galaxies formed hundreds of millions of years later; the last-scattering surface predates them by a huge margin.

questions.prompt: Order these epochs/events from EARLIEST to LATEST in cosmic time.

items.text: Universe is a hot, opaque, fully ionized plasma
Temperature falls to ~3000 K (z ≈ 1100)
Electrons and protons combine into neutral hydrogen
Photons free-stream; universe becomes transparent (the CMB)

questions.explanation: The universe starts as a hot ionized plasma, cools with expansion to ~3000 K at z ≈ 1100, at which point electrons bind to protons (recombination), collapsing the free-electron density so photons can finally free-stream — the light we now see as the CMB.

lessons.label: The 2.725 K Blackbody and the Dipole: What COBE/FIRAS Actually Measured

sections.heading: The most perfect blackbody ever measured
sections.body: The CMB spectrum is a thermal blackbody at T = 2.725 K (about 2.7 K — the peak of its Planck curve lands in the microwave, near 160 GHz / 1.9 mm wavelength, by Wien's law). This was not obvious in advance: a blackbody spectrum is the unavoidable signature of radiation that was once in thermal equilibrium with matter, so measuring it is the single strongest proof that the universe really passed through a hot, dense phase — the "hot Big Bang." The Far-InfraRed Absolute Spectrophotometer (FIRAS) instrument aboard NASA's COBE satellite, led by John Mather, measured the spectrum in 1990 and found it matched a blackbody to extraordinary precision: deviations smaller than about 50 parts per million. When Mather presented the FIRAS spectrum at the January 1990 American Astronomical Society meeting, the data points fell so exactly on the theoretical curve — with error bars smaller than the line width — that the audience gave a standing ovation. Mather and George Smoot shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for the COBE results.

sections.heading: The prediction came first — and was nearly missed
sections.body: A hot early universe was predicted to leave relic radiation of a few kelvin by George Gamow and his students Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman in the late 1940s (Alpher & Herman estimated ~5 K in 1948). The prediction was largely forgotten. In 1964–65 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs, using a horn antenna in Holmdel, New Jersey, found an unremovable excess noise of about 3.5 K they could not eliminate (they famously even cleaned out pigeon droppings from the antenna). Nearby at Princeton, Robert Dicke, Jim Peebles, Peter Roll and David Wilkinson were building a receiver to search for exactly this relic. The two groups connected, and back-to-back papers appeared in the Astrophysical Journal in 1965: Penzias & Wilson reported the measurement (without interpreting it), and the Princeton group supplied the cosmological interpretation. Penzias and Wilson received the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sections.heading: The dipole: our motion through the CMB rest frame
sections.body: The CMB is nearly uniform across the sky, but the single largest anisotropy is a dipole — one side of the sky is slightly hotter, the opposite side slightly cooler, by about ±3.36 millikelvin. This is not primordial. It is a Doppler shift caused by OUR motion: the Solar System is moving at roughly 370 km/s relative to the frame in which the CMB is isotropic. Toward the direction of motion the CMB looks blueshifted (hotter); away from it, redshifted (cooler). This gives us the closest thing to an absolute cosmic rest frame — not a violation of relativity (there is no preferred frame for the laws of physics), but a preferred frame in which the matter and radiation of the universe are, on average, at rest. Once the dipole is subtracted, the remaining temperature fluctuations are the primordial anisotropies (~1 part in 100,000) that encode the physics of the early universe.

lessons.workedExample: Convert the CMB dipole into our velocity. The measured dipole amplitude is ΔT ≈ 3.36 mK on a mean temperature T = 2.725 K, a non-relativistic Doppler effect: ΔT/T = v/c. Solving, v = c × (ΔT/T) = (3.0 × 10⁵ km/s) × (3.36 × 10⁻³ K / 2.725 K) = (3.0 × 10⁵) × (1.23 × 10⁻³) ≈ 370 km/s. That is the Solar System's speed relative to the CMB rest frame, pointed roughly toward the constellation Leo. Compare scales to appreciate how quiet the sky is: the dipole (3.36 mK, ~10⁻³ of T) is our motion; the primordial anisotropies are far smaller, ΔT ~ 30 µK, about 10⁻⁵ of T — a part in 100,000. So subtracting the dipole is essential before you can even see the cosmological signal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the CMB dipole to check whether a student can separate a LOCAL kinematic effect from a COSMOLOGICAL one. The dipole looks like a giant anisotropy but carries no early-universe information — it is just our velocity. A student who explains "the dipole is our 370 km/s motion via ΔT/T = v/c, and you subtract it to reveal the real 10⁻⁵ primordial fluctuations" shows they understand what part of the map is signal versus artifact. Getting the blackbody point right (FIRAS to ~50 ppm, proving the hot Big Bang) is the other classic probe — it is the observation that rules out steady-state alternatives.

questions.prompt: Why is the CMB's near-perfect blackbody spectrum such strong evidence for the hot Big Bang?

options.text: Blackbody spectra can only be produced by stars
A blackbody is the signature of radiation that was once in thermal equilibrium with dense matter, which requires a hot, dense early phase
It proves the universe is infinitely old
Blackbody radiation is emitted only by black holes

explanations.a: Any system in thermal equilibrium radiates as a blackbody; it is not unique to stars. Summed starlight, in fact, does NOT make a smooth blackbody.
explanations.b: Correct — a precise blackbody spectrum requires the radiation to have thermalized in a hot, dense, opaque medium, exactly the early-universe plasma the hot Big Bang predicts. Steady-state models struggle to produce it.
explanations.c: The blackbody spectrum constrains the thermal history, not the age being infinite; it actually supports a finite hot origin.
explanations.d: Black holes emit faint Hawking radiation, but the CMB blackbody comes from the early-universe plasma, not from black holes.

questions.prompt: The CMB dipole (±3.36 mK) is caused by:

options.text: A primordial density fluctuation on the largest scales
The Solar System's ~370 km/s motion relative to the CMB rest frame (a Doppler shift)
The rotation of the Milky Way's dark-matter halo only
Instrumental noise that cannot be removed

explanations.a: The dipole is not primordial; it is a kinematic Doppler effect that must be subtracted to reveal the true ~10⁻⁵ primordial anisotropies.
explanations.b: Correct — our net motion (Solar System through the CMB frame at ~370 km/s) blueshifts the sky ahead and redshifts it behind, producing the dipole via ΔT/T = v/c.
explanations.c: Galactic rotation contributes to our net velocity, but the dipole reflects the TOTAL motion of the Solar System relative to the CMB frame, not the halo rotation alone.
explanations.d: The dipole is a real, well-measured cosmic signal, not noise; COBE, WMAP, and Planck all measure it consistently.

questions.prompt: Match each person/team to their contribution to CMB history.

left.text: Predicted relic radiation of a few kelvin (late 1940s)
Measured the excess microwave noise in 1964–65 (Nobel 1978)
Led FIRAS, measured the blackbody to ~50 ppm (Nobel 2006)
Provided the cosmological interpretation in the companion 1965 paper

right.text: Gamow, Alpher & Herman
Penzias & Wilson
John Mather (with George Smoot on COBE)
Dicke, Peebles, Roll & Wilkinson

questions.explanation: Gamow, Alpher & Herman predicted a few-kelvin relic (~5 K, 1948); Penzias & Wilson serendipitously measured it at Bell Labs (Nobel 1978); the Princeton group (Dicke, Peebles, Roll & Wilkinson) supplied the interpretation in the back-to-back 1965 ApJ paper; John Mather led the COBE/FIRAS blackbody measurement, sharing the 2006 Nobel with George Smoot.

questions.prompt: After the dipole is removed, the remaining primordial CMB temperature fluctuations are of order:

options.text: ~1 part in 10 (10⁻¹)
~1 part in 100,000 (10⁻⁵), i.e., tens of microkelvin
Exactly zero — the CMB is perfectly smooth

explanations.a: 10⁻¹ is vastly too large; such huge fluctuations would be trivially visible and inconsistent with the observed smoothness.
explanations.b: 10⁻³ is the scale of the DIPOLE (our motion), not of the primordial anisotropies, which are ~100× smaller.
explanations.c: Correct — the intrinsic anisotropies are ΔT ~ 30 µK on 2.725 K, about 1 part in 100,000, first mapped by COBE's DMR and precisely by WMAP and Planck.
explanations.d: The CMB is NOT perfectly smooth; the ~10⁻⁵ fluctuations are exactly the seeds of structure and the data behind the acoustic peaks.

lessons.label: Acoustic Oscillations in the Photon-Baryon Fluid: The Physics Behind the Peaks

sections.heading: A tug-of-war: gravity versus radiation pressure
sections.body: Before recombination, photons and baryons were tightly coupled by Thomson scattering into a single "photon-baryon fluid." This fluid felt two competing forces in and around the dark-matter potential wells seeded by primordial density fluctuations. Gravity pulled the fluid INTO overdense regions, compressing it. But as the gas compressed, the photon pressure shot up (radiation pressure is enormous) and pushed the fluid back OUT. The result is exactly what happens when you compress any gas: it oscillates. Overdense regions collapsed, overshot, rebounded, and re-collapsed — sound waves ringing through the primordial plasma. These are literally acoustic oscillations: standing sound waves in the early universe. Dark matter, which does not feel photon pressure, provided the stationary gravitational scaffolding but did not oscillate with the fluid — a distinction that matters for reading the peaks.

sections.heading: The sound speed and the sound horizon
sections.body: The speed of these waves is the sound speed of a photon-dominated fluid, cs ≈ c/√3 ≈ 0.58c ≈ 1.7 × 10⁵ km/s — an astonishing fraction of the speed of light, because the "pressure" is provided by relativistic photons. (Adding baryons lowers it somewhat: cs = c/√[3(1 + R)], where R = 3ρ_baryon/4ρ_photon.) The maximum distance a sound wave could travel from the Big Bang to recombination is the "sound horizon," r_s ≈ 150 Mpc in comoving units (about 490 million light-years). This is a fixed physical length — a standard ruler frozen into the universe at last scattering. Every mode that had time to complete a whole number of oscillations by recombination reaches an extremum (maximum compression or maximum rarefaction) at that instant, and those special modes are what we see as the peaks in the power spectrum.

sections.heading: Frozen at recombination: turning sound into a spectrum
sections.body: Recombination acts like a camera shutter. The instant the electrons bind into atoms, the photon pressure vanishes (no more Thomson scattering), the sound waves stop, and the pattern of compressions and rarefactions is frozen into the temperature of the released photons: maximally compressed regions are hotter, maximally rarefied regions cooler. Because different wavelengths were caught at different phases of their oscillation, the CMB temperature varies with angular scale in a very specific, calculable way. Modes caught at maximum compression (having completed a half-integer or integer number of oscillations) produce the strongest temperature contrast → the acoustic PEAKS; modes caught mid-swing produce the troughs. The whole story was worked out in the late 1960s–70s (Peebles & Yu 1970; Sunyaev & Zeldovich 1970) and is why the CMB is a snapshot of a ringing plasma, not a featureless glow.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate the sound speed and why the first acoustic scale is about a degree on the sky. Take the photon-fluid sound speed cs ≈ c/√3 = (3.0 × 10⁵ km/s)/1.732 ≈ 1.73 × 10⁵ km/s — the plasma "rings" at ~58% of light speed. Over the ~380,000 years to recombination, sound imprints a characteristic comoving length, the sound horizon r_s ≈ 150 Mpc. That ruler sits on the last-scattering surface, whose comoving distance from us is D ≈ 14,000 Mpc. Its angular size is θ ≈ r_s / D ≈ 150 / 14,000 ≈ 0.011 rad ≈ 0.6°–1°. On the power-spectrum axis of multipole ℓ (roughly ℓ ≈ 180°/θ), that angular scale corresponds to ℓ ≈ 200–300 by this crude estimate; the careful projection puts the first (fundamental) acoustic peak at ℓ ≈ 220. So the sound speed of light-pressure and the age at recombination, together, predict a degree-scale hot/cold pattern — and that is what the peaks are.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "what physically makes the CMB peaks?" wants to hear the mechanism, not just the word "oscillations." The signature of understanding is the tug-of-war framing: gravity compresses the photon-baryon fluid, radiation pressure resists, and the fluid rings as sound waves until recombination freezes the pattern. Students who add that the sound speed is ~c/√3 and that dark matter provides the wells but does not oscillate have grasped the two ingredients that later let you read baryon and dark-matter densities off the peak heights. A hand-wave like "quantum fluctuations made hot and cold spots" misses the acoustic physics entirely.

questions.prompt: The acoustic oscillations in the early universe arose from a competition between:

options.text: Dark energy pushing out and dark matter pulling in
Gravity compressing the photon-baryon fluid and photon (radiation) pressure pushing it back out
Magnetic fields and neutrino pressure
The expansion of space and the contraction of black holes

explanations.a: Dark energy was dynamically negligible in the early universe, and dark matter does not provide pressure — it only supplies the gravitational wells. The oscillation needs a restoring pressure.
explanations.b: Correct — gravity pulled the tightly coupled photon-baryon fluid into overdense regions, photon pressure resisted and pushed it back, and the fluid rang like a compressed gas: sound waves.
explanations.c: Magnetic fields and neutrino pressure are not the dominant drivers of the acoustic peaks; the photon-baryon pressure vs. gravity balance is.
explanations.d: Black hole contraction plays no role; the peaks come from sound waves in the plasma before recombination.

questions.prompt: The sound speed of the photon-baryon fluid is approximately:

options.text: The speed of sound in air, ~340 m/s
c/√3 ≈ 0.58c ≈ 1.7 × 10⁵ km/s, because relativistic photons provide the pressure
Exactly the speed of light, c
Zero — the fluid did not move

explanations.a: That is sound in ordinary cool air; the early-universe fluid was radiation-dominated, giving a sound speed a huge fraction of c.
explanations.b: Correct — for a photon-dominated fluid cs = c/√3 ≈ 0.58c (slightly reduced by baryon loading, cs = c/√[3(1+R)]), because the restoring pressure comes from relativistic photons.
explanations.c: The sound speed is a bit below c/√3, not c itself; no signal exceeds c, and the fluid speed is ~0.58c.
explanations.d: The fluid oscillated vigorously — that motion is exactly what creates the acoustic peaks.

questions.prompt: What role did dark matter play in the acoustic oscillations?

options.text: It oscillated in lockstep with the photons, amplifying the pressure
It provided stationary gravitational potential wells but did not oscillate, since it does not feel photon pressure
It scattered the photons and kept them trapped
It had no effect on the CMB at all

explanations.a: Dark matter does not couple to photons, so it cannot oscillate with the fluid; only the photon-baryon fluid rings.
explanations.b: Correct — dark matter is pressureless and only gravitates, so it forms the stationary wells the fluid falls into and rebounds from, without oscillating itself.
explanations.c: Photon trapping was done by free electrons (Thomson scattering), not dark matter.
explanations.d: Dark matter has a big effect — its potential wells set the oscillation and, via the third peak, its density is read off the spectrum.

questions.prompt: Order the causal chain that turns primordial sound waves into CMB peaks, EARLIEST to LATEST.

items.text: Primordial density fluctuations seed dark-matter potential wells
Photon-baryon fluid falls in and rebounds — sound waves ring
Recombination removes photon pressure and freezes the pattern
Compressions/rarefactions become hot/cold spots seen as power-spectrum peaks

questions.explanation: Primordial fluctuations create potential wells; the photon-baryon fluid oscillates (rings) in and out of them; recombination shuts off photon pressure and freezes the compression/rarefaction pattern; that frozen pattern appears as hot/cold spots whose statistics form the acoustic peaks.

lessons.label: Reading the Planck Power Spectrum: First-Peak Geometry, Baryon Loading, and the Damping Tail

sections.heading: The first peak is a standard ruler for geometry
sections.body: The CMB power spectrum plots temperature-fluctuation power against multipole moment ℓ (small ℓ = large angular scales, large ℓ = small scales). Its most prominent feature is the first acoustic peak at ℓ ≈ 220, corresponding to an angular scale of about 1°. The physical size of that feature is the sound horizon (~150 Mpc), a known ruler; the ANGLE it subtends depends on the geometry of space between us and the last-scattering surface. In a flat universe the ruler subtends ~1° and the peak lands at ℓ ≈ 220; in a positively curved (closed) universe light paths would make it look larger (peak shifts to smaller ℓ), and in an open universe smaller (larger ℓ). Measuring the first peak at ℓ ≈ 220 was the decisive evidence — from BOOMERANG and MAXIMA (2000), then WMAP and Planck — that the universe is spatially flat to within about 2% (Ω_total = 1.00 ± 0.02).

sections.heading: Baryon loading: odd peaks versus even peaks
sections.body: Baryons add mass to the oscillating fluid, deepening the compressions (falling further into the wells) more than the rarefactions. Compression phases produce the ODD-numbered peaks (first, third, …) and rarefaction phases the EVEN-numbered peaks (second, …). So MORE baryons enhance the odd peaks relative to the even ones: the second peak is suppressed relative to the first. The precise ratio of first-to-second peak height is therefore a direct baryometer. Planck (2018) uses this to pin the physical baryon density to Ω_b h² = 0.02237 ± 0.00015 — a ~1% measurement of how much ordinary matter the universe contains, read purely off the relative heights of the acoustic peaks. This is one of the two independent baryon counts the next lessons compare.

sections.heading: The third peak weighs the dark matter
sections.body: The third peak carries information about the dark-matter density. More dark matter changes the balance between the gravitational driving and the radiation, altering how the peak heights decay and especially boosting the third peak relative to the second. From the full peak structure Planck measures the cold-dark-matter density Ω_c h² ≈ 0.120 — roughly five to six times the baryon density — quantitative confirmation that most matter is non-baryonic. Together with the flat-geometry result, this yields the concordance ΛCDM budget: about 5% baryons, 27% dark matter, 68% dark energy, with H₀ ≈ 67.4 km/s/Mpc from Planck.

sections.heading: The damping tail: Silk damping smooths small scales
sections.body: At small angular scales (high ℓ, beyond the third peak) the power falls off steeply — the "damping tail." This is Silk damping (Joseph Silk, 1968): near recombination, photons diffused (random-walked) out of the smallest overdensities before the pattern froze, washing out fluctuations on scales below the photon mean free path. The damping tail is not a nuisance — its precise shape independently constrains the baryon density and the number of relativistic species, and its measurement by high-resolution experiments (the South Pole Telescope, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, and Planck) sharpens the whole cosmological fit.

lessons.workedExample: Read the first peak as a geometry test. The first acoustic peak sits at multipole ℓ₁ ≈ 220. The rough correspondence between multipole and angle is θ ≈ 180°/ℓ, so θ ≈ 180°/220 ≈ 0.8°. Now compare to the prediction: the sound horizon r_s ≈ 150 Mpc at a last-scattering distance D ≈ 14,000 Mpc subtends r_s/D ≈ 0.011 rad ≈ 0.6°–0.8° — but ONLY if space is flat, so that light travels in straight lines and the ruler keeps its Euclidean angular size. Had the universe been closed, that same 150 Mpc ruler would appear magnified (peak pushed to ℓ < 220); had it been open, demagnified (peak at ℓ > 220). Observing ℓ₁ ≈ 220 therefore measures Ω_total = 1.00 ± 0.02: the universe is spatially flat. Then the first-to-second peak height ratio gives Ω_b h² = 0.0224, and the third peak gives Ω_c h² ≈ 0.120 — three numbers, all read off one curve.
lessons.judgeFraming: The power spectrum is the richest single figure in cosmology, and judges love to ask "what does each peak tell you?" because a rehearsed student can recite "there are peaks" without knowing what they measure. The strong answer maps features to physics: first-peak POSITION → spatial flatness (standard ruler); odd/even peak height RATIO → baryon density (baryon loading); third peak → dark-matter density; damping tail → Silk diffusion. A student who can say "the peak at ℓ ≈ 220 means the universe is flat, and the suppressed second peak means ~5% baryons" is reading the data, not memorizing a shape.

questions.prompt: The position of the first acoustic peak at ℓ ≈ 220 primarily tells us:

options.text: The age of the universe in years
That space is spatially flat (Ω_total ≈ 1), because the sound-horizon ruler subtends ~1°
The temperature of the CMB today
The number of galaxies in the universe

explanations.a: The peak position is a geometry measurement; the age comes from the full fit of parameters, not directly from ℓ₁.
explanations.b: Correct — the sound horizon is a known physical ruler, and the angle it subtends (peak at ℓ ≈ 220, ~1°) depends on spatial curvature, pinning Ω_total ≈ 1 (flat).
explanations.c: The CMB temperature (2.725 K) comes from the blackbody spectrum, not the peak position.
explanations.d: Galaxy counts are unrelated to the first-peak position, which is a curvature/geometry probe.

questions.prompt: Increasing the baryon density mainly does what to the acoustic peaks?

options.text: Shifts all peaks to smaller ℓ
Enhances the odd (compression) peaks relative to the even (rarefaction) peaks — e.g., raises the first relative to the second
Removes the peaks entirely
Only affects the damping tail and nothing else

explanations.a: Peak POSITIONS are set mainly by geometry/sound horizon; baryon density changes relative HEIGHTS, not the overall position shift described here.
explanations.b: Correct — added baryon mass deepens the compressions, boosting the odd-numbered peaks (first, third) relative to the even ones (second), so the first-to-second height ratio is a baryometer.
explanations.c: Baryons modulate peak heights; they do not erase the peaks.
explanations.d: Baryon density does affect the damping scale, but its signature relevant here is the odd/even peak-height ratio.

questions.prompt: The steep fall-off of power at small angular scales (the damping tail) is due to:

options.text: Silk damping — photons diffusing out of the smallest overdensities near recombination, erasing small-scale fluctuations
Dark energy stretching the fluctuations
Instrumental beam smoothing only
Absorption by interstellar dust

explanations.a: Correct — Joseph Silk (1968) showed photons random-walk (diffuse) out of the smallest overdensities before recombination froze the pattern, damping high-ℓ power; its shape constrains baryons and relativistic species.
explanations.b: Dark energy acts on large scales and late times, not the small-scale damping at recombination.
explanations.c: Beam smoothing must be corrected for, but the physical damping tail is Silk diffusion in the plasma, a real cosmological effect.
explanations.d: Interstellar dust is a foreground handled separately; it is not the origin of the intrinsic damping tail.

questions.prompt: Match each feature of the CMB power spectrum to the quantity it constrains.

right.text: Spatial curvature / flatness (Ω_total ≈ 1)
Baryon density (Ω_b h² ≈ 0.0224)
Dark-matter density (Ω_c h² ≈ 0.120)
Silk (photon-diffusion) damping scale

questions.explanation: The first-peak POSITION is the standard-ruler geometry test (flatness); the first-to-second peak height RATIO is the baryometer (baryon loading); the third peak's height constrains the dark-matter density; and the high-ℓ damping tail encodes Silk photon-diffusion damping.

lessons.label: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis: The Deuterium Bottleneck and Predicting Primordial Helium

sections.heading: The first three minutes: cooking the light elements
sections.body: Long before recombination — in the first few minutes, when the universe was a billion kelvin — and seconds earlier had been denser than the Sun's core — nuclear reactions forged the lightest elements from protons and neutrons. This is Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN). It produced essentially all the primordial deuterium (²H), helium-3, helium-4, and a trace of lithium-7, but almost no heavier elements (the mass gaps at A = 5 and A = 8, plus the rapidly dropping density, halt the chain). Heavier elements had to wait for stars. The idea traces to George Gamow and the famous "αβγ" paper (Alpher, Bethe & Gamow, 1948) — Gamow whimsically added Hans Bethe's name for the pun — with the detailed modern calculation done by Wagoner, Fowler & Hoyle (1967). BBN is one of the three observational pillars of the hot Big Bang, alongside the CMB and the expansion of the universe.

sections.heading: The neutron-to-proton ratio freezes at about 1:7
sections.body: The helium yield is set by how many neutrons survive to be incorporated into nuclei. At high temperature, weak interactions kept neutrons and protons interconverting, holding their ratio near the thermal equilibrium value n/p = exp(−Δm·c²/kT), where Δm·c² = 1.293 MeV is the neutron-proton mass difference. As the universe cooled below kT ≈ 0.8 MeV (about 1 second in), the weak reactions became too slow to keep up and the ratio "froze out" near n/p ≈ 1/6. Free neutrons then decayed (lifetime ≈ 880 s) during the few-minute delay before nucleosynthesis could begin, dropping the ratio to about n/p ≈ 1/7 by the time deuterium started forming. Nearly every surviving neutron ends up locked into a helium-4 nucleus, so that frozen ratio essentially DICTATES the primordial helium abundance.

sections.heading: The deuterium bottleneck
sections.body: Building helium requires deuterium as the stepping stone (p + n → D, then D + D or D + p reactions build up to ⁴He). But deuterium is fragile: its binding energy is only 2.22 MeV, and with a billion-plus photons per baryon, the high-energy photon tail photodissociates any deuterium as fast as it forms — even after the average temperature drops well below 2.22 MeV. This is the "deuterium bottleneck": nucleosynthesis STALLS until the temperature falls to about kT ≈ 0.07–0.08 MeV (T ≈ 10⁹ K, at ~3 minutes), when deuterium can finally accumulate. Then the reactions proceed almost explosively and quickly lock the available neutrons into ⁴He. The bottleneck is the same photon-to-baryon physics that delayed recombination — high entropy postpones both.

sections.heading: The prediction: about 25% helium by mass
sections.body: The upshot is a firm, largely parameter-free prediction: the primordial helium mass fraction is Y_p ≈ 0.247, i.e., about 25% of the ordinary (baryonic) mass emerged from the Big Bang as helium-4, with essentially all the rest as hydrogen. This value is remarkably insensitive to the exact baryon density (it depends mostly on the frozen n/p ratio and neutron lifetime), which is why it is such a clean prediction. Observations of helium in the most metal-poor, least-processed gas clouds and dwarf galaxies give Y_p ≈ 0.245, in striking agreement. Deuterium, by contrast, IS highly sensitive to the baryon density — the more baryons, the more efficiently deuterium is burned into helium, leaving less D behind — which is exactly what makes deuterium the precision baryometer of the next lesson.

lessons.workedExample: Predict the primordial helium fraction from the frozen neutron-to-proton ratio. Freeze-out fixes roughly n/p ≈ 1/7 by the time nucleosynthesis begins. Assume every neutron is paired with a proton into a ⁴He nucleus (each ⁴He has 2 neutrons + 2 protons). Take 7 protons for every 1 neutron. The 1 neutron pairs with 1 proton and, together with one more neutron... simpler bookkeeping: for every 2 neutrons you need 2 protons to make one ⁴He (mass 4), and with n/p = 1/7 the leftover protons stay as hydrogen. The standard result is Y_p = 2(n/p)/(1 + n/p). Plugging n/p = 1/7: Y_p = 2(1/7)/(1 + 1/7) = (2/7)/(8/7) = 2/8 = 0.25. So ~25% of baryonic mass is helium-4 and ~75% hydrogen — a prediction fixed almost entirely by the neutron-proton mass difference (1.293 MeV) and the neutron lifetime (~880 s), matching the observed Y_p ≈ 0.245 in pristine gas.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe BBN to see whether a student understands that the ~25% helium abundance is a PREDICTION of the hot Big Bang, fixed by nuclear and weak physics, not a fitted number. The key moves are: the n/p ratio freezes near 1/7, essentially all surviving neutrons go into ⁴He, so Y_p = 2(n/p)/(1+n/p) ≈ 0.25. Bonus credit for explaining the deuterium bottleneck — why nucleosynthesis waits until ~10⁹ K despite deuterium's 2.22 MeV binding energy, because of the huge photon-to-baryon ratio. A student who says "helium was just always 25%" without the mechanism has memorized the answer, not the physics.

questions.prompt: The primordial helium-4 mass fraction predicted by Big Bang Nucleosynthesis is approximately:

options.text: ~25% (Y_p ≈ 0.247), with the rest mostly hydrogen

explanations.a: 2% is far too low; that is closer to the total mass fraction of elements heavier than helium made in stars, not primordial helium.
explanations.b: Correct — with n/p ≈ 1/7 at nucleosynthesis and nearly all neutrons ending in ⁴He, Y_p = 2(n/p)/(1+n/p) ≈ 0.25, matching the observed ~0.245 in pristine gas.
explanations.c: ~75% is the primordial HYDROGEN fraction, not helium; the two are swapped.
explanations.d: 50% would require n/p ≈ 1/3, far from the observed freeze-out value near 1/7.

questions.prompt: The "deuterium bottleneck" refers to:

options.text: A shortage of protons in the early universe
Nucleosynthesis stalling because the huge photon-to-baryon ratio photodissociates fragile deuterium until T drops to ~10⁹ K
Deuterium being too heavy to form at all
A traffic jam of neutrons decaying too fast

explanations.a: Protons were abundant; the bottleneck is about deuterium survival, not a proton shortage.
explanations.b: Correct — deuterium's low 2.22 MeV binding plus a billion-plus photons per baryon means the photon tail destroys D as fast as it forms, stalling the chain until kT ≈ 0.07–0.08 MeV (~10⁹ K).
explanations.c: Deuterium forms readily via p + n → D; the problem is that it is photodissociated, not that it cannot form.
explanations.d: Neutron decay matters for the n/p ratio, but the bottleneck specifically is deuterium photodissociation by energetic photons.

questions.prompt: Which quantity is the helium yield Y_p MOST sensitive to?

options.text: The exact baryon density (it changes Y_p by tens of percent)
The frozen neutron-to-proton ratio (set by the n-p mass difference and neutron lifetime)
The present-day dark-energy density
The number of galaxies at recombination

explanations.a: Y_p is only weakly dependent on baryon density — it is DEUTERIUM that is the sensitive baryometer, not helium.
explanations.b: Correct — Y_p ≈ 2(n/p)/(1+n/p), so it is governed by the n/p ratio at nucleosynthesis, fixed mainly by the 1.293 MeV mass difference and the ~880 s neutron lifetime.
explanations.c: Dark energy is irrelevant in the first minutes of a radiation-dominated universe.
explanations.d: Galaxies did not exist during BBN; they form far later and have no role in setting Y_p.

questions.prompt: Order these BBN events from EARLIEST to LATEST.

items.text: Weak reactions freeze the n/p ratio near 1/6 (kT ≈ 0.8 MeV, ~1 s)
Free neutrons decay during the delay, dropping n/p toward ~1/7
Deuterium bottleneck breaks at T ≈ 10⁹ K (~3 min) as D finally accumulates
Surviving neutrons are rapidly locked into ⁴He, fixing Y_p ≈ 0.25

questions.explanation: The n/p ratio freezes out near 1/6 at ~1 s; free neutrons then decay during the delay, lowering n/p toward ~1/7; the deuterium bottleneck breaks near 10⁹ K at ~3 minutes; and the surviving neutrons are quickly bound into ⁴He, setting the ~25% helium yield.

lessons.label: Two Baryon Counts That Agree: BBN Deuterium vs. the CMB Third Peak

sections.heading: Deuterium as a precision baryometer
sections.body: Of all the BBN products, deuterium is the sharpest tool for counting baryons. The reason is a steep, monotonic dependence: the more baryons per photon, the more efficiently deuterium is processed into helium, so the leftover primordial D/H ratio FALLS steeply as the baryon density rises. This makes D/H a sensitive "baryometer" — a small change in D/H implies a well-defined baryon density. The catch is that deuterium is destroyed inside stars (it is never made astrophysically, only destroyed), so you must measure it in the most PRISTINE gas available. The breakthrough was measuring D/H in absorption against distant quasars, using high-redshift, near-primordial gas clouds along the sightline (pioneered by David Tytler and Scott Burles in the late 1990s, and refined to ~1% by Ryan Cooke and collaborators, 2014–2018).

sections.heading: The number: D/H and the baryon density from BBN
sections.body: The best measurements give a primordial abundance D/H ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ (about 25 deuterium atoms per million hydrogen atoms). Folding that through standard BBN nuclear reaction rates yields a baryon density of Ω_b h² ≈ 0.0219 ± 0.0005, corresponding to a baryon-to-photon ratio η ≈ 6 × 10⁻¹⁰. This count comes from nuclear physics operating in the first three minutes — an entirely different epoch, and entirely different physics, from the CMB.

sections.heading: The CMB's independent count — and the agreement
