sections.body: The CMB measures the SAME baryon density by a completely independent route: the relative heights of the acoustic peaks (baryon loading — the odd/even peak ratio from Lesson 4). Planck (2018) gives Ω_b h² = 0.02237 ± 0.00015 from the power spectrum at recombination, z ≈ 1100, using photon-plasma acoustics rather than nuclear reactions. The two numbers — 0.0219 from deuterium at 3 minutes, 0.02237 from the CMB at 380,000 years — agree to within a couple of percent. This is one of the most powerful consistency checks in all of cosmology: two independent probes, separated by ~380,000 years and relying on unrelated physics (weak/nuclear reactions vs. photon-baryon acoustics), converge on the same baryon-to-photon ratio η ≈ 6 × 10⁻¹⁰. It is a quantitative triumph of the hot Big Bang, and it also reveals that ordinary (baryonic) matter is only ~5% of the total — the CMB's much larger TOTAL matter density then demands the non-baryonic dark matter of Lesson 4's third peak.

sections.heading: Why concordance matters — and the small tensions that remain
sections.body: A single number matching by luck is unremarkable; two independent methods converging is a genuine test that could have failed. If BBN and the CMB had disagreed badly, it would have signaled new physics (extra relativistic species, non-standard expansion, or errors in the framework). Historically the lithium-7 abundance is the one persistent discrepancy — BBN predicts about 3× more ⁷Li than is observed in old halo stars, the unresolved "primordial lithium problem" — a reminder that concordance is strong but not perfect. Still, the deuterium-CMB agreement on the baryon density stands as a textbook example of how cosmology cross-checks itself across vastly different epochs and physical mechanisms.

lessons.workedExample: Compare the two independent baryon counts head-to-head. From primordial deuterium: measured D/H ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ in pristine quasar-absorption gas → through BBN reaction networks → Ω_b h² ≈ 0.0219 (baryon-to-photon ratio η ≈ 6.0 × 10⁻¹⁰). From the CMB: Planck fits the acoustic peak heights (baryon loading, first-to-second peak ratio) at z ≈ 1100 → Ω_b h² = 0.02237. The fractional difference is (0.02237 − 0.0219)/0.0219 ≈ 0.02, i.e., about 2% — well within the combined uncertainties. Two clocks separated by ~380,000 years of cosmic history, one reading nuclear reaction yields and the other reading sound waves in plasma, report the same baryon-to-photon ratio. Converting Ω_b h² ≈ 0.022 with h ≈ 0.674 gives Ω_b ≈ 0.049 — baryons are just ~5% of the cosmic energy budget, forcing the remaining matter (~27%) to be non-baryonic dark matter.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the capstone consistency argument, and judges reward students who can articulate WHY two agreeing measurements are more compelling than either alone. The strong answer names both independent routes — BBN deuterium (nuclear physics at ~3 minutes) and the CMB acoustic peaks (photon-baryon physics at ~380,000 years) — and stresses that they rely on unrelated physics yet converge on Ω_b h² ≈ 0.022 (η ≈ 6 × 10⁻¹⁰). Extra credit for noting this pins baryons at only ~5% of the universe, and for honesty about the lingering lithium-7 problem. A student who just says "the Big Bang is confirmed" has missed the structure of the argument: independent probes agreeing is the whole point.

questions.prompt: Why is primordial deuterium such a good "baryometer"?

options.text: Its abundance is completely independent of the baryon density
Its abundance falls steeply and monotonically as the baryon density rises, so measured D/H pins the baryon density tightly
Deuterium is continuously produced in stars, giving a large sample
Deuterium is the most abundant element, so it is easy to measure

explanations.a: The opposite — deuterium is HIGHLY sensitive to baryon density, which is exactly what makes it useful.
explanations.b: Correct — more baryons burn deuterium into helium more efficiently, so leftover D/H drops steeply with baryon density; a precise D/H measurement therefore yields a precise Ω_b h².
explanations.c: Deuterium is only DESTROYED in stars, never made, which is why it must be measured in pristine, unprocessed gas.
explanations.d: Deuterium is rare (~25 per million H atoms); its value is its sensitivity, not its abundance.

questions.prompt: The BBN-deuterium baryon density and the CMB acoustic-peak baryon density are powerful because they:

options.text: Use the exact same physics at the same epoch, so agreement is guaranteed
Are independent probes — nuclear reactions at ~3 minutes vs. photon-baryon acoustics at ~380,000 years — that nonetheless converge on Ω_b h² ≈ 0.022
Both simply assume the answer in advance
Disagree by a factor of ten, revealing new physics

explanations.a: They use DIFFERENT physics (weak/nuclear reactions vs. plasma acoustics) at DIFFERENT epochs, so agreement is a real test, not guaranteed.
explanations.b: Correct — two unrelated methods separated by ~380,000 years both give Ω_b h² ≈ 0.022 (η ≈ 6 × 10⁻¹⁰), a genuine independent cross-check that could have failed.
explanations.c: Neither assumes the answer; each derives Ω_b h² from independent data (D/H, or peak heights).
explanations.d: They AGREE to within about 2%, not disagree by a factor of ten.

questions.prompt: The concordant baryon density (Ω_b ≈ 0.05) combined with the CMB's total matter density implies:

options.text: All matter is ordinary baryonic matter
Ordinary baryons are only ~5% of the universe, so most matter must be non-baryonic dark matter
There is no dark matter
The universe is 100% dark energy

explanations.a: If all matter were baryonic, the total matter density would equal ~0.05, but the CMB measures ~0.31 in matter — far more.
explanations.b: Correct — both baryon counts give Ω_b ≈ 0.05, yet the CMB's total matter density is much larger (~0.27 in dark matter), so most matter is non-baryonic.
explanations.c: The mismatch between the baryon count and the total matter density is direct evidence FOR dark matter, not against it.
explanations.d: Dark energy is ~68% of the energy budget, but there is also ~5% baryons and ~27% dark matter; it is not 100% dark energy.

questions.prompt: Match each baryon-density probe to its defining physics and epoch.

right.text: Nuclear reactions in the first ~3 minutes (D/H ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵)
Photon-baryon acoustics at z ≈ 1100 (Ω_b h² = 0.02237)
The single number both probes agree on, ≈ 6 × 10⁻¹⁰
Lithium-7, predicted ~3× higher than observed in halo stars

questions.explanation: BBN deuterium (D/H ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵) counts baryons via nuclear reactions in the first ~3 minutes; the CMB counts them via acoustic-peak heights at z ≈ 1100 (Ω_b h² = 0.02237); both agree on the baryon-to-photon ratio η ≈ 6 × 10⁻¹⁰; and the lingering exception is the lithium-7 problem, where BBN predicts ~3× more ⁷Li than observed in old halo stars.

units.label: Structure, Dark Matter, and Dark Energy Evidence

lessons.label: Baryon Acoustic Oscillations: A 150-Mpc Standard Ruler Frozen into Galaxy Clustering

sections.heading: Sound waves in the primordial plasma
sections.body: Before recombination — the epoch about 380,000 years after the Big Bang (redshift z ≈ 1100) when the universe cooled enough for electrons and protons to combine into neutral hydrogen — ordinary matter (baryons) and photons were locked together in a single hot fluid by Thomson scattering. In that photon–baryon fluid, the gravity of dark-matter overdensities pulled matter in, while photon pressure pushed it back out, launching spherical pressure (sound) waves that raced outward at the relativistic sound speed, close to c/√3 (about 57% of the speed of light). At recombination the photons suddenly decoupled and streamed away as the cosmic microwave background (CMB); with the pressure gone, each sound wave stalled. The distance a wave had travelled by that instant — the "sound horizon at the drag epoch," written r_d — was frozen into the matter distribution. Its comoving value is about 147 Mpc (roughly 100 h⁻¹ Mpc, ≈ 490 million light-years), a length precisely fixed by the physics of the early universe.

sections.heading: A bump in the galaxy correlation function
sections.body: The frozen wave leaves a subtle imprint: galaxies are very slightly MORE likely to be found separated by exactly r_d than by nearby separations — a single broad bump in the two-point correlation function of galaxies, or equivalently a series of wiggles in the power spectrum. It is a tiny excess (about a 1% enhancement in clustering probability), so detecting it needs enormous galaxy catalogs. It was first securely measured in 2005, independently, by Daniel Eisenstein and collaborators in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) luminous-red-galaxy sample — the acoustic peak sat at ~100 h⁻¹ Mpc — and by Shaun Cole and colleagues in the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey. Later surveys (BOSS, eBOSS, and now DESI) mapped millions of galaxies to pin the scale down to sub-percent precision across a range of redshifts.

sections.heading: Why it is a standard ruler
sections.body: Because r_d is a KNOWN physical length (calibrated by the same early-universe physics that shapes the CMB), measuring its APPARENT size at a given redshift turns it into a standard ruler for geometry — the spatial analogue of a standard candle. Seen on the sky it subtends an angle Δθ = r_d / D_M(z), which measures the (comoving angular-diameter) distance D_M(z). Measured along the line of sight it spans a redshift interval Δz = H(z)·r_d / c, which measures the Hubble expansion rate H(z) directly. So a single feature yields both a distance and an expansion rate at each redshift, tracing the expansion history and tightly constraining Ω_m, dark energy, and the curvature of space. Crucially, BAO is a geometric, largely model-independent measurement — it does not rely on stellar astrophysics the way the Cepheid/supernova distance ladder does, making it a powerful independent cross-check.

lessons.workedExample: Take the radial BAO feature at redshift z = 0.35 (roughly the SDSS luminous-red-galaxy sample). In a flat ΛCDM universe with H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc, Ω_m = 0.3, the expansion rate there is H(z) = H₀·√(Ω_m(1+z)³ + Ω_Λ) = 70·√(0.3·1.35³ + 0.7) = 70·√(0.738 + 0.7) = 70·√1.438 ≈ 84 km/s/Mpc. With a comoving sound horizon r_d ≈ 147 Mpc, the acoustic feature spans a redshift interval Δz = H(z)·r_d / c = (84 km/s/Mpc · 147 Mpc) / (3×10⁵ km/s) ≈ 0.041. So along the line of sight the "ruler" appears as a ~0.04-wide bump in redshift. Transversely at the same z it subtends an angle of roughly 6 degrees (Δθ = r_d/D_M ≈ 147/1376 rad ≈ 0.107 rad). Measuring both the radial Δz and the transverse Δθ, and demanding they describe the SAME physical sphere, is the Alcock–Paczynski test — it independently constrains H(z), D_M(z), and Ω_m.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about BAO to see whether a student understands the difference between a physically CALIBRATED ruler and an empirical correlation. The tell of real understanding is naming WHERE the 150-Mpc scale comes from (a sound wave frozen at recombination, not an arbitrary clustering length) and WHY that makes it independent of the Cepheid/supernova ladder — so BAO can arbitrate the Hubble tension rather than inherit its calibrations. A student who says "galaxies just cluster at 150 Mpc" has memorized a number; one who traces it to the photon–baryon sound horizon and explains the radial-vs-transverse measurement has understood the tool.

questions.prompt: Physically, what does the ~150-Mpc BAO scale represent?

options.text: The typical size of a galaxy cluster today
The distance a sound wave travelled in the photon–baryon plasma before recombination (the sound horizon), frozen in when photons decoupled
The wavelength of the cosmic microwave background radiation
The mean free path of a photon in the present-day intergalactic medium

explanations.a: Clusters are ~1–3 Mpc across, roughly a hundred times smaller; the BAO scale is not a cluster size.
explanations.b: Correct — pressure waves in the coupled photon–baryon fluid travelled at ~c/√3 until recombination; the distance reached (the sound horizon, r_d ≈ 147 Mpc comoving) was frozen into the matter distribution as a preferred galaxy separation.
explanations.c: The CMB peaks at millimetre wavelengths; that has nothing to do with the 150-Mpc clustering scale.
explanations.d: A photon mean free path is a microscopic scattering length, unrelated to the frozen acoustic scale in galaxy clustering.

questions.prompt: Why is BAO called a "standard ruler," and what makes it valuable as a cosmological probe?

options.text: Its physical length is known from early-universe physics, so its apparent size at a redshift yields distances and H(z) independently of the stellar distance ladder
Every galaxy is exactly the same physical size, so galaxies serve as rulers
It has a known intrinsic luminosity, so its apparent brightness gives distance
It can only be measured in the local universe (z < 0.01)

explanations.a: Correct — because r_d is a calibrated physical LENGTH, its measured angular size gives D_M(z) and its radial redshift span gives H(z), all without Cepheids or supernovae, making it an independent geometric cross-check.
explanations.b: Galaxies vary enormously in size; the ruler is the acoustic scale imprinted in their statistical clustering, not any individual galaxy.
explanations.c: A known luminosity describes a standard CANDLE (like a Type Ia supernova); BAO is a standard RULER, defined by a length, not a brightness.
explanations.d: The opposite — BAO is measured across a wide redshift range (z ≈ 0.1 to 2+ with surveys like BOSS, eBOSS, and DESI), which is precisely why it traces the expansion history.

questions.prompt: Which pair of surveys first securely detected the baryon acoustic peak in galaxy clustering, in 2005?

options.text: COBE and WMAP
The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (Eisenstein et al.) and the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey (Cole et al.)
The Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes
LIGO and Virgo

explanations.a: COBE and WMAP are CMB satellites — they measured the acoustic oscillations in the microwave background, not the BAO peak in the galaxy distribution.
explanations.b: Correct — in 2005 Daniel Eisenstein and collaborators found the acoustic peak in SDSS luminous red galaxies, and Shaun Cole and collaborators found it in the 2dF survey, the two independent galaxy-clustering detections.
explanations.c: Hubble and JWST are imaging observatories, not the wide-field redshift surveys needed to map millions of galaxy positions for BAO.
explanations.d: LIGO and Virgo are gravitational-wave detectors, unrelated to galaxy clustering.

questions.prompt: Match each BAO measurement direction to what it primarily constrains.

left.text: Requiring transverse and radial to describe the same sphere

right.text: The comoving angular-diameter distance D_M(z)
The Hubble expansion rate H(z) at that redshift
The Alcock–Paczynski constraint on H(z)·D_M and Ω_m

questions.explanation: The angle the ruler subtends on the sky measures the distance D_M(z); the redshift interval it spans along the line of sight measures the expansion rate H(z); and demanding the same physical sphere look consistent in both directions is the Alcock–Paczynski test, which pins down the product H(z)·D_M and Ω_m.

lessons.label: From CMB Ripples to the Cosmic Web: The Growth of Structure and sigma_8

sections.heading: Tiny seeds, gravitational amplification
sections.body: The CMB shows the universe at 380,000 years old was astonishingly smooth: temperature fluctuations of only about one part in 100,000 (ΔT/T ≈ 10⁻⁵), which trace density fluctuations of similar tiny amplitude. Yet today the universe is lumpy — galaxies, clusters, and vast voids. The bridge is gravitational instability: a region slightly denser than average pulls in more matter, grows denser still, and runs away. In the matter-dominated era a density contrast δ = δρ/ρ grows in linear theory in proportion to the scale factor, δ ∝ a, i.e. it grows as the universe expands. When δ reaches order unity the region "turns around," detaches from the expansion, and collapses into a bound structure. Structure formation is therefore hierarchical and bottom-up: small clumps collapse first and merge into larger ones.

sections.heading: Why cold dark matter is required
sections.body: Ordinary (baryonic) matter could not have done this alone. Before recombination, baryons were tied to photons, and photon pressure prevented baryonic overdensities from growing — they oscillated (the acoustic waves of the previous lesson) instead of collapsing. Dark matter, by contrast, does not couple to photons, so dark-matter overdensities could begin collapsing much earlier, from around matter–radiation equality at z ≈ 3400. That head start is essential. If only baryons existed, a fluctuation of δ ≈ 10⁻⁵ at recombination growing as δ ∝ a would reach only δ ≈ 10⁻⁵ × 1100 ≈ 0.01 by today — nowhere near the δ ≈ 1 needed to collapse. Dark matter, having grown since z ≈ 3400, built deep gravitational wells that baryons fell into AFTER recombination, catching up quickly. The matter must also be "cold" (slow-moving, non-relativistic) so it clumps on small scales; hot dark matter (fast neutrinos) would erase small-scale structure. This is the CDM in ΛCDM.

sections.heading: The cosmic web and sigma_8
sections.body: The result is the cosmic web: dense nodes (galaxy clusters) linked by filaments, bounded by sheet-like walls, surrounding near-empty voids tens of megaparsecs across. It was revealed observationally by redshift surveys — the CfA survey (Margaret Geller and John Huchra, whose 1989 map showed the "Great Wall"), then 2dF and SDSS — and reproduced in landmark N-body simulations, notably the Millennium Simulation (Volker Springel and colleagues, 2005). The amplitude of clumpiness is captured by a single number, σ₈ (sigma-eight): the root-mean-square matter density fluctuation in randomly placed spheres of radius 8 h⁻¹ Mpc. Its value is about 0.8. Combined with the matter density as S₈ = σ₈·√(Ω_m/0.3), it is one of the most-quoted structure-growth parameters — and the source of a live tension, since weak-lensing surveys (KiDS, DES) tend to prefer a slightly LOWER S₈ than the value the Planck CMB predicts, a mild (~2–3σ) discrepancy that may hint at new physics or unmodeled systematics.

lessons.workedExample: Quantify why dark matter is needed. Model linear growth as δ ∝ a (density contrast tracks the scale factor in the matter era). A baryon-only fluctuation has amplitude δ ≈ 2×10⁻⁵ at recombination (z ≈ 1100). By today the scale factor has grown by a factor (1 + z) = 1101, so δ_today ≈ 2×10⁻⁵ × 1101 ≈ 0.02 — still deep in the linear regime, far below the δ ≈ 1 required to collapse into a galaxy. Now add cold dark matter, whose fluctuations began growing at matter–radiation equality (z ≈ 3400). Its extra growth factor of roughly 3400/1100 ≈ 3 (plus the fact that baryons fall into the pre-built dark-matter wells rather than starting from scratch) lets the total matter perturbation reach δ ≈ 1 and collapse by z ≈ 1–2, matching the observed epoch of galaxy formation. The arithmetic is the classic proof that the 10⁻⁵ CMB ripples could not have grown into today's galaxies without a dark, pressureless component.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the CMB-to-cosmic-web link to test whether a student sees structure formation as a QUANTITATIVE growth calculation, not a just-so story. The decisive move is the amplitude argument: 10⁻⁵ ripples growing as δ ∝ a fall short of collapse in a baryon-only universe, so a pressureless dark component that started growing earlier is logically forced. A student who can state σ₈ ≈ 0.8 as "how clumpy the universe is on 8 h⁻¹ Mpc scales" and explain the S₈ tension between lensing and the CMB shows they understand structure growth as a measurable, testable prediction of ΛCDM.

questions.prompt: Roughly how large are the density fluctuations imprinted in the CMB that seeded all later structure?

options.text: About one part in 100,000 (ΔT/T ≈ 10⁻⁵)
About 10% (ΔT/T ≈ 0.1)
Order unity (ΔT/T ≈ 1)
Exactly zero — the CMB is perfectly smooth

explanations.a: Correct — the CMB temperature (and density) fluctuations are about 10⁻⁵, the tiny seeds that gravity amplified over billions of years into galaxies and clusters.
explanations.b: 10% fluctuations would make the early universe grossly lumpy and the CMB sky wildly patchy; the real anisotropies are far smaller.
explanations.c: Order-unity fluctuations would mean structure had already collapsed at recombination, contradicting the observed near-uniform CMB.
explanations.d: The CMB is very smooth but NOT perfectly so; the ~10⁻⁵ anisotropies (mapped by COBE, WMAP, Planck) are exactly the seeds of structure.

questions.prompt: Why could baryonic matter NOT have grown the CMB fluctuations into today's galaxies on its own?

options.text: Baryons are repelled by gravity
Before recombination baryons were coupled to photons, whose pressure prevented collapse; only after recombination could they grow, leaving too little time to reach δ ≈ 1
Baryons move faster than light and cannot clump
There are no baryons in the early universe

explanations.a: Baryons feel ordinary attractive gravity; the problem is pressure support before recombination, not repulsion.
explanations.b: Correct — photon pressure held baryonic overdensities up (they oscillated) until recombination; starting to grow only then, a 10⁻⁵ fluctuation growing as δ ∝ a reaches only ~0.01 today, far short of collapse — so a pressureless dark component that grew earlier is required.
explanations.c: Nothing moves faster than light; baryons are ordinary slow matter, and speed is not the issue here.
explanations.d: Baryons certainly exist in the early universe (they make the CMB and BBN abundances); the issue is timing of their collapse, not their absence.

questions.prompt: What does the parameter σ₈ (sigma-eight) quantify?

options.text: The age of the universe in billions of years
The root-mean-square matter density fluctuation in spheres of radius 8 h⁻¹ Mpc — a measure of how clumpy the universe is
The number of galaxies within 8 Mpc of the Milky Way
The temperature of the CMB, 8 K above absolute zero

explanations.a: The age (~13.8 Gyr) is a separate parameter; σ₈ is about clumpiness, not time.
explanations.b: Correct — σ₈ ≈ 0.8 is the amplitude of matter fluctuations measured in 8 h⁻¹ Mpc spheres, the standard normalization of the matter power spectrum and a key structure-growth parameter.
explanations.c: σ₈ is a statistical fluctuation amplitude, not a local galaxy count.
explanations.d: The CMB temperature is 2.725 K, and σ₈ is unrelated to it; the "8" refers to the 8 h⁻¹ Mpc sphere radius, not a temperature.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of cosmic structure growth from earliest to latest.

items.text: CMB-era density fluctuations of ~10⁻⁵ are present
Cold-dark-matter overdensities grow and form deep gravitational wells
Baryons decouple from photons and fall into the dark-matter wells
Nonlinear collapse builds the cosmic web of nodes, filaments, and voids

questions.explanation: The ~10⁻⁵ seeds exist at recombination; dark matter (uncoupled to photons) grows first and digs the gravitational wells; after recombination baryons decouple and fall into those wells; continued nonlinear growth then assembles the cosmic web of clusters, filaments, and voids.

lessons.label: Weighing the Universe: Cluster Dynamics, Gravitational Lensing, and the Bullet Cluster

sections.heading: Zwicky and the virial theorem
sections.body: The first hint of dark matter came from weighing a galaxy cluster. In 1933 Fritz Zwicky studied the Coma cluster and applied the virial theorem — for a gravitationally bound, relaxed system, 2K + U = 0, so the total kinetic energy of the galaxies' random motions is balanced by their mutual gravitational binding. From the observed spread in galaxy velocities (a line-of-sight velocity dispersion of roughly 1000 km/s) he inferred the mass needed to keep the fast-moving galaxies bound. It came out hundreds of times larger than the mass visible as stars. Zwicky coined the term "dunkle Materie" (dark matter). The virial mass estimate is, in order of magnitude, M ≈ σ²R/G, where σ is the velocity dispersion and R the cluster radius — a formula that turns a measured spread of velocities directly into a mass.

sections.heading: Rotation curves and gravitational lensing
sections.body: A second independent line came from Vera Rubin and Kent Ford in the 1970s, who measured the rotation curves of spiral galaxies (including Andromeda, M31) and found that orbital speeds stay flat far beyond the visible disk instead of falling off as Keplerian gravity from the luminous mass predicts — implying extended halos of unseen mass. A third, purely geometric line is gravitational lensing: mass bends light (a prediction of general relativity confirmed in 1919). Strong lensing produces dramatic arcs and Einstein rings around massive clusters; weak lensing produces tiny, coherent distortions in the shapes of thousands of background galaxies, which can be statistically inverted into a map of the total mass — luminous or not — along the line of sight. Lensing weighs a cluster without any assumption that it is relaxed or in equilibrium, sidestepping the main caveat of the virial method.

sections.heading: The Bullet Cluster: dark matter caught in the act
sections.body: The most direct empirical case that dark matter is real, collisionless, and distinct from ordinary matter is the Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-558), analyzed by Douglas Clowe and collaborators in 2006. It is a system of two galaxy clusters that recently collided and passed through each other. The hot X-ray-emitting gas — which is most of the ORDINARY (baryonic) mass — was slowed by ram pressure during the collision and now lags behind, sitting between the two clusters (mapped by the Chandra X-ray Observatory). But the gravitational-lensing mass map shows the bulk of the mass sailed straight through, tracking the nearly collisionless galaxies, offset from the gas. Since the mass is spatially separated from the dominant baryonic (gas) component, the mass must be dark, collisionless matter — a result very hard to explain by modifying gravity alone (as in MOND), because in a pure modified-gravity picture the lensing signal should follow the visible baryons (the gas), not lead it.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate a cluster's mass from its galaxy motions. Take a velocity dispersion σ = 1000 km/s = 1×10⁶ m/s and a radius R = 1 Mpc = 3.086×10²² m. The virial estimate M ≈ σ²R/G with G = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² gives M ≈ (10⁶)² × (3.086×10²²) / (6.674×10⁻¹¹) = (10¹² × 3.086×10²²) / (6.674×10⁻¹¹) = 3.086×10³⁴ / 6.674×10⁻¹¹ ≈ 4.6×10⁴⁴ kg. Dividing by the solar mass (2×10³⁰ kg) gives M ≈ 2×10¹⁴ M_sun. The stars and gas of such a cluster total only ~10¹²–10¹³ M_sun — so the dynamical mass exceeds the visible mass by a factor of ~10–100, exactly Zwicky's "missing mass." The same ~10¹⁴ M_sun answer emerges independently from lensing and from the X-ray gas temperature, and the three agreeing is what makes the dark-matter conclusion robust rather than a quirk of one method.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the Bullet Cluster specifically because it separates students who recite "dark matter exists" from those who understand WHY it beats the leading alternative. The key insight is the SPATIAL SEPARATION: the lensing mass and the X-ray gas sit in different places, which modified-gravity theories struggle to reproduce because they tie the gravitational source to the visible baryons. A student who can also state the virial logic (M ≈ σ²R/G, mass from a velocity spread) and note that dynamics, lensing, and X-ray temperature give the SAME cluster mass demonstrates they grasp dark matter as a multiply-confirmed measurement.

questions.prompt: What did Fritz Zwicky conclude from applying the virial theorem to the Coma cluster in 1933?

options.text: The galaxies were moving too slowly, so the cluster was collapsing
The galaxies' high velocities required far more mass to remain bound than was visible as stars — evidence for unseen "dark matter"
The cluster contained no dark matter at all
The universe was contracting

explanations.a: The galaxies were moving too FAST for the visible mass to bind them, not too slowly; the cluster is bound only because extra unseen mass is present.
explanations.b: Correct — from a ~1000 km/s velocity dispersion the virial theorem implied a mass hundreds of times the luminous mass, and Zwicky named the excess "dunkle Materie" (dark matter).
explanations.c: The opposite — his measurement was the first strong evidence FOR dark matter.
explanations.d: Zwicky's cluster result concerns local dynamics, not the global expansion or contraction of the universe.

questions.prompt: Why is the Bullet Cluster considered especially direct evidence for collisionless dark matter?

options.text: It is the most distant galaxy cluster known

Its gravitational-lensing mass is spatially offset from the X-ray gas (most of the ordinary matter), which lagged behind in the collision — so the dominant mass is dark and collisionless, not the visible gas
It contains no ordinary matter at all
Its galaxies rotate faster than the speed of light

explanations.a: The Bullet Cluster is notable for the collision geometry, not for being a distance record.
explanations.b: Correct — the collision separated the ram-pressure-slowed X-ray gas (most of the baryons) from the lensing mass, which passed straight through with the collisionless galaxies; the mass leading the gas is hard for modified gravity to explain because that ties gravity to the visible baryons.
explanations.c: It contains plenty of ordinary matter — the hot X-ray gas IS the ordinary matter; the point is that the total mass is offset from it.
explanations.d: Nothing moves faster than light; the argument is about the spatial offset of mass from gas, not galaxy speeds.

questions.prompt: In the virial mass estimate M ≈ σ²R/G, what does σ represent?

options.text: The surface brightness of the cluster
The velocity dispersion — the spread in the galaxies' line-of-sight speeds
The Stefan–Boltzmann constant
The cluster's redshift

explanations.a: Surface brightness measures light, not the kinematics that the virial theorem uses.
explanations.b: Correct — σ is the velocity dispersion; a larger spread of galaxy speeds requires more binding mass, so mass scales as σ² (times R/G).
explanations.c: The Stefan–Boltzmann constant (also written σ) is a thermal-radiation constant, a different σ entirely and not what appears in the virial mass.
explanations.d: Redshift gives the cluster's distance/recession, not the internal velocity spread that sets the virial mass.

questions.prompt: Match each dark-matter probe to the observation it relies on.

right.text: The velocity dispersion of galaxies in a cluster
Orbital speeds staying flat far beyond the visible disk
Coherent shape distortions of thousands of background galaxies
Lensing mass map offset from the Chandra X-ray gas

questions.explanation: Zwicky used the cluster velocity dispersion (virial theorem); Rubin & Ford used flat rotation curves beyond the visible disk; weak lensing statistically inverts the coherent shear of background-galaxy shapes into a mass map; and the Bullet Cluster case rests on the lensing mass being offset from the X-ray-emitting gas.

lessons.label: Why Lambda-CDM Is 'Concordance': Independent Probes Converging on the Same Parameters

sections.heading: A model with only a handful of numbers
sections.body: The standard model of cosmology, ΛCDM (Lambda Cold Dark Matter), describes a spatially flat, expanding universe whose contents today are roughly 5% ordinary baryonic matter, 27% cold dark matter, and 68% dark energy (a cosmological constant, Λ). Remarkably, the entire observable universe — the CMB, the abundance of light elements, galaxy clustering, the expansion history — is captured by only about six free parameters (for example the physical baryon density Ω_b h², the cold-dark-matter density Ω_c h², the Hubble constant H₀, the primordial fluctuation amplitude and tilt n_s, and the reionization optical depth). Planck (2018) fixes these tightly: Ω_m ≈ 0.31, Ω_Λ ≈ 0.69, H₀ ≈ 67.4 km/s/Mpc, n_s ≈ 0.965, σ₈ ≈ 0.81. The power of a model is not that it fits one dataset with six knobs, but that the SAME six values fit many independent datasets at once.

sections.heading: The concordance: independent probes intersecting
sections.body: ΛCDM earned the nickname "concordance model" because physically unrelated measurements agree on the same parameters. Type Ia supernovae (standard candles) constrain a combination of Ω_m and Ω_Λ along one direction in parameter space. The CMB constrains the total density to be flat, Ω_m + Ω_Λ ≈ 1, a nearly perpendicular direction. Galaxy clustering and BAO independently pin Ω_m. Plot these constraint bands together and they intersect in one small region near (Ω_m, Ω_Λ) ≈ (0.3, 0.7). This "cosmic triangle" was set out by Neta Bahcall, Jeremiah Ostriker, Saul Perlmutter, and Paul Steinhardt in 1999; the term "concordance model" itself traces to Ostriker and Steinhardt (1995). Independent lines of evidence, each with different systematics, converging on the same answer is the strongest kind of scientific argument — no single measurement could be so persuasive.

sections.heading: Big Bang nucleosynthesis: a wholly separate check
sections.body: A completely independent pillar is Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN). In the first few minutes the universe forged the light elements — mostly hydrogen and helium-4, with traces of deuterium and lithium — and the yields depend sensitively on the baryon-to-photon ratio, i.e. on Ω_b h². The measured primordial deuterium abundance (from absorption in distant, chemically pristine gas clouds) gives Ω_b h² ≈ 0.022. The CMB, using entirely different physics 380,000 years later, independently gives Ω_b h² ≈ 0.0224. Two clocks — nuclear reactions at one minute and photon decoupling at 380,000 years — agreeing on the baryon density to a few percent is a striking, non-trivial success. Yet ΛCDM is not without cracks: the Hubble tension (Planck's H₀ ≈ 67 versus the Cepheid-calibrated supernova ladder's ≈ 73 km/s/Mpc, a ~5σ gap) and the milder S₈ tension keep the "concordance" from being complete, and are the field's most active debates.

lessons.workedExample: Turn the BBN/CMB baryon density into a picture of the cosmic budget. Both give Ω_b h² ≈ 0.022. Using the Planck Hubble constant H₀ = 67.4 km/s/Mpc, the reduced Hubble parameter is h = 0.674, so h² = 0.454. Then the baryon density parameter is Ω_b = 0.022 / 0.454 ≈ 0.049 — about 5% of the critical density is ordinary matter. But the total matter density is Ω_m ≈ 0.31, so dark matter contributes Ω_c ≈ 0.31 − 0.05 ≈ 0.26, roughly five times the baryons. The remaining Ω_Λ ≈ 1 − 0.31 ≈ 0.69 is dark energy (using flatness, Ω_total ≈ 1 from the CMB). The result — 5% baryons, 26% dark matter, 69% dark energy — comes from stitching together nucleosynthesis, the CMB, and the flatness constraint, three independent measurements, and it is the same budget every probe returns.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use ΛCDM to test whether a student understands what makes a model scientifically compelling: not fitting one curve, but the CONVERGENCE of independent probes on the same few parameters. The strong answer names at least two unrelated measurements (say, BBN deuterium and the CMB) that agree on Ω_b h², and explains why agreement between methods with different systematics is more persuasive than any single fit. A student who also acknowledges the open cracks — the Hubble tension especially — shows they see concordance as a hard-won, still-tested result, not dogma.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate present-day energy budget of the universe in ΛCDM?

options.text: ~5% ordinary matter, ~27% dark matter, ~68% dark energy
~50% ordinary matter, ~50% dark energy, no dark matter
~90% ordinary matter, ~10% dark energy
~33% each of matter, radiation, and dark energy

explanations.a: Correct — ΛCDM gives roughly 5% baryonic matter, 27% cold dark matter (so ~32% total matter), and ~68% dark energy today.
explanations.b: Dark matter dominates the matter sector (~5× the baryons), so a no-dark-matter split contradicts clustering, lensing, and the CMB.
explanations.c: Ordinary matter is only ~5%, not 90%; most of the universe is dark matter and dark energy.
explanations.d: Radiation is negligible today (~10⁻⁴ of the budget); the split is matter (~32%) and dark energy (~68%), not thirds.

questions.prompt: Why is ΛCDM called the "concordance" model?

options.text: Because a single dataset can be fit with a large number of free parameters
Because many independent probes (supernovae, the CMB, BAO, BBN) converge on the same handful of parameter values despite having different systematics
Because all cosmologists signed an agreement to use it
Because it was the first cosmological model ever proposed

explanations.a: Fitting one dataset with many knobs is unremarkable; concordance is precisely the OPPOSITE — few parameters fitting MANY independent datasets.
explanations.b: Correct — "concordance" means unrelated measurements with different systematics agree on the same parameters (e.g. (Ω_m, Ω_Λ) ≈ (0.3, 0.7)), the hallmark of a robust model.
explanations.c: "Concordance" refers to agreement among measurements, not a social agreement among scientists.
explanations.d: ΛCDM is a modern (1990s–2000s) synthesis, not the first cosmological model; the name reflects agreement of data, not primacy.

questions.prompt: Big Bang nucleosynthesis and the CMB independently agree on which quantity, using completely different physics and epochs?

options.text: The baryon density Ω_b h² (≈ 0.022)
The number of galaxies in the Local Group
The rotation speed of the Milky Way
The surface temperature of the Sun

explanations.a: Correct — BBN (nuclear reactions in the first minutes, via primordial deuterium) and the CMB (photon decoupling at 380,000 years) both yield Ω_b h² ≈ 0.022, a striking independent cross-check on the baryon density.
explanations.b: Local Group galaxy counts are a local, low-precision quantity, not what BBN and the CMB jointly constrain.
explanations.c: The Milky Way's rotation speed is a local dynamical measurement, unrelated to the primordial baryon density.
explanations.d: The Sun's temperature is stellar astrophysics; BBN and the CMB agree on a cosmological parameter (the baryon density), not solar properties.

questions.prompt: Match each cosmological probe to the parameter constraint it primarily provides.

right.text: A combination of Ω_m and Ω_Λ (the acceleration/expansion history)
Spatial flatness, Ω_m + Ω_Λ ≈ 1
The baryon density Ω_b h² from light-element abundances
A geometric standard-ruler distance/H(z) at each redshift

questions.explanation: Type Ia supernovae constrain the Ω_m–Ω_Λ combination via the expansion/acceleration history; the CMB fixes spatial flatness (Ω_m + Ω_Λ ≈ 1); BBN sets the baryon density Ω_b h² from primordial light-element abundances; and BAO provides a geometric standard-ruler measurement of distance and H(z). Their intersection is the concordance.

lessons.label: What Dark Energy Might Be: Cosmological Constant, Quintessence, or Modified Gravity

sections.heading: The equation of state and the acceleration condition
sections.body: Whatever drives cosmic acceleration is characterized by its equation-of-state parameter w = P/ρ, the ratio of its pressure to its energy density. From general relativity, the second Friedmann equation says the expansion accelerates (ä > 0) only when the total ρ + 3P < 0, i.e. when a component has w < −1/3 — a sufficiently NEGATIVE pressure. Ordinary matter has w = 0 (pressureless) and radiation w = +1/3; both decelerate the expansion. Dark energy must have strongly negative pressure. The simplest candidate is Einstein's cosmological constant Λ, which behaves as the energy of empty space (vacuum energy) with a constant density and w = −1 exactly. In ΛCDM, Λ is dark energy, and all current data are consistent with w = −1 to within a few percent.

sections.heading: The cosmological constant problem, and quintessence
sections.body: A cosmological constant fits the data but comes with the worst quantitative prediction in physics. Quantum field theory says the vacuum should have a zero-point energy density, but naïve estimates exceed the observed Λ by up to ~10¹²⁰ — an embarrassment known as the cosmological constant problem, plus the "coincidence problem" (why is dark energy comparable to matter density right now, not vastly earlier or later?). These puzzles motivate dynamical alternatives. Quintessence replaces the constant Λ with a slowly evolving scalar field whose energy density changes over time, giving an equation of state that can differ from −1 and vary with redshift (typically −1 < w < −1/3), often parametrized as w(a) = w₀ + w_a(1 − a). A field with w < −1 ("phantom" energy) would drive an ever-faster expansion ending in a "Big Rip." Distinguishing these from a pure constant requires measuring whether w equals −1 and whether it changes with time.

sections.heading: Modified gravity and the GW170817 constraint
sections.body: A radically different option is that there is no dark energy at all — instead general relativity itself is wrong on cosmological scales, and modifying it (theories like f(R) gravity or DGP braneworld models) mimics acceleration. Many such theories predicted that gravitational waves would travel at a speed slightly different from that of light. That door was slammed on 17 August 2017 by GW170817, the binary neutron-star merger detected by LIGO and Virgo: its gravitational-wave signal and the accompanying gamma-ray burst arrived within about 1.7 seconds of each other after travelling roughly 130 million light-years, forcing the gravitational-wave speed to equal the speed of light to about one part in 10¹⁵. That single multi-messenger event ruled out large classes of modified-gravity dark-energy models. Meanwhile the best current fits (Planck combined with BAO and supernovae) give w ≈ −1.03 ± 0.03, consistent with a cosmological constant — although in 2024 the DESI survey reported a mild preference for an EVOLVING dark energy, a result now under intense scrutiny and debate.

lessons.workedExample: Show why acceleration demands w < −1/3. The acceleration equation gives ä/a ∝ −(ρ + 3P) = −ρ(1 + 3w) for a component with w = P/ρ. Test the candidates: matter (w = 0) gives 1 + 3(0) = +1 > 0, so ä/a < 0 — the expansion DECELERATES, as expected for gravitating matter. Radiation (w = +1/3) gives 1 + 3(1/3) = +2 > 0 — decelerates even more strongly. A cosmological constant (w = −1) gives 1 + 3(−1) = −2 < 0, so ä/a > 0 — the expansion ACCELERATES. The threshold is where 1 + 3w = 0, i.e. w = −1/3: any component with w below −1/3 pushes the universe apart. Dark energy at w ≈ −1 sits well past that threshold, which is why a dark-energy universe transitions from decelerating to accelerating. Note these are two distinct epochs: the deceleration-to-acceleration transition occurred at z ≈ 0.7 (acceleration needs only 2Ω_Λ > Ω_m(1+z)³), whereas dark energy became the dominant component — Λ-domination, where Ω_Λ = Ω_m — later, at z ≈ 0.3. Acceleration began before Λ actually dominated the energy budget.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe dark energy to see if a student can separate WHAT is measured (an equation of state w near −1, driving acceleration) from the competing INTERPRETATIONS (vacuum energy, a dynamical field, or modified gravity). The strong answer states the acceleration condition w < −1/3 and explains that pinning down whether w = −1 exactly, and whether it evolves, is how we tell a cosmological constant from quintessence. Citing GW170817 as the event that killed many modified-gravity models — because gravitational waves were shown to travel at the speed of light — signals a student who tracks how real observations arbitrate between theories.

questions.prompt: For a component to drive accelerating cosmic expansion, its equation-of-state parameter w = P/ρ must satisfy which condition?

options.text: w < −1/3 (sufficiently negative pressure)
w = +1/3 exactly

explanations.a: Positive w (like matter or radiation) gives ρ + 3P > 0 and DECELERATES the expansion, the opposite of what is needed.
explanations.b: Correct — acceleration (ä > 0) requires ρ + 3P < 0, i.e. 1 + 3w < 0, so w < −1/3; a cosmological constant (w = −1) satisfies this easily.
explanations.c: w = +1/3 is radiation, which strongly decelerates the expansion.
explanations.d: w = 0 is pressureless matter, which also decelerates; only w < −1/3 accelerates.

questions.prompt: What is the "cosmological constant problem"?

options.text: The cosmological constant changes rapidly with time, making it hard to measure
Quantum field theory's naïve estimate of the vacuum energy exceeds the observed value of Λ by an enormous factor (up to ~10¹²⁰)
The cosmological constant makes the universe collapse
There is no way to measure dark energy at all

explanations.a: A cosmological constant is by definition constant in time (w = −1); the problem is its magnitude, not its variation.
explanations.b: Correct — theoretical vacuum-energy estimates overshoot the tiny observed Λ by as much as 120 orders of magnitude, often called the worst prediction in physics.
explanations.c: A positive Λ drives acceleration and expansion, not collapse.
explanations.d: Dark energy is measured (via supernovae, BAO, the CMB); the problem is explaining WHY Λ is so small, not whether it can be observed.

questions.prompt: How did the 2017 event GW170817 constrain modified-gravity explanations of dark energy?

options.text: It measured the mass of dark matter directly

Its gravitational waves and gamma-rays arrived within ~1.7 s after ~130 million light-years, showing gravitational waves travel at the speed of light — ruling out many modified-gravity models that predicted a different speed
It proved dark energy does not exist
It measured the Hubble constant to be exactly 70 km/s/Mpc

explanations.a: GW170817 was a neutron-star merger; it did not measure a dark-matter particle mass.
explanations.b: Correct — the near-simultaneous arrival of the gravitational-wave and electromagnetic signals fixed the gravitational-wave speed to equal the speed of light to ~1 part in 10¹⁵, eliminating broad classes of modified-gravity dark-energy theories.
explanations.c: The event constrained WHICH explanation of acceleration works; it did not show acceleration/dark energy is absent.
explanations.d: Standard-siren mergers can help measure H₀, but GW170817's dark-energy relevance is the GW-speed constraint, and its H₀ estimate was not a precise "exactly 70."

questions.prompt: Match each dark-energy candidate to its defining feature.

right.text: Constant vacuum energy density, w = −1 exactly
A dynamical scalar field with evolving w, typically −1 < w < −1/3
w < −1, driving an ever-faster expansion toward a "Big Rip"
No new energy — general relativity itself altered on large scales

questions.explanation: The cosmological constant is constant vacuum energy with w = −1; quintessence is a dynamical scalar field with an evolving w between −1 and −1/3; phantom energy has w < −1 and ends in a Big Rip; modified gravity postulates no new energy component but alters general relativity on cosmological scales.

lessons.label: Complementary Dark-Energy Probes: Supernovae, BAO, and Weak Lensing Together

sections.heading: Geometry versus growth
sections.body: No single measurement can characterize dark energy; the strategy is to combine probes that constrain DIFFERENT physics. Geometric probes measure the background expansion history — the distance-redshift relation and H(z). Type Ia supernovae are standard candles giving the luminosity distance d_L(z); BAO is a standard ruler giving the angular-diameter distance D_M(z) and H(z). Growth-of-structure probes instead measure how fast density fluctuations grow over time — captured by the quantity fσ₈(z). Weak gravitational lensing (cosmic shear), redshift-space distortions, and cluster counts all measure growth. The distinction matters because dark energy and modified gravity can produce the SAME expansion history H(z) while predicting DIFFERENT growth rates: measuring both geometry and growth is the cleanest way to tell "new energy" from "new gravity."

sections.heading: Breaking degeneracies by combining
sections.body: Each probe alone is degenerate — its constraint is a broad band in parameter space — but the bands point in different directions, so their intersection is tight. Supernovae measure only RELATIVE distances well (their absolute calibration carries nuisance parameters), while BAO supplies an ABSOLUTE ruler anchored to the CMB sound horizon; combining them calibrates the supernova ladder and breaks the Ω_m–Ω_Λ degeneracy. Adding weak lensing brings in growth, separating dark energy from modified gravity. The Dark Energy Task Force (Albrecht and colleagues, 2006) formalized this with a "figure of merit" — essentially the inverse area of the allowed region in the w₀–w_a plane — to compare how much each survey combination tightens the dark-energy constraints.

sections.heading: The surveys, past and future
sections.body: These probes have been pursued by dedicated programs: the Supernova Cosmology Project and High-z Team (the 1998 discovery), then wide surveys such as the Dark Energy Survey (DES), the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS), and Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) for lensing, and BOSS/eBOSS for BAO. The current "Stage IV" generation is designed to combine all three at unprecedented scale: DESI (spectroscopic BAO and redshift-space distortions across tens of millions of galaxies), the Euclid space telescope (launched 2023, weak lensing plus clustering), the Vera C. Rubin Observatory with its LSST (deep imaging for lensing and thousands of supernovae), and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Their power is complementarity — geometry from BAO and supernovae, growth from lensing and RSD — cross-checking dark energy and the growth history simultaneously.

lessons.workedExample: Use a Type Ia supernova as a standard candle to get a distance, then note the cross-check. A Type Ia at peak has an absolute magnitude M ≈ −19.3 (after light-curve standardization). Suppose one is observed with peak apparent magnitude m = 20.0. The distance modulus is μ = m − M = 20.0 − (−19.3) = 39.3. Inverting μ = 5·log₁₀(d_L/10 pc) gives d_L = 10^(μ/5 + 1) pc = 10^(39.3/5 + 1) pc = 10^(7.86 + 1) pc = 10^8.86 pc ≈ 7.2×10⁸ pc ≈ 720 Mpc, corresponding to z ≈ 0.16. That single supernova gives a luminosity distance at z ≈ 0.16. A BAO measurement at the SAME redshift independently gives an angular-diameter distance and H(z) at z ≈ 0.16 from a standard ruler — no supernova physics involved. Demanding the geometric candle and the geometric ruler agree, and then checking the growth rate fσ₈ from weak lensing at that redshift, is exactly the multi-probe consistency test that pins down dark energy.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask why cosmologists use several dark-energy probes rather than just the "best" one to test whether a student grasps degeneracy-breaking and the geometry-versus-growth split. The strong answer explains that supernovae and BAO both measure GEOMETRY (the expansion history) while weak lensing measures GROWTH, and that a theory of modified gravity can mimic the geometry but not the growth — so combining them is how you distinguish new energy from new gravity. A student who names Stage IV surveys (DESI, Euclid, Rubin/LSST, Roman) and ties each to a probe shows they understand the current experimental landscape, not just textbook history.

questions.prompt: Type Ia supernovae and BAO are both primarily which kind of dark-energy probe?

options.text: Growth-of-structure probes, measuring fσ₈(z)
Geometric probes, measuring the expansion history (distances and H(z))
Probes of the CMB temperature
Direct detectors of dark-matter particles

explanations.a: Growth probes are weak lensing, redshift-space distortions, and cluster counts; supernovae and BAO measure geometry, not the growth rate.
explanations.b: Correct — supernovae (standard candles → d_L) and BAO (standard ruler → D_M, H(z)) both trace the background expansion history, i.e. geometry.
explanations.c: Neither is a CMB-temperature probe; they use the low-redshift galaxy/supernova distribution.
explanations.d: Neither detects dark-matter particles; they constrain dark energy through cosmic geometry.

questions.prompt: Why is combining geometric probes with growth-of-structure probes especially powerful?

options.text: It doubles the number of supernovae observed
Dark energy and modified gravity can share the same expansion history H(z) but predict different growth rates, so measuring both distinguishes new energy from new gravity
Growth probes are always more accurate than geometric probes
It removes the need to measure redshifts

explanations.a: Combining probe TYPES is about breaking degeneracies, not simply increasing supernova counts.
explanations.b: Correct — a modified-gravity theory can mimic the geometry (H(z)) while predicting a different fσ₈ growth history, so only measuring BOTH geometry and growth can tell the two interpretations apart.
explanations.c: Neither type is universally more accurate; their VALUE is complementarity, since they constrain different physics.
explanations.d: All these probes rely on redshifts; combining them does not eliminate that need.

questions.prompt: A standardized Type Ia supernova (M ≈ −19.3) is observed at peak apparent magnitude m = 20.0. Its approximate luminosity distance is:

options.text: ~720 Mpc (distance modulus μ ≈ 39.3)
~10 pc
~1 Mpc
~14,000 Mpc (the edge of the observable universe)

explanations.b: 10 pc is the reference distance where apparent and absolute magnitude are equal (μ = 0); here μ = 39.3, far larger.
explanations.c: 1 Mpc would give μ ≈ 25, not 39.3; the supernova is hundreds of times more distant.
explanations.d: ~14,000 Mpc corresponds to a much larger distance modulus (μ ≈ 48); μ = 39.3 gives ~720 Mpc.

questions.prompt: Match each Stage IV / recent survey to its primary dark-energy probe.

right.text: Spectroscopic BAO and redshift-space distortions from tens of millions of galaxy redshifts
Space-based weak lensing plus galaxy clustering over a wide area
Ground-based weak-lensing (cosmic shear) imaging surveys
Deep repeated imaging yielding thousands of supernovae plus lensing

questions.explanation: DESI is a spectroscopic survey specializing in BAO and redshift-space distortions; Euclid is a space telescope combining weak lensing with clustering; KiDS and HSC are ground-based cosmic-shear (weak-lensing) imaging surveys; and the Rubin Observatory's LSST provides deep repeated imaging that delivers thousands of supernovae along with lensing.

units.label: Landmark Studies and Open Debates

lessons.label: Penzias and Wilson 1965: The Antenna 'Noise' That Was the Big Bang (Nobel 1978)

sections.heading: A horn antenna, a stubborn hiss, and pigeons
sections.body: In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, radio astronomers at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Holmdel, New Jersey, were commissioning a large horn-reflector antenna — built for early Echo/Telstar satellite communication — to make careful measurements of the Milky Way at a wavelength of 7.35 cm (a frequency of 4080 MHz). To do sensitive work they needed to account for every source of noise, so they compared the antenna's output against a cold reference load cooled with liquid helium. They found a persistent excess: an antenna temperature of about 3.5 K (they quoted 3.5 ± 1.0 K) that would not go away. It was the same in every direction they pointed (isotropic), showed no daily or seasonal variation, and was unpolarized. They checked everything — receiver electronics, the join in the antenna, and famously a pair of pigeons nesting in the horn whose droppings they cleaned out (the 'white dielectric material'). Nothing removed the hiss. Their measurement was published in 1965 in the Astrophysical Journal as 'A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s' — a deliberately modest four-column title for one of the most important observations of the century.

sections.heading: The theorists next door had predicted exactly this
sections.body: Forty kilometers away at Princeton, Robert Dicke, Jim Peebles, Peter Roll, and David Wilkinson were independently building a radiometer to search for exactly such a relic radiation: if the universe began hot and dense, the early plasma would have been in thermal equilibrium with light, and as the universe expanded and cooled that light should survive today as a faint microwave blackbody bath. (Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman had already predicted a temperature of roughly 5 K back in 1948, a prediction that had been largely forgotten.) When Penzias phoned Dicke about the unexplained noise, Dicke reportedly hung up and told his group, 'Boys, we've been scooped.' The two groups published back-to-back papers in the same 1965 volume: Penzias and Wilson reported the measurement without claiming to know its origin, and the Princeton group (Dicke, Peebles, Roll, Wilkinson) supplied the cosmological interpretation — this was the cosmic microwave background (CMB), the afterglow of the Big Bang. Penzias and Wilson shared half of the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery (the other half went to Pyotr Kapitsa for unrelated low-temperature work).

sections.heading: Why a uniform 3 K microwave glow is the smoking gun
sections.body: The CMB is decisive because a hot-Big-Bang origin predicts three specific, checkable properties, all of which the CMB has. First, it must be a near-perfect thermal blackbody, because it was emitted by matter and radiation in equilibrium — later confirmed exquisitely by COBE (Lesson 3), with a temperature now pinned at 2.725 K. Second, it must be nearly isotropic — the same temperature in every direction — because the early universe was smooth; Penzias and Wilson already saw this. Third, it must fill all of space rather than come from discrete sources like stars or galaxies. No rival model of the 1960s could produce a smooth, all-sky, thermal microwave background as a natural consequence; the Steady-State universe (Lesson 2) in particular had no mechanism for it. The 7.35 cm wavelength Penzias and Wilson used sits on the long-wavelength Rayleigh–Jeans tail of the 2.725 K spectrum, so they caught the CMB well away from its peak — but the temperature they extracted was already the right ballpark for the whole spectrum.

lessons.workedExample: Where does a 2.725 K blackbody actually peak, and why is it called 'microwave'? Wien's displacement law says the peak wavelength is λ_max = b / T with b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K. So λ_max = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.725 ≈ 1.06 × 10⁻³ m ≈ 1.06 mm — squarely in the microwave band, which is why it is the cosmic MICROWAVE background. Now compare Penzias and Wilson's observing wavelength: 7.35 cm = 73.5 mm, about 70 times longer than the peak, deep on the Rayleigh–Jeans tail. That they could still detect a ~3.5 K excess so far from the peak, isotropically and without seasonal change, is exactly what a diffuse cosmic blackbody predicts and what a local or instrumental artifact would not. Sanity check the temperature they reported (3.5 ± 1.0 K) against today's precise value (2.725 K): the modern number sits inside their error bar — a striking vindication of a 1965 measurement made while cleaning pigeon droppings out of a horn.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love the Penzias–Wilson story because it tests whether a student understands EVIDENCE versus anecdote. The memorable bits (helium-cooled load, pigeons, the phone call to Dicke) are fun, but a strong student can state WHY the observation clinched the Big Bang: a smooth, all-sky, thermal microwave glow at ~3 K is exactly what a hot early universe predicts and what no discrete-source or Steady-State model naturally gives. A judge may ask 'how did they know it wasn't just noise?' — the winning answer names the three signatures (isotropic, unpolarized, no seasonal variation) and that the Princeton group had independently predicted the same relic radiation, so theory and accident met in the same 1965 journal volume.

questions.prompt: What did Penzias and Wilson actually measure at their 7.35 cm (4080 MHz) horn antenna in 1964–65?

options.text: A sharp radio spike coming from one specific point on the sky
A uniform excess antenna temperature of about 3.5 K, the same in every direction, with no seasonal or daily variation
The 21 cm hydrogen line from the Milky Way
Radar echoes from the Echo communications satellite

explanations.a: The signal was the opposite of a point source — it was isotropic, filling the whole sky equally, which is why a local or discrete origin was ruled out.
explanations.b: Correct — an isotropic, unpolarized ~3.5 K excess with no daily/seasonal change is exactly what a diffuse cosmic blackbody (the CMB) produces, and it survived every attempt to remove it as instrumental noise.
explanations.c: The 21 cm line is a specific spectral feature at a different wavelength; they were observing at 7.35 cm and found a broadband, structureless excess.
explanations.d: The antenna had been built for satellite work, but the excess was not a satellite echo — it was present with the antenna pointed anywhere at the sky.

questions.prompt: Why does a smooth ~3 K microwave background strongly favor a hot Big Bang over its rivals?

options.text: Because only stars can emit microwaves

Because a hot, dense early universe in thermal equilibrium naturally leaves a near-perfect blackbody that is isotropic and fills all space, which rival 1960s models (like Steady-State) could not reproduce
Because the microwave background is polarized in a way only Steady-State predicts
Because it proves the universe is contracting

explanations.a: Stars produce discrete, non-thermal-across-the-whole-sky emission; the CMB is a diffuse, all-sky blackbody, which is not a stellar signature.
explanations.b: Correct — thermal equilibrium in a hot early universe predicts a blackbody spectrum, isotropy, and space-filling radiation; no competing model of the era generated all three naturally.
explanations.c: The CMB is very nearly unpolarized at the level Penzias and Wilson measured; Steady-State made no such prediction.
explanations.d: The CMB is evidence of a hot, expanding past, not of contraction.

questions.prompt: Match each person or group to their role in the 1965 CMB discovery.

right.text: Measured the unexplained ~3.5 K isotropic excess and published the observation
Supplied the cosmological interpretation (this is the Big Bang afterglow) in a companion paper
Predicted a relic background near ~5 K back in 1948, a forecast later forgotten
Awarded the Physics prize for the discovery of the cosmic microwave background

questions.explanation: Penzias and Wilson measured the excess and reported it without claiming its origin; the Princeton group (Dicke, Peebles, Roll, Wilkinson) published the companion paper interpreting it as the CMB; Alpher and Herman had predicted ~5 K in 1948; and the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Penzias and Wilson for the discovery.

questions.prompt: Penzias and Wilson observed at 7.35 cm, but a 2.725 K blackbody peaks near 1.06 mm. What does that imply about their measurement?

options.text: Their wavelength was wrong, so the CMB temperature they reported is meaningless
They observed on the long-wavelength Rayleigh–Jeans tail, far from the peak, yet still recovered a temperature consistent with the whole blackbody spectrum
They observed exactly at the spectral peak of the CMB
The CMB has no defined temperature away from its peak

explanations.a: The wavelength was fine — a blackbody has one temperature, recoverable from any point on its spectrum, and their value later proved consistent with 2.725 K.
explanations.b: Correct — 7.35 cm is about 70 times longer than the 1.06 mm peak, so they sampled the Rayleigh–Jeans tail, but a single blackbody temperature describes the entire curve, so their tail measurement still pinned the temperature.
explanations.c: The peak near 1.06 mm is far shorter than their 7.35 cm; they were nowhere near it.
explanations.d: A blackbody has a single temperature that characterizes its emission at every wavelength, peak or tail.

lessons.label: Big Bang vs. Steady State: Hoyle, the Perfect Cosmological Principle, and How the CMB Decided It

sections.heading: Two universes: one with a beginning, one eternal
sections.body: By the late 1940s cosmologists agreed the universe was expanding — Hubble's 1929 law v = H₀·d showed galaxies receding faster the farther away they lie. But expansion admits two very different stories. The Big Bang picture (championed by George Gamow and colleagues) runs the expansion backward to a hot, dense beginning a finite time ago. The Steady-State picture, proposed in 1948 by Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold in one paper and Fred Hoyle in a separate one, kept the expansion but denied any beginning: the universe is eternal and, on large scales, looks the same at every epoch. Ironically, it was Hoyle — Steady-State's fiercest defender — who coined the term 'Big Bang,' reportedly in a 1949 BBC radio broadcast, as a vivid (some say dismissive) label for the rival theory. The name stuck to the theory Hoyle spent his career opposing.

sections.heading: The Perfect Cosmological Principle demands continuous creation
sections.body: Steady-State rested on the Perfect Cosmological Principle: the universe is homogeneous and isotropic not only in space (the ordinary Cosmological Principle — no special place) but also in TIME (no special epoch). If the universe never changes its large-scale appearance yet is expanding and diluting, something must replenish it. Steady-State therefore required the continuous creation of matter — new hydrogen atoms appearing throughout space to keep the average density constant as galaxies fly apart. Hoyle formalized this with a 'creation field' (the C-field). The required creation rate is astonishingly tiny — of order one hydrogen atom per cubic kilometer per year (see the worked example) — far below any hope of direct detection, which was both the theory's escape hatch and its critics' complaint: an unfalsifiable trickle of matter conjured to preserve an aesthetic principle. The theory's appeal was real, though: it needed no singular beginning, and it gave a definite, testable prediction that the universe should look statistically the same at all distances (hence all look-back times).

sections.heading: How the data decided — and why it took the CMB
sections.body: Several observations turned against Steady-State through the 1950s–60s. Martin Ryle's radio-source counts at Cambridge showed there were MORE faint (distant, hence earlier) radio sources than a non-evolving universe should have — the distant universe looked different from the nearby one, contradicting the Perfect Cosmological Principle. The discovery that quasars were common in the early universe but rare nearby reinforced this cosmic evolution. But the decisive blow was the 1965 CMB (Lesson 1): a smooth ~3 K thermal blackbody filling all of space is a natural relic of a hot dense beginning, whereas Steady-State — with no hot early phase — had no mechanism to produce an all-sky thermal background at the observed temperature. Hoyle and a few collaborators tried to rescue the idea (e.g., thermalizing starlight via hypothetical intergalactic dust), but the fixes were contrived and unpersuasive. Together with Big Bang nucleosynthesis correctly predicting the primordial helium abundance (~25% by mass), the CMB moved the community decisively to the hot Big Bang. Steady-State is the textbook example of a serious, testable theory that lost cleanly to evidence.

lessons.workedExample: How much matter creation would Steady-State actually need? To hold the density constant against expansion, the creation rate per unit volume must roughly replace what expansion dilutes: dρ/dt ≈ 3·H₀·ρ. Take the critical density ρ ≈ 9 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/m³ and H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹, so 3H₀ ≈ 6.8 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Then dρ/dt ≈ 6.8 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 9 × 10⁻²⁷ ≈ 6 × 10⁻⁴⁴ kg/m³/s. Dividing by a hydrogen-atom mass (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) gives ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ atoms per cubic meter per second. Multiply by the seconds in a year (3.15 × 10⁷) to get ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁹ atoms per cubic meter per year — i.e. about ONE atom per cubic kilometer per year (a cubic kilometer is 10⁹ m³). That rate is far too small to detect in any laboratory, which is precisely why Steady-State could not be killed by a direct search for created matter — and why it had to be defeated instead by indirect cosmic evidence like the CMB and radio-source counts.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson is a judge's favorite for probing the nature of science: 'Steady-State was a good theory that turned out wrong — why do we still respect it?' A strong student explains that Steady-State was scientific precisely because it made falsifiable predictions (the universe should look the same at all epochs), and that it was DEFEATED BY DATA — radio-source counts, quasar evolution, and above all the CMB — not by fiat. Naming the Perfect Cosmological Principle and continuous matter creation, and then explaining why a smooth thermal 3 K background is fatal to a universe with no hot beginning, shows a student who understands theory-versus-evidence rather than just memorizing 'the Big Bang won.'

questions.prompt: What extra assumption distinguishes the Perfect Cosmological Principle (Steady-State) from the ordinary Cosmological Principle?

options.text: That the universe is the same at every point in SPACE
That the universe is the same at every point in space AND at every moment in TIME (no special epoch)
That the universe is finite in extent
That the universe is not expanding

explanations.a: Spatial homogeneity is the ORDINARY Cosmological Principle, shared by the Big Bang model; it is not what makes Steady-State distinctive.
explanations.b: Correct — the Perfect Cosmological Principle adds temporal homogeneity: no special epoch, so the universe looks statistically the same at all times, which forces continuous matter creation to offset expansion.
explanations.c: Finiteness is not the distinguishing assumption; the key addition is sameness in time.
explanations.d: Steady-State fully accepted expansion — that is exactly why it needed continuous creation to keep the density constant.

questions.prompt: Why did the Steady-State model require the continuous creation of matter?

options.text: To explain where dark matter comes from
Because an expanding universe that must always look the same needs new matter to replace what expansion dilutes, keeping the average density constant
To account for the energy of the CMB
Because matter was observed appearing in laboratories

explanations.a: Continuous creation was about preserving average density under expansion, not about dark matter (which the model did not address).
explanations.b: Correct — expansion dilutes density, but the Perfect Cosmological Principle demands an unchanging large-scale appearance, so new hydrogen (Hoyle’s C-field) had to appear to hold the density steady.
explanations.c: Steady-State had no natural CMB mechanism at all; that was its downfall, not the reason for continuous creation.
explanations.d: No such creation was ever observed in the lab — the required rate (~1 atom per km³ per year) is undetectably small.

questions.prompt: Which single observation is usually credited with decisively defeating Steady-State?

options.text: Hubble’s 1929 discovery of cosmic expansion
The 1965 discovery of the smooth ~3 K cosmic microwave background, a natural relic of a hot beginning that Steady-State could not reproduce
The detection of gravitational waves in 2015
The measurement of the deflection of starlight in 1919

explanations.a: Expansion was common ground — BOTH models accepted it — so Hubble’s law did not distinguish them.
explanations.b: Correct — a smooth, all-sky thermal ~3 K background is the expected afterglow of a hot dense early universe, and Steady-State (with no hot beginning) had no natural way to produce it.
explanations.c: Gravitational waves came decades after the debate was settled and were not part of it.
explanations.d: The 1919 eclipse test confirmed general relativity, not the Big Bang over Steady-State.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the Big Bang vs. Steady-State story from earliest to latest.

items.text: Hubble's law v = H₀·d establishes cosmic expansion (1929)
Bondi, Gold, and Hoyle propose the Steady-State model (1948)
Hoyle coins the term 'Big Bang' on BBC radio (1949)
Penzias and Wilson detect the CMB, tipping the balance to the Big Bang (1965)

questions.explanation: Expansion came first (Hubble, 1929), setting up the debate; Steady-State was proposed in 1948; Hoyle coined 'Big Bang' in a 1949 broadcast; and the CMB detection in 1965 decided the contest in the Big Bang's favor.

lessons.label: COBE, WMAP, and Planck: Three Generations That Made Cosmology Precise

sections.heading: COBE (1989): the perfect blackbody and the first ripples
sections.body: The Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE), launched by NASA in 1989, carried two decisive instruments. FIRAS (the Far-Infrared Absolute Spectrophotometer), led by John Mather, measured the CMB spectrum and found it to be a blackbody at T = 2.725 K with deviations smaller than about 50 parts per million — the most perfect blackbody ever observed in nature, exactly as a hot Big Bang predicts. DMR (the Differential Microwave Radiometer), led by George Smoot, mapped the sky's temperature and in 1992 detected the first anisotropies: tiny fluctuations of order 30 microkelvin, or about one part in 100,000, on top of the uniform 2.725 K. These ripples are the seeds of all later structure — the slightly denser patches that grew into galaxies and clusters. COBE's angular resolution was coarse (~7°), so it saw only the largest-scale ripples, but it proved they existed. Mather and Smoot shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work.

sections.heading: WMAP (2001): the acoustic peaks and the 13.7-billion-year universe
sections.body: The Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP), launched by NASA in 2001 and named for CMB pioneer David Wilkinson, improved the resolution to about 0.2° (13 arcminutes) — sharp enough to resolve the CMB's acoustic peaks. Before recombination the photon–baryon plasma rang like a bell: sound waves compressed and rarefied it, imprinting a characteristic angular scale. The first and largest acoustic peak sits at multipole ℓ ≈ 220, corresponding to an angular scale near 1°, and its position revealed that the universe is spatially FLAT (total density very close to critical). WMAP's spectrum yielded a precise inventory: an age of about 13.7 billion years and a composition of roughly 4–5% ordinary (baryonic) matter, ~23% dark matter, and ~72–73% dark energy. This is when cosmology became a genuinely precise, parameter-fitting science rather than a field of factor-of-two arguments.

sections.heading: Planck (2009): the high-precision benchmark
sections.body: The European Space Agency's Planck satellite, launched in 2009, pushed resolution to ~5–10 arcminutes and much lower noise, measuring the acoustic-peak structure out to high multipoles across nine frequency bands (which is essential for subtracting foreground emission from our own Galaxy). Planck's 2018 results are the modern benchmark for the standard ΛCDM model: a Hubble constant H₀ ≈ 67.4 km/s/Mpc, an age of 13.8 billion years, matter density Ω_m ≈ 0.315, and dark-energy density Ω_Λ ≈ 0.685, with a nearly flat geometry and a spectrum of primordial fluctuations consistent with inflation (Lesson 4). The COBE → WMAP → Planck lineage is a textbook case of instruments getting sharper by more than an order of magnitude in angular resolution across three decades, each generation confirming the last while adding precision — and Planck's H₀ ≈ 67 is one side of the Hubble tension (Lesson 5).

lessons.workedExample: How does an acoustic peak at multipole ℓ ≈ 220 translate to an angle on the sky, and which mission could resolve it? A useful rule of thumb links multipole to angular scale by θ ≈ 180° / ℓ. For the first peak, θ ≈ 180° / 220 ≈ 0.8° — just under one degree. Now compare instrument resolutions: COBE at ~7° is far too coarse to resolve a 0.8° feature (7° ≫ 0.8°), which is why COBE saw only the broad ripples and could not map the acoustic peaks. WMAP at ~0.2° comfortably resolves a 0.8° peak (0.2° < 0.8°), which is exactly why WMAP could pin the first peak at ℓ ≈ 220 and thereby show the universe is flat. Planck at ~5 arcmin (≈0.08°) resolves not just the first peak but a long series of higher-ℓ peaks (ℓ up to ~2500), tightening every parameter. The lesson: angular resolution sets the largest multipole (smallest angle) you can measure, and each mission's resolution is what unlocked its science.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the COBE/WMAP/Planck lineage to check whether a student grasps that BETTER INSTRUMENTS drive discovery, not just cleverer theory. A judge may ask 'why did we need three CMB satellites?' The strong answer ties each to a capability: COBE proved the blackbody (FIRAS) and the ripples (DMR) at coarse ~7° resolution; WMAP's ~0.2° resolution resolved the acoustic peaks and fixed the age and flatness; Planck's ~5-arcmin resolution across nine bands set the precision benchmark (H₀ ≈ 67, age 13.8 Gyr). A student who can connect a specific instrument/resolution to a specific result — rather than saying 'they all looked at the CMB' — shows real command of how observational precision advances.

questions.prompt: What did COBE's FIRAS instrument establish about the CMB spectrum?

options.text: That it is a jagged spectrum full of emission lines
That it is a near-perfect blackbody at 2.725 K, with deviations below ~50 parts per million
That its temperature varies wildly across the sky
That the CMB does not follow a blackbody curve at all

explanations.a: The CMB spectrum is smooth and featureless, not a line spectrum — FIRAS found it followed the Planck blackbody curve to extraordinary precision.
explanations.b: Correct — FIRAS (Mather) measured a 2.725 K blackbody with deviations under ~50 ppm, the most perfect blackbody known in nature and a clean confirmation of a hot early universe.
explanations.c: The spectrum is nearly identical everywhere; the tiny sky-to-sky variations (the anisotropies) were the job of the DMR instrument, not FIRAS, and are only ~30 μK.
explanations.d: FIRAS showed the opposite — an essentially perfect blackbody fit.

questions.prompt: The first acoustic peak in the CMB power spectrum sits at multipole ℓ ≈ 220 (about 1° on the sky). What did resolving it reveal?

options.text: That the universe is spatially FLAT (total density near critical)
That the CMB is polarized by dust
That dark matter does not exist
That the universe is only a few million years old

explanations.a: Correct — the angular position of the first acoustic peak (near 1°, ℓ ≈ 220) is a standard ruler; finding it there shows light traveled through a flat geometry, so total density is very near critical.
explanations.b: Dust foregrounds are a nuisance to subtract, not what the acoustic-peak position reveals; the peak position measures geometry.
