questions.explanation: First obtain the public data and covariance; then compute model distance moduli (marginalizing over M); then evaluate χ² with the inverse covariance and find the minimum; finally report the best-fit parameter with a Δχ²-based uncertainty, stated assumptions, and a model comparison — the falsifiable, error-barred, reproducible result.

units.label: Foundations: The Physics and Geometry of an Indirect Detection

lessons.label: Why Exoplanets Are Nearly Invisible: The Contrast and Angular-Separation Problem

sections.heading: Two disasters at once: the planet is faint AND it hides in the glare
sections.body: To photograph a planet around another star you must beat two independent problems simultaneously, and each alone is brutal. The first is CONTRAST: a planet shines only by reflecting a sliver of its star's light. For Jupiter, the reflected-light flux ratio is roughly the geometric albedo times the square of the planet's radius over its orbital distance — about 0.5 × (71,492 km / 7.78×10⁸ km)² ≈ 4×10⁻⁹. The planet is a few HUNDRED MILLION times fainter than the star sitting right next to it. Earth is worse still: ~0.3 × (6,371 km / 1.496×10⁸ km)² ≈ 5×10⁻¹⁰, roughly two billion times fainter than the Sun. The second problem is ANGULAR SEPARATION: the planet sits a tiny angle away from a blindingly bright point source, and that angle, θ ≈ a/d (in arcseconds when a is in AU and d in parsecs), is minuscule. Jupiter seen from 10 parsecs is only 5.2/10 = 0.52 arcsec from its star; Earth from the same distance is 1.0/10 = 0.10 arcsec. You are trying to see a firefly one-billionth as bright, a fraction of an arcsecond from a searchlight.

sections.heading: The diffraction limit sets the wall — and starlight overflows it anyway
sections.body: Even a perfect telescope smears a point source into a blob of finite width set by diffraction: θ ≈ 1.22 λ/D, the wavelength over the aperture diameter. Hubble (D = 2.4 m) at 500 nm has a diffraction limit of 1.22 × 500×10⁻⁹ / 2.4 ≈ 2.5×10⁻⁷ rad ≈ 0.05 arcsec. So an Earth analog at 0.10 arcsec is barely two resolution elements out — formally resolvable, but the star's diffraction pattern (its Airy rings and scattered-light halo) still floods that location with far more than 10⁻¹⁰ of the peak. Ground-based telescopes are worse: atmospheric turbulence blurs stars to ~1 arcsec unless adaptive optics corrects the wavefront in real time. The blocker is not raw resolution so much as the enormous dynamic range — a detector able to record a 10¹⁰-to-1 brightness difference within a fraction of an arcsecond does not exist off the shelf.

sections.heading: Why direct imaging works only in a narrow corner — and what actually cracked it
sections.body: Direct imaging succeeds today only where the physics is kindest: YOUNG, massive, self-luminous giant planets far from their stars, observed in the infrared. A newly formed giant is still hot from gravitational contraction (hundreds to ~1000 K), so in the infrared it GLOWS by its own thermal emission rather than by feeble reflection — pushing the contrast from ~10⁻⁹ up to a far friendlier ~10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁶. The landmark result was HR 8799: Christian Marois and colleagues in 2008 directly imaged three planets (a fourth followed in 2010) orbiting a young A-type star, the first multi-planet system ever imaged. Beta Pictoris b was imaged around the same era. Instruments beat the glare with a CORONAGRAPH (a mask that blocks the star's core), adaptive optics, and ANGULAR DIFFERENTIAL IMAGING (rotating the field so the fixed instrument speckles can be subtracted while a real planet moves). The takeaway that shapes the whole field: because direct detection is so hard for ordinary mature planets, nearly every exoplanet we know was found INDIRECTLY — by watching what the planet does to its star, not by seeing the planet itself.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to know whether Hubble could, in principle, directly image an Earth-twin orbiting a Sun-like star 10 parsecs away. First the geometry: θ = a/d = 1.0 AU / 10 pc = 0.10 arcsec. Hubble's diffraction limit is θ_min = 1.22 λ/D = 1.22 × 500×10⁻⁹ m / 2.4 m = 2.5×10⁻⁷ rad. Converting (1 rad = 206,265 arcsec) gives ≈ 0.052 arcsec, so the planet at 0.10 arcsec is just about resolvable — the separation is NOT the dealbreaker. The dealbreaker is contrast: the Earth-twin reflects only ~0.3 × (6,371 km / 1.496×10⁸ km)² ≈ 5×10⁻¹⁰ of the star's light, and at 0.10 arcsec the star's scattered-light halo is orders of magnitude brighter than that. Conclusion: geometry says "barely resolvable," but the ~2-billion-to-1 brightness ratio buries the planet — which is exactly why we detect Earth analogs by their transit or reflex wobble, not by imaging.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe "why can't you just take a picture of it?" to see whether a student grasps that exoplanet science is fundamentally INDIRECT and why. A strong answer separates the two obstacles — the ~10⁹–10¹⁰ contrast ratio and the sub-arcsecond angular separation — and explains that direct imaging only cracks the narrow regime of young, hot, wide-orbit giants glowing in the infrared. That distinction shows the student understands the measurement problem, not just the buzzwords.

questions.prompt: Roughly what is the visible-light contrast (planet-to-star flux ratio) of a Jupiter-like planet in reflected light?

options.text: About 10⁻² (1 percent)
About 10⁻⁹ (one billionth)
About 1 (equal brightness)
About 10⁻⁹⁰

explanations.a: 10⁻² is closer to a transit DEPTH for a hot Jupiter, not the reflected-light brightness ratio; a planet reflecting sunlight is far fainter than 1 percent of its star.
explanations.b: Correct — albedo × (Rₚ/a)² ≈ 0.5 × (71,492/7.78×10⁸)² ≈ 4×10⁻⁹, so Jupiter is roughly a billion times fainter than its star in reflected visible light.
explanations.c: A planet reflects only a tiny fraction of the light it receives; it is nowhere near as bright as its star.
explanations.d: 10⁻⁹⁰ is astronomically too small — that is far beyond any real flux ratio; the reflected-light contrast is about 10⁻⁹.

questions.prompt: A planet orbits at 5 AU around a star 25 parsecs away. What is its approximate angular separation from the star?

options.text: 0.2 arcsec
5 arcsec
125 arcsec
0.002 arcsec

explanations.a: Correct — θ (arcsec) ≈ a (AU) / d (pc) = 5 / 25 = 0.2 arcsec.
explanations.b: 5 arcsec would be the answer if you used the AU value alone and ignored the 25 pc distance; distance divides the separation down.
explanations.c: 125 = 5 × 25 multiplies instead of divides; separation shrinks with distance, so you divide by parsecs.
explanations.d: 0.002 arcsec is 100× too small — it would come from dividing by 2500 rather than 25.

questions.prompt: Why does direct imaging work for the HR 8799 planets (Marois et al. 2008) but not for a mature Earth-like planet?

options.text: HR 8799 is much closer than any other star
The HR 8799 planets are young, hot, self-luminous giants seen in the infrared, giving a far more favorable contrast (~10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶) than a mature reflecting planet
Earth-like planets do not emit or reflect any light at all
HR 8799 has no host star to create glare

explanations.a: HR 8799 is about 40 parsecs away — not unusually close. Its imageability comes from the planets' own thermal glow and wide orbits, not proximity.
explanations.b: Correct — freshly formed giants are still hot from contraction and glow by thermal emission in the infrared, raising the contrast to ~10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ (versus ~10⁻¹⁰ reflected for an Earth analog), and they orbit far out at large angular separation.
explanations.c: Earth-like planets do reflect (and thermally emit) light; the problem is the ~10⁻¹⁰ contrast, not zero flux.
explanations.d: HR 8799 is a real star with substantial glare; coronagraphy and angular differential imaging suppress it — the star is not absent.

questions.prompt: Rank these targets from EASIEST to HARDEST to directly image, given the contrast/separation physics.

items.text: A young, hot, self-luminous giant on a wide orbit, seen in the infrared
A mature Jupiter-like reflecting planet at ~5 AU
A mature Earth-like reflecting planet at 1 AU around a Sun-like star

questions.explanation: A young hot giant glows by its own thermal emission (contrast ~10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶) and sits far out, so it is easiest. A mature reflecting Jupiter (~10⁻⁹, wider separation) is harder. A mature Earth analog (~10⁻¹⁰ contrast at just 0.1 arcsec) is hardest of all.

lessons.label: The Five Detection Channels and What Each One Physically Measures

sections.heading: Each method measures a different physical quantity — none measures "a planet" directly
sections.body: Because direct imaging is so limited, the field runs on five INDIRECT channels, and the single most important habit is to know exactly what each one measures — and, just as importantly, what it does NOT. (1) RADIAL VELOCITY (Doppler) watches the star's spectral lines shift back and forth as the planet tugs it toward and away from us; it measures the star's line-of-sight velocity and yields the orbital period and a MINIMUM mass, m·sin(i), because we never see the inclination i on its own. (2) TRANSIT photometry watches the star dim as the planet crosses its face; it measures the fractional flux drop, depth = (Rₚ/R★)², giving the planet's RADIUS ratio, the period, and (from the transit shape) the inclination. (3) DIRECT IMAGING spatially resolves the planet's own light, giving its luminosity/temperature and projected separation. (4) MICROLENSING watches a foreground star+planet gravitationally magnify a background star; the planet adds a brief spike, giving the planet-to-star MASS RATIO and projected separation — even for planets thousands of parsecs away. (5) ASTROMETRY measures the star's tiny two-dimensional wobble on the sky, which — because it captures the full orbit, not just the line-of-sight piece — yields a TRUE mass.

sections.heading: The complementarity: radius from transit, mass from Doppler, density from both
sections.body: The channels are powerful precisely because they measure DIFFERENT things and can be combined. A transit gives radius but not mass; radial velocity gives (minimum) mass but not radius. When a planet both transits AND is bright enough for radial-velocity follow-up, the transit pins the inclination near 90°, so sin(i) ≈ 1 and the RV minimum mass becomes a true mass — and now you have both mass and radius, hence a bulk DENSITY that tells you whether the planet is rocky, watery, or a gas giant. This is why the workhorse discovery strategy is "find by transit, confirm and weigh by radial velocity." Astrometry (star's sky-plane wobble) and radial velocity are also complementary: RV is blind to face-on orbits (no line-of-sight motion) while astrometry is blind to edge-on orbits (no sky-plane spread), so together they cover all geometries.

sections.heading: Two histories worth getting right: the pulsar planets and 51 Pegasi b
sections.body: A judge-ready detail: the FIRST confirmed exoplanets were not found by any of the "starlight" methods. In 1992 Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail detected planets around the millisecond pulsar PSR B1257+12 by PULSAR TIMING — the planets' gravity perturbed the exquisitely regular arrival times of the pulsar's radio pulses. The first planet around a normal, Sun-like star came three years later: in 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced 51 Pegasi b, a Jupiter-mass world on a scorching 4.23-day orbit, detected by radial velocity — a result so paradigm-shifting (a giant planet where none was expected) that it won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. A sixth channel, TRANSIT TIMING VARIATIONS (TTV), deserves mention: in a multi-planet system, planets tug on each other, so transits arrive slightly early or late, and the pattern of those deviations reveals the masses of the perturbing planets — this is how many Kepler systems were weighed without any radial-velocity data at all.

lessons.workedExample: A team finds a periodic 0.5-percent transit dip on a Sun-like star (R★ = 1 R☉) and then measures a radial-velocity semi-amplitude for the same star. From the transit alone they get only a radius: depth = (Rₚ/R★)² = 0.005, so Rₚ/R★ = √0.005 ≈ 0.071, i.e. Rₚ ≈ 0.071 R☉ ≈ 0.69 R_Jupiter — but they have NO mass yet. The radial-velocity curve gives a minimum mass m·sin(i); crucially, because the planet TRANSITS, the orbit is nearly edge-on, so i ≈ 90° and sin(i) ≈ 1, meaning the RV minimum mass IS essentially the true mass. Now, with both a radius (from transit) and a true mass (from RV, unlocked by the transit geometry), they compute a bulk density and can argue whether the planet is a puffy sub-Saturn or a dense rocky world. The lesson: neither channel alone answers "what is this planet?"; the combination does.
lessons.judgeFraming: A frequent judge question is "what does your method actually measure?" Students who confuse a transit's radius with a mass, or claim radial velocity gives a true mass without a transit to fix the inclination, reveal a shallow grasp. Naming each channel's literal observable — Doppler shift → line-of-sight velocity → m·sin(i); flux dip → radius ratio; astrometric wobble → true mass — and explaining why transit + RV together yield a density is exactly the fluency that distinguishes a rigorous project from a repeated headline.

questions.prompt: Match each detection channel to the primary physical quantity it directly measures.

right.text: Star's line-of-sight velocity → minimum mass m·sin(i)
Fractional flux drop → planet radius ratio (Rₚ/R★)²
Gravitational magnification → planet-to-star mass ratio
Star's 2-D sky-plane wobble → true mass

questions.explanation: Radial velocity reads the star's Doppler-shifted line-of-sight velocity (giving m·sin i); a transit reads the flux drop (giving the radius ratio); microlensing reads a transient magnification (giving a mass ratio); astrometry reads the star's full two-dimensional wobble (giving a true mass because it captures the whole orbit).

questions.prompt: Why does a transit detection let radial velocity yield a TRUE mass rather than only a minimum mass?

options.text: The transit measures the mass directly and RV is not needed
A transit requires a nearly edge-on orbit, so i ≈ 90° and sin(i) ≈ 1, turning the RV minimum mass m·sin(i) into essentially the true mass
Transits slow the planet down so its mass can be weighed
The transit depth equals the planet mass

explanations.a: A transit gives a radius, not a mass; you still need RV to weigh the planet. The transit's role is to fix the inclination.
explanations.b: Correct — to transit, the orbit must be seen nearly edge-on (i near 90°), so sin(i) ≈ 1 and the RV's m·sin(i) collapses to the true mass m.
explanations.c: Transits do not change the planet's motion; they are just a geometric alignment that lets us see the dip.
explanations.d: Transit depth encodes radius, (Rₚ/R★)², not mass.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the history of exoplanet detection is accurate?

options.text: The first confirmed exoplanets were found around the pulsar PSR B1257+12 by Wolszczan & Frail in 1992, via pulsar timing
51 Pegasi b was the first exoplanet ever confirmed, in 1992
The first exoplanets were directly imaged in the 1980s
Mayor & Queloz discovered 51 Pegasi b using the transit method

explanations.a: Correct — Wolszczan and Frail confirmed planets around the millisecond pulsar PSR B1257+12 in 1992 using pulsar timing, the first confirmed exoplanets.
explanations.b: 51 Pegasi b (Mayor & Queloz) was 1995 and orbits a Sun-like star; it was the first around a NORMAL star, but the pulsar planets came first, in 1992.
explanations.c: The first direct images of exoplanets (e.g. HR 8799) came in 2008, not the 1980s.
explanations.d: Mayor & Queloz found 51 Pegasi b by RADIAL VELOCITY, not transits — work that won the 2019 Nobel Prize.

questions.prompt: A single transit light curve, with no other data, tells you the planet's ___.

options.text: Mass and density
Radius ratio, orbital period, and orbital inclination — but not its mass
True mass directly
Atmospheric composition only

explanations.a: A transit gives no mass on its own, so density (mass/volume) is out of reach without RV or TTV follow-up.
explanations.b: Correct — the depth gives (Rₚ/R★)², the repetition gives the period, and the ingress/egress shape gives the inclination; mass needs a separate channel.
explanations.c: True mass comes from radial velocity (with the transit fixing sin i), astrometry, or TTVs — not from photometry alone.
explanations.d: Transmission spectroscopy during transit can probe an atmosphere, but a plain broadband light curve gives geometry, not composition.

lessons.label: Geometric Transit Probability: Why We See So Few and Which Planets We Miss

sections.heading: The alignment lottery: probability ≈ R★ / a
sections.body: A transit only happens if the planet's orbit is tilted so that, from OUR particular line of sight, the planet passes across the stellar disk. For a randomly oriented circular orbit, the geometric probability of that alignment is beautifully simple: P_transit ≈ R★ / a (more precisely (R★ + Rₚ)/a, but the planet's radius is usually negligible). The intuition: the planet transits only when the observer lies within a thin band of viewing angles set by the star's angular size as seen from the orbit. Plug in numbers and the consequences are stark. The Sun's radius is 0.00465 AU, so an Earth analog at a = 1 AU has P ≈ 0.00465/1 ≈ 0.0047 — under HALF A PERCENT. A hot Jupiter at a = 0.05 AU has P ≈ 0.00465/0.05 ≈ 0.093 — about 9 percent. Close-in planets are roughly twenty times more likely to transit than an Earth-like planet, purely because of geometry.

sections.heading: The selection effect this bakes in — and how to correct it
sections.body: Because P_transit scales as 1/a, transit surveys are massively BIASED toward short-period, close-in planets — they are the low-hanging fruit, both because they transit more often geometrically and because they transit more often in time (a 3-day planet gives you 100+ transits per year to stack, an Earth analog gives you one). This is a textbook SELECTION EFFECT: the raw catalog is not a fair sample of what exists. To turn a pile of detections into a true OCCURRENCE RATE — how many planets of a given size and period the average star hosts — astronomers must DEBIAS: for every detected planet, divide by its transit probability (and by the survey's completeness) to estimate how many similar planets went unseen because they simply were not aligned. An Earth analog you did detect statistically stands in for ~200 identical planets whose orbits happened to be tilted out of the transit geometry. Skipping this correction makes hot Jupiters look far more common than they are — they are actually rare (~1 percent of stars), just easy to catch.

sections.heading: Eccentricity, grazing transits, and the planets we systematically miss
sections.body: Two refinements matter. First, ECCENTRICITY changes the odds: a planet on an eccentric orbit spends variable distance from the star, and averaging over orbital phase gives P_transit ≈ (R★/a) × 1/(1 − e²), so eccentric orbits are somewhat MORE likely to transit than circular ones of the same semi-major axis. Second, even among transiting systems, GRAZING transits (where the planet clips only the stellar limb) are shallow, V-shaped, and easy to miss or mistake for noise. The planets we systematically miss are therefore the long-period ones (tiny R★/a, and few transits to catch in a finite survey) and any world whose orbital plane is simply tilted away from us — which is most of them. This is why "we detected N transiting planets" is never the same statement as "N planets exist here"; the geometry guarantees the transiting sample is a small, biased slice of the true population.

lessons.workedExample: A survey monitors Sun-like stars (R★ = 1 R☉ = 0.00465 AU) and wants to compare its sensitivity to hot Jupiters versus Earth analogs. Hot Jupiter at a = 0.05 AU: P_transit ≈ 0.00465/0.05 = 0.093, about 9 percent — roughly 1 in 11 such systems transits. Earth analog at a = 1 AU: P_transit ≈ 0.00465/1 = 0.0047, about 0.47 percent — only ~1 in 213 transits. So the survey is ~20× more likely to catch the hot Jupiter by geometry ALONE, before even counting that the hot Jupiter also delivers dozens more transits per year to stack. If the team detects, say, 5 transiting Earth analogs, debiasing implies the true number of Earth analogs among the monitored stars is roughly 5 / 0.0047 ≈ 1,060 — the vast majority tilted out of view. Reporting the raw 5 as the occurrence would understate reality by more than two hundredfold.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love to ask "if you only found a handful, how can you claim planets are common?" — because it tests whether a student understands SELECTION EFFECTS. The winning answer states the geometric probability P ≈ R★/a, shows why it makes close-in planets vastly over-represented, and explains the debiasing step (divide detections by transit probability and completeness) that converts a biased catalog into a real occurrence rate. That reasoning is the difference between counting dots and doing population statistics.

questions.prompt: For a randomly oriented circular orbit, the geometric probability that a planet transits its star is approximately:

options.text: a / R★
R★ / a
(R★ / a)²
R★ × a

explanations.a: a/R★ is the inverse and would exceed 1 for any real orbit (distances are far larger than stellar radii), which is impossible for a probability.
explanations.b: Correct — P_transit ≈ R★/a; the star's radius over the orbital distance sets the thin band of viewing angles that produce a transit.
explanations.c: (R★/a)² is the transit DEPTH-like scaling for a size ratio, not the alignment probability, which goes as the first power R★/a.
explanations.d: Multiplying gives units of area, not a dimensionless probability; the correct form is the ratio R★/a.

questions.prompt: An Earth analog orbits a Sun-like star (R★ = 0.00465 AU) at a = 1 AU. Its transit probability is closest to:

options.text: About 9 percent
About 0.5 percent
About 50 percent
About 100 percent (it always transits)

explanations.a: ~9 percent is the hot-Jupiter case at a ≈ 0.05 AU; an Earth at 1 AU is 20× less likely.
explanations.b: Correct — P ≈ 0.00465/1 ≈ 0.0047 ≈ 0.5 percent, so only about 1 in 213 such systems transits from a random viewing angle.
explanations.c: 50 percent would require the star to fill half the sky as seen from the orbit — vastly larger than reality.
explanations.d: Most orbits are tilted out of the transit geometry; transits are the rare aligned minority, not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Why do raw transit-survey catalogs make hot Jupiters look more common than they truly are?

options.text: Hot Jupiters are physically the most abundant type of planet
Their small a gives a high transit probability (R★/a) and many transits per year, so they are over-represented — a selection effect that must be debiased
Hot Jupiters emit their own light and are directly imaged
Their orbits are always perfectly edge-on

explanations.a: Hot Jupiters are actually rare (~1 percent of stars); they only APPEAR common because they are easy to catch.
explanations.b: Correct — small orbital distance means a high geometric transit probability and dozens of transits per year to stack, so they dominate raw catalogs until you debias by dividing out transit probability and completeness.
explanations.c: Transit surveys detect them by dimming, not direct imaging; their over-representation is geometric, not from self-luminosity.
explanations.d: Hot Jupiters do not always transit; only the small aligned fraction does — that fraction is just larger than for distant planets.

questions.prompt: How does orbital eccentricity affect transit probability, all else equal?

options.text: It has no effect; only semi-major axis matters
Averaged over orbital phase, eccentricity slightly RAISES the transit probability, by a factor 1/(1 − e²)
It makes transits impossible
It reduces probability to exactly zero for e > 0

explanations.a: Eccentricity does matter; the standard correction multiplies R★/a by 1/(1 − e²).
explanations.b: Correct — P_transit ≈ (R★/a) × 1/(1 − e²), so an eccentric orbit is somewhat more likely to transit than a circular one of the same semi-major axis.
explanations.c: Eccentric orbits still transit — Kepler and TESS found many; eccentricity modifies the odds, it does not forbid transits.
explanations.d: Only a face-on (i ≈ 0) geometry forbids transits; nonzero eccentricity alone does not drive the probability to zero.

lessons.label: The Reflex Wobble: Center-of-Mass Reasoning and the Star's Response to a Planet

sections.heading: Both bodies orbit the barycenter — the star is not fixed
sections.body: The bedrock of radial velocity and astrometry is Newton's third law made orbital: a star does not hold a planet in orbit while sitting still; both bodies orbit their common center of mass, the BARYCENTER. The lever-arm relation is m★ · r★ = mₚ · rₚ, so the star traces a small circle whose radius is smaller than the planet's by the mass ratio. For the Sun–Jupiter system the barycenter actually lies just OUTSIDE the Sun's surface — about 1.07 solar radii from the Sun's center — so the Sun genuinely loops around a point in space, and a distant alien astronomer could in principle detect Jupiter by watching that loop. This tiny, periodic motion is the "reflex wobble," and its two observable projections are the star's back-and-forth line-of-sight speed (radial velocity) and its side-to-side position on the sky (astrometry).

sections.heading: The radial-velocity semi-amplitude and its scaling law
sections.body: What radial velocity measures is the SEMI-AMPLITUDE K — how fast the star swings toward and away from us. For a circular orbit a convenient scaling captures the physics: K ≈ 28.4 m/s × (mₚ sin i / M_Jup) × (M★ / M☉)^(−2/3) × (P / 1 yr)^(−1/3). Read it slowly: heavier planets tug harder (K grows with planet mass); heavier stars are harder to move (K falls with M★); and — less obviously — SHORTER-period planets whip the star faster (K grows as P shrinks). Two anchor cases. Jupiter around the Sun (P = 11.86 yr): K ≈ 28.4 × 1 × 1 × (11.86)^(−1/3) ≈ 28.4/2.28 ≈ 12.5 m/s — the Sun's reflex speed from Jupiter is about 12–13 m/s, a slow walk. Earth around the Sun (P = 1 yr, mₚ ≈ 0.00315 M_Jup): K ≈ 28.4 × 0.00315 ≈ 0.09 m/s — 9 centimeters per second, the speed of a strolling ant, which is why detecting a true Earth twin by radial velocity is at the ragged edge of the possible.

sections.heading: The sin(i) ambiguity and what the wobble cannot tell you alone
sections.body: Radial velocity sees only the LINE-OF-SIGHT component of the reflex motion, so an unknown orbital inclination i sneaks into every mass: the method returns mₚ · sin(i), a MINIMUM mass. A face-on orbit (i = 0) produces no radial-velocity signal at all — the star loops in the plane of the sky and never moves toward or away from us — while an edge-on orbit (i = 90°) gives the full signal and the true mass. Because we usually do not know i, an RV "planet" of minimum mass 0.5 M_Jup could be a 0.5 M_Jup planet seen edge-on or a much heavier object seen nearly face-on. This is exactly why a companion transit (which forces i ≈ 90°), an astrometric orbit (which captures the sky-plane motion and breaks the degeneracy), or dynamical modeling is so valuable — each removes the sin(i) veil and converts a minimum mass into a real one.

lessons.workedExample: Reconstruct the discovery of 51 Pegasi b (Mayor & Queloz, 1995). It has a minimum mass of about 0.47 M_Jup and an orbital period of P = 4.23 days = 0.0116 yr around a roughly Sun-mass star. Predict the radial-velocity semi-amplitude: K ≈ 28.4 m/s × (0.47) × (1)^(−2/3) × (0.0116)^(−1/3). The period term (0.0116)^(−1/3) ≈ 4.42, so K ≈ 28.4 × 0.47 × 4.42 ≈ 59 m/s. That matches the historic measurement (~59 m/s) that Mayor and Queloz reported — a signal large ONLY because the planet's 4.23-day orbit is so short that it whips the star quickly. Contrast with Jupiter's 12.5 m/s despite Jupiter being twice as massive: the 51 Peg b signal wins on the P^(−1/3) term. And because a later transit was found (fixing i ≈ 90°), the minimum mass is essentially the true mass. The worked chain — barycenter → K scaling → sin(i) caveat resolved by transit — is the entire logic of the field in one system.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "why does the star move at all?" and "what is a minimum mass?" to see whether a student truly owns center-of-mass reasoning or just parrots "Doppler wobble." A strong answer invokes m★r★ = mₚrₚ (the barycenter), predicts K with the 28.4 m/s scaling and its counterintuitive P^(−1/3) dependence, and explains the sin(i) ambiguity — that RV gives only mₚ sin i until a transit or astrometry fixes the inclination. Getting the 51 Peg b number (~59 m/s) right shows the physics is real, not memorized.

questions.prompt: The barycenter relation m★·r★ = mₚ·rₚ implies that as seen by radial velocity, the star:

options.text: Stays perfectly fixed while the planet orbits it
Traces its own small orbit around the common center of mass, moving less than the planet by the mass ratio
Orbits the planet
Moves only if the planet is more massive than the star

explanations.a: The star is not fixed; Newton's third law makes it orbit the shared barycenter — that reflex motion is the whole signal.
explanations.b: Correct — both bodies orbit the barycenter, and the star's orbit is smaller than the planet's by the factor mₚ/m★.
explanations.c: Both orbit their common center of mass; the star does not orbit the planet — the barycenter sits between them (very close to the star).
explanations.d: The star wobbles for ANY planet mass, just by a tiny amount; the effect does not require the planet to outweigh the star.

questions.prompt: Using K ≈ 28.4 m/s × (mₚ sin i / M_Jup) × (M★/M☉)^(−2/3) × (P/yr)^(−1/3), roughly what reflex speed does Jupiter (P = 11.86 yr) induce on the Sun?

options.text: About 0.09 m/s
About 12.5 m/s
About 59 m/s
About 500 m/s

explanations.a: 0.09 m/s (9 cm/s) is the EARTH-induced value; Jupiter, being ~318× heavier, moves the Sun far more.
explanations.c: ~59 m/s is the 51 Pegasi b value, driven up by its very short 4.23-day period; Jupiter's long period gives a much smaller K.
explanations.d: 500 m/s is far too large for a planet; that regime belongs to stellar or brown-dwarf companions.

questions.prompt: Radial velocity yields only mₚ·sin(i), a MINIMUM mass, because:

options.text: The Doppler effect is inherently inaccurate
RV measures only the line-of-sight component of the star's motion, so an unknown inclination i enters as sin(i); a face-on orbit gives no signal at all
Planets have no well-defined mass
The star's mass is unknown

explanations.a: The ambiguity is geometric, not a precision flaw — even a perfect spectrograph returns only mₚ sin i.
explanations.b: Correct — only the line-of-sight velocity is measured, so the unknown inclination appears as sin(i); an i = 0 (face-on) orbit produces zero radial-velocity signal.
explanations.c: Planets have definite masses; the method just cannot isolate the mass from the inclination without more information.
explanations.d: The host star's mass is estimated separately (from its spectrum/models); the sin(i) issue is about the ORBIT's tilt, not the star's mass.

questions.prompt: Order these systems by the star's radial-velocity semi-amplitude K, from SMALLEST to LARGEST.

items.text: Earth around the Sun (P = 1 yr) → K ≈ 0.09 m/s
Jupiter around the Sun (P = 11.86 yr) → K ≈ 12.5 m/s
51 Pegasi b (0.47 M_Jup, P = 4.23 d) → K ≈ 59 m/s

questions.explanation: Earth's reflex is tiny (~9 cm/s). Jupiter, far heavier, gives ~12.5 m/s despite its long period. 51 Pegasi b, though lighter than Jupiter, is on a 4.23-day orbit whose short period (via the P^(−1/3) term) pushes K up to ~59 m/s — the largest of the three.

lessons.label: Signal Versus Noise: Photon Statistics, Stellar Variability, and the Detection Floor

sections.heading: The photon floor: you cannot beat √N
sections.body: Every exoplanet signal is a faint change measured against a noisy background, so the discipline is really about signal-to-noise. The most fundamental noise is PHOTON (Poisson) noise: light arrives in discrete quanta, and if you collect N photons the intrinsic statistical fluctuation is √N. The fractional noise is therefore √N/N = 1/√N — so to measure a change of, say, 100 parts per million (10⁻⁴) at all, you need the fractional noise below that, i.e. 1/√N < 10⁻⁴, which means N > 10⁸ photons. This is why an Earth transit, at a depth of only (1/109)² ≈ 84 parts per million, is so demanding: to detect an 84-ppm dip at the usual 5σ threshold you must beat down the noise to ~17 ppm, requiring on the order of a few ×10⁹ photons collected across the relevant transits. Photon noise is the irreducible floor set by physics; no clever processing gets below it for a given photon count.

sections.heading: The star fights back: stellar variability and jitter
sections.body: Nature adds a second, nastier noise source: the STAR ITSELF is not a steady lamp. Its surface roils with GRANULATION (convective cells rising and sinking), it oscillates (helioseismic p-modes), it is peppered with dark STARSPOTS and bright faculae that rotate in and out of view, and it occasionally FLARES. In photometry, spots crossing the disk create brightness wiggles that can mimic or bury a shallow transit; the Sun's own photometric variability is tens of parts per million on transit-relevant timescales, comparable to an Earth transit's depth. In radial velocity, the same activity produces "stellar jitter": convective blueshift suppression in spots and granulation shifts the spectral lines by ~1 m/s or more, an astrophysical noise floor that does NOT average away like photon noise because it is correlated with the star's rotation and activity cycle. This is the crux of the Earth-detection problem: Earth's 9 cm/s reflex is buried a factor of ~10 below the meter-per-second jitter of even a quiet Sun-like star.

sections.heading: White noise averages down; red noise does not — and that sets the real floor
sections.body: The reason variability is so pernicious is the difference between WHITE and RED (correlated) noise. White noise — like photon noise — is independent point to point, so averaging M measurements beats it down as 1/√M; collect more data and it fades. RED noise is correlated across time (granulation persists for minutes, spots for days, activity cycles for years), so it does NOT shrink as 1/√M — averaging is far less effective, and beyond some point piling on more observations barely helps. The practical DETECTION FLOOR of an instrument is therefore set not by its raw precision but by this correlated astrophysical noise. Modern spectrographs illustrate the point: HARPS reached ~1 m/s and ESPRESSO pushes to ~10 cm/s in raw precision — enough, on paper, to see Earth's 9 cm/s — yet stellar jitter of order 1 m/s remains the true barrier, which is why the frontier is now as much about MODELING and removing stellar activity as about building quieter instruments.

lessons.workedExample: A team asks whether their photometry can detect an Earth-sized transit (depth ≈ 84 ppm = 8.4×10⁻⁵) around a Sun-like star at 5σ. Start with photon noise. To reach a per-point fractional precision fine enough that the combined transit signal clears 5σ, they need the effective noise on the transit measurement below depth/5 ≈ 17 ppm = 1.7×10⁻⁵. Since fractional photon noise is 1/√N, that requires 1/√N ≈ 1.7×10⁻⁵, i.e. N ≈ (1/1.7×10⁻⁵)² ≈ 3.5×10⁹ photons collected over the observed transits. That is achievable from space with a big enough aperture and many stacked transits (Kepler did exactly this). BUT the team then checks the STELLAR floor: their target is spotted, with photometric variability ~50 ppm on transit timescales — larger than the 84-ppm signal itself and, being red noise tied to rotation, not something more integration time averages away. Their honest conclusion: the transit is detectable in principle against PHOTON noise, but the star's intrinsic variability, not the telescope, is the limiting factor — so they must either pick a quieter star or model the spot signal explicitly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "what actually limits your sensitivity?" to separate students who think the answer is "a bigger telescope" from those who understand noise. The rigorous reply distinguishes PHOTON noise (irreducible, but beatable as √N by collecting more light) from STELLAR variability / red noise (correlated, does NOT average down, and sets the true detection floor). Citing that Earth's 9 cm/s reflex sits below the ~1 m/s stellar jitter — so the frontier is activity modeling, not just instrument precision — signals genuine command of the measurement.

questions.prompt: If you collect N photons, the fractional photon (Poisson) noise scales as:

options.text: √N
N

explanations.a: 1/N falls too fast; the standard deviation of N counts is √N, so the FRACTIONAL noise is √N/N = 1/√N, not 1/N.
explanations.b: Correct — Poisson noise on N counts is √N, so fractional noise is √N/N = 1/√N; quadrupling photons halves the fractional noise.
explanations.c: √N is the absolute noise, not the fractional noise; dividing by the signal N gives 1/√N.
explanations.d: Noise does not grow in proportion to N; the fractional noise DECREASES as more photons are collected.

questions.prompt: Why is a true Earth twin so hard to detect by radial velocity even with a 10 cm/s-precision spectrograph like ESPRESSO?

options.text: Earth induces a huge reflex velocity that saturates the detector
Earth's ~9 cm/s reflex sits below the ~1 m/s stellar jitter (granulation, spots, activity), a correlated astrophysical noise that does not average away like photon noise
Earth has no gravitational effect on the Sun
Spectrographs cannot measure Doppler shifts smaller than 100 m/s

explanations.a: Earth's reflex is tiny (~9 cm/s), the opposite of saturating; the challenge is that it is too small, not too large.
explanations.b: Correct — the instrument may reach 10 cm/s, but stellar activity produces ~1 m/s of correlated jitter that buries Earth's 9 cm/s and, being red noise, does not shrink with more data.
explanations.c: Earth does tug the Sun (~9 cm/s reflex); the signal exists but is buried in stellar noise.
explanations.d: Modern spectrographs measure sub-m/s shifts; the 100 m/s figure is far coarser than reality.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between white noise and red (correlated) noise for a detection?

options.text: White noise cannot be reduced, but red noise averages away quickly
White noise averages down as 1/√M with more measurements, while red noise is correlated in time and does NOT shrink that way, setting the real detection floor
They are the same thing under different names
Red noise only affects imaging, never spectroscopy

explanations.a: It is the reverse: white noise (independent) averages down, while red (correlated) noise is the stubborn one.
explanations.b: Correct — independent white noise falls as 1/√M with M measurements, but time-correlated red noise (granulation, spots, activity) resists averaging and becomes the limiting floor.
explanations.c: They differ fundamentally in their time correlation, which is exactly why one averages down and the other does not.
explanations.d: Red noise appears in both photometry (spot-crossing wiggles) and spectroscopy (activity-driven RV jitter); it is not imaging-only.

questions.prompt: An Earth-sized transit around a Sun-like star has a depth of about:

options.text: About 1 percent (10,000 ppm)
About 84 parts per million
About 50 percent
About 1 part per trillion

explanations.a: ~1 percent is a hot-JUPITER depth; a Jupiter is ~10× Earth's radius, so its depth is ~100× larger than Earth's.
explanations.b: Correct — depth = (R⊕/R☉)² ≈ (1/109)² ≈ 8.4×10⁻⁵ ≈ 84 ppm, which is why space missions are needed to catch it.
explanations.c: 50 percent would require the planet to be comparable in size to the star — impossible for a planet.
explanations.d: 1 part per trillion is far too small; the Earth-transit depth is ~84 ppm, about ten million times larger.

lessons.label: Candidate, Validated, or Confirmed: The Language and Burden of an Exoplanet Claim

sections.heading: Three words that are not synonyms: candidate, validated, confirmed
sections.body: Precise language is not pedantry in this field — the words CANDIDATE, VALIDATED, and CONFIRMED denote genuinely different levels of evidence, and a judge will notice if you use them loosely. A CANDIDATE is a signal that passed initial vetting but could still be a false positive — Kepler labeled these KOIs (Kepler Objects of Interest) and TESS labels them TOIs (TESS Objects of Interest). A CONFIRMED planet has an independent line of evidence, most commonly a dynamical MASS measurement — a radial-velocity detection of the same body, or transit-timing variations — that establishes it is planetary and not an impostor. A VALIDATED planet sits between: no mass has been measured, but a statistical argument shows the FALSE-POSITIVE PROBABILITY is very low (typically below ~1 percent), so the signal is almost certainly a real planet even though it has not been dynamically confirmed. These are rungs on a ladder of certainty, not interchangeable synonyms.

sections.heading: Why the ladder exists: false positives are the rule, not the exception
sections.body: The ladder exists because a periodic dip is far more often NOT a planet. The dominant impostors are ECLIPSING BINARIES — two stars orbiting and mutually eclipsing, which produce deep, periodic dips — and, more insidiously, BACKGROUND (blended) eclipsing binaries, where a faint eclipsing pair sits in the same photometric aperture as your bright target star and dilutes down to a shallow, planet-looking dip. Grazing binaries and instrumental artifacts add more. Statistical VALIDATION works by computing, for a given candidate, the probability of each astrophysical false-positive scenario against the probability it is a genuine planet, folding in the transit shape, the stellar field density, follow-up imaging, and priors — the tool BLENDER and Timothy Morton's VESPA (vespa, Morton 2015) formalized this. Its power is scale: Morton and colleagues (2016) statistically VALIDATED 1,284 Kepler planets in a single paper, because obtaining radial-velocity masses one by one for thousands of faint Kepler stars was simply infeasible.

sections.heading: The burden of proof: extraordinary claims and the honest label
sections.body: The governing ethic is the burden of proof: the claimant, not the skeptic, must rule out the mundane explanations, and the strength of the claim must match the strength of the evidence. A student who folds one TESS light curve, sees a dip, and announces "I discovered a planet" has skipped the entire ladder — the honest statement is "a transit-like CANDIDATE, pending vetting." As evidence accumulates — odd/even depth consistency, no secondary eclipse, centroid stability, a low false-positive probability from validation, and ultimately an independent mass — the claim can be upgraded rung by rung to "validated" and then "confirmed." Judges reward this calibrated language precisely because it demonstrates the scientific temperament: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and the discipline of naming your rung on the certainty ladder is what separates a defensible project from a wishful headline.

lessons.workedExample: A team finds a clean, repeating 200-ppm dip in a TESS light curve. Walk the ladder honestly. Step 1 — CANDIDATE: it is a TOI, a transit-like signal, nothing more; they must not call it a planet yet. Step 2 — rule out impostors: odd and even transits match in depth (arguing against an eclipsing binary of two unequal stars), there is no secondary eclipse half a period later (arguing against a self-luminous companion), and the flux centroid does not shift during the dip (arguing against a blended background binary in the aperture). Step 3 — VALIDATE: running a tool like VESPA, they fold in the U-shaped transit, the local stellar density, and archival high-resolution imaging to compute a false-positive probability of 0.3 percent — below the ~1 percent threshold — so the object is now statistically VALIDATED, even with no mass. Step 4 — CONFIRM: months later, a radial-velocity campaign detects a matching 6 m/s reflex signal at the same period, delivering a true mass and CONFIRMING the planet. The team's report tracks its language to its evidence at every step — the exact discipline the ladder demands.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges deliberately test whether a student overclaims: "you found a dip — is that a planet?" The credibility-winning answer places the result on the correct rung — candidate, validated, or confirmed — and explains what evidence each rung requires (initial vetting; a sub-1-percent false-positive probability from statistical validation; an independent mass for confirmation). Knowing that most periodic dips are eclipsing-binary or blended false positives, and that Morton et al. (2016) validated 1,284 Kepler planets statistically, shows a student who understands the BURDEN of proof, not just the vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Match each status term to the evidence standard it requires.

right.text: A signal that passed initial vetting but could still be a false positive (e.g. a KOI/TOI)
No mass measured, but a statistical false-positive probability shown to be very low (~<1%)
An independent dynamical mass (radial velocity or TTVs) establishing it is planetary

questions.explanation: A candidate is a vetted-but-uncertain signal (KOI/TOI); a validated planet has a demonstrated low false-positive probability but no mass; a confirmed planet has an independent dynamical mass measurement establishing its planetary nature.

questions.prompt: Statistical VALIDATION (e.g. with VESPA) establishes a planet by:

options.text: Directly imaging the planet
Computing that the false-positive probability of the signal is very low (typically <1%), without necessarily measuring a mass
Measuring the planet's radial-velocity mass
Waiting for the planet to be seen with the naked eye

explanations.a: Validation is a statistical argument, not an image; it works for faint Kepler stars that can never be directly imaged.
explanations.b: Correct — validation compares the probability of astrophysical false positives against a genuine planet and declares the planet real when the false-positive probability is very low (~<1%), no mass required.
explanations.c: Measuring an RV mass is CONFIRMATION, a stronger and different standard than statistical validation.
explanations.d: Exoplanets are never resolved by naked eye; validation is a quantitative false-positive calculation.

questions.prompt: What is the most common astrophysical false positive that mimics a transiting planet?

options.text: A passing comet
An eclipsing binary (including a blended/background eclipsing binary in the same aperture)
A solar flare on our own Sun
Cosmic microwave background fluctuations

explanations.a: A comet would not produce a strictly periodic, repeating, planet-shaped dip tied to an orbital period.
explanations.b: Correct — eclipsing binaries (two stars mutually eclipsing), and especially blended background eclipsing binaries diluted into a shallow dip, are the dominant transit false positives.
explanations.c: A flare on our Sun is an additive brightening in our own sky, not a periodic dip on a distant target star.
explanations.d: The CMB is a smooth cosmological background, utterly unrelated to a periodic stellar light-curve dip.

questions.prompt: Order the rungs of an exoplanet claim from WEAKEST to STRONGEST evidence.

items.text: Candidate (TOI/KOI): a vetted signal that could still be a false positive
Validated: false-positive probability shown to be <1%, but no mass
Confirmed: an independent dynamical mass (RV or TTV) measured

questions.explanation: A candidate is the weakest rung (an unconfirmed signal); validation adds a low false-positive probability but no mass; confirmation, with an independent dynamical mass, is the strongest standard.

units.label: The Transit Method in Depth: Anatomy of a Light Curve

lessons.label: Reading a Transit: Depth, the Four Contacts, and Total vs. Flat Duration (T14 and T23)

sections.heading: Depth is the easy part — and it is just an area ratio
sections.body: When a planet crosses in front of its star, it blocks a fraction of the starlight equal to the ratio of the two disks’ areas. Because area scales as radius squared, the fractional dip in brightness — the transit depth δ — is (Rp/Rs)², the planet’s radius over the star’s radius, squared. A Jupiter (radius ≈10% of the Sun’s) blocks about (0.1)² = 0.01, a 1% dip; an Earth across the Sun blocks only (6371 km / 696,000 km)² ≈ 84 parts per million, which is why space photometry (Kepler, TESS) rather than ground telescopes was needed to find small planets. The very first transiting exoplanet, HD 209458 b, was caught this way in 1999 by two independent teams — David Charbonneau, Timothy Brown, and colleagues (STARE), and the Gregory Henry team (Henry, Marcy, Butler & Vogt 2000) — after Michel Mayor’s Geneva group had announced the radial-velocity discovery of the planet, showing a clean ≈1.5% dip that pinned the planet’s radius once the star’s radius was known. Crucially, depth gives you a RADIUS, not a mass; a transit alone cannot tell a puffy Jupiter from a dense one.

sections.heading: The four contacts: where ingress and egress begin and end
sections.body: A real transit is not an instantaneous on/off — the planet’s disk takes time to slide onto and off of the stellar disk, and astronomers mark four contact points to describe this geometry. FIRST CONTACT is the instant the planet’s leading edge first touches the stellar limb from outside (ingress begins). SECOND CONTACT is when the planet’s trailing edge finally crosses the limb, so the whole planet is now silhouetted on the disk (ingress ends). THIRD CONTACT is when the leading edge reaches the far limb and starts to exit (egress begins). FOURTH CONTACT is when the trailing edge clears the disk entirely (egress ends). Between first and fourth contact the star is dimmed; between second and third the planet is fully on the disk and the dip is at (or near) its deepest. This vocabulary is borrowed directly from the classical description of Venus and Mercury transits across the Sun, observed since the 1600s.

sections.heading: Two durations carry two different pieces of information
sections.body: From the four contacts come two measurable durations. T14 (first-to-fourth contact) is the TOTAL transit duration — the full width of the dip. T23 (second-to-third contact) is the FLAT or FULL duration — the interval the planet is entirely on the disk. The difference, roughly (T14 − T23)/2, is the ingress/egress time, set by how long the planet’s own diameter takes to cross the limb. In the idealized “boxcar” picture (no limb darkening, planet crossing the star’s center), the light curve is a trapezoid: a sloped ingress from first to second contact, a flat bottom from second to third, and a sloped egress from third to fourth. The ratio T23/T14 is not a throwaway detail — it encodes how centrally the planet crosses the star (the impact parameter, Lesson 2). A transit with almost no flat bottom (T23 → 0, a V-shape) is a warning sign explored later in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: Take HD 209458 b: an inflated hot Jupiter of radius ≈1.38 R_Jupiter (≈98,700 km) transiting a star of radius ≈1.16 R_Sun (≈807,000 km). The depth is (98,700/807,000)² = (0.122)² ≈ 0.0149, i.e. a 1.5% dip — consistent with the ~1.5–1.7% dip seen in the discovery light curves. Now compare an Earth-radius planet across the same star: (6371/807,000)² ≈ 6.2×10⁻⁵, about 62 ppm — 240 times shallower and utterly invisible from the ground, but detectable by Kepler, whose photometric precision reached tens of ppm on bright stars. The lesson: a student reading a light curve reports a radius ratio from the depth, then multiplies by the (independently known) stellar radius — never claims a mass from the dip alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student knows what a transit actually measures. The classic trap is claiming to have “measured the planet’s mass” from a light curve — you have not; depth gives (Rp/Rs)², a radius ratio, and mass needs radial velocities or transit-timing. A student who states “the 1% dip means the planet’s radius is about 10% of the star’s, and I got the absolute radius by scaling to the known stellar radius” demonstrates they understand the observable, its limits, and the four-contact geometry behind the trapezoid they plotted.

questions.prompt: A planet produces a transit depth of 0.0049 (0.49%). What is the planet-to-star radius ratio Rp/Rs?

options.text: About 0.0049
About 0.07
About 0.49
It cannot be determined from depth alone

explanations.a: That is the depth itself (the area ratio), not the radius ratio — you must take the square root.
explanations.b: Correct — depth = (Rp/Rs)², so Rp/Rs = √0.0049 = 0.07; the planet’s radius is about 7% of the star’s.
explanations.c: 0.49 would be the radius ratio if depth equaled Rp/Rs directly, but depth is the SQUARE of the radius ratio.
explanations.d: The radius ratio is exactly what depth gives you; it is the absolute radius (needing the stellar radius) and the mass (needing RV) that depth alone cannot supply.

questions.prompt: Order the four contact points as they occur in time during a transit.

items.text: Leading edge first touches the stellar limb (ingress begins)
Trailing edge crosses onto the disk; planet fully silhouetted (ingress ends)
Leading edge reaches the far limb (egress begins)
Trailing edge clears the disk entirely (egress ends)

questions.explanation: First contact (ingress begins) → second contact (planet fully on the disk, ingress ends) → third contact (egress begins) → fourth contact (planet fully off the disk, egress ends). T14 spans first-to-fourth, T23 spans second-to-third.

questions.prompt: Match each transit quantity to what it is/measures.

right.text: (Rp/Rs)² — the planet-to-star area (radius-squared) ratio
Total duration: first-to-fourth contact
Flat/full duration: second-to-third contact (planet fully on disk)
The ingress/egress time — roughly how long the planet’s diameter takes to cross the limb

questions.explanation: Depth is the area ratio (Rp/Rs)²; T14 is the total first-to-fourth-contact width; T23 is the flat second-to-third-contact interval; and half the difference between them is the ingress/egress time set by the planet’s own diameter crossing the limb.

questions.prompt: Why did detecting Earth-sized transits require space telescopes like Kepler rather than ground-based photometry?

options.text: Earth-sized planets orbit too far from their stars to ever transit
An Earth across a Sun-like star dims it by only ~80 ppm, below the precision achievable through Earth’s turbulent atmosphere
Ground telescopes cannot see the infrared light transits emit
Earth-sized planets produce no measurable depth at all

explanations.a: Transit geometry depends on orbital inclination, not planet size; small planets transit just as readily as large ones when aligned.
explanations.b: Correct — an Earth‑radius planet gives a dip of order (R_Earth/R_Sun)² ≈ 84 ppm, and atmospheric scintillation limits ground photometry to roughly a part in a thousand, so the tiny signal is buried without going to space.
explanations.c: A transit is a broadband dimming, not infrared emission; the issue is the signal’s tiny amplitude, not its wavelength.
explanations.d: It does produce a depth (~84 ppm) — small but real; the problem is measuring it, not that it is zero.

lessons.label: Impact Parameter and Inclination: How Orbit Tilt Reshapes Ingress and Egress

sections.heading: The impact parameter: how far off-center the planet crosses
sections.body: No planet is guaranteed to cross the exact middle of the stellar disk. The IMPACT PARAMETER b measures how far from the star’s center the planet’s path passes, in units of the stellar radius: b = 0 is a dead-center transit across the full diameter, while b ≈ 1 is a grazing pass that just clips the limb. For a circular orbit, b is fixed by the orbital geometry: b = (a/Rs)·cos i, where a is the orbital semi-major axis and i the inclination (i = 90° is a perfectly edge-on orbit). Because a/Rs is often large (tens), even a couple of degrees away from 90° pushes b close to 1 or out of transit entirely — which is why transiting planets are geometrically rare and why the geometric transit probability for a circular orbit is just Rs/a.

sections.heading: Impact parameter reshapes the light curve: T23/T14 tells you b
sections.body: A central transit (b = 0) has the longest possible flat bottom relative to its total width — the planet spends most of the event fully on the disk, so T23 is nearly as long as T14 and the trapezoid has a broad flat floor. As b increases, the chord across the star gets shorter, the planet spends more of its time straddling the limb, and the flat portion T23 shrinks. In the grazing limit (b → 1 + something, where the planet never fully covers), the flat bottom disappears entirely and the light curve becomes a V — pure ingress running straight into egress with no flat middle. So the ratio T23/T14 is a direct handle on the impact parameter, and by extension on the inclination once a/Rs is known. This is why a well-sampled ingress/egress shape is worth as much as the depth: it breaks geometric degeneracies.

sections.heading: Why the depth–b degeneracy matters for radius measurements
sections.body: Here is a subtlety that trips up careless analyses: the OBSERVED depth of a limb-darkened transit depends slightly on where the planet crosses, because a planet transiting near the limb blocks fainter (limb-darkened) parts of the star than one crossing the bright center. Ignoring this, a high-b transit can look shallower and yield an underestimated Rp/Rs if you fit it with a central-transit model. More importantly, b, a/Rs, and Rp/Rs are partially degenerate in a light-curve fit — a slightly larger planet at higher impact parameter can mimic a smaller planet crossing centrally. Breaking this needs good ingress/egress sampling (to nail b) and, ideally, an independent constraint on the stellar density (Lesson 4). This is exactly why modern pipelines fit the full transit shape, not just the depth and width.

lessons.workedExample: For HD 209458 b, the scaled semi-major axis is a/Rs ≈ 8.76 and the measured inclination is i ≈ 86.7°. The impact parameter is then b = (a/Rs)·cos i = 8.76 × cos(86.7°) = 8.76 × 0.0576 ≈ 0.50 — the planet crosses about halfway between the star’s center and its limb. That intermediate b still leaves a clear flat bottom (T23 well short of, but not near, zero), consistent with the trapezoidal light curve observed. Contrast a hypothetical b = 0.98 case: cos i would be 0.98/8.76 = 0.112, so i ≈ 83.6° — just 3° more tilt — and the transit would go V-shaped and grazing, with the depth no longer a clean (Rp/Rs)² read. A 3° change in inclination is the difference between a textbook transit and a false-positive-prone grazing event.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows transits will ask, “how do you know the planet crossed the middle of the star?” — because if it grazed, your depth-to-radius conversion is compromised. The strong answer cites the impact parameter and how the flat-bottom-to-total-width ratio (T23/T14) constrains it: “my transit has a well-defined flat bottom, so b is moderate, and I fit b jointly with the radius rather than assuming a central crossing.” That shows you understand geometry, not just that you plotted a dip.

questions.prompt: For a circular orbit, the impact parameter is b = (a/Rs)·cos i. A planet has a/Rs = 10 and inclination i = 88°. What is b, approximately?

options.text: About 0.35
About 0.09
About 1.7
About 10

explanations.a: Correct — cos 88° ≈ 0.0349, so b = 10 × 0.0349 ≈ 0.35, a moderately off-center transit with a clear flat bottom.
explanations.b: 0.09 would come from using cos 89.5° or a much smaller a/Rs; with i = 88° and a/Rs = 10 the product is ~0.35.
explanations.c: 1.7 exceeds 1, which would mean NO transit (the planet misses the disk); the arithmetic gives 0.35.
explanations.d: 10 is a/Rs itself, which would require cos i = 1 (i = 0°, a face-on orbit that never transits).

questions.prompt: As the impact parameter b increases toward a grazing value, how does the light-curve shape change?

options.text: The flat bottom (T23) lengthens until the transit is nearly all flat
The flat bottom shrinks toward zero and the transit becomes V-shaped
The depth increases without bound
The transit duration T14 stays exactly the same but gets deeper

explanations.a: The opposite — a longer flat bottom corresponds to a MORE central transit (small b), not a grazing one.
explanations.b: Correct — a higher b means a shorter chord across the star and more time spent straddling the limb, so T23 collapses and the trapezoid degenerates into a V (pure ingress into egress).
explanations.c: Depth is set mainly by (Rp/Rs)²; it does not grow without bound as b rises — if anything limb darkening makes a high-b transit look slightly shallower.
explanations.d: Higher b actually shortens the chord and thus T14; it does not hold duration fixed while deepening the dip.

questions.prompt: For a circular orbit, the geometric probability that a randomly oriented planet transits its star is approximately:

options.text: Rs/a (stellar radius over semi-major axis)
a/Rs (semi-major axis over stellar radius)
(Rp/Rs)² (the transit depth)
Always 50%, since the orbit is either edge-on or not

explanations.a: Correct — the alignment must be within a narrow band of inclinations, giving a transit probability of about Rs/a for a circular orbit; close-in planets (small a) transit far more often, which is why hot Jupiters dominated early transit surveys.
explanations.b: a/Rs is much greater than 1 and cannot be a probability; the correct ratio is its reciprocal, Rs/a.
explanations.c: The depth sets how DEEP a transit is, not how LIKELY one is to be geometrically aligned.
explanations.d: Transit probability is not 50%; it is the small geometric fraction Rs/a, typically a few percent or less for close-in planets and far smaller for distant ones.

questions.prompt: Why can a naive central-transit fit underestimate a planet’s radius when the true transit is at high impact parameter?

options.text: High-b transits emit extra light that fills in the dip
Near the limb the star is fainter (limb-darkened), so the planet blocks less flux and the depth reads shallower than a central crossing of the same planet
The planet physically shrinks when it crosses the limb
Impact parameter has no effect on measured radius

explanations.a: No extra light is emitted; the planet is a dark disk. The effect is about which part of the STAR it covers.
explanations.b: Correct — a limb-crossing planet occults dimmer, limb-darkened stellar surface, so the observed depth is slightly smaller; fitting it with a central model underestimates Rp/Rs unless b is fit jointly.
explanations.c: The planet’s radius is fixed; the apparent effect comes from the star’s brightness profile, not the planet changing size.
explanations.d: Impact parameter does affect the measured depth (via limb darkening) and is degenerate with radius, which is exactly why it must be fit.

lessons.label: Limb Darkening: Why Real Transits Are Round-Bottomed, Not Boxcars

sections.heading: Stars are not uniform disks — the limb is dimmer than the center
sections.body: The idealized trapezoid of Lesson 1 assumes the star is a flat, uniformly bright disk. Real stars are not: they are brighter at the center and progressively fainter toward the edge, an effect called LIMB DARKENING that has been known from the Sun since the 1800s. The cause is optical depth in the stellar atmosphere. When you look at the center of the disk you peer straight down into hotter, deeper layers; when you look at the limb your line of sight grazes tangentially and reaches only the higher, cooler, more rarefied layers before the gas becomes opaque. Since hotter gas radiates more (per the Stefan–Boltzmann and Planck laws), the center looks bright and the limb looks dim. The effect is stronger at bluer wavelengths and for cooler stars.

sections.heading: The consequence: round-bottomed, not flat-bottomed, transits
sections.body: Because the planet blocks a brighter patch when it crosses the star’s center than when it is near the limb, the transit does not have a truly flat floor. Instead the light curve is ROUND-BOTTOMED: the dip deepens smoothly as the planet moves toward the disk center (blocking the brightest region) and shallows again toward third contact. The corners at second and third contact are softened rather than sharp. Modelers describe the stellar brightness profile with a limb-darkening law — most commonly the QUADRATIC law I(μ)/I(1) = 1 − u₁(1 − μ) − u₂(1 − μ)², where μ = cosθ is the cosine of the angle from disk center (μ = 1 at center, μ = 0 at the limb) and u₁, u₂ are coefficients. Claret and others have tabulated these coefficients from stellar-atmosphere models for a grid of temperatures, gravities, and metallicities.

sections.heading: The Mandel–Agol model and why limb darkening cannot be ignored
sections.body: In 2002 Kaisey Mandel and Eric Agol published exact analytic formulae for the flux blocked by a planet crossing a limb-darkened star — a workhorse still used in essentially every transit-fitting package today. Getting limb darkening right matters for real science: if you fit a round-bottomed transit with a flat-bottomed boxcar you bias the inferred radius ratio and impact parameter, and you can distort a transmission spectrum (the wavelength dependence of depth used to probe atmospheres). Because limb darkening is stronger in the blue, the transit is measurably more “rounded” in blue bands than red — a chromatic signature that must be modeled, not fit away. In practice authors either fix u₁, u₂ to tabulated theoretical values or fit them (or a reparameterized combination) when the data are precise enough.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a Sun-like star with quadratic limb-darkening coefficients around u₁ ≈ 0.4, u₂ ≈ 0.25 in a red band. At disk center μ = 1, so the bracket (1 − μ) terms vanish and the intensity is at its full value I(1). At the extreme limb μ = 0, the intensity is I(1)×[1 − 0.4(1) − 0.25(1)] = I(1)×(1 − 0.65) = 0.35 I(1) — the edge of the star is only about a third as bright as its center. So a planet crossing at b = 0 blocks a patch nearly three times brighter than the same planet grazing at b ≈ 1, which is precisely why the transit floor sags in the middle instead of sitting flat, and why a high-impact-parameter transit reads shallower. A student fitting a boxcar to such data would misestimate both the depth and the ingress shape.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use limb darkening to separate students who ran a real transit fit from those who eyeballed a flat-bottomed cartoon. If your light curve has rounded corners and a sagging floor, that is not noise — it is the star’s brightness profile, and saying so (“the round bottom is limb darkening; I used a quadratic law with coefficients for this stellar temperature”) shows genuine command of the model. Claiming the star is a uniform disk, or treating the round bottom as a measurement error, signals a surface-level understanding.

questions.prompt: What physically causes limb darkening — the fact that a star’s limb looks fainter than its center?

options.text: The limb is physically cooler because the star is colder at its equator
A line of sight to the limb grazes tangentially and samples only higher, cooler atmospheric layers, while a line to the center reaches hotter, deeper layers
Dust between us and the star absorbs the edges more than the center
The planet’s shadow darkens the limb during transit

explanations.a: Limb darkening is not about equator-vs-pole temperature; it appears all around the disk edge and is a line-of-sight/optical-depth effect.
explanations.b: Correct — at the limb your sightline exits the atmosphere through cooler, higher layers (which radiate less), whereas at center you see down into hotter, deeper, brighter gas.
explanations.c: Interstellar dust dims and reddens starlight overall but does not create the smooth center-to-limb brightness gradient across a single stellar disk.
explanations.d: Limb darkening exists whether or not a planet is transiting; it is a property of the star, not a shadow.

questions.prompt: Using the quadratic law I(μ)/I(1) = 1 − u₁(1−μ) − u₂(1−μ)² with u₁ = 0.4 and u₂ = 0.25, what is the relative intensity at the extreme limb (μ = 0)?

options.text: 1.00 (same as the center)
0.00 (the limb is completely dark)

explanations.a: 1.00 is the CENTER value (μ = 1), where the (1−μ) terms vanish; the limb is fainter.
explanations.b: 0.65 is the amount SUBTRACTED (u₁ + u₂ = 0.65 at μ = 0), not the remaining intensity.
explanations.c: Correct — at μ = 0 the intensity is 1 − 0.4 − 0.25 = 0.35, so the limb is about 35% as bright as the center.
explanations.d: The limb is dimmer but not black; the law gives 0.35, a nonzero value.

questions.prompt: Whose 2002 work gave the analytic formulae for a planet transiting a limb-darkened star, now standard in transit-fitting codes?

options.text: Mandel & Agol
Mayor & Queloz
Penzias & Wilson
Payne-Gaposchkin

explanations.a: Correct — Kaisey Mandel and Eric Agol (2002) derived the exact analytic light-curve formulae for limb-darkened transits, still embedded in modern fitting packages.
explanations.b: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz discovered 51 Pegasi b (1995) via radial velocity — a landmark, but not the limb-darkened transit model.
explanations.c: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detected the cosmic microwave background (1965); unrelated to transits.
explanations.d: Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin showed stars are mostly hydrogen (1925); a stellar-composition landmark, not a transit model.

questions.prompt: Match each transit-modeling choice to its consequence.

left.text: Fitting a flat-bottomed boxcar to a limb-darkened transit
Using a quadratic limb-darkening law with tabulated coefficients
Observing the same transit in a bluer band

right.text: Biases the inferred radius ratio and impact parameter
Correctly reproduces the round-bottomed shape and unbiased parameters
Produces a more strongly rounded transit, since limb darkening is stronger in the blue

questions.explanation: A boxcar fit to a truly round-bottomed transit biases Rp/Rs and b; a proper quadratic law recovers the shape and unbiased parameters; and because limb darkening is stronger at bluer wavelengths, the same transit looks more rounded in a blue band than a red one.

lessons.label: Transit Duration as a Clock: Recovering Stellar Density and Orbital Distance

sections.heading: Duration encodes how fast the planet crosses — which encodes geometry
sections.body: The transit duration is not just cosmetic — it is a clock. The planet sweeps across a chord of the stellar disk at its orbital speed, so the total duration T14 depends on the chord length (set by Rs and the impact parameter b), the orbital speed (set by the semi-major axis a and period P), and the geometry of the crossing. For a central transit (b = 0) of a small planet on a circular orbit, a good approximation is T14 ≈ (P/π)·arcsin(Rs/a) ≈ (P/π)·(Rs/a) when a ≫ Rs. The key structural fact is that the duration divided by the period gives you Rs/a — the STELLAR radius in units of the orbital distance. Rearranged, the light curve alone hands you a/Rs, the scaled semi-major axis, a purely geometric quantity independent of any absolute distance calibration.

sections.heading: From a/Rs to stellar density: the Seager–Mallén-Ornelas result
sections.body: In 2003 Sara Seager and Gabriela Mallén-Ornelas showed that a single well-measured transit light curve — depth, total duration, and flat duration — determines the mean density of the STAR, without ever resolving the star or knowing its distance. The chain is: the light curve gives a/Rs; Kepler’s third law relates a, P, and the total system mass (dominated by the star); combining them cancels the star’s absolute size and leaves its mean density. Explicitly, ρ★ ≈ (3π/G)·(1/P²)·(a/Rs)³ (neglecting the planet’s mass). This is remarkable: the shape of a brightness dip, plus the orbital period, tells you how dense the host star is — a technique now called “asterodensity profiling.” It is used to sanity-check host-star properties and to flag false positives whose implied “stellar density” is physically absurd.

sections.heading: Eccentricity, the caveats, and why density is a cross-check
sections.body: The clean density result assumes a circular orbit. On an eccentric orbit the planet’s speed at transit differs from the circular-orbit value, so a transit caught near periastron is shorter (planet moving fast) and near apoastron is longer than expected — meaning the density you derive assuming circularity can be wrong by a factor that depends on eccentricity and the orientation of the orbit. This is actually useful: if you know the true stellar density independently (e.g. from asteroseismology or Gaia-based stellar parameters), the MISMATCH between it and the transit-derived density constrains the orbital eccentricity — the “photo-eccentric effect” exploited by Dawson & Johnson (2012). So transit duration is simultaneously a stellar-density probe (if you assume circular) and an eccentricity probe (if you know the density). Either way it is far more than a number to report — it is a physical constraint.

lessons.workedExample: Take HD 209458 b again: period P = 3.5247 days = 304,530 s and scaled semi-major axis a/Rs ≈ 8.76 from the light-curve shape. Plug into ρ★ = (3π/G)·(1/P²)·(a/Rs)³: with (a/Rs)³ = 672, 1/P² = 1.08×10⁻¹¹ s⁻², and 3π/G = 1.41×10¹¹, the product is ≈ 1024 kg/m³. That is about 0.73 times the Sun’s mean density (1408 kg/m³), correctly flagging HD 209458 as a slightly evolved, puffed-up star a bit less dense than the Sun — a conclusion reached from the transit shape and period ALONE, with no parallax and no spectrum. A student who reports “my transit implies a stellar density of ~1000 kg/m³, consistent with a slightly evolved solar-type star” has extracted real astrophysics from a light curve.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is a favorite advanced-judge question: “what, besides the planet’s radius, can you get from the light curve?” The impressive answer is the stellar density, via a/Rs and Kepler’s third law (Seager & Mallén-Ornelas 2003), plus the caveat that it assumes a circular orbit and can otherwise reveal eccentricity. A student who can derive or at least explain ρ★ ∝ (a/Rs)³/P² demonstrates they see the light curve as a geometric and dynamical instrument, not just a dip whose depth they read off.

questions.prompt: What quantity does the transit duration (relative to the period) most directly give you, independent of distance?

options.text: The planet’s mass
The scaled semi-major axis a/Rs (equivalently Rs/a)
The star’s surface temperature
The planet’s albedo

explanations.a: Mass comes from radial velocities or transit-timing, not from how long the transit lasts.
explanations.b: Correct — for a circular orbit T14/P ≈ (1/π)·(Rs/a), so the duration and period together yield the scaled semi-major axis a/Rs, a purely geometric quantity.
explanations.c: Temperature comes from the star’s spectrum/color, not from transit duration.
explanations.d: Albedo is probed by the secondary eclipse and reflected light, not by the primary transit’s duration.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of the Seager–Mallén-Ornelas method that turns a light curve into a stellar density.

items.text: Measure depth, total duration, and flat duration from the light curve
Solve the light-curve geometry for the scaled semi-major axis a/Rs
Apply Kepler’s third law relating a, P, and the (star-dominated) system mass
Cancel the star’s absolute size to obtain its mean density ρ★ ∝ (a/Rs)³/P²

questions.explanation: You first measure the observables (depth, T14, T23), solve the geometry for a/Rs, invoke Kepler’s third law to bring in P and the stellar mass, and combine them so the absolute stellar radius cancels, leaving the mean stellar density ρ★ ∝ (a/Rs)³/P².

questions.prompt: A transit-derived stellar density assumes a circular orbit. If the true orbit is eccentric and the transit happens near periastron, the transit will be:

options.text: Longer than the circular-orbit prediction, because the planet moves slower there
Shorter than the circular-orbit prediction, because the planet moves faster near periastron
Exactly the same, because eccentricity does not affect duration
Undetectable, because eccentric planets do not transit

explanations.a: Near periastron the planet moves FASTER (Kepler’s second law), not slower, so the transit is shorter, not longer.
explanations.b: Correct — at periastron the planet’s orbital speed is highest, so it crosses the disk more quickly and the transit is shorter than a circular orbit of the same period would give; this mismatch is what the “photo-eccentric” method (Dawson & Johnson 2012) exploits.
explanations.c: Eccentricity strongly affects the transit speed and hence duration; that is the whole basis of extracting eccentricity from durations.
explanations.d: Eccentric planets transit just fine; eccentricity changes the transit’s timing and duration, not whether it occurs.

questions.prompt: For HD 209458 b (P ≈ 3.52 d, a/Rs ≈ 8.76), the transit-derived mean stellar density comes out near 1000 kg/m³, versus the Sun’s ~1408 kg/m³. The best interpretation is that:

options.text: The measurement is wrong, because all stars have the Sun’s density
The host is a slightly evolved, somewhat inflated solar-type star, less dense than the Sun
The planet must be extremely massive
The orbit must be exactly circular for the number to mean anything at all

explanations.a: Stars span a huge range of mean densities (from ~150 kg/m³ for evolved subgiants to far higher for dwarfs); a value below solar is physically sensible, not an error.
explanations.b: Correct — ~1000 kg/m³ (≈0.73 ρ_Sun) indicates a slightly evolved, puffed-up solar-type star, exactly what independent studies of HD 209458 find, and it was obtained from the transit shape and period alone.
explanations.c: The derived quantity is the STAR’s density; it is insensitive to the planet’s mass, which is neglected in the formula.
explanations.d: Assuming circularity gives a specific density value, but a slightly eccentric orbit would just shift it — the number is still interpretable as a density estimate/cross-check.

lessons.label: Grazing Transits, Blends, and the Eclipsing-Binary False Positive

sections.heading: The core problem: a dip is not a planet
sections.body: A transit survey does not detect planets — it detects periodic dimmings, and many things dim periodically. The dominant astrophysical false positives are ECLIPSING BINARIES (EBs): two stars orbiting each other so that one passes in front of the other. Because a small, faint star (an M dwarf) or a brown dwarf can be nearly the same SIZE as a giant planet despite being far more massive, a shallow, planet-like dip can be produced by a stellar or substellar companion.
