Transit surveys like Kepler and TESS therefore treat every candidate as guilty until proven innocent; historically a large fraction of raw transit candidates turn out to be some flavor of EB, and the whole enterprise of “vetting” exists to weed them out before expensive follow-up.

sections.heading: Three telltale EB signatures — and the grazing V-shape
sections.body: Several features betray an eclipsing binary. (1) A SECONDARY ECLIPSE that is too deep: when the companion passes behind the primary you may see a second dip; for a star-star pair this secondary can be a substantial fraction of the primary, whereas a planet’s secondary is tiny. (2) ODD–EVEN DEPTH DIFFERENCES: in a near-equal binary at twice the true period, alternate eclipses (one star in front, then the other) have slightly different depths, so “odd” and “even” transits differ — a planet’s transits are all identical. (3) An ELLIPSOIDAL/reflection phase variation from tidally distorted stars. (4) A GRAZING, V-SHAPED eclipse: a grazing EB never fully occults, so like a high-impact-parameter transit it shows a V with no flat bottom — and a V-shape is a red flag because the depth-to-radius mapping is unreliable and the companion may be stellar. Kepler’s vetting explicitly flags V-shaped events for scrutiny.

sections.heading: Blends: the background eclipsing binary hiding in the aperture
sections.body: The most insidious false positive is the BLEND, especially a background eclipsing binary (BEB). Photometric apertures are large (Kepler pixels are ~4 arcsec, TESS ~21 arcsec), so light from a faint, deeply eclipsing binary a few arcseconds away leaks into the target’s aperture. A 50% eclipse of a faint background star, diluted by the bright foreground target, can masquerade as a shallow, few-percent — or even sub-percent — planet-like dip on the target. Detecting blends drove a suite of techniques: CENTROID MOTION analysis (the photocenter shifts slightly during the eclipse if the source is off-target), high-resolution imaging to find nearby stars, and radial-velocity checks. When a candidate is too faint or crowded for a direct mass measurement, astronomers turn to STATISTICAL VALIDATION — computing the probability the signal is a planet versus each false-positive scenario. Tools like BLENDER (used to validate Kepler‑10c and others, while Kepler‑10b itself was radial-velocity-confirmed via Keck-HIRES) and Timothy Morton’s vespa framework formalized this, enabling the wholesale validation of thousands of Kepler candidates that could never be individually mass-confirmed.

lessons.workedExample: Imagine a TESS candidate: a clean, periodic 1.2% dip, period 2.7 days, but the light curve is distinctly V-shaped with no flat bottom, and folding at TWICE the period reveals that alternate dips differ by ~15% in depth. Each clue points away from a planet. The V-shape says grazing (unreliable radius, possibly stellar); the odd–even depth difference says this is really a near-equal eclipsing binary at half the assumed period, with the two similar stars alternately eclipsing. A follow-up check for a shallow secondary eclipse at phase 0.5 seals it: a stellar secondary of a fraction of a percent appears, far deeper than any planet’s reflected/thermal secondary. The verdict is an eclipsing binary, not a planet — and catching it from the discovery light curve alone (V-shape + odd–even + secondary) saved a night of large-telescope radial-velocity time.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love the question “how do you know it’s really a planet and not two stars?” because it is exactly what professionals worry about most. A strong answer lists concrete vetting signatures — V-shape (grazing/stellar), odd–even depth differences (near-equal EB at double the period), a too-deep secondary eclipse, and centroid shifts (a blended background binary) — and names the remedy (radial velocities, high-res imaging, or statistical validation à la vespa/BLENDER). A student who says “it dipped periodically so it’s a planet” has skipped the single hardest and most important step in the whole field.

questions.prompt: Why can an eclipsing binary containing a small M dwarf mimic a giant-planet transit?

options.text: M dwarfs are the same MASS as giant planets
A low-mass star or brown dwarf can be nearly the same RADIUS as a giant planet, producing a similar-depth dip despite being far more massive
M dwarfs emit no light, so they look exactly like planets
Giant planets and M dwarfs have identical temperatures

explanations.a: They are not the same mass — an M dwarf is tens to hundreds of times more massive than a giant planet; the resemblance is in size, not mass.
explanations.b: Correct — because transit depth depends only on RADIUS, and small stars/brown dwarfs are radius-comparable to Jupiter, they can carve a planet-depth dip; only a mass measurement (or vetting) reveals the imposter.
explanations.c: M dwarfs do emit light; the mimicry is geometric (similar radius), not a matter of invisibility.
explanations.d: Their temperatures differ greatly; the false positive arises from similar radii, not similar temperatures.

questions.prompt: A candidate’s transits show an “odd–even depth difference” — alternate dips have slightly different depths. What does this most strongly suggest?

options.text: A genuine multi-planet system
A near-equal eclipsing binary detected at twice its true period, with the two stars alternately eclipsing
Strong limb darkening on the planet
That the planet has rings

explanations.a: Different planets have different periods and would not produce a clean odd–even alternation at a single folded period.
explanations.b: Correct — if two similar stars eclipse each other, folding at half the true period lines up star-A-in-front with star-B-in-front, giving slightly unequal “odd” and “even” depths; a real planet’s transits are all identical.
explanations.c: Limb darkening rounds the transit bottom but does not make alternate transits differ in depth.
explanations.d: Rings would alter a single transit’s shape, not create a systematic odd-vs-even depth alternation.

questions.prompt: What is a "blend" (e.g., a background eclipsing binary) as a transit false positive?

options.text: Two planets transiting the same star simultaneously
Light from a nearby, deeply eclipsing binary leaking into the target’s photometric aperture, diluted to look like a shallow transit on the target
A planet whose atmosphere blends into the star’s
Two exposures accidentally averaged together

explanations.a: Simultaneous double transits are real (multi-planet) events, not blends; a blend involves contaminating light from a DIFFERENT source.
explanations.b: Correct — large apertures (Kepler ~4", TESS ~21") admit light from nearby stars, so a deep eclipse of a faint background binary, diluted by the bright target, appears as a shallow planet-like dip on the target.
explanations.c: A planet’s atmosphere causes tiny transmission signals, not the aperture-contamination false positive called a blend.
explanations.d: A blend is an astrophysical contamination by a real eclipsing source, not a data-averaging artifact.

questions.prompt: Match each vetting signature or tool to what it reveals or does.

right.text: Flags a grazing event with an unreliable radius, possibly a stellar companion
Detects a photocenter shift during eclipse, exposing an off-target blended source
Indicates a stellar (not planetary) companion, whose reflected/thermal secondary would be far shallower
Computes the probability the signal is a planet vs. false-positive scenarios to validate candidates that cannot be mass-confirmed

questions.explanation: A V-shape flags a grazing/possibly stellar event; centroid motion exposes an off-target blend; a too-deep secondary eclipse betrays a stellar companion; and statistical-validation frameworks (vespa, BLENDER) compute planet-vs-false-positive probabilities to validate candidates without a direct mass.

lessons.label: Beyond the Dip: Secondary Eclipse, Occultation Depth, and Full-Orbit Phase Curves

sections.heading: The secondary eclipse: catching the planet’s own light disappear
sections.body: Half an orbit after the transit, a transiting planet passes BEHIND its star — the SECONDARY ECLIPSE, or occultation. During transit the planet blocks starlight; during the secondary eclipse the STAR blocks the planet, so the tiny drop you measure is the planet’s OWN light (thermal emission plus reflected starlight) being removed from the combined system. The occultation depth is therefore ≈ (Fp/Fs)·(Rp/Rs)² — the planet’s surface brightness relative to the star’s, times the same area ratio as the transit. Because a hot Jupiter is far cooler than its star, this is a small effect in visible light but grows dramatically in the infrared, where the planet’s thermal glow competes better with the star. The occultation is the cleanest way to measure a planet’s dayside brightness, since it directly isolates the planet’s flux without needing to spatially resolve it.

sections.heading: Spitzer and the first exoplanet thermal detections (2005)
sections.body: The breakthrough came in 2005 with NASA’s Spitzer Space Telescope. Two teams independently detected secondary eclipses in the infrared: David Charbonneau and colleagues measured the occultation of TrES-1, and Drake Deming and colleagues measured HD 209458 b — the first direct detections of light from planets orbiting other stars. These occultations, at depths of a few tenths of a percent in the mid-infrared, yielded the planets’ dayside brightness temperatures (roughly 1000 K and above for these hot Jupiters), turning exoplanets from points inferred by their shadows into worlds with measured temperatures. It was a landmark: no image of the planet was ever made, yet its thermal emission was cleanly separated by watching it wink out behind its star.

sections.heading: Phase curves: the whole orbit, hotspots, and eccentricity
sections.body: Between and beyond the two eclipses, the system brightness varies continuously as the planet shows changing fractions of its hot dayside and cool nightside — a PHASE CURVE, the exoplanet analogue of lunar phases. Its amplitude gives the day–night temperature contrast; the phase at which it peaks reveals whether the hottest point is at the substellar point or shifted by winds. In 2007 Heather Knutson and collaborators used Spitzer to map HD 189733 b’s 8-µm phase curve and found the brightness peak offset from the substellar point — evidence that a super-rotating equatorial jet blows the hotspot downwind, a foundational result for exoplanet meteorology. Separately, the TIMING of the secondary eclipse constrains orbital ECCENTRICITY: on a circular orbit the occultation falls exactly halfway between transits, but on an eccentric orbit it shifts earlier or later (the offset scales with e·cosω), so measuring when the planet disappears behind the star is a direct eccentricity probe.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a hot Jupiter with Rp/Rs ≈ 0.12 (transit depth ≈ 1.5%) is observed in the mid-infrared, where its dayside surface brightness is about 3% of the star’s (Fp/Fs ≈ 0.03) because the planet is hot (≈1200 K) and the contrast is much more favorable than in visible light. The predicted secondary-eclipse depth is (Fp/Fs)·(Rp/Rs)² ≈ 0.03 × 0.0149 ≈ 4.5×10⁻⁴, about 0.045% — a few hundred ppm, right in the regime Spitzer measured for real hot Jupiters like HD 209458 b and TrES-1 in 2005. Now imagine the occultation is observed to occur 12 minutes LATER than the exact transit-to-transit midpoint: that timing offset (∝e·cosω) reveals a small but nonzero orbital eccentricity, information the primary transit alone could not provide. The student thus extracts a dayside temperature AND an eccentricity constraint from parts of the light curve most people ignore.
lessons.judgeFraming: An advanced judge may ask “what else is in the light curve besides the transit?” — and the secondary eclipse and phase curve are the sophisticated answers. Explaining that the occultation depth ≈ (Fp/Fs)(Rp/Rs)² measures the planet’s own dayside light (first done with Spitzer in 2005 for TrES-1 and HD 209458 b), that a phase-curve hotspot offset reveals atmospheric winds (Knutson et al. 2007, HD 189733 b), and that occultation TIMING constrains eccentricity, shows a student who understands a transiting system as a full-orbit laboratory, not just a single dip.

questions.prompt: During a secondary eclipse (occultation), what is actually being blocked, and what does the depth measure?

options.text: The planet blocks the star; the depth measures the planet’s radius
The star blocks the planet; the depth measures the planet’s own emitted-plus-reflected light, ≈ (Fp/Fs)(Rp/Rs)²
Nothing is blocked; it is an instrumental artifact
The planet’s moon blocks the star

explanations.a: That describes the PRIMARY transit; during the secondary eclipse the roles reverse and the star hides the planet.
explanations.b: Correct — at secondary eclipse the star occults the planet, so the removed flux is the planet’s own dayside light (thermal + reflected), giving an occultation depth ≈ (Fp/Fs)(Rp/Rs)².
explanations.c: The secondary eclipse is a real astrophysical event — the planet passing behind the star — not an artifact.
explanations.d: No moon is required; the secondary eclipse is the planet itself passing behind its host star.

questions.prompt: Why are secondary eclipses of hot Jupiters far easier to detect in the infrared than in visible light?

options.text: Planets only emit infrared and never visible or reflected light
In the infrared the planet’s thermal emission is a much larger fraction of the star’s flux, so the planet-to-star contrast Fp/Fs is far more favorable
Infrared telescopes have larger apertures by law
The star stops shining in the infrared

explanations.a: Hot Jupiters do reflect some visible light; the point is that their THERMAL emission peaks in the infrared, boosting contrast there.
explanations.b: Correct — a ~1000–1500 K planet radiates strongly in the infrared while the much hotter star’s output there is relatively lower, so Fp/Fs (and thus the occultation depth) is much larger in the IR — exactly why Spitzer succeeded in 2005.
explanations.c: Aperture size is not fixed by wavelength or law; the advantage is the physical planet-to-star flux contrast.
explanations.d: The star still shines brightly in the infrared; it is simply that the planet’s relative contribution is larger there.

questions.prompt: Knutson et al. (2007) mapped HD 189733 b’s 8-µm phase curve with Spitzer and found the brightness peak offset from the substellar point. What did this reveal?

options.text: The planet has no atmosphere
A super-rotating equatorial jet carries the hottest region downwind of the substellar point
The planet is tidally spinning up and about to be destroyed
The star is variable and the planet is irrelevant

explanations.a: A shifted hotspot requires an atmosphere to redistribute heat; the offset is evidence FOR an atmosphere, not against one.
explanations.b: Correct — the eastward offset of the brightness peak indicates winds (a super-rotating jet) advecting heat downwind of the substellar point, a foundational result in exoplanet atmospheric dynamics.
explanations.c: The phase-curve offset is about heat transport by winds, not about the planet’s rotational destruction.
explanations.d: The signal tracks the planet’s orbital phase and its dayside/nightside, so it is a planetary atmosphere effect, not stellar variability.

questions.prompt: If a secondary eclipse occurs measurably earlier or later than exactly halfway between two transits, what does that timing offset constrain?

options.text: The planet’s radius
The star’s metallicity
The orbital eccentricity (the offset scales with e·cosω)
Nothing physical; eclipses are always exactly at the midpoint

explanations.a: Radius comes from the transit depth, not from the timing of the secondary eclipse.
explanations.b: Metallicity is a spectroscopic property of the star, unrelated to eclipse timing.
explanations.c: Correct — a circular orbit puts the occultation exactly halfway between transits, so any shift (to leading order ∝ e·cosω) directly constrains the orbital eccentricity and orientation.
explanations.d: They are only at the midpoint for circular orbits; an eccentric orbit shifts the occultation, which is precisely the useful signal.

units.label: The Radial-Velocity Method in Depth: Fitting the Doppler Orbit

lessons.label: From Line Shift to Orbit: The Six Keplerian Elements Behind an RV Curve

sections.heading: A time series of line shifts, not a single Doppler number
sections.body: The Core taught the one-line idea: a planet tugs its star, the star’s spectral lines shift by Δλ/λ = v_r/c, and the line-of-sight velocity v_r wobbles. The depth beyond that is realizing a real detection is never one Doppler shift — it is a *time series*. You point a spectrograph at the star night after night, measure v_r on each visit (often to better than 1 m/s), and accumulate dozens to hundreds of velocity points spread over months or years. The science lives in fitting a physical model to that scatter of points. That model is a Keplerian orbit: the star and planet orbit their common center of mass on ellipses, and the star’s line-of-sight velocity is the projection of its half of that motion onto your sightline. Fitting an RV curve means recovering the orbit that produced the points.

sections.heading: The six classical orbital elements — and which ones RV can see
sections.body: A Keplerian orbit in three dimensions is specified by six numbers, the classical orbital elements: the semi-major axis a (size), eccentricity e (shape), inclination i (tilt of the orbit plane to your sightline), longitude of the ascending node Ω (the orbit’s orientation on the sky), argument of periastron ω (where in the orbit the closest approach sits), and a time reference such as the time of periastron passage T_p (the clock’s zero). Radial velocity is a purely line-of-sight measurement, so it is blind to some of these. From an RV curve you cleanly recover the *period* P (hence a, once you know the stellar mass, via Kepler’s third law), the eccentricity e, the argument of periastron ω, the time of periastron T_p, plus two amplitude-type quantities the Core did not separate out: the systemic velocity γ (the whole system’s bulk drift toward or away from us) and the semi-amplitude K (half the peak-to-trough swing). What RV *cannot* isolate are the inclination i and the node Ω — the sky-plane orientation — which is the root of the famous M·sin i degeneracy of the next lessons.

sections.heading: The RV equation and Kepler’s equation underneath it
sections.body: The star’s modeled radial velocity as a function of time is v_r(t) = γ + K[cos(ω + ν(t)) + e·cos ω], where ν(t) is the *true anomaly*, the planet’s angular position in its orbit measured from periastron. For a circular orbit (e = 0) this collapses to a pure sinusoid, v_r = γ + K·cos(ω + ν), which is why the Core could get away with "a clean sine wave." For e > 0 the curve is skewed, because ν does not advance uniformly in time. Getting ν(t) requires solving Kepler’s equation, M = E − e·sin E, where the mean anomaly M = 2π(t − T_p)/P ticks uniformly and E is the eccentric anomaly; ν then follows from tan(ν/2) = √[(1+e)/(1−e)]·tan(E/2). Kepler’s equation is transcendental — you solve it numerically (Newton’s method) at each time step — which is exactly why RV fitting is a computational job, not a ruler-and-protractor one.

lessons.workedExample: You have 60 HARPS velocities of a Sun-like star scattered over 300 nights. A periodogram of the residuals peaks sharply at P = 14.65 days. You fit the six-parameter model v_r(t) = γ + K[cos(ω+ν) + e·cos ω]. The optimizer returns γ = −13.402 km/s (the star’s bulk motion), K = 4.2 m/s, e = 0.12, ω = 47°, and T_p at a specific Julian date. Notice what you did and did not get: you nailed P, K, e, ω, T_p, γ — but nowhere in that list is the inclination i. So you can quote the planet’s minimum mass M·sin i from K and P (next lesson), and its orbital distance a from P and the stellar mass, but you cannot yet say whether the orbit is edge-on or tilted 30° to your line of sight. That missing i is not a fitting failure — it is geometrically invisible to a line-of-sight-only technique.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges press "what exactly did your fit measure?" to see whether a student treats RV as a slot machine that spits out "a planet mass" or as a Keplerian model with named parameters. The strong answer lists the parameters RV actually constrains — P, K, e, ω, T_p, γ — and explains that inclination i and node Ω are geometrically unobservable in line-of-sight data, which is *why* the derived mass is a minimum. A student who says "I fit a sine wave and got the mass" has skipped both the eccentric physics and the inclination caveat, and a judge will probe exactly there.

questions.prompt: Which set of quantities can a radial-velocity curve, on its own, actually constrain?

options.text: Period P, inclination i, and node Ω
Period P, semi-amplitude K, eccentricity e, argument of periastron ω, time of periastron T_p, and systemic velocity γ
The planet’s true mass and radius directly
Only the systemic velocity γ and nothing time-varying

explanations.a: Inclination i and node Ω are the sky-plane orientation, which is invisible to a line-of-sight-only measurement — RV cannot constrain them.
explanations.b: Correct — these six are exactly the parameters of the RV model v_r = γ + K[cos(ω+ν) + e·cos ω]; P, K, e, ω, T_p and γ are all recoverable from the time series.
explanations.c: RV gives a minimum mass M·sin i, not the true mass, and says nothing about the planet’s physical radius (that needs a transit).
explanations.d: γ is the constant offset; the periodic wobble (K, P, e, ω, T_p) is the whole point of the measurement.

questions.prompt: Why is the inclination i geometrically absent from a radial-velocity solution?

options.text: Because spectrographs are not precise enough to detect it
Because RV measures only the line-of-sight component of the star’s velocity, so a tilt of the orbit plane cannot be separated from a change in the true velocity amplitude
Because inclination only matters for circular orbits
Because i is fixed at 90° for every planetary system

explanations.a: It is not a precision problem — even a perfect spectrograph measures only line-of-sight motion, so i stays hidden.
explanations.b: Correct — you see v_r = v·sin i-type projection, so an unknown tilt trades off against the true speed; RV alone cannot break that.
explanations.c: Inclination affects the observed amplitude for orbits of any eccentricity, not just circular ones.
explanations.d: Orbits take all inclinations; only transiting systems happen to be near edge-on (i ≈ 90°).

questions.prompt: Why must Kepler’s equation M = E − e·sin E be solved numerically inside an RV fit?

options.text: Because the systemic velocity γ changes every night
Because it is transcendental — E cannot be written as a closed-form elementary function of M — so the true anomaly ν(t) needed for an eccentric curve is found iteratively (e.g. Newton’s method)
Because the period P is unknown until the orbit is solved
Because radial velocity is measured in km/s, not m/s

explanations.a: γ is a single constant offset, not a per-night variable, and has nothing to do with Kepler’s equation.
explanations.b: Correct — M = E − e·sin E has no elementary inverse, so you iterate for E (then ν) at each time; this is what makes RV fitting computational.
explanations.c: P is found first from a periodogram; the numerical solve is needed even with P known, to get ν from time.
explanations.d: Units are irrelevant to the transcendental nature of the equation.

questions.prompt: Match each RV-fit parameter to what it physically represents.

right.text: Orbital period (spacing of the wobble in time)
Eccentricity — how elongated/skewed the orbit and curve are
Semi-amplitude — half the peak-to-trough velocity swing
Systemic velocity — the whole system’s bulk line-of-sight drift

questions.explanation: P sets the wobble’s repeat time; e sets the curve’s skew away from a sinusoid; K is half the peak-to-trough velocity swing and encodes the tug (hence M·sin i); γ is the constant offset from the system’s bulk motion through the galaxy.

lessons.label: The Semi-Amplitude K and the Mass Function: What the Wobble Actually Encodes

sections.heading: K is the single number carrying the planet’s mass
sections.body: The semi-amplitude K — half the peak-to-trough swing of the RV curve — is where the planet’s mass hides. Physically, the star and planet orbit a common center of mass, so a heavier planet on a closer, faster orbit yanks the star harder and produces a bigger K. The full relation is K = (2πG/P)^{1/3} · (M_p sin i)/(M_★ + M_p)^{2/3} · 1/√(1−e²). For the common case of a planet far lighter than its star (M_p ≪ M_★), this simplifies to the widely used scaling K = 28.4 m/s · (M_p sin i / M_Jup) · (M_★/M_☉)^{−2/3} · (P/yr)^{−1/3} / √(1−e²). Read off what makes K big: large planet mass, short period, low stellar mass, and (mildly) high eccentricity all raise it. This is why the first RV planets were hot Jupiters — massive planets on days-long orbits give tens of m/s, easy to catch.

sections.heading: The mass function: what you can state without knowing i
sections.body: Because RV cannot see the inclination, the cleanest thing you can write down that involves *only observed quantities* is the spectroscopic mass function: f(m) = (M_p sin i)³/(M_★ + M_p)² = P·K³·(1−e²)^{3/2}/(2πG). Everything on the right — P, K, e — comes straight from the fit, so f(m) is a hard, model-independent number. It bundles the unknown i into the combination M_p sin i. If you additionally know the stellar mass M_★ (from spectroscopy plus stellar models, or an asteroseismic/Gaia constraint) and assume M_p ≪ M_★, you invert it to the planet’s *minimum mass* M_p sin i. That "minimum" wording is exact: since sin i ≤ 1, the true mass M_p = (M_p sin i)/sin i is always at least the minimum, and equals it only for an edge-on orbit (i = 90°).

sections.heading: Real amplitudes: from hot Jupiters down to Earth’s 9 cm/s
sections.body: Putting numbers to it calibrates the whole hunt. Jupiter, on its 11.86-yr orbit, makes the Sun swing by only K ≈ 12.5 m/s — a slow, decade-long wobble. Earth makes the Sun move at K ≈ 0.09 m/s, i.e. 9 cm/s, over a year: about the speed of a strolling ant, and the reason an Earth twin is the hardest RV target there is. 51 Pegasi b, the first hot Jupiter (Mayor & Queloz 1995, Nobel 2019), produced K ≈ 59 m/s on a 4.23-day orbit — enormous by these standards, which is precisely why 1990s spectrographs could catch it. The historical precision ladder — ~15 m/s in the early 1990s, ~1 m/s with HARPS in the 2000s, and ~10 cm/s the goal for ESPRESSO — is literally a ladder of which planets K lets you reach.

lessons.workedExample: A G-type star (M_★ = 1.0 M_☉) shows a clean RV signal: P = 4.23 days, K = 59 m/s, e ≈ 0. Convert P to years: 4.23/365.25 = 0.01158 yr. Apply the scaling K = 28.4 · (M_p sin i / M_Jup) · (1.0)^{−2/3} · (0.01158)^{−1/3} / 1. Now (0.01158)^{−1/3} = 1/0.2258 = 4.43, so 59 = 28.4 · (M_p sin i / M_Jup) · 4.43, giving M_p sin i / M_Jup = 59/(28.4·4.43) = 59/125.8 = 0.47. So M_p sin i ≈ 0.47 M_Jup — recovering exactly Mayor & Queloz’s result for 51 Peg b. If a follow-up transit later showed the orbit is edge-on (sin i ≈ 1), that minimum *is* the true mass, ≈ 0.47 M_Jup; if instead the system were tilted to i = 30° (sin i = 0.5), the true mass would double to ≈ 0.94 M_Jup. Same K, same fit — the mass you report hinges entirely on the unknown i.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love to ask "so how much does your planet weigh?" specifically to hear whether the student volunteers "minimum mass, M·sin i" and can say why. The mass function is the concept that lets a student answer honestly: f(m) is built only from P, K, and e — all measured — so it is a claim you can defend without hand-waving about geometry. A student who quotes a single-valued mass with no sin i, or who cannot say that the true mass is *larger* than the minimum, has not internalized what the wobble amplitude does and does not encode.

questions.prompt: Two planets have the same mass and stellar host. Planet A orbits in 4 days, planet B in 400 days, both circular. How do their RV semi-amplitudes compare?

options.text: Equal, because mass is the same
A is larger, because K scales as P^(−1/3) — the shorter-period planet tugs the star faster
B is larger, because a wider orbit sweeps more velocity
Cannot be compared without the inclination

explanations.a: Mass is only one factor; K also depends on period as P^(−1/3), so equal masses do not give equal K.
explanations.b: Correct — K ∝ P^(−1/3), so A (P = 4 d) has K about (400/4)^(1/3) ≈ 4.6× larger than B (P = 400 d). Short periods make bigger, faster wobbles.
explanations.c: A wider orbit means a slower star and smaller K, not larger — the star’s reflex speed drops with distance.
explanations.d: The ratio of amplitudes at fixed mass and (here) edge-on comparison follows from P alone; inclination scales both equally.

questions.prompt: What makes the mass function f(m) = P·K³·(1−e²)^{3/2}/(2πG) especially useful?

options.text: It gives the planet’s true mass without any assumptions
It is built only from directly fitted quantities (P, K, e), so it is a model-independent number that bundles the unknown inclination into M_p sin i
It removes the need to know the stellar mass
It gives the planet’s radius

explanations.a: It does not give the true mass — the unknown sin i and the assumption M_p ≪ M_★ still stand between f(m) and a planet mass.
explanations.b: Correct — P, K, and e all come straight from the RV fit, so f(m) = (M_p sin i)³/(M_★+M_p)² is a hard observable independent of orbital models.
explanations.c: To turn f(m) into M_p sin i you still need M_★ from spectroscopy/stellar models; f(m) itself just packages the observables.
explanations.d: Radius comes from a transit depth, (R_p/R_★)², not from the RV mass function.

questions.prompt: An RV fit gives M_p sin i = 0.5 M_Jup. A later transit shows the system is edge-on (sin i ≈ 1). What is the true mass, and what if instead i were 30°?

options.text: 0.5 M_Jup edge-on; still 0.5 M_Jup at 30°, because RV already gave the mass
0.5 M_Jup edge-on; ≈ 1.0 M_Jup at i = 30°, because M_p = (M_p sin i)/sin i and sin 30° = 0.5
0.25 M_Jup edge-on; 0.5 M_Jup at 30°
Undefined, because mass cannot be recovered even with i known

explanations.a: M_p sin i is a minimum; only edge-on gives the true mass. At 30° the true mass is larger, not equal.
explanations.b: Correct — the true mass is the minimum divided by sin i. Edge-on (sin i = 1) leaves it at 0.5 M_Jup; at i = 30° (sin i = 0.5) it doubles to ≈ 1.0 M_Jup.
explanations.c: Edge-on means sin i ≈ 1, so the true mass equals the minimum (0.5), not half of it.
explanations.d: Once i is known, M_p = (M_p sin i)/sin i is fully determined.

questions.prompt: Order these bodies from the SMALLEST to the LARGEST RV semi-amplitude K they induce on a Sun-like host (all at their real orbits).

items.text: Earth (1 yr): K ≈ 0.09 m/s
Jupiter (11.86 yr): K ≈ 12.5 m/s

questions.explanation: Earth’s 9 cm/s is the tiniest (light planet, 1-yr orbit); Jupiter’s 12.5 m/s is larger (massive, but slow decade-long orbit); 51 Peg b’s 59 m/s is largest — sub-Jupiter mass but a 4.23-day orbit, since short periods sharply boost K (∝ P^(−1/3)).

lessons.label: Eccentric Orbits: How a Skewed, Non-Sinusoidal RV Curve Reveals Shape

sections.heading: Why eccentricity skews the curve away from a sine wave
sections.body: A circular orbit gives a perfect sinusoid because the star’s reflex velocity varies smoothly and symmetrically. Eccentricity breaks that symmetry through Kepler’s second law: the star sweeps equal areas in equal times, so it moves fastest at periastron (closest approach) and slowest at apastron. In velocity terms, the RV curve spends a long, lazy time near one extreme and then whips rapidly through a sharp spike near periastron — a skewed, sawtooth-like or "shark-fin" shape rather than a smooth sine. The two controlling parameters are the eccentricity e (how extreme the skew) and the argument of periastron ω (which rotates the asymmetry — a curve with a sharp peak looks different from one with a sharp trough, and ω sets which you see). Fitting both e and ω to the curve’s *shape* is how eccentricity is measured, with no imaging required.

sections.heading: Eccentric giants that broke the tidy formation picture
sections.body: Early expectations, shaped by the near-circular planets of our own Solar System, were that planets form on roughly circular orbits from a flat disk. Radial velocity demolished that: many giant exoplanets turned up on strikingly eccentric orbits. HD 80606 b (Naef et al. 2001, Geneva team) has e ≈ 0.93 — its RV curve is a dramatic narrow spike, and the planet plunges from a Mercury-like distance to a scorching skim of the star every 111 days. Others, like HD 20782 b, reach e ≈ 0.97, among the most eccentric known. These "eccentric giants" forced theorists to add dynamical histories to the story: planet–planet scattering (Rasio & Ford 1996), in which close encounters between forming giants fling one onto an eccentric orbit, and the Kozai–Lidov mechanism, in which a distant stellar or planetary companion pumps up eccentricity, followed by tidal circularization if the planet gets close enough. The *shape* of an RV curve became evidence about how planetary systems assemble.

sections.heading: Practical hazards: eccentric planets and the aliasing trap
sections.body: Eccentricity is not just a curiosity — it is a place RV analyses go wrong. A single moderately eccentric planet can, if the data are sparsely or unluckily sampled, mimic the signal of two planets on circular orbits (the harmonic content of an eccentric curve has power at the period’s multiples). This is a known false-positive route: several claimed multi-planet systems were later reinterpreted as one eccentric planet once denser data arrived. Conversely, forcing a circular fit onto a genuinely eccentric orbit biases the derived K, period, and even mass. The discipline is to let e float, check whether the eccentric solution is statistically justified (many teams report both), and sample the orbit densely enough — especially near the fast periastron passage, where a few well-placed points pin down the shape and a gap there can hide or fake a planet.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose an RV curve of a Sun-like star shows a shallow, broad dip for most of a 111-day cycle, then a sudden sharp velocity spike lasting only a couple of days before snapping back. A pure-sine (circular) fit leaves large systematic residuals right at the spike — a tell-tale that the orbit is eccentric. Letting e and ω float, the fit locks onto e ≈ 0.93 with ω placing periastron at the spike, and the residuals collapse into the noise. That is essentially HD 80606 b: the planet spends most of its "year" far out moving slowly, then races through a close periastron where the star’s reflex velocity swings hardest and fastest. The lesson for a student’s own data: if a sinusoid leaves a repeating kink at one phase, do not add a second planet reflexively — first test whether one eccentric orbit explains it, because an eccentric curve’s spike is exactly the feature a circular model cannot reproduce.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe eccentricity because a skewed RV curve is where students either show real orbital understanding or reveal they only know "sine wave = planet." The concept a judge wants to hear is that the curve’s *asymmetry* is physical — Kepler’s second law makes the star race through periastron — and that e and ω are read from the shape, not assumed to be zero. It is also a favorite because an eccentric single planet can masquerade as two circular ones, so a student who says "I checked whether one eccentric orbit fit before claiming a second planet" demonstrates exactly the skepticism a judge is testing for.

questions.prompt: Why is the RV curve of an eccentric orbit skewed rather than a symmetric sine wave?

options.text: Because the spectrograph loses precision at high velocities
Because Kepler’s second law makes the star move fastest at periastron and slowest at apastron, so the velocity spikes sharply near closest approach and lingers near the far point
Because eccentric orbits have two periods
Because the systemic velocity γ changes over the orbit

explanations.a: The skew is physical, not instrumental — it appears in perfectly measured data.
explanations.b: Correct — equal areas in equal times means fast motion at periastron and slow motion at apastron, producing a sharp velocity spike and a lazy far-side, i.e. a skewed curve.
explanations.c: An eccentric orbit still has a single period P; the skew comes from non-uniform speed within that one period.
explanations.d: γ is a constant offset; it does not vary around the orbit and cannot skew the curve.

questions.prompt: What does the argument of periastron ω control in an RV curve?

options.text: The overall amplitude of the wobble
The orientation of the asymmetry — whether the sharp feature appears as a peak or a trough and at what orbital phase
The orbital period
The systemic velocity offset

explanations.a: Amplitude is set by K, not ω.
explanations.b: Correct — ω rotates where periastron sits, which flips/shifts the skew so the sharp velocity excursion shows up as a peak or trough at a particular phase.
explanations.c: Period is P; ω is an orientation angle, not a timescale.
explanations.d: The systemic offset is γ; ω is unrelated to it.

questions.prompt: Why did eccentric giant planets like HD 80606 b (e ≈ 0.93) matter theoretically?

options.text: They proved planets cannot form in disks at all
They contradicted the expectation of near-circular orbits from a flat disk, motivating dynamical mechanisms like planet–planet scattering and Kozai–Lidov excitation
They showed the RV method does not work for giant planets
They demonstrated that eccentricity cannot be measured from RV

explanations.a: Planets still form in disks; the point is that later dynamics can excite eccentricity, not that disk formation fails.
explanations.b: Correct — highly eccentric giants clashed with tidy circular-disk formation and pushed theorists toward scattering (Rasio & Ford 1996) and Kozai–Lidov pumping plus tidal circularization.
explanations.c: RV works fine — indeed it is how these eccentricities were measured.
explanations.d: Eccentricity is precisely what the curve’s skew lets you measure; these are textbook cases of doing so.

questions.prompt: A sparsely sampled RV dataset shows extra structure. Before claiming a two-planet system, what should you check first?

options.text: Whether a single eccentric orbit reproduces the curve, since an eccentric planet can mimic two circular ones
Whether the telescope was in focus
Whether the star is a different spectral type
Whether the systemic velocity is exactly zero

explanations.a: Correct — an eccentric single planet has harmonic power that can imitate two circular signals; several claimed systems were later reduced to one eccentric planet with denser data.
explanations.b: Focus affects photometric imaging, not the Doppler velocities that make an RV curve.
explanations.c: Spectral type sets the lines used but does not create spurious extra orbital signals of this kind.
explanations.d: γ being nonzero is normal (bulk motion) and is not what generates fake second planets.

lessons.label: Breaking the M·sin i Degeneracy with Transits, Astrometry, and Imaging

sections.heading: The degeneracy, stated precisely — and why it needs outside help
sections.body: RV delivers M_p sin i, the true mass multiplied by the sine of an unknown inclination. Nothing in a line-of-sight-only dataset can separate the two: a heavy planet on a face-on-ish orbit and a light planet on an edge-on orbit can produce identical RV curves. Breaking the degeneracy therefore always requires a *second, geometry-sensitive* observation that constrains i (or the full orbit) independently. Three techniques do this, and they are complementary in the regimes where each works: transit photometry (for close-in planets that happen to cross the star), astrometry (for the plane-of-sky wobble), and direct imaging (for wide, bright, young planets). Each supplies the missing tilt, converting a minimum mass into a real one.

sections.heading: Transits: the geometry does the work for free
sections.body: A transit is only visible if the orbit is seen close to edge-on, so a detected transit *immediately* implies sin i ≈ 1 — the inclination is pinned near 90° by the mere fact that the planet crosses the stellar disk. That collapses M_p sin i into the true mass M_p. This is why the RV+transit combination is the workhorse of exoplanet characterization: the transit depth gives the radius via (R_p/R_★)², the RV gives the (now true) mass, and dividing mass by volume gives the *density* — the single number that distinguishes a puffy hydrogen gas giant from a dense rocky super-Earth. The precision the pairing enabled is why space photometry from Kepler and TESS is so often followed up with HARPS/ESPRESSO velocities: neither technique alone gives density, but together they do.

sections.heading: Astrometry and imaging: the full orbit, no transit required
sections.body: Transits only work for the small fraction of systems aligned edge-on. Astrometry measures the star’s tiny *two-dimensional* path on the sky as it orbits the barycenter, tracing the projected ellipse whose shape directly yields the inclination i and node Ω — the exact quantities RV lacks — so it delivers a true mass for any orientation, including face-on systems RV would show weakly and transits would miss entirely. The catch is the signal is minute (micro-arcseconds); ESA’s Gaia mission is now delivering astrometric orbits and true masses for the brighter, wider RV planets, and historic astrometric "detections" (e.g. the long-disputed Barnard’s Star claims of the 1960s) are a cautionary tale about the difficulty. Direct imaging is the third route: for young, wide-orbit giant planets bright enough to resolve, tracking orbital motion over years gives the inclination geometrically, again turning M_p sin i into M_p. The three methods tile the parameter space — transits for hot close-in planets, astrometry for intermediate separations, imaging for wide young giants.

lessons.workedExample: An RV survey finds a planet with M_p sin i = 0.9 M_Jup on a 3.5-day orbit around a Sun-like star. On its own you can only say "at least 0.9 Jupiter masses." A photometric follow-up then catches a 1.0% transit repeating on exactly 3.5 days. Two things happen at once. First, the transit’s existence forces sin i ≈ 1, so the true mass is essentially the minimum, M_p ≈ 0.9 M_Jup. Second, the depth gives the size: (R_p/R_★)² = 0.010, so R_p/R_★ = 0.10, and with R_★ ≈ 1 R_☉ ≈ 7.0×10^5 km, R_p ≈ 7.0×10^4 km — a Jupiter-sized radius. Now combine: mass ≈ 0.9 M_Jup packed into ≈ 1 Jupiter radius gives a density comparable to Jupiter’s (~1.3 g/cm³), confirming a genuine gas giant rather than an inflated low-density puffball or a dense rocky impostor. Neither the RV nor the transit alone could have said that; the geometry the transit supplied is what unlocked both the true mass and the density.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the concept judges circle back to hardest: "your RV gave a minimum mass — how did you get the real one?" The answer they are listening for names a *geometry-supplying* second measurement and says what it pins down: a transit forces sin i ≈ 1 (and adds a radius, hence density); astrometry or imaging measures the plane-of-sky orbit and yields i directly. A student who can explain that density — the payoff that separates gas giants from rocky worlds — only becomes accessible once mass (via broken degeneracy) and radius (via transit) are both in hand has shown they understand why exoplanet science leans so heavily on combining methods.

questions.prompt: Why does the detection of a transit immediately break the M·sin i degeneracy?

options.text: Because transits measure the planet’s mass directly
Because a transit is only geometrically possible for a near-edge-on orbit, forcing sin i ≈ 1, so M_p sin i becomes the true mass M_p
Because transits change the systemic velocity γ
Because transits eliminate the need for radial velocity entirely

explanations.a: Transits measure radius (via depth), not mass; the mass still comes from RV.
explanations.b: Correct — to cross the stellar disk the orbit must be seen nearly edge-on, so i ≈ 90° and sin i ≈ 1, turning the RV minimum mass into the true mass.
explanations.c: A transit is a photometric dip; it does not alter the star’s systemic velocity.
explanations.d: RV is still required for the mass — the transit supplies the geometry and the radius, not the mass.

questions.prompt: What can RV + transit together yield that neither gives alone?

options.text: The planet’s orbital period
The planet’s bulk density, from a true mass (RV, with sin i ≈ 1) and a radius (transit depth)
The star’s distance
The planet’s surface temperature exactly

explanations.a: Period is available from either technique alone; it is not the unique payoff of combining them.
explanations.b: Correct — the transit fixes i (true mass) and gives the radius, and mass ÷ volume is density, the number that separates gas giants from rocky worlds.
explanations.c: Distance comes from parallax (e.g. Gaia), not from RV+transit.
explanations.d: Equilibrium temperature can be estimated from insolation, but it is not what the RV+transit density combination provides.

questions.prompt: Which advantage does astrometry have over transits for measuring a true planet mass?

options.text: It works only for edge-on orbits
It measures the star’s two-dimensional path on the sky, yielding the inclination and node for orbits of any orientation — including non-transiting, face-on-ish systems
It requires no knowledge of the stellar mass
It gives the planet’s radius directly

explanations.a: The opposite — astrometry does not need an edge-on alignment; that is its strength over transits.
explanations.b: Correct — astrometry traces the projected orbital ellipse on the sky, directly giving i and Ω, so it yields true masses even for systems that never transit.
explanations.c: You still need M_★ to convert the astrometric wobble into a planet mass.
explanations.d: Radius comes from a transit; astrometry constrains the orbit geometry and mass, not the physical size.

questions.prompt: Match each degeneracy-breaking technique to the regime where it works best.

right.text: Close-in planets aligned near edge-on (also gives radius → density)
Any orientation via the plane-of-sky wobble; best for brighter, wider RV planets (e.g. Gaia)
Wide-orbit, young, self-luminous giants bright enough to resolve

questions.explanation: Transits catch close-in, near-edge-on planets and add a radius; astrometry recovers the full orbit (i, Ω) for any orientation and is now delivered by Gaia for brighter/wider systems; direct imaging resolves wide, young, bright giants and gets inclination from tracked orbital motion.

lessons.label: Stellar Jitter, Spots, and Activity Cycles: The False-Positive Problem in RV

sections.heading: The star is not a quiet mirror — it makes its own velocity signals
sections.body: An RV planet detection assumes the star’s spectral lines shift bodily because the whole star moves. But the star’s surface is turbulent and magnetically active, and those processes distort line shapes in ways a spectrograph reads as spurious velocity — collectively "stellar jitter." The sources span a wide range of timescales: p-mode oscillations (asteroseismic ringing) over minutes at the ~1 m/s level; granulation and supergranulation (convective boiling) over minutes to a day; rotating starspots and magnetic active regions over the stellar rotation period (days to weeks); and long-term magnetic activity cycles (the Sun’s is 11 years) over years. Every one of these can produce a periodic RV signal that has nothing to do with a planet — the central obstacle to finding low-mass worlds, because their true signals (an Earth’s 9 cm/s) sit far below typical jitter.

sections.heading: How a spot fakes — or hides — a planet
sections.body: The clearest culprit is a dark starspot. As the star rotates, a spot on the approaching (blueshifted) limb removes blue-shifted light from the averaged line, shifting its centroid redward; half a rotation later it sits on the receding limb and shifts it blueward. The line’s measured velocity therefore oscillates *at the rotation period* (and its harmonics) even though the star’s center of mass is not moving — a textbook false positive. Worse, spots also suppress the star’s convective blueshift locally, adding a second activity-linked velocity term. Because a spot signal is tied to rotation, a favorite red flag is a claimed "planet" whose period equals the stellar rotation period or half of it. Activity can also *mask* a real planet by adding correlated noise that buries the Keplerian signal, so jitter both invents and conceals.

sections.heading: Diagnostics and cautionary tales
sections.body: The defense is to prove the signal is a genuine bodily shift, not a line-shape change. A real Doppler shift moves the whole line identically; a spot changes the line’s *asymmetry*. So analysts compute the bisector inspan/velocity span of the cross-correlation profile and check it does *not* correlate with the RV; they monitor chromospheric activity indicators — Ca II H&K (the log R′_HK index), Hα — and the stellar rotation period, and demand the candidate period differ from these. Modern pipelines model the correlated activity noise with Gaussian-process regression tied to the rotation period. The history is humbling: the 2012 claim of Alpha Centauri Bb (Dumusque et al.), a 51 cm/s, 3.24-day signal, was shown by Rajpaul, Aigrain & Roberts (2016) to be an artifact of the observing-window sampling, not a planet, and retracted; several GJ 581 candidates and an early Barnard’s Star signal were likewise contested as activity. These are not embarrassments so much as the field learning, publicly, how hard sub-m/s work is.

lessons.workedExample: A team reports a candidate at K = 2 m/s with a 26-day period around an active K dwarf. Before celebrating, they run the checklist. First, the star’s rotation period, estimated from photometric spot modulation and the Ca II H&K index, is ~26 days — the candidate period *equals the rotation period*, an immediate red flag that a spot, not a planet, may be responsible. Second, they compute the line-bisector span and find it correlates with the measured RV (Pearson r ≈ 0.6): a real bodily Doppler shift would leave the line shape unchanged, so a bisector that tracks the velocity signals a shape distortion from an active region. Third, a Gaussian-process activity model keyed to the 26-day rotation absorbs most of the "signal," and the planet’s statistical significance collapses. Conclusion: this is stellar jitter masquerading as a planet, exactly the trap that felled Alpha Cen Bb. Had the period instead been, say, 9 days — well away from rotation — with a flat bisector and no activity correlation, the candidate would have survived the vetting.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges treat stellar activity as the ultimate "how do you know it is real?" question for any low-amplitude RV claim, because it is where overexcited students get burned. The answer that impresses names the mechanism (a rotating spot shifts the line centroid at the rotation period without moving the star’s center of mass) and the vetting (period ≠ rotation period; flat line bisector; no correlation with Ca II H&K or Hα; GP activity modeling). Citing the retracted Alpha Cen Bb detection shows a student knows this is not hypothetical — even expert teams have mistaken jitter for planets, so a good project states explicitly how it ruled activity out.

questions.prompt: How can a rotating starspot fake a radial-velocity planet signal?

options.text: By physically pushing the star back and forth
By removing light from the approaching then receding limb as it rotates, shifting the averaged line centroid at the stellar rotation period even though the star’s center of mass does not move
By increasing the star’s overall brightness
By changing the systemic velocity γ permanently

explanations.a: A spot does not move the star’s center of mass; the false signal comes from a line-shape distortion, not real bulk motion.
explanations.b: Correct — a dark spot subtracts blue- then red-shifted light as it crosses the disk, moving the measured line centroid periodically at the rotation period, mimicking a Doppler wobble.
explanations.c: A spot slightly dims the star (photometric variability), but the RV false positive comes from the line-profile distortion, not brightness.
explanations.d: γ is a stable bulk offset; a spot does not permanently change it.

questions.prompt: Why is a candidate whose orbital period equals the stellar rotation period treated with suspicion?

options.text: Because planets cannot orbit that fast
Because spot-induced RV signals recur at the rotation period (and its harmonics), so a match strongly suggests activity rather than a planet
Because the systemic velocity forbids it
Because rotation periods are always exactly one year

explanations.a: Planets can and do orbit at many periods; coincidence with rotation is the issue, not a speed limit.
explanations.b: Correct — starspots produce velocity signals locked to rotation, so a candidate period equal to (or half) the rotation period is a classic activity red flag.
explanations.c: γ is unrelated to the coincidence between orbital and rotation periods.
explanations.d: Rotation periods range from hours to months depending on the star; they are not fixed at a year.

questions.prompt: A real Doppler shift and a spot distortion differ in one testable way. Which diagnostic exploits it?

options.text: The line bisector: a true bulk shift leaves line shape unchanged, while a spot changes line asymmetry, so a bisector that correlates with the RV signals activity
The star’s apparent magnitude in a single filter
The telescope’s aperture diameter
The exposure time of each spectrum

explanations.a: Correct — a genuine Doppler shift translates the whole line rigidly (flat bisector vs. RV), whereas a spot distorts the profile, so a bisector span that tracks the RV betrays a line-shape origin.
explanations.b: Single-filter magnitude tracks brightness variability but does not distinguish a bulk shift from a shape change the way the bisector does.
explanations.c: Aperture affects photon collection, not whether the line shifted bodily or changed shape.
explanations.d: Exposure time affects signal-to-noise, not the bodily-shift-vs-distortion distinction.

questions.prompt: What is the lesson of the retracted Alpha Centauri Bb detection (claimed 2012, refuted 2016)?

options.text: That radial velocity never works below 100 m/s
That even an expert team can mistake an artifact of activity and observing-window sampling for a sub-m/s planet, so low-amplitude claims demand rigorous activity vetting
That Alpha Centauri B has no planets of any kind, ever
That transits are the only valid detection method

explanations.a: RV reaches well below 100 m/s (HARPS ~1 m/s, ESPRESSO ~10 cm/s); the issue is jitter, not a hard floor at 100 m/s.
explanations.b: Correct — Rajpaul, Aigrain & Roberts (2016) showed the 51 cm/s "signal" arose from the data sampling/window function plus activity, a cautionary tale that sub-m/s detections need careful vetting.
explanations.c: The retraction concerns one specific candidate signal, not a blanket claim that the star can never host planets.
explanations.d: The episode motivates better RV vetting, not the abandonment of RV for transits.

lessons.label: Chasing Earth-Analogs: HARPS, ESPRESSO, and the Sub-Meter-Per-Second Frontier

sections.heading: The 9 cm/s target and the instruments built to reach it
sections.body: Detecting an Earth twin around a Sun-like star means measuring a 9 cm/s wobble spread over a full year — the flagship challenge of precision RV. HARPS (the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher), on ESO’s 3.6 m telescope at La Silla since 2003, was the machine that first made ~1 m/s routine. Its design philosophy is stability above all: the spectrograph sits in a vacuum vessel, temperature-controlled to milli-kelvin levels, fed by fiber optics that scramble the light so the star’s image jitter does not masquerade as a velocity, and wavelength-calibrated against a stable reference so instrumental drift can be subtracted. ESPRESSO, commissioned on the 8.2 m Very Large Telescope in 2018, pushed the design to a ~10 cm/s goal and can even combine light from all four VLT unit telescopes; its wavelength scale is anchored by a laser frequency comb, a ruler of evenly spaced calibration lines far more stable than the older thorium-argon lamps. The engineering theme is that at these amplitudes, every source of instrumental drift is a potential fake planet.

sections.heading: A landmark within reach: Proxima Centauri b
sections.body: The nearest star to the Sun hosts a planet found this way. Proxima Centauri b, announced by Anglada-Escudé et al. (2016) from the "Pale Red Dot" HARPS campaign, produces a K ≈ 1.4 m/s signal on an 11.2-day period, implying a minimum mass of ≈ 1.3 Earth masses — and, because Proxima is a cool M dwarf, that 11.2-day orbit lands in the star’s habitable zone where liquid water could exist. It is a signal a thousand times smaller than 51 Peg b’s, and detecting it required years of velocities plus careful activity modeling to separate the planet from the flare-prone star’s jitter. Proxima b is the modern poster child for what precision RV around nearby M dwarfs can do: small stars give proportionally larger wobbles for the same planet (K scales as M_★^(−2/3)), and their close-in habitable zones give short, easily sampled periods, which is why the search for potentially habitable worlds leans heavily on red dwarfs.

sections.heading: The wall: the stellar activity floor and the next-generation fight
sections.body: The frontier is no longer mainly instrumental — comb-calibrated spectrographs are stable below the Earth-signal level. The wall is astrophysical: granulation, oscillations, and magnetic activity produce an RV "jitter floor" of order a m/s even on quiet stars, still an order of magnitude above Earth’s 9 cm/s. Beating it is the goal of a new generation — ESPRESSO, plus EXPRES, NEID, and the Keck Planet Finder (KPF) — and the strategies are as much about analysis as hardware: intensive time sampling to average over short-timescale convective noise, Gaussian-process and line-by-line activity modeling to subtract the star’s contribution, correction of telluric (Earth-atmosphere) absorption lines, and careful selection of the quietest stars. Whether a true Sun–Earth analog can be pulled out of the activity floor with RV alone is an open, actively debated question, and it is why complementary techniques (transits from PLATO, astrometry from Gaia) are pursued in parallel. The sub-m/s hunt is where instrumentation, stellar physics, and statistics meet.

lessons.workedExample: Compare the RV difficulty of three worlds around Sun-like or near-Sun-like stars to see why Earth is the hard case. 51 Peg b: K ≈ 59 m/s — detectable by 1990s spectrographs with ~15 m/s precision, so it was found first. Proxima b: K ≈ 1.4 m/s — needs a HARPS-class ~1 m/s instrument plus multi-year campaigns and activity modeling, achieved in 2016; note the boost from Proxima being a low-mass M dwarf (K ∝ M_★^(−2/3), so a lighter star wobbles more for the same planet). An Earth twin around a G star: K ≈ 0.09 m/s (9 cm/s) — an order of magnitude below even ESPRESSO’s ~10 cm/s design goal *and* buried under the ~1 m/s stellar activity floor. The arithmetic makes the strategy obvious: the same planet is far easier to detect around a small star, which is exactly why the nearest potentially habitable RV detections are around M dwarfs like Proxima, not solar twins, and why a genuine Sun–Earth analog remains at or beyond the current RV frontier.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the Earth-analog problem to test whether a student grasps that a detection limit is set by *both* instrument and star. A strong answer quantifies the target (≈ 9 cm/s over a year), names why it is hard (below the ~1 m/s stellar activity floor, and near the edge of instrument precision), and explains the M-dwarf strategy (K ∝ M_★^(−2/3), so smaller stars give bigger wobbles and closer habitable zones — the reason Proxima b was reachable). A student who thinks better telescopes alone will find Earth twins has missed the astrophysical floor; one who names HARPS/ESPRESSO precision, activity mitigation, and target selection together shows they understand where the real frontier is.

questions.prompt: Roughly what radial-velocity semi-amplitude must be measured to detect an Earth twin around a Sun-like star, and over what period?

options.text: About 59 m/s over 4 days
About 9 cm/s (0.09 m/s) over one year
About 12 m/s over 12 years
About 1 km/s over one month

explanations.a: That is 51 Peg b, a hot Jupiter — enormous compared to Earth’s signal.
explanations.b: Correct — Earth makes the Sun wobble at ≈ 9 cm/s spread over its 1-year orbit, the benchmark Earth-analog RV target.
explanations.c: That is roughly Jupiter’s reflex signal (12.5 m/s, 11.86 yr), not Earth’s.
explanations.d: A km/s is stellar bulk-motion scale, ten thousand times larger than Earth’s reflex signal.

questions.prompt: What is the primary barrier now standing between current spectrographs and an Earth-twin RV detection?

options.text: Telescopes cannot collect enough light
The astrophysical stellar activity/jitter floor (granulation, oscillations, magnetic activity) of order ~1 m/s, about ten times larger than Earth’s 9 cm/s signal
The speed of light is not known precisely enough
Earth’s orbit is too short to sample

explanations.a: Light-gathering is not the bottleneck; comb-calibrated spectrographs are stable below the Earth signal — the star itself is the problem.
explanations.b: Correct — stellar granulation, oscillations, and magnetic activity create a ~1 m/s jitter floor that dwarfs the 9 cm/s target, so activity mitigation, not just hardware, is the frontier.
explanations.c: The speed of light is a defined constant; it is not a limiting uncertainty here.
explanations.d: A 1-year period is easily sampled; the challenge is amplitude below the jitter, not period length.

questions.prompt: Why is the search for potentially habitable RV planets concentrated on M dwarfs like Proxima Centauri?

options.text: Because M dwarfs are the brightest stars, giving the best spectra
Because their low mass gives a larger reflex wobble for the same planet (K ∝ M_★^(−2/3)) and their close-in habitable zones give short, easily sampled orbital periods
Because M dwarfs have no starspots or activity
Because M dwarfs are the only stars close to the Sun

explanations.a: M dwarfs are faint, not bright; the advantage is dynamical, not luminosity.
explanations.b: Correct — a lighter star wobbles more for a given planet (K scales as M_★^(−2/3)), and the habitable zone sits close-in, giving short periods that are quick to sample — how Proxima b (K ≈ 1.4 m/s, 11.2 d) was found.
explanations.c: M dwarfs are notoriously active and flare-prone; activity is a major challenge, handled with careful modeling, not absent.
explanations.d: Many spectral types lie near the Sun; M dwarfs are simply the most numerous and dynamically favorable for this search.

questions.prompt: Order these RV detections/targets from EASIEST to HARDEST to detect by semi-amplitude.

items.text: 51 Peg b (K ≈ 59 m/s)
Proxima b (K ≈ 1.4 m/s)
Earth twin around a Sun-like star (K ≈ 0.09 m/s)

questions.explanation: 51 Peg b’s 59 m/s was reachable with 1990s ~15 m/s instruments; Proxima b’s 1.4 m/s needed HARPS-class ~1 m/s precision plus activity modeling (2016); an Earth twin’s 9 cm/s sits below both the ~10 cm/s instrument goal and the ~1 m/s stellar jitter floor, making it the hardest.

units.label: From Signal to Physical Planet: Radius, Mass, Density, and Class

lessons.label: Combining Transit and RV: Deriving Radius, True Mass, and Bulk Density

sections.heading: Two measurements, two different quantities
sections.body: The transit method and the radial-velocity (RV) method each measure something a single one cannot finish. A transit — a planet crossing the face of its star — gives the planet's SIZE: the fractional dip in brightness equals the ratio of areas, δ = (R_p / R_star)². A 1% dip on a Sun-like star means R_p / R_star = √0.01 = 0.1, so the planet is one-tenth the star's radius. But a transit says nothing about mass; a Styrofoam ball and a lead ball of the same size block the same light. The RV method measures the star's reflex wobble — the tiny back-and-forth Doppler shift of its spectral lines as the planet tugs it — which gives the planet's MASS. This is the technique Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz used to find 51 Pegasi b in 1995 (Nobel Prize in Physics 2019). Radius from transit, mass from RV: together they are the whole planet; apart, each is half a description.

sections.heading: The sin i problem, and why a transit fixes it
sections.body: RV alone does not give the true mass — it gives M_p · sin i, where i is the orbital inclination (the angle between the orbit plane and our line of sight). We only feel the component of the star's motion along our line of sight, so a face-on orbit (i = 0) produces no RV signal at all, and any RV-only mass is a LOWER LIMIT (a "minimum mass"). The elegant fix: a transit only happens when the orbit is very nearly edge-on to us, i ≈ 90°, so sin i ≈ 1. That means for any transiting planet the messy M_p · sin i collapses to the true M_p. This complementarity is exactly why the two methods are so powerful in combination — the transit both delivers the radius AND certifies the inclination that makes the RV mass real, not just a floor.

sections.heading: Radius plus mass equals density — the first real clue to composition
sections.body: Once you have a true radius and a true mass, you get bulk density, ρ = M_p / (4/3 · π · R_p³), and density is the first genuine window into what a planet is made of. A dense world (Earth is 5.5 g/cm³) is rock and iron; a low-density world (Saturn is 0.69 g/cm³, less than water) is a gas giant with a deep hydrogen/helium envelope; something near 1–3 g/cm³ may be a water world or a rock core under a thick atmosphere. The first exoplanet caught in transit, HD 209458 b, was found by David Charbonneau and colleagues and independently by Gregory Henry's team in 1999–2000, and its combined transit-plus-RV solution revealed a startling density well under that of water — a genuinely puffy, inflated hot Jupiter. Density is where a "detection" becomes a "characterization": you stop reporting that a planet exists and start arguing about what kind of world it is.

lessons.workedExample: Take HD 209458 b around its Sun-like star (R_star ≈ 1.2 R_sun). The transit depth is about δ ≈ 1.5%, so R_p / R_star = √0.015 ≈ 0.122, giving R_p ≈ 0.122 × 1.2 R_sun ≈ 0.147 R_sun ≈ 1.4 R_Jupiter — noticeably bigger than Jupiter. The RV wobble has a semi-amplitude K ≈ 85 m/s, which for this ~3.5-day orbit works out to a true mass (transit fixes sin i ≈ 1) of M_p ≈ 0.69 M_Jupiter. Now the payoff: mass 0.69 M_Jup ≈ 1.3 × 10²⁷ kg, radius 1.4 R_Jup ≈ 9.9 × 10⁷ m, volume 4/3·π·R³ ≈ 4.0 × 10²⁴ m³, so ρ ≈ 1.3 × 10²⁷ / 4.0 × 10²⁴ ≈ 330 kg/m³ ≈ 0.33 g/cm³. That is one-third the density of water — less than Saturn — a planet more mass than half a Jupiter puffed up bigger than Jupiter itself. Neither the 1.5% dip nor the 85 m/s wobble alone could have told you that; only the two together.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges press exoplanet students on "how do you know its mass, and is that the real mass or a lower limit?" because the sin i subtlety is the single most common place a project overclaims. A student who says "the transit forces i ≈ 90°, so my RV gives the true mass, not just M·sin i, and combining radius and mass gives a density of X g/cm³ that says rock versus gas" has demonstrated they understand why BOTH measurements are needed. One who reports a mass from RV alone without mentioning inclination, or a radius from transit and calls the planet "characterized," has missed the core logic of the field.

questions.prompt: A planet produces a transit depth of 0.25% (0.0025) on a star. What is R_p / R_star?

explanations.a: This is the depth itself; the depth equals the SQUARE of the radius ratio, so you must take a square root, not report the depth as the ratio.
explanations.b: Correct — depth δ = (R_p/R_star)², so R_p/R_star = √0.0025 = 0.05. The planet is 5% of the star's radius.
explanations.c: This is the depth squared; you went the wrong direction — square the ratio to get the depth, so invert by taking a root of the depth.
explanations.d: This would require a depth of 0.25 (25%), which no planet produces; you took the root of the wrong number.

questions.prompt: Why does a radial-velocity measurement of a NON-transiting planet give only a minimum mass?

options.text: Because spectrographs are not precise enough to measure the true mass
Because RV measures M_p · sin i, and without a transit the inclination i is unknown, so the true mass could be larger
Because the star's mass is unknown
Because the planet's radius is unknown

explanations.a: Precision is not the issue — even a perfect spectrograph measures only the line-of-sight velocity component, so the geometric sin i factor remains.
explanations.b: Correct — RV senses only the line-of-sight motion, so it constrains M_p · sin i. A more face-on orbit (smaller i, smaller sin i) means the true M_p must be larger to produce the same wobble, so the RV value is a floor.
explanations.c: The stellar mass is needed to interpret the wobble but is usually known from the star's spectrum; it is not the reason for the sin i degeneracy.
explanations.d: Radius (from transit) is irrelevant to the mass wobble; the minimum-mass issue is purely the unknown inclination.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to turn raw signals into a bulk density for a transiting planet.

items.text: Measure transit depth δ and convert to radius: R_p = R_star · √δ
Measure the RV semi-amplitude K of the star's wobble
Use the transit (i ≈ 90°, sin i ≈ 1) to convert M·sin i into true mass M_p
Combine M_p and R_p into density ρ = M_p / (4/3 · π · R_p³)

questions.explanation: The transit depth gives the radius; the RV amplitude gives the mass signal; the transit's near-edge-on geometry removes sin i to yield the true mass; and only with both a true mass and a true radius can you form the density. Density is the last step because it requires both prior products.

questions.prompt: A transiting planet is found to have a bulk density of 0.4 g/cm³. What does this most strongly suggest?

options.text: A dense iron-rich rocky planet
A gas-dominated giant with a deep hydrogen/helium envelope
A pure-water ocean world
A measurement error, since no planet can be that low

explanations.a: Rock-and-iron worlds like Earth are ~4–8 g/cm³, roughly ten to twenty times denser than this; 0.4 g/cm³ cannot be rocky.
explanations.b: Correct — 0.4 g/cm³ is below the density of water and comparable to Saturn (0.69 g/cm³) or the puffy hot Jupiter HD 209458 b, indicating a light hydrogen/helium-dominated gas giant.
explanations.c: A water world is around 1–2 g/cm³ (water is 1.0); 0.4 g/cm³ is far too low for even pure water and demands a light gas envelope.
explanations.d: Real planets such as HD 209458 b and WASP-17 b genuinely have densities this low; it is a physical result, not an error.

lessons.label: Kepler's Third Law in Practice: Orbital Distance from Period and Stellar Mass

sections.heading: From a period you can time to a distance you cannot see
sections.body: A transit gives you the orbital PERIOD directly and precisely — you just measure the spacing between dips, and repeated transits over years pin the period to many decimal places. But the quantity you actually want for the physics (equilibrium temperature, insolation, tidal forces, whether the planet is in the habitable zone) is the orbital DISTANCE, and you never see that distance directly. The bridge is Kepler's third law. Johannes Kepler published it in 1619 (Harmonices Mundi) as an empirical pattern for the Solar System: the square of a planet's period is proportional to the cube of its orbital semi-major axis. Isaac Newton later derived it from gravity and, crucially, showed the proportionality constant depends on the total mass — turning Kepler's pattern into a mass-measuring tool.

sections.heading: The Newtonian form, and the convenient solar-unit shortcut
sections.body: Newton's generalized third law is P² = 4π²a³ / [G(M_star + M_p)]. For a planet, M_p is almost always negligible next to the star, so P² ≈ 4π²a³ / (G·M_star). The messy constants vanish if you choose the right units: measure the period P in years, the semi-major axis a in astronomical units (AU), and the stellar mass M_star in solar masses, and the law becomes simply a³ = M_star · P². (For the Sun, M_star = 1 and you recover Earth's a³ = 1·1² = 1 AU.) So the recipe to characterize a transiting planet's orbit is: get P from the transit spacing, get M_star from the star's spectral type or asteroseismology, then solve a = (M_star · P²)^(1/3). This is one of the highest-leverage calculations in exoplanet work because it converts two things you CAN measure into the distance you need.

sections.heading: Why the stellar mass matters, and where the uncertainty hides
sections.body: The orbital distance you derive is only as good as the stellar mass you feed in — and because a enters as the cube root of M_star, the distance is fairly forgiving of stellar-mass error (a 30% error in mass gives only about a 9% error in a, since 1.3^(1/3) ≈ 1.09). This is why exoplanet characterization leans so heavily on getting the STAR right first: a planet's radius scales with the stellar radius (from the transit depth), its mass scales with the stellar mass (from RV), and its orbital distance scales with the stellar mass through Kepler's law. The mantra "know thy star" is not a slogan — the Gaia mission's precise parallaxes and the stellar parameters from spectroscopy are what let modern surveys convert the same raw light curve into a physically reliable planet. A wrong stellar mass propagates into a wrong distance, a wrong temperature, and a wrong verdict on habitability.

lessons.workedExample: Consider 51 Pegasi b, the first exoplanet found around a Sun-like star. It was detected by radial velocity — no transit has ever been seen — but Kepler's third law needs only the orbital period and the stellar mass, so it works for RV-only planets just as well. Its RV-measured period is P ≈ 4.23 days, and its host star is slightly more massive than the Sun, M_star ≈ 1.11 M_sun. Convert the period to years: P = 4.23 / 365.25 ≈ 0.01158 yr. Apply the solar-unit law: a³ = M_star · P² = 1.11 × (0.01158)² = 1.11 × 1.341 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 1.488 × 10⁻⁴. Take the cube root: a = (1.488 × 10⁻⁴)^(1/3) ≈ 0.053 AU. That matches the published value (~0.052 AU) and confirms 51 Peg b as a "hot Jupiter" orbiting roughly one-twentieth of Earth's distance from the Sun — a result so unexpected in 1995 that it forced theorists to invent planetary migration. Notice the whole distance came from a timing measurement (the period) and a stellar mass; the AU itself was never observed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "you measured a period — how did you get the orbital distance, and what did that require?" because it tests whether a student understands that the physically interesting quantities are DERIVED, not measured, and that they rest on the stellar mass. A strong answer states Kepler's third law in the a³ = M_star · P² solar-unit form, names where the stellar mass came from, and notes that because a depends on the cube root of the mass the distance is relatively robust to stellar-mass error. That shows the student can chain measurements into physics rather than treating "distance" as something the telescope handed them.

questions.prompt: In solar units (P in years, a in AU, M in solar masses), Kepler's third law for a planet is:

options.text: a² = M_star · P³
a³ = M_star · P²
a = M_star · P
P³ = M_star · a²

explanations.a: The exponents are swapped — it is the CUBE of the distance that equals the SQUARE of the period, not the reverse.
explanations.b: Correct — with P in years, a in AU, and M_star in solar masses, the constants cancel and P² = a³/M_star, i.e. a³ = M_star · P². For the Sun and Earth this gives 1³ = 1·1².
explanations.c: This linear form is dimensionally wrong and does not reproduce Earth's known values; the relation is a power law with cube and square, not linear.
explanations.d: This inverts the powers; the period is squared and the axis is cubed, so P² = a³/M_star, not P³ = M_star·a².

questions.prompt: A transiting planet has period P = 8 days around a star of mass 1.0 M_sun. Approximately what is its orbital distance?

options.text: About 0.08 AU
About 0.35 AU
About 1.0 AU
About 8 AU

explanations.a: Correct — P = 8/365.25 ≈ 0.0219 yr, so a³ = 1.0 × (0.0219)² ≈ 4.8 × 10⁻⁴, and a ≈ (4.8 × 10⁻⁴)^(1/3) ≈ 0.078 ≈ 0.08 AU, a classic short-period orbit.
explanations.b: This overestimates; you likely forgot to convert 8 days into years before squaring, or took a root incorrectly.
explanations.c: 1 AU corresponds to a 1-year (365-day) period around a Sun-mass star, not an 8-day one; an 8-day orbit is far tighter.
explanations.d: This is off by orders of magnitude — an 8 AU orbit around the Sun would have a period of about 22 years, not 8 days.

questions.prompt: Why is the derived orbital distance relatively insensitive to errors in the stellar mass?

options.text: Because the stellar mass does not appear in Kepler's law at all
Because a depends on the cube root of M_star, so even a 30% mass error yields only about a 9% distance error
Because the planet's mass cancels the stellar mass
Because the period measurement is imprecise anyway

explanations.a: The stellar mass is central — a³ = M_star · P². It does appear; the point is how weakly it propagates.
explanations.b: Correct — since a ∝ M_star^(1/3), fractional errors are cut by a factor of three: 1.30^(1/3) ≈ 1.09, so 30% in mass becomes ~9% in distance.
explanations.c: The planet's mass is negligible and dropped from the equation; it does not "cancel" the stellar mass.
explanations.d: The period is typically the MOST precise quantity in the whole problem (measured over many transits), so it is not the source of forgiveness here.

questions.prompt: Match each measured/known input to the planet property it lets you derive.

left.text: RV amplitude + stellar mass (transit fixes sin i)

right.text: Planet radius
Planet true mass
Orbital distance (via Kepler's third law)

questions.explanation: Transit depth against areas (with the stellar radius) gives the planet radius; the RV amplitude with the stellar mass and the transit-fixed inclination gives the true planet mass; the period with the stellar mass, through a³ = M_star·P², gives the orbital distance. Each planet property is anchored to a corresponding stellar property.
