lessons.label: Equilibrium Temperature, Albedo, and the Insolation a Planet Receives

sections.heading: Insolation: how much starlight actually reaches the planet
sections.body: Once Kepler's law gives the orbital distance a, you can compute the INSOLATION — the stellar flux the planet intercepts — which is just the star's luminosity spread over a sphere of radius a: S = L_star / (4π·a²). The inverse-square falloff is the whole story: a planet twice as far from its star receives one-quarter the flux. Astronomers usually quote insolation in units of Earth's (S⊕, the ~1361 W/m² solar constant), because that immediately tells you whether a world is being baked or frozen relative to home. A hot Jupiter at 0.05 AU around a Sun-like star soaks up roughly (1/0.05)² = 400 times Earth's insolation; a planet at 5 AU gets 1/25 of it. Insolation, not raw distance, is what sets a planet's thermal fate, and it folds in the star's luminosity so a cool red dwarf's habitable zone sits far closer in than the Sun's.

sections.heading: Equilibrium temperature: balancing absorbed and emitted energy
sections.body: The equilibrium temperature T_eq is what you get by demanding energy balance: the power a planet absorbs from starlight equals the thermal power it radiates as a blackbody. Working that balance out gives T_eq = T_star · √(R_star / 2a) · (1 − A)^(1/4), where T_star and R_star are the star's temperature and radius, a is the orbital distance, and A is the Bond albedo — the fraction of incident starlight the planet reflects rather than absorbs. Two features matter. First, T_eq falls only as the SQUARE ROOT of distance (T ∝ a^(−1/2)), a gentler dependence than insolation's inverse square, because temperature goes as the fourth root of flux. Second, albedo enters weakly, as the FOURTH root of (1 − A): a perfectly reflective world (A = 1) would be at absolute zero, but going from a dark A = 0 to a bright A = 0.5 multiplies T_eq by (0.5)^(1/4) ≈ 0.84, only about a 16% reduction.

sections.heading: Why equilibrium temperature is a floor, not the surface temperature
sections.body: T_eq is a physicist's idealization — the temperature of an airless (or thin-atmosphere) blackbody in radiative balance — and it is deliberately NOT the surface temperature of a planet with a real atmosphere. Greenhouse gases absorb the planet's outgoing infrared and re-radiate some back down, warming the surface ABOVE T_eq. Earth is the textbook case: its equilibrium temperature is about 255 K (−18 °C, below freezing), yet its actual surface averages ~288 K (15 °C) — the ~33 K difference is the natural greenhouse effect, without which our oceans would freeze. Venus is the extreme: T_eq near 230 K but a surface of ~735 K under a runaway CO₂ greenhouse. So when a survey reports a planet's "equilibrium temperature," a careful student reads it as a baseline set by starlight and albedo, knowing the true surface could be much hotter if the planet holds a thick atmosphere. The habitable-zone concept (formalized by James Kasting and colleagues in 1993) is built on exactly this reasoning — the range of orbits where a rocky planet with a plausible atmosphere could sustain liquid surface water.

lessons.workedExample: Compute Earth's equilibrium temperature from scratch. Use T_star = 5772 K (the Sun), R_star = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, a = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, and Earth's Bond albedo A = 0.30. First the geometric factor: R_star / (2a) = 6.96 × 10⁸ / (2 × 1.496 × 10¹¹) = 2.33 × 10⁻³, and its square root is 0.0482. Multiply by T_star: 5772 × 0.0482 ≈ 278 K — that is the temperature of a perfectly absorbing (A = 0) Earth. Now apply albedo: (1 − 0.30)^(1/4) = 0.70^(0.25) ≈ 0.915, so T_eq ≈ 278 × 0.915 ≈ 255 K. That is the famous −18 °C figure — below freezing. Earth's real average surface temperature is ~288 K; the 33 K gap is exactly the greenhouse effect, and reproducing the 255 K value is how atmospheric scientists first quantified how much warming our atmosphere supplies.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe "what is the equilibrium temperature and is that the surface temperature?" because conflating the two is a signature of a student who plugged into a formula without understanding it. The give-away of real understanding is stating that T_eq is a radiative-balance blackbody baseline set by insolation and albedo, that it scales only as a^(−1/2) and weakly with albedo, and that a real atmosphere's greenhouse effect makes the surface hotter — citing Earth's 255 K vs 288 K. A student who reports 255 K as "Earth's temperature" without the greenhouse caveat has revealed they do not grasp what the number means.

questions.prompt: A planet's orbital distance is doubled (same star). How does the insolation it receives change?

options.text: It halves
It drops to one-quarter
It stays the same
It doubles

explanations.a: Halving would be a 1/a dependence, but flux spreads over the surface of a sphere, which grows as a², so the falloff is steeper.
explanations.b: Correct — insolation S = L/(4π·a²) follows the inverse-square law, so doubling a multiplies flux by (1/2)² = 1/4.
explanations.c: Flux definitely changes with distance; the inverse-square law guarantees a farther planet gets less light.
explanations.d: It decreases, not increases — moving away from the star can only reduce the flux received.

questions.prompt: Equilibrium temperature depends on orbital distance as:

options.text: T_eq ∝ a⁻² (inverse square, like insolation)
T_eq ∝ a⁻¹ᐟ² (inverse square root)
T_eq ∝ a (linear)
T_eq is independent of distance

explanations.a: Insolation (flux) goes as a⁻², but temperature is the FOURTH root of flux, so the two inverse-square powers become a^(−2/4) = a^(−1/2).
explanations.b: Correct — since flux ∝ a⁻² and blackbody flux ∝ T⁴, temperature ∝ (flux)^(1/4) ∝ a^(−2/4) = a^(−1/2). Temperature falls more gently than flux.
explanations.c: Temperature falls, not rises, with distance, and not linearly; the dependence is a negative fractional power.
explanations.d: Distance strongly affects temperature through the flux; it is certainly not independent.

questions.prompt: Earth's equilibrium temperature is about 255 K, yet its average surface temperature is about 288 K. Why the difference?

options.text: The equilibrium formula is simply wrong for Earth
The greenhouse effect: atmospheric gases absorb outgoing infrared and re-radiate some downward, warming the surface above the blackbody baseline
Earth reflects less light than the formula assumes
Internal heat from Earth's core supplies the extra 33 K

explanations.a: The formula is correct as the radiative-balance baseline; the point is that it deliberately ignores atmospheric greenhouse warming, so 255 K is right for what it models.
explanations.b: Correct — greenhouse gases (water vapor, CO₂) trap outgoing infrared and warm the surface ~33 K above the 255 K equilibrium value; this is the natural greenhouse effect.
explanations.c: The 255 K value already uses Earth's albedo (0.30); reflection is accounted for and is not the source of the extra warming.
explanations.d: Geothermal heat flux at the surface is minuscule compared with sunlight (~0.09 W/m² versus ~240 W/m² absorbed) and cannot supply 33 K of warming.

questions.prompt: Two identical rocky planets orbit the same star at the same distance, but one has albedo A = 0 (perfectly black) and the other A = 0.5. How do their equilibrium temperatures compare?

options.text: The A = 0.5 planet is about half as hot
The A = 0.5 planet is only about 16% cooler, because albedo enters as (1 − A)^(1/4)
They are identical, since albedo does not affect temperature
The A = 0.5 planet is hotter, because it reflects more energy

explanations.a: Halving would require (1 − A) to enter linearly, but it enters as a fourth root, greatly softening the effect.
explanations.b: Correct — T_eq ∝ (1 − A)^(1/4), so going from A = 0 to A = 0.5 multiplies temperature by (0.5)^(1/4) ≈ 0.84, about a 16% reduction.
explanations.c: Albedo does affect temperature — a more reflective planet absorbs less starlight and runs cooler; it simply enters weakly.
explanations.d: Reflecting more light means absorbing LESS, so a higher-albedo planet is cooler, not hotter.

lessons.label: The Mass-Radius Diagram: Rocky, Water, Gas, and Degenerate Interiors

sections.heading: The master diagnostic plot of the field
sections.body: Plot every well-characterized planet with mass on one axis and radius on the other, overlay theoretical curves for different compositions, and you have the mass-radius diagram — the single most-used interpretive tool in exoplanet science. Because a point on this plot is really a density (ρ = M / (4/3·π·R³)), a planet's position relative to the theoretical curves tells you what it is made of without ever landing on it. The composition curves, computed by matching the equation of state of candidate materials to hydrostatic balance, stack from bottom to top: pure iron (densest, smallest radius for a given mass), Earth-like rock (silicate mantle over iron core), pure water/ice, and hydrogen/helium gas (least dense, largest radius). A measured planet that lands on the "rock" curve is rock; one that sits well above the water curve must have a light gas envelope. Foundational modern reference curves come from work like Sara Seager and colleagues (2007) and Jonathan Fortney and colleagues (2007).

sections.heading: For rocky and icy planets, bigger mass means bigger radius — but sublinearly
sections.body: For solid planets (rock, iron, water) radius grows with mass, but slowly: adding mass compresses the interior, so the radius rises roughly as R ∝ M^0.27 for terrestrial worlds. Double a rocky planet's mass and its radius grows only ~20%, because the extra material is squeezed into a denser interior rather than puffing the planet out. This sublinear growth is why "super-Earths" a few times Earth's mass are only modestly larger than Earth in radius. The curves for different solid compositions run roughly parallel and offset: at any given mass, a water world has a larger radius (lower density) than a rock world, which is larger than a pure-iron world. Mercury, unusually dense for its size, sits low toward the iron curve; this is how the diagram flags composition anomalies.

sections.heading: The turnover: where degeneracy pressure makes more mass mean SMALLER radius
sections.body: The most counterintuitive feature is at the top. For gas giants, radius increases with mass only up to about a Jupiter mass, then FLATTENS — Jupiter and Saturn have nearly the same radius despite Jupiter being three times more massive — and beyond a few Jupiter masses the radius actually DECREASES with added mass. The reason is electron degeneracy pressure: in very massive, dense hydrogen/helium bodies the electrons are packed so tightly that quantum (Pauli) pressure, not thermal pressure, holds the object up, and for a degeneracy-supported sphere adding mass increases the self-gravity faster than the pressure can resist, so the object shrinks. This is the same physics that governs white dwarfs, where it culminates in the Chandrasekhar mass — about 1.4 solar masses — the maximum mass a white dwarf's electron degeneracy pressure can support before it collapses. Zapolsky and Salpeter worked out this mass-radius behavior for cold spheres back in 1969. So the mass-radius diagram spans a continuous physical story: from compressible rock, through the H/He plateau, into the degenerate regime shared by giant planets, brown dwarfs, and white dwarfs.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose you have characterized a planet at M_p = 5 M⊕ and R_p = 1.5 R⊕ and want to read its composition off the diagram. First get the density: in Earth units, ρ/ρ⊕ = (M/M⊕)/(R/R⊕)³ = 5 / (1.5)³ = 5 / 3.375 ≈ 1.48, so about 1.5 times Earth's 5.5 g/cm³, i.e. ~8.2 g/cm³. That is DENSER than Earth — the planet plots below the Earth-composition curve, toward the iron curve, so it is a rock-iron super-Earth, likely with a large metallic core, not a water world. Contrast a second planet at M_p = 5 M⊕ but R_p = 2.4 R⊕: now ρ/ρ⊕ = 5 / (2.4)³ = 5 / 13.8 ≈ 0.36, only ~2 g/cm³. That plots ABOVE the pure-water curve, too puffy to be rock or even pure water — it needs a hydrogen/helium envelope, marking it a sub-Neptune. Same mass, radically different worlds, and the diagram reads the difference straight off the radius.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "what does your planet's spot on the mass-radius diagram tell you, and why does the top of the diagram turn over?" because it distinguishes students who treat the plot as a lookup table from those who understand the physics behind each regime. A strong answer explains that position encodes density and hence composition (iron vs rock vs water vs gas), that solid planets grow sublinearly (R ∝ M^~0.27), and that beyond ~1 Jupiter mass electron degeneracy pressure flattens and then reverses the trend — the same physics that gives white dwarfs the ~1.4-solar-mass Chandrasekhar limit. That connects a single planet to the deep physics of matter under pressure.

questions.prompt: On the mass-radius diagram, why do more massive gas giants (beyond ~1 Jupiter mass) have SMALLER radii?

options.text: They lose mass to their star, shrinking over time
Electron degeneracy pressure supports them, and for a degenerate sphere added mass increases gravity faster than pressure can resist, so it contracts
They are made of denser elements than smaller giants
Their higher temperature makes them contract

explanations.a: Mass loss is not the cause of the mass-radius turnover; the trend is a static structural property of degenerate matter, seen even in stable objects.
explanations.b: Correct — in massive, dense H/He bodies electrons become degenerate and quantum pressure dominates; for such objects the mass-radius relation inverts, so more mass means a smaller radius, the same physics as white dwarfs.
explanations.c: Composition is essentially the same H/He; the shrinkage comes from the degenerate equation of state, not a switch to heavier elements.
explanations.d: Higher temperature would tend to inflate a gas body, not shrink it; the contraction is due to degeneracy pressure's equation of state, not heat.

questions.prompt: A planet plots with a density about 1.5 times Earth's on the mass-radius diagram. Its most likely composition is:

options.text: A hydrogen/helium gas giant
A rock-iron world, possibly iron-enriched, denser than Earth
A pure-water ocean world
A sub-Neptune with a thick gas envelope

explanations.a: Gas giants have densities near or below water (~0.7–1.3 g/cm³), an order of magnitude lower than 1.5× Earth (~8 g/cm³); this planet is far too dense to be gaseous.
explanations.b: Correct — a density above Earth's points to a rock-iron composition with a substantial metallic core (like Mercury's high density), plotting toward the iron curve.
explanations.c: A water world is LESS dense than Earth (water is 1.0 g/cm³ versus Earth's 5.5); 1.5× Earth's density rules out a water-dominated interior.
explanations.d: A sub-Neptune is puffy and low-density; a super-Earth-density planet is the opposite of that.

questions.prompt: The Chandrasekhar mass (~1.4 solar masses) is:

options.text: The maximum mass of any exoplanet
The maximum mass a white dwarf's electron degeneracy pressure can support before collapse
The mass of the Sun in a different unit system
The minimum mass a star needs to fuse hydrogen

explanations.a: Exoplanets top out far below a stellar mass; the Chandrasekhar limit is a stellar-remnant concept, not a planetary one, though it shares the degeneracy physics.
explanations.b: Correct — it is the ceiling (~1.4 M_sun) above which electron degeneracy pressure can no longer hold up a white dwarf, driving collapse; the same degeneracy physics flattens the giant-planet mass-radius curve.
explanations.c: It is about 1.4 solar masses, a physical limit, not merely a re-expressed solar mass.
explanations.d: The hydrogen-fusion threshold (~0.08 M_sun) is a different limit; the Chandrasekhar mass concerns degeneracy support in remnants.

questions.prompt: Match each composition to its position on the mass-radius diagram (at a fixed mass).

right.text: Smallest radius / highest density
Small radius, denser than water
Larger radius, lower density than rock
Largest radius / lowest density

questions.explanation: At a fixed mass, composition sets the radius by density: iron is densest (smallest radius), then silicate rock, then water/ice (puffier), then hydrogen/helium gas (least dense, largest radius). This ordering is exactly what lets the diagram read composition off a measured mass and radius.

lessons.label: The Radius Valley: Super-Earths, Sub-Neptunes, and the Gap Between Them

sections.heading: A gap that turned up when the radii got precise enough
sections.body: When you histogram the radii of small close-in planets, you do not get a smooth distribution — you get two peaks with a valley between them. Small planets cluster around ~1.3 Earth radii (super-Earths) and around ~2.4 Earth radii (sub-Neptunes), with a conspicuous DEFICIT of planets near ~1.8 R⊕. This "radius valley" (also called the Fulton gap) was revealed in 2017 by Benjamin Fulton and collaborators using the California-Kepler Survey, which obtained precise host-star radii (later sharpened by Gaia parallaxes) and thereby precise PLANET radii. The gap had been predicted theoretically before it was seen — but it only became visible once stellar and planetary radii were measured to a few percent, a reminder that "know thy star" is what makes fine features in planet demographics detectable at all.

sections.heading: Two populations, one likely origin: rocky cores with and without envelopes
sections.body: The leading interpretation is that both peaks are rocky cores of similar mass, and the split is about whether a core kept a thin hydrogen/helium envelope. The super-Earth peak (below ~1.5 R⊕) is bare rocky cores — their measured densities are consistent with Earth-like rock. The sub-Neptune peak (~2–3 R⊕) is the SAME kind of core but wrapped in a hydrogen/helium envelope just a percent or two of the planet's mass — yet because gas is so extended, even a tiny envelope roughly doubles the observed radius. The valley at ~1.8 R⊕ is then the "forbidden" in-between: a core either holds enough gas to be a puffy sub-Neptune or loses essentially all of it to become a bare super-Earth, and little sits in the middle. Crucially, the valley's location shifts with orbital period and stellar mass in ways these models predict, which is why demographics — not just individual planets — became decisive evidence.

sections.heading: The mechanism debate: photoevaporation versus core-powered mass loss
sections.body: What strips the envelopes is genuinely contested, with two leading mechanisms making similar predictions. PHOTOEVAPORATION (developed by James Owen and Yanqin Wu, notably 2013 and 2017) holds that high-energy X-ray and ultraviolet radiation from the young star in its first ~100 million years heats and blows off the envelope; planets closer in, or around more active stars, lose more, carving the valley. CORE-POWERED MASS LOSS (Sivan Ginzburg and colleagues 2018; Akash Gupta and Hilke Schlichting 2019) instead argues the escaping energy comes from the planet's OWN cooling luminosity — the hot rocky core radiates its formation heat outward over ~billions of years, slowly driving the envelope off, no strong stellar X-rays required. Both predict a bimodal radius distribution with a valley near ~1.8 R⊕, so telling them apart relies on subtle differences — how the valley's position depends on stellar mass, orbital period, and stellar age, and on the exact envelope-mass distribution. This is a live front in the field, precisely the kind of open question where new precise radii keep tipping the balance.

lessons.workedExample: You have two close-in planets around similar stars. Planet A: M = 4 M⊕, R = 1.3 R⊕. Planet B: M = 5 M⊕, R = 2.5 R⊕. Compute densities in Earth units. Planet A: ρ/ρ⊕ = 4 / (1.3)³ = 4 / 2.20 ≈ 1.8, so ~1.8× Earth — consistent with bare Earth-like rock (in fact slightly iron-enhanced); it sits in the super-Earth peak below the valley. Planet B: ρ/ρ⊕ = 5 / (2.5)³ = 5 / 15.6 ≈ 0.32, only ~0.3× Earth (~1.8 g/cm³) — far too low for rock or even pure water, so despite a rocky core it must carry a hydrogen/helium envelope; it sits in the sub-Neptune peak above the valley. Notice their MASSES are nearly the same (4 vs 5 M⊕); what separates them across the ~1.8 R⊕ gap is not the core but whether an envelope survived — exactly the picture the photoevaporation and core-powered-mass-loss models are competing to explain.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "why is there a gap in the small-planet radius distribution, and what makes it?" because it rewards students who think in POPULATIONS and understand an open debate rather than reciting one planet. A strong answer names the radius valley near ~1.8 R⊕ (Fulton et al. 2017), explains the two peaks as rocky cores with versus without a thin H/He envelope, and lays out the two competing loss mechanisms — stellar-driven photoevaporation (Owen & Wu) versus internally-driven core-powered mass loss (Gupta & Schlichting) — noting they are hard to distinguish because both predict the same valley. Naming a genuine, unresolved controversy accurately is exactly the mark of scientific maturity judges look for.

questions.prompt: The "radius valley" (Fulton gap) refers to:

options.text: A gap in the orbital distances of hot Jupiters
A deficit of small planets near ~1.8 Earth radii, between super-Earth and sub-Neptune peaks
The gap between the innermost planet and its star
A gap in planet masses near one Jupiter mass

explanations.a: The valley is about planet RADII of small planets, not the orbital-distance distribution of giant planets.
explanations.b: Correct — Fulton et al. (2017) found the small-planet radius distribution is bimodal, peaking near ~1.3 and ~2.4 R⊕ with a deficit around ~1.8 R⊕.
explanations.c: It is a feature of the planet SIZE distribution across many systems, not a spatial gap within one system.
explanations.d: The valley is in radius, not mass; the mass-radius turnover near a Jupiter mass is a separate phenomenon (degeneracy).

questions.prompt: Why does a sub-Neptune (~2.4 R⊕) have roughly double the radius of a super-Earth (~1.3 R⊕) even when their rocky cores are similar in mass?

options.text: The sub-Neptune's core is made of much lighter rock
A thin hydrogen/helium envelope of only ~1–2% of the mass is so extended that it roughly doubles the observed radius
The sub-Neptune is much hotter and thermally expanded rock
The sub-Neptune has a larger iron core

explanations.a: The cores are essentially the same rocky composition; the difference is the envelope, not a lighter rock.
explanations.b: Correct — hydrogen/helium is extremely low-density and puffy, so even a tiny envelope by mass adds a large gas layer, roughly doubling the radius over a bare core.
explanations.c: Thermal expansion of rock is negligible at these scales and cannot account for a doubling in radius; a gas envelope can.
explanations.d: A larger iron core would make it SMALLER and denser, the opposite of the puffy sub-Neptune.

questions.prompt: Match each envelope-loss mechanism to its defining energy source and key proponents.

right.text: Young star's high-energy X-ray/UV radiation over ~100 Myr (Owen & Wu)
The planet's own cooling luminosity over ~Gyr (Gupta & Schlichting)

questions.explanation: Photoevaporation (Owen & Wu) drives the envelope off using the young star's X-ray/UV flux in its first ~100 million years; core-powered mass loss (Gupta & Schlichting 2019, following Ginzburg et al. 2018) instead uses the planet's internal heat of formation radiating outward over billions of years. Both predict a radius valley near ~1.8 R⊕, which is why they are hard to distinguish.

questions.prompt: Why did the radius valley only become clearly visible around 2017, not in early Kepler data?

options.text: Kepler had not yet found enough planets
Precise host-star radii (from the California-Kepler Survey, later Gaia) were needed to pin down planet radii to a few percent and resolve the gap
The valley only appeared after 2017 as planets evolved
Early Kepler could not measure orbital periods accurately

explanations.a: Kepler had already found thousands of small planets; the limitation was the PRECISION of their radii, not the sample size.
explanations.b: Correct — a planet's radius is only as precise as its host star's radius (transit depth gives R_p/R_star), so better stellar parameters from the California-Kepler Survey and Gaia sharpened planet radii enough to reveal the gap.
explanations.c: The valley is a long-standing demographic feature, not something that physically materialized in 2017; only its DETECTION is recent.
explanations.d: Kepler measured periods extremely well from the start; the bottleneck was radius precision, which depends on the stellar radius.

lessons.label: Inflated Hot Jupiters: The Radius-Anomaly Puzzle and Its Candidate Explanations

sections.heading: Planets bigger than the models allow
sections.body: Standard planet-structure models predict that a Jupiter-mass, hydrogen/helium planet, left to cool over billions of years, should settle to a radius close to Jupiter's (about 1 R_Jup) or a bit smaller. Yet a large fraction of hot Jupiters — gas giants on short, hot orbits — are measurably LARGER, from ~1.2 up to nearly 2 R_Jup. The very first transiting planet, HD 209458 b, was already a puzzle: at ~1.4 R_Jup and only ~0.7 M_Jup, its density (~0.3 g/cm³) is far too low for an old, quietly cooling giant. The extreme cases are even more striking: WASP-17 b is about 2 R_Jup with a density near 0.1 g/cm³, less than cork. These planets are "inflated" — they are hotter and puffier inside than an isolated giant of the same age and mass should be — and explaining the extra internal heat is the radius-anomaly problem, an active puzzle for two decades.

sections.heading: The clinching clue: radius correlates with the starlight received
sections.body: The decisive observational fact is that the amount of inflation tracks the INSOLATION. Planets that receive more stellar flux are, on average, more inflated — a correlation quantified in analyses by Brice-Olivier Demory and Sara Seager (2011), by Gregory Laughlin and colleagues (2011), and by Neil Miller and Jonathan Fortney (2011), who noted that below a threshold of roughly 2 × 10⁸ erg/s/cm² of incident flux, giant planets are NOT anomalously large, while above it they increasingly are. This flux dependence is the central constraint any explanation must satisfy: whatever inflates hot Jupiters must be powered by, or switched on by, the intense irradiation of a close-in orbit. It immediately rules out explanations that do not scale with starlight and points toward mechanisms that deposit stellar energy deep in the planet or slow its ability to cool and shrink.

sections.heading: Competing mechanisms, none yet decisive
sections.body: Several mechanisms remain in contention, and the community has not settled on one. OHMIC DISSIPATION (Konstantin Batygin and David Stevenson, 2010) proposes that the hot, partially-ionized atmosphere's fast winds sweep through the planet's magnetic field, driving electrical currents whose resistive (ohmic) heating warms the deep interior — naturally tied to irradiation because hotter atmospheres are more ionized and windier. TIDAL HEATING can inflate a planet if its orbit is eccentric, as flexing dissipates energy inside, though many hot Jupiters have circularized orbits, limiting this channel. ENHANCED ATMOSPHERIC OPACITY / DELAYED COOLING holds that strong irradiation and metal-rich atmospheres trap the planet's internal heat, slowing the contraction so the planet stays large longer. THERMAL TIDES and turbulent downward heat transport have also been proposed. A key discriminator is REINFLATION: some planets appear to swell as their star brightens with age, which is hard for mechanisms (like tidal heating during migration) that act only early and favors mechanisms that continuously inject or trap heat, such as ohmic dissipation. The radius-anomaly puzzle is a textbook example of a well-established EMPIRICAL correlation (inflation with flux) whose underlying MECHANISM is still genuinely open.

lessons.workedExample: Take HD 209458 b and test it against the flux threshold. Its host is Sun-like (L ≈ 1 L_sun) and it orbits at a ≈ 0.047 AU. Insolation relative to Earth is S/S⊕ = (L/L_sun)/(a/AU)² = 1 / (0.047)² ≈ 1 / 0.0022 ≈ 450 — roughly 450 times Earth's insolation. In cgs that is about 450 × 1.36 × 10⁶ erg/s/cm² ≈ 6 × 10⁸ erg/s/cm², comfortably ABOVE the ~2 × 10⁸ erg/s/cm² threshold identified by Miller & Fortney (2011). The model prediction: this planet should be inflated — and indeed it is, at ~1.4 R_Jup versus the ~1.0–1.1 R_Jup a non-irradiated 0.7 M_Jup giant would settle to. Now contrast a cool giant far from its star, receiving only a few times Earth's flux, below the threshold: it is expected to (and does) sit at the normal ~1 R_Jup. The single variable that best predicts which giants are puffed up is not their mass or age but the starlight they drink in — the observation every candidate mechanism must reproduce.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the inflated-hot-Jupiter problem with "your planet is bigger than models predict — why, and how sure are you of the cause?" because it tests whether a student can hold a firmly established observation and an unresolved mechanism in mind at once. The strongest answer states the empirical anchor (radius correlates with insolation above a ~2 × 10⁸ erg/s/cm² flux threshold, per Miller & Fortney 2011 and Demory & Seager 2011), then lays out competing mechanisms — ohmic dissipation (Batygin & Stevenson 2010), tidal heating, delayed cooling — and explicitly says which is favored and why (e.g., reinflation evidence disfavors early-only mechanisms). Distinguishing "what we observe" from "what we think causes it" is exactly the intellectual honesty judges reward.

questions.prompt: What is the "radius anomaly" of hot Jupiters?

options.text: Their radii shrink faster than models predict
Many are substantially LARGER (~1.2 to ~2 R_Jup) than cooling models predict for their mass and age
Their radii cannot be measured because they are too hot
They all have exactly the same radius

explanations.a: The anomaly is the opposite — they are too LARGE, not too small; they fail to shrink as much as an isolated cooling giant should.
explanations.b: Correct — a large fraction of hot Jupiters are inflated well beyond the ~1 R_Jup that standard structure models predict for an old H/He giant, some reaching nearly 2 R_Jup.
explanations.c: Their radii are measured precisely from transit depths; measurability is not the issue.
explanations.d: They span a range of radii; the anomaly is that many are inflated, not that they are uniform.

questions.prompt: What is the key OBSERVATIONAL correlation that any inflation mechanism must explain?

options.text: Inflation increases with the planet's orbital eccentricity only
Inflation increases with the stellar insolation the planet receives, above a threshold near 2 × 10⁸ erg/s/cm²
Inflation increases with the planet's age
Inflation is independent of everything measurable

explanations.a: Eccentricity-driven tidal heating is one candidate MECHANISM, but the robust empirical correlation is with insolation; many inflated hot Jupiters have circular orbits.
explanations.b: Correct — Demory & Seager (2011), Laughlin et al. (2011), and Miller & Fortney (2011) showed inflation tracks incident flux, with anomalies appearing above roughly 2 × 10⁸ erg/s/cm²; this is the constraint every model must match.
explanations.c: Age alone does not drive inflation; if anything, isolated giants shrink with age, so age is not the controlling correlation.
explanations.d: Inflation is strongly correlated with insolation, which is precisely what makes the phenomenon tractable to study.

questions.prompt: The ohmic dissipation mechanism (Batygin & Stevenson, 2010) explains inflation by:

options.text: Radioactive decay in the planet's core
Ionized atmospheric winds crossing the planet's magnetic field, driving currents whose resistive heating warms the deep interior
Collisions with asteroids heating the planet
The planet fusing hydrogen like a small star

explanations.a: Radioactive decay is far too weak to inflate a gas giant and does not scale with starlight, contradicting the insolation correlation.
explanations.b: Correct — hot, partially ionized atmospheres driven by fast winds act as moving conductors in the planet's magnetic field, generating currents whose ohmic (resistive) heating deposits energy deep inside; because hotter atmospheres are more ionized, it naturally scales with irradiation.
explanations.c: Impacts cannot supply sustained internal heat and do not correlate with insolation.
explanations.d: Hydrogen fusion requires ~80 Jupiter masses (~0.08 M_sun); hot Jupiters at ~1 M_Jup are nowhere near it and are not fusing anything.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps by which a student diagnoses a hot Jupiter as anomalously inflated.

items.text: Measure radius from transit depth and mass from RV, giving a low bulk density
Compute the insolation from stellar luminosity and orbital distance
Compare the measured radius to a standard cooling model for that mass and age
Note that the excess radius correlates with high insolation, implicating an irradiation-powered mechanism

questions.explanation: First you characterize the planet (radius, mass, density); then you quantify how much starlight it receives; then you compare its radius against what an un-inflated cooling model predicts; and finally you interpret the excess in light of the insolation correlation, pointing to an irradiation-driven heating or cooling-delay mechanism. The interpretation step must come last because it rests on all three measurements.

units.label: Atmospheres and Habitability: Characterizing Distant Worlds

lessons.label: Transmission Spectroscopy: Scale Height and the Wavelength-Dependent Planet Radius

sections.heading: The transit depth is set by the planet’s silhouette — and the silhouette has an atmosphere
sections.body: The depth of a transit is one of the cleanest measurements in astronomy: when a planet crosses its star it blocks a fraction of the light equal to the ratio of areas, δ = (Rp/Rs)². A hot Jupiter (Rp ≈ 1.4 Jupiter radii ≈ 1.0×10⁸ m) crossing a Sun-like star (Rs ≈ 7×10⁸ m) blocks about (1.0×10⁸ / 7×10⁸)² ≈ 0.02, a 2% dip. But the planet is not a hard disk. It has a gaseous atmosphere that is transparent at some wavelengths and opaque at others, so the size of the silhouette depends on the color of light you measure it in. At a wavelength where an atmospheric molecule absorbs strongly, starlight that grazes the planet’s limb is blocked out to a higher altitude, the effective radius Rp(λ) grows, and the transit gets slightly deeper. Measure the transit depth as a function of wavelength and you have a transmission spectrum — a fingerprint of what the atmosphere is made of, obtained without ever resolving the planet as more than a point.

sections.heading: Scale height: how thick the annulus of absorbing gas is
sections.body: The vertical structure of the atmosphere is governed by hydrostatic balance, which gives pressure falling off exponentially with altitude. The e-folding length is the scale height H = kT / (μ g), where k is Boltzmann’s constant (1.38×10⁻²³ J/K), T the atmospheric temperature, μ the mean molecular mass, and g the surface gravity. H is the natural ruler of a transmission spectrum: a strong absorption band raises the opaque radius by a handful of scale heights above the continuum. Everything that makes H large makes the signal large — high temperature, low gravity, and low mean molecular weight. A puffy, hot, hydrogen-dominated atmosphere (μ ≈ 2.3 amu, the H₂/He value) has a scale height of hundreds of kilometers; a cool, high-gravity, water- or nitrogen-rich atmosphere (μ ≈ 18–28 amu) has one an order of magnitude smaller. This is exactly why the first atmospheres were detected on hot Jupiters and why a rocky planet with a heavy secondary atmosphere is so much harder — its scale height, and therefore its spectral signal, is tiny.

sections.heading: From scale height to a measurable signal — and the history
sections.body: The amplitude of a spectral feature in the transit depth is approximately Δδ ≈ 2 Rp n H / Rs², where n is the number of scale heights the band rises above the continuum (typically a few). Because it goes as Rp/Rs², a big planet around a small star wins twice. This is a parts-per-million measurement: even a favorable hot Jupiter gives a feature amplitude of only a few hundred ppm on top of a percent-level transit, which is why space telescopes above the turbulent atmosphere were essential. The first exoplanet atmosphere was detected this way by David Charbonneau and collaborators in 2002, who saw the 589 nm sodium doublet make the transit of HD 209458 b about 0.02% deeper with the Hubble Space Telescope — the opening measurement of the entire field of exoplanet atmospheric characterization.

lessons.workedExample: Take HD 209458 b — a hot Jupiter with T ≈ 1450 K, g ≈ 9 m/s², a hydrogen-dominated atmosphere (μ ≈ 2.3 amu = 2.3×1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg), Rp ≈ 1.38 RJ ≈ 9.9×10⁷ m, orbiting a star of Rs ≈ 1.2 R☉ ≈ 8.4×10⁸ m. First the continuum transit depth: (Rp/Rs)² = (9.9×10⁷ / 8.4×10⁸)² ≈ (0.118)² ≈ 0.014, a 1.4% dip — matching the observed ~1.5%. Now the scale height: H = kT/(μg) = (1.38×10⁻²³ × 1450) / (3.82×10⁻²⁷ × 9) ≈ 2.0×10⁻²⁰ / 3.44×10⁻²⁶ ≈ 5.8×10⁵ m ≈ 580 km. The signal per scale height is Δδ ≈ 2 Rp H / Rs² = 2 × 9.9×10⁷ × 5.8×10⁵ / (8.4×10⁸)² ≈ 1.15×10¹⁴ / 7.0×10¹⁷ ≈ 1.6×10⁻⁴, i.e. about 160 ppm per scale height. A strong band standing ~3 scale heights above the continuum is therefore a ~500 ppm bump on a 14,000 ppm transit — small, but exactly the size Hubble measured for sodium and water on this planet.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will ask "why does the planet look bigger at some wavelengths than others?" to check whether a student understands that a transmission spectrum is a radius-versus-wavelength measurement, not a direct image. The tell of real understanding is naming scale height and its dependence on T, μ, and g — a student who can explain why a hot, low-gravity, hydrogen-rich planet gives a big signal while a rocky world with a nitrogen atmosphere gives a tiny one has grasped why target selection, not just telescope time, decides what is detectable.

questions.prompt: A transit is 1.6% deep in white light. What does the transit depth most directly tell you?

options.text: The planet’s mass relative to the star
The ratio of the planet’s radius to the star’s radius, since depth ≈ (Rp/Rs)²
The planet’s orbital period
The atmospheric composition directly, in one number

explanations.a: Mass comes from radial velocity or transit timing, not from how much light is blocked; depth is an area (radius) measurement.
explanations.b: Correct — the fraction of light blocked equals the ratio of the projected areas, so depth ≈ (Rp/Rs)² and a 1.6% dip implies Rp/Rs ≈ 0.126.
explanations.c: Period comes from the time between transits, not from the depth of a single one.
explanations.d: Composition requires measuring how the depth changes with wavelength; a single white-light depth gives only a size ratio.

questions.prompt: Two planets have identical temperature and gravity. Planet A has a hydrogen/helium atmosphere (μ ≈ 2.3 amu); planet B has a water-vapor atmosphere (μ ≈ 18 amu). Which has the larger transmission signal, and why?

options.text: Planet B, because heavier molecules absorb more light
Planet A, because its scale height H = kT/(μg) is larger at lower mean molecular weight
They are equal, because temperature and gravity are the same
Planet B, because a higher μ raises the scale height

explanations.a: Absorption strength per molecule is not what sets the amplitude; the vertical extent of the atmosphere (scale height) does, and that grows with lower μ.
explanations.b: Correct — H = kT/(μg), so at fixed T and g the low-μ hydrogen atmosphere has a scale height ~8× larger, spreading its absorbing annulus over more kilometers and producing a bigger feature.
explanations.c: Equal T and g do not make the signals equal, because the mean molecular weights differ and H depends on μ.
explanations.d: This inverts the relation — a higher μ lowers the scale height (H is inversely proportional to μ), shrinking the signal.

questions.prompt: Why were the first exoplanet atmospheres detected from space (HST) rather than the ground, and on hot Jupiters rather than rocky planets?

options.text: Ground telescopes cannot see planets at all
The features are ~hundreds of ppm on a percent-level transit, so they need the photometric stability above the atmosphere, and hot Jupiters maximize Rp/Rs² and scale height
Hot Jupiters are the only planets with atmospheres
Sodium can only be seen from space

explanations.a: Ground telescopes routinely observe transits; the issue is the tiny, wavelength-dependent depth change, not seeing the transit at all.
explanations.b: Correct — a transmission feature is a few-hundred-ppm change on a ~1% transit, demanding the stable photometry of space, and hot Jupiters give the largest signal because they maximize both Rp/Rs² and the scale height (hot, low-gravity, hydrogen-rich).
explanations.c: Rocky planets have atmospheres too; they are just far harder because their heavy, cool, high-gravity atmospheres have tiny scale heights.
explanations.d: Sodium has since been detected from the ground as well; the space requirement was about photometric precision, not the element.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in reasoning from a raw transit to a transmission spectrum.

items.text: Measure the transit depth in many separate wavelength channels
Convert each depth to an effective planet radius via δ(λ) = (Rp(λ)/Rs)²
Plot effective radius versus wavelength
Identify molecular bands where the radius rises above the continuum

questions.explanation: You first measure depth in each wavelength channel, convert each depth to an effective radius through δ = (Rp/Rs)², assemble those radii into a radius-versus-wavelength plot, and only then read off the bands where the atmosphere is opaque and the radius bulges above the continuum.

lessons.label: Reading a Transmission Spectrum: Molecular Bands, Rayleigh Slopes, and Flat Clouds

sections.heading: Molecular bands: the peaks that name the molecules
sections.body: A transmission spectrum is read like a bar code. Each molecule imprints absorption at characteristic wavelengths, so a bump in the effective radius at the right place identifies a gas. Water vapor is the workhorse of near-infrared exoplanet spectroscopy, with a strong band at 1.4 μm that sits squarely in the Hubble WFC3 grism and additional bands near 0.9 and 1.9 μm. Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide absorb in the infrared (CO near 2.3 and 4.6 μm, CO₂ with a sharp feature at 4.3 μm); methane has bands in the near-IR that dominate cooler atmospheres. In the optical, the alkali metals sodium (589 nm) and potassium (770 nm) produce narrow cores with pressure-broadened wings that probe deep, clear layers. The pattern of which bands are present and how deep they are constrains both composition and, through relative band strengths, the temperature and metallicity of the gas.

sections.heading: The Rayleigh slope: why the blue end rises
sections.body: Even where no molecule absorbs, small particles and molecules scatter light, and scattering is strongly wavelength-dependent. Rayleigh scattering has a cross-section that falls as λ⁻⁴, so blue light is scattered far more than red. In transmission this makes the atmosphere effectively opaque to higher altitude at short wavelengths, so the planet looks larger in the blue — a spectrum that slopes upward toward shorter wavelengths. The steepness of that slope is diagnostic: a slope consistent with λ⁻⁴ over several scale heights points to small-particle Rayleigh scattering by hazes, and some planets show "super-Rayleigh" slopes steeper than λ⁻⁴, a sign of a particular haze particle-size distribution. The blue slope and the infrared molecular bands are read together — the slope tells you about aerosols, the bands about gases.

sections.heading: Clouds and the flat, featureless spectrum
sections.body: The single most important complication is clouds and hazes. A deck of condensate or photochemical haze acts as a gray, wavelength-independent screen: it sets a high-altitude opaque floor that hides the gas below, muting or entirely erasing molecular bands. A transmission spectrum that comes back flat and featureless is therefore not a null result — it is a positive detection of high-altitude aerosols. The textbook case is GJ 1214 b, a warm sub-Neptune whose spectrum Laura Kreidberg and collaborators showed in 2014 (Nature) to be flat to high precision with Hubble, ruling out a clear atmosphere and demanding high clouds. On the population scale, David Sing and collaborators (2016, Nature) surveyed ten hot Jupiters with Hubble and Spitzer and found a continuum from clear atmospheres with strong water bands to cloudy ones with muted water — reframing "we didn’t see water" from an absence of the molecule to a presence of clouds hiding it.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose you observe a warm sub-Neptune and expect a hydrogen-rich atmosphere with a scale height of about 200 km, so a strong water band should raise the radius by ~3 scale heights ≈ 600 km, a feature of roughly a few hundred ppm. Instead your spectrum from 0.8 to 1.7 μm is flat to within ±30 ppm — no 1.4 μm water bump, no blue slope. You do not conclude "no water." The expected water feature is ~10× larger than your error bars, so its absence means something is capping the atmosphere above the altitude where water would show. The correct inference is a high-altitude cloud or haze deck sitting above roughly the millibar level, flattening the spectrum — exactly the conclusion Kreidberg et al. drew for GJ 1214 b, where a clear atmosphere was excluded at high confidence and only a high cloud top reproduced the flat data.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love to hand a student a flat transmission spectrum and ask "what did you learn?" because the naive answer — "nothing" or "no atmosphere" — is wrong, and the right one shows real physical reasoning. A flat spectrum where a bump was expected is a detection of high clouds or haze, not an absence of molecules. A student who can say "the features are muted relative to the scale height I predicted, so aerosols are capping the atmosphere" demonstrates they understand that clouds are a signal, and that predicted feature size versus noise is how you interpret a null-looking result.

questions.prompt: Match each spectral feature to what it reveals about the atmosphere.

left.text: Rising effective radius toward the blue (λ⁻⁴)
A flat, featureless spectrum where bands were expected
A narrow core with broad wings at 589 nm

right.text: Water vapor absorption
Rayleigh scattering by small haze particles
High-altitude clouds/haze muting the bands
Pressure-broadened sodium probing deep clear layers

questions.explanation: The 1.4 μm bump is the near-IR water band; a λ⁻⁴ rise to the blue is Rayleigh scattering by small aerosols; a flat spectrum where features were predicted is high clouds/haze capping the atmosphere; and a narrow-core, broad-winged 589 nm feature is pressure-broadened sodium seen down into deep, clear layers.

questions.prompt: A transmission spectrum slopes upward toward shorter (bluer) wavelengths. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The star is bluer than the Sun
Rayleigh scattering by small particles, whose cross-section rises as λ⁻⁴, making the planet look larger in the blue
The planet is hotter on its blue side
Water vapor absorbs mostly in the blue

explanations.a: The stellar color is divided out in forming the transmission spectrum; the slope is a property of the planet’s atmosphere, not the star.
explanations.b: Correct — Rayleigh scattering scales as λ⁻⁴, so short-wavelength light is scattered out to higher altitude, the effective radius grows toward the blue, and the spectrum slopes up.
explanations.c: Planets do not have a "blue side"; the slope is a scattering effect versus wavelength, not a spatial temperature difference.
explanations.d: Water’s strong bands are in the near-infrared (e.g., 1.4 μm), not a smooth blue-optical slope.

questions.prompt: Kreidberg et al. (2014) measured a flat, featureless Hubble transmission spectrum for the sub-Neptune GJ 1214 b. What did they conclude?

options.text: The planet has no atmosphere at all
High-altitude clouds/haze cap the atmosphere and hide the molecular bands, since a clear atmosphere was ruled out to high precision
The instrument was broken
The atmosphere is pure hydrogen with no other molecules

explanations.a: A flat spectrum is not a bare rock; the data ruled out a clear atmosphere and required a high cloud/haze deck sitting above the layers where bands form.
explanations.b: Correct — the expected features were far larger than the tiny error bars, so their absence meant high-altitude aerosols were flattening the spectrum, a positive detection of clouds/haze rather than a null result.
explanations.c: The precision of the flat measurement is exactly what made the cloud interpretation robust; it was a real, high-quality spectrum.
explanations.d: A pure clear hydrogen atmosphere would still show molecular bands from trace species and a Rayleigh slope; the flatness specifically requires an aerosol layer.

questions.prompt: Why is measuring the predicted feature size (in scale heights) before observing so important when interpreting a flat spectrum?

options.text: It tells you the planet’s mass
It lets you judge whether "flat" means clouds (features suppressed below the noise) or simply that your data are not precise enough to see the expected bump
It sets the orbital period
It has no bearing on interpretation

explanations.a: Scale height depends on T, μ, and g, not on mass directly; predicting feature size is about signal amplitude, not weighing the planet.
explanations.b: Correct — if the predicted feature is many times your error bars and you still see nothing, aerosols are suppressing it; if the predicted feature is below your noise, a flat spectrum is uninformative. The comparison is what makes the cloud conclusion valid.
explanations.c: Period comes from transit timing, unrelated to feature amplitude.
explanations.d: It is central: without knowing the expected amplitude you cannot tell a real detection of clouds from a non-detection due to insufficient precision.

lessons.label: Emission Spectroscopy, Thermal Inversions, and High-Resolution Cross-Correlation

sections.heading: Secondary eclipse: catching the planet’s own light
sections.body: Transmission reads the light passing through the terminator; emission spectroscopy reads the planet’s own thermal glow. When the planet passes behind the star (the secondary eclipse) its light is removed, and the small dip measures the planet-to-star flux ratio directly: the eclipse depth is (Rp/Rs)² × (Fp/Fs), where Fp/Fs is the ratio of the planet’s to the star’s brightness at that wavelength. For a hot Jupiter this is largest in the infrared, where a ~1500 K planet is bright relative to a ~6000 K star. Because emission comes from the dayside, an emission spectrum probes the vertical temperature structure of the atmosphere, not just its composition — you are seeing to different depths at different wavelengths, and how bright each layer is depends on how hot it is.

sections.heading: Absorption versus emission features: reading the temperature gradient
sections.body: The direction a spectral feature points tells you which way temperature runs with altitude. In a normal atmosphere temperature falls with height, so a molecular band lets you see up to cooler, higher layers and appears as an absorption dip in the emission spectrum. But if temperature rises with altitude — a thermal inversion (stratosphere) — the same band shows the hotter upper layer and appears in emission, as a peak. Inversions on the hottest planets are driven by high-altitude optical absorbers: gaseous titanium oxide and vanadium oxide were proposed by Fortney, Hubeny, Spiegel and others in the late 2000s, and on ultra-hot Jupiters (dayside temperatures above ~2200 K) atomic metals and molecules like iron and hydrogen anion opacity do the heating. Emission features of water and CO seen in emission on planets such as WASP-121 b and WASP-18 b are the direct evidence that these stratospheres exist.

sections.heading: High-resolution cross-correlation and the JWST era
sections.body: A powerful ground-based technique sidesteps clouds and low resolution entirely. High-resolution cross-correlation spectroscopy (HRCCS) uses spectrographs at resolving power R ≈ 100,000 to resolve thousands of individual molecular lines. Because the planet moves fast along its orbit, its lines are Doppler-shifted by tens of km/s over a few hours while the star and Earth’s telluric lines stay nearly fixed — so cross-correlating the changing spectrum against a molecular template pulls the planet’s signal out and measures its orbital velocity. Ignas Snellen and collaborators used this in 2010 (Nature) to detect carbon monoxide in HD 209458 b and measure the planet’s orbital velocity semi-amplitude Kp ≈ 140 km/s, which pins the orbital inclination and hence the true mass. The James Webb Space Telescope has since transformed the space side: its transiting-exoplanet program delivered the first unambiguous carbon-dioxide detection in an exoplanet, WASP-39 b, via a strong 4.3 μm band (JWST Transiting Exoplanet Community ERS Team, published 2023 in Nature), along with photochemically produced sulfur dioxide — pushing atmospheric characterization from a few molecules on hot Jupiters toward the small-planet frontier.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate a secondary-eclipse depth for a hot Jupiter in the mid-infrared. Take Rp/Rs ≈ 0.12 (so (Rp/Rs)² ≈ 0.0144), a dayside temperature Tp ≈ 1450 K, and a stellar temperature Ts ≈ 6000 K. At long infrared wavelengths the Planck function is roughly linear in temperature (Rayleigh–Jeans), so Fp/Fs ≈ Tp/Ts ≈ 1450/6000 ≈ 0.24. The eclipse depth is then (Rp/Rs)² × (Fp/Fs) ≈ 0.0144 × 0.24 ≈ 0.0035, about 3500 ppm — a healthy signal, and far larger than the ~100 ppm transmission features, which is why dayside emission was measured (first by Spitzer in 2005) even for planets whose transmission spectra were hard. Contrast the HRCCS approach: rather than a broadband depth, Snellen’s CO detection tracked the planet’s lines sweeping through Kp ≈ 140 km/s of Doppler shift in a single night, turning the planet’s orbital motion itself into the signal and yielding its true mass.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing emission spectroscopy will ask "how can a spectral feature appear in emission rather than absorption?" — because the answer forces a student to reason about the vertical temperature structure, not just list molecules. Features in emission mean temperature rises with altitude (a thermal inversion); features in absorption mean it falls. A student who connects an emission peak to a high-altitude absorber like TiO/VO heating a stratosphere, and who can contrast a broadband secondary eclipse with the Doppler-tracking logic of high-resolution cross-correlation, shows they understand that an emission spectrum is a thermometer of the atmosphere’s layers.

questions.prompt: A secondary eclipse (the planet passing behind the star) measures which quantity?

options.text: The transmission of starlight through the terminator
The planet-to-star flux ratio, (Rp/Rs)² × (Fp/Fs), i.e. the planet’s own emitted light
The planet’s orbital period only
The stellar radius alone

explanations.a: That is the primary transit (transmission); the secondary eclipse hides the planet, removing its own light.
explanations.b: Correct — when the planet disappears behind the star the missing light is the planet’s thermal emission, so the eclipse depth is (Rp/Rs)² × (Fp/Fs), a direct measure of the dayside brightness.
explanations.c: Timing gives the period, but the eclipse depth specifically measures the planet’s emitted flux ratio.
explanations.d: The stellar radius is not what the eclipse depth isolates; it is the planet-to-star flux ratio.

questions.prompt: In an emission spectrum, a molecular band appears as an emission peak rather than an absorption dip. What does this imply?

options.text: Temperature decreases with altitude (normal profile)
Temperature increases with altitude — a thermal inversion (stratosphere)
The molecule is absent
The planet has no atmosphere

explanations.a: A falling temperature profile produces absorption features, because the band lets you see up to cooler, higher layers.
explanations.b: Correct — an emission feature means the band probes a hotter layer above, so temperature rises with altitude: a thermal inversion, often driven by high-altitude optical absorbers like TiO/VO or atomic metals on ultra-hot Jupiters.
explanations.c: An emission peak is a strong detection of the molecule, not its absence; the direction of the feature encodes the temperature gradient.
explanations.d: Emission features require an atmosphere with a specific (inverted) temperature structure; they are not a sign of a bare planet.

questions.prompt: How does high-resolution cross-correlation spectroscopy (HRCCS) pull a planet’s signal out of overwhelming starlight from the ground?

options.text: By spatially resolving the planet from the star
By exploiting the planet’s large, changing orbital Doppler shift (tens of km/s over hours) to separate its thousands of molecular lines from the fixed stellar and telluric lines
By waiting for the planet to get brighter than the star
By blocking the star with a coronagraph

explanations.a: These planets are not spatially resolved; HRCCS works on unresolved, blended light.
explanations.b: Correct — at R ≈ 100,000 the planet’s many lines are resolved and shift by tens of km/s along the orbit while stellar and telluric lines stay put, so cross-correlating against a molecular template isolates the moving planet and measures its velocity (e.g., Snellen 2010, CO in HD 209458 b, Kp ≈ 140 km/s).
explanations.c: The planet never outshines its star; the method relies on Doppler separation, not brightness.
explanations.d: HRCCS does not use a coronagraph; it separates signals in velocity space, not in angle.

questions.prompt: What did JWST’s transiting-exoplanet program report for WASP-39 b (2023) that had not been unambiguously seen before in any exoplanet?

options.text: The first detection of hydrogen
The first unambiguous carbon-dioxide detection (a strong 4.3 μm band), plus photochemically produced sulfur dioxide
The first image of an exoplanet surface
The first measurement of an exoplanet’s mass

explanations.a: Hydrogen-dominated atmospheres were already inferred; the landmark was CO₂, not hydrogen.
explanations.b: Correct — JWST resolved the 4.3 μm CO₂ band cleanly, the first unambiguous CO₂ detection in an exoplanet atmosphere, and also revealed SO₂ produced by photochemistry.
explanations.c: JWST measured a transmission spectrum, not a surface image; these planets remain spatially unresolved points.
explanations.d: Masses were measured for exoplanets decades earlier via radial velocity; the WASP-39 b result was about atmospheric chemistry.

lessons.label: The Habitable Zone as Climate Physics: Runaway Greenhouse and Its Moving Edges

sections.heading: Equilibrium temperature is only the starting point
sections.body: The naive picture of the habitable zone — the orbital band where a planet’s equilibrium temperature allows liquid water — gets you started but is physically incomplete. Equilibrium temperature Teq balances absorbed sunlight against thermal re-radiation: Teq = Ts (Rs/2d)^(1/2) (1−A)^(1/4), where A is the Bond albedo and d the orbital distance. For Earth with A ≈ 0.3, Teq ≈ 255 K — below freezing. The surface is 288 K only because the atmosphere’s greenhouse effect adds ~33 K. That gap is the whole point: habitability is not set by the bare radiative balance but by what an atmosphere does to it. The real habitable zone is defined by climate physics — the range of insolation over which a planet can maintain surface liquid water given a self-regulating atmosphere — and its edges are set by two runaway feedbacks, not by Teq crossing 273 K.

sections.heading: The inner edge: the runaway greenhouse
sections.body: Move a planet closer to its star and you do not simply warm it smoothly. Water vapor is itself a powerful greenhouse gas, so a warmer surface evaporates more water, which traps more heat, which evaporates more water — a positive feedback. There is a ceiling to how much thermal radiation a water-saturated atmosphere can emit to space, the Kombayashi–Ingersoll limit (around 280–310 W/m² of outgoing longwave radiation). Once absorbed sunlight exceeds that ceiling, the atmosphere cannot cool fast enough and temperature runs away, boiling the oceans — the runaway greenhouse thought to have befallen Venus. Even short of full runaway, a "moist greenhouse" lifts water high into the stratosphere where ultraviolet light dissociates it and the hydrogen escapes to space, desiccating the planet over time. This inner edge, not a simple boiling point, sets the hot side of the habitable zone.

sections.heading: The outer edge, the moving boundaries, and the history
sections.body: The outer edge is set by the opposite failure. Far from the star a planet must lean on carbon dioxide to stay warm, but CO₂ helps only up to a point: pile on enough and Rayleigh scattering by the CO₂ raises the albedo and CO₂ begins to condense, so added CO₂ stops warming and starts cooling — the maximum-greenhouse limit. The modern framework traces to James Kasting, Daniel Whitmire, and Ray Reynolds (1993, Icarus), who computed these edges for the Sun and other stars; Ravi Kopparapu and collaborators updated them in 2013, placing the Sun’s conservative habitable zone at roughly 0.99–1.70 AU (moist-greenhouse inner edge to maximum-greenhouse outer edge — the moist-greenhouse limit is the conservative inner edge, slightly farther out than the runaway-greenhouse edge near 0.97 AU). Crucially, the edges move: they depend on planet mass, atmospheric composition, rotation rate, and especially clouds. Three-dimensional climate models by Yang, Cowan, and Abbot (2013) showed that on slowly rotating planets a thick dayside cloud deck raises the albedo and pushes the inner edge substantially closer to the star than 1D models predict. The habitable zone is a physics calculation with real uncertainties, not a fixed ring on a map.

lessons.workedExample: Check Earth against the physics. Equilibrium temperature: Teq = Ts (Rs/2d)^(1/2)(1−A)^(1/4). A convenient form for Sun-like illumination is Teq ≈ 278.3 K × (L/L☉)^(1/4) × (1−A)^(1/4) / (d/AU)^(1/2). For Earth (L = L☉, d = 1 AU, A = 0.3): Teq ≈ 278.3 × (0.7)^(1/4) ≈ 278.3 × 0.915 ≈ 255 K. The observed surface temperature is 288 K, so the greenhouse effect supplies 288 − 255 ≈ 33 K — the atmosphere, not the orbit, keeps Earth liquid. Now the zone edges scale with the square root of luminosity: the conservative inner (moist-greenhouse) edge sits where the stellar flux reaches the critical value, d_inner ≈ (L/L☉ / Seff,inner)^(1/2) AU. Using Kopparapu’s conservative Seff,inner ≈ 1.015 (the moist-greenhouse limit) and Seff,outer ≈ 0.35 for the Sun gives d_inner ≈ 0.99 AU and d_outer ≈ 1.69 AU — Earth at 1.00 AU sits just outside the conservative inner edge, which is exactly why its climate is sensitive and its habitability is not guaranteed by orbit alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "why isn’t the habitable zone just where the temperature is between freezing and boiling?" to separate students who memorized a definition from those who understand the feedbacks. The strong answer names the two runaways: the inner edge is a water-vapor runaway greenhouse (with the Kombayashi–Ingersoll ceiling on outgoing radiation), and the outer edge is the maximum-greenhouse limit where more CO₂ stops helping. A student who adds that the edges move with clouds and rotation — citing Kasting 1993 and the Kopparapu 2013 update — shows they treat habitability as climate physics with uncertainty, not a fixed ring, which is exactly the sophistication a judge rewards.

questions.prompt: Earth’s equilibrium temperature is about 255 K, yet its surface averages 288 K. What accounts for the ~33 K difference?

options.text: Earth is closer to the Sun than its equilibrium calculation assumes
The greenhouse effect — the atmosphere traps outgoing thermal radiation, warming the surface above the bare radiative balance
Radioactive heating from Earth’s interior
The equilibrium calculation is simply wrong

explanations.a: The 255 K already uses Earth’s actual distance and albedo; distance is not the missing ingredient.
explanations.b: Correct — equilibrium temperature is the no-atmosphere radiative balance; the observed 288 K is higher because greenhouse gases (chiefly water vapor and CO₂) trap outgoing infrared, adding ~33 K.
explanations.c: Geothermal heat flux is negligible (~0.09 W/m²) compared with the ~240 W/m² of absorbed sunlight; it cannot supply 33 K.
explanations.d: The calculation is correct for a no-atmosphere world; the point is that the atmosphere’s greenhouse effect adds the extra warmth.

questions.prompt: What sets the INNER edge of the habitable zone?

options.text: The point where water boils at 373 K
The runaway greenhouse: rising insolation drives a water-vapor feedback past the Kombayashi–Ingersoll limit on outgoing radiation, so temperature runs away
The point where CO₂ condenses
The star’s magnetic activity level

explanations.a: The boiling point of water at 1 atm is not the physical edge; the runaway happens through a vapor feedback well before a simple boiling threshold.
explanations.b: Correct — water vapor is a greenhouse gas, so more warmth means more vapor means more warmth; once absorbed sunlight exceeds the maximum outgoing radiation a saturated atmosphere can emit (Kombayashi–Ingersoll limit), temperature runs away and the oceans are lost.
explanations.c: CO₂ condensation is relevant at the OUTER edge (maximum greenhouse), not the inner one.
explanations.d: Stellar activity matters for atmospheric escape but does not define the classical inner edge, which is a climate-feedback limit.

questions.prompt: What sets the OUTER edge of the habitable zone?

options.text: The maximum-greenhouse limit: beyond a point, added CO₂ raises albedo (Rayleigh scattering) and condenses, so it no longer warms the planet
The point where the planet becomes tidally locked
The runaway water-vapor greenhouse
The orbit where the year exceeds one Earth year

explanations.a: Correct — far out, a planet relies on CO₂ for warmth, but past the maximum-greenhouse limit more CO₂ scatters sunlight (higher albedo) and begins to condense, so it stops warming and the surface can no longer stay above freezing.
explanations.b: Tidal locking depends on the star and distance but is not what defines the outer habitable-zone edge.
explanations.c: The water-vapor runaway is the INNER edge; the outer edge is the CO₂ maximum-greenhouse limit.
explanations.d: Orbital period is a consequence of distance, not the physical criterion for the outer edge.

questions.prompt: Match each contribution to what it established about the habitable zone.

right.text: The foundational climate-physics framework for the HZ edges around the Sun and other stars
Updated conservative HZ limits (~0.99–1.70 AU for the Sun)
3D models showing dayside clouds move the inner edge inward on slow rotators

questions.explanation: Kasting, Whitmire & Reynolds (1993) built the foundational 1D climate framework for the HZ edges; Kopparapu et al. (2013) updated the conservative limits to about 0.99–1.70 AU for the Sun; and Yang, Cowan & Abbot (2013) used 3D climate models to show that dayside cloud feedback on slowly rotating planets moves the inner edge closer to the star.

lessons.label: M-Dwarf Worlds: Tidal Locking, Flares, and Why Nearby Habitability Is Contested

sections.heading: Why M dwarfs are where we look first
sections.body: M dwarfs — cool, low-mass red stars — make up roughly three-quarters of all stars in the Galaxy, and they are the easiest place to find and study small habitable-zone planets. A low-luminosity star has its habitable zone pulled in close, to roughly 0.02–0.1 AU, and that proximity is a gift to detection: the planet-to-star radius ratio is large (deeper transits from a small star), the reflex radial-velocity wobble is bigger (lower stellar mass), and the short orbital periods of days mean transits repeat often. The nearest examples are landmark systems: Proxima Centauri b, an ~1.3 Earth-mass planet in the habitable zone of the closest star, found by Guillem Anglada-Escudé and collaborators via radial velocity in 2016; and TRAPPIST-1, where Michaël Gillon and collaborators announced in 2017 seven Earth-sized transiting planets, several in the habitable zone — the richest nearby laboratory for small-planet atmospheres.

sections.heading: Tidal locking and the atmospheric-collapse worry
sections.body: A planet orbiting that close is likely tidally locked, rotating synchronously so one hemisphere faces the star permanently — eternal day on one side, eternal night on the other. The early worry (Steven Dole, 1964) was that the night side would get so cold that the atmosphere itself would freeze out there — carbon dioxide and even nitrogen condensing onto the dark hemisphere and permanently collapsing the atmosphere. But climate modeling changed the picture: Manoj Joshi and collaborators (1997) showed that a modestly thick atmosphere transports heat efficiently from the substellar point around to the night side, keeping it warm enough to prevent collapse. Tidal locking reshapes the climate — a hot substellar region, strong day-to-night winds, possibly a persistent dayside cloud deck — but it does not automatically forbid habitability. Whether a given planet retains its atmosphere is now the central question.

sections.heading: Flares, XUV, water loss — and the contested verdict
sections.body: The real threats are magnetic. M dwarfs are extraordinarily active: they flare frequently and emit disproportionate high-energy ultraviolet and X-ray (XUV) radiation, and they stay active for billions of years. Worse, M dwarfs spend a long, luminous pre-main-sequence phase — up to a billion years — brighter than their eventual steady state, so a planet that ends up in the habitable zone may spend its youth well inside the runaway-greenhouse line. Rodrigo Luger and Rory Barnes (2015) argued this can boil off a planet’s entire water inventory; the resulting hydrogen escape can leave behind large amounts of abiotic oxygen — both a habitability threat and a biosignature false-positive source. Stellar wind and XUV-driven escape can also strip atmospheres outright from unmagnetized planets. The verdict is genuinely contested: proponents note M dwarfs are abundant, their planets are detectable, and their long lifetimes give biology time; skeptics point to tidal locking, flares, XUV erosion, and early water loss. JWST is now testing it directly — Thomas Greene and collaborators (2023) found that the innermost TRAPPIST-1 planet, TRAPPIST-1 b, has a dayside near ~500 K consistent with a bare rock and little or no atmosphere, an early data point that nearby M-dwarf worlds may struggle to keep their air.

lessons.workedExample: Locate the habitable zone of TRAPPIST-1 and check a planet against it. TRAPPIST-1 is an ultracool dwarf with luminosity L ≈ 5.5×10⁻⁴ L☉. The habitable zone scales as the square root of luminosity, so the inner edge sits near d_inner ≈ (L/L☉ / Seff,inner)^(1/2) ≈ (5.5×10⁻⁴ / 1.05)^(1/2) ≈ 0.023 AU — a hundredth of Earth’s orbit, with planets whose "years" are only a few Earth days. Now the equilibrium temperature of TRAPPIST-1 e at d ≈ 0.029 AU: Teq ≈ 278.3 × (L/L☉)^(1/4) / (d/AU)^(1/2) (ignoring albedo) ≈ 278.3 × (5.5×10⁻⁴)^(1/4) / (0.029)^(1/2) ≈ 278.3 × 0.153 / 0.170 ≈ 250 K — close to Earth’s 255 K equilibrium value, which is why TRAPPIST-1 e is a prime habitable-zone target. But the same proximity that gives 250 K also means near-certain tidal locking and exposure to frequent flares and XUV from an active star — the numbers put it in the zone while the stellar environment is exactly why its habitability stays contested.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will press "M-dwarf planets are the easiest to find — so why do scientists argue about whether they’re habitable?" to see if a student can hold both sides. The detectability advantages (deep transits, big RV signal, frequent short-period transits, abundant stars) are real, but so are the threats: tidal locking, frequent flares and XUV, a superluminous pre-main-sequence phase that can strip water (Luger & Barnes 2015), and atmospheric escape. A student who names a concrete recent test — JWST finding TRAPPIST-1 b consistent with a bare, airless rock — shows they follow the live debate rather than repeating a textbook "red dwarfs are promising" line.

questions.prompt: Why is the habitable zone of an M dwarf located so close to the star (~0.02–0.1 AU)?

options.text: M dwarfs have strong gravity that pulls the zone inward
M dwarfs are low-luminosity, so a planet must orbit close to receive enough flux for liquid water; the zone distance scales as √L
M dwarfs are hotter than the Sun
M dwarfs have no habitable zone at all

explanations.a: The zone location is set by radiative flux, not by the star’s gravity acting on the planet’s orbit.
explanations.b: Correct — because the habitable zone distance scales as the square root of luminosity, a faint M dwarf (thousandths of a solar luminosity) has its zone pulled in to a few hundredths of an AU.
explanations.c: M dwarfs are cooler and much less luminous than the Sun, which is exactly why the zone is close in.
explanations.d: M dwarfs do have habitable zones; they are simply much closer to the star.

questions.prompt: A close-in M-dwarf planet is likely tidally locked. Does this automatically make it uninhabitable?

options.text: Yes — the night side always freezes out the atmosphere completely
No — climate models (e.g., Joshi et al. 1997) show a modestly thick atmosphere transports heat to the night side and prevents collapse, though the climate is reshaped
Yes — tidal locking stops the planet from having any atmosphere
No — tidally locked planets rotate too fast to have a permanent night side

explanations.a: The atmospheric-collapse worry was the early (Dole 1964) concern, but it is not automatic; heat transport can prevent it.
explanations.b: Correct — Joshi et al. (1997) showed that even a modestly thick atmosphere circulates heat from the substellar point to the night side, keeping it warm enough to avoid freeze-out; tidal locking reshapes the climate rather than forbidding habitability.
explanations.c: Tidal locking does not remove an atmosphere; it fixes the rotation so one side always faces the star.
explanations.d: A tidally locked planet rotates synchronously (once per orbit), which is exactly what creates a permanent day and night side.

questions.prompt: Luger & Barnes (2015) argued that M-dwarf habitable-zone planets may be desiccated during the star’s youth. What is the mechanism?

options.text: M dwarfs are too cold when young to allow liquid water

M dwarfs have a long, superluminous pre-main-sequence phase, so a future HZ planet spends its youth inside the runaway-greenhouse line, losing water via photodissociation and hydrogen escape — leaving abiotic O₂ behind
The planets are too massive to hold water
Tidal heating boils the oceans away

explanations.a: The problem is the opposite: the young M dwarf is too bright, not too cold, for planets that later cool into the habitable zone.
explanations.b: Correct — M dwarfs are superluminous for up to ~1 Gyr before settling, so a planet destined for the HZ endures an early runaway greenhouse; water is lifted high, photodissociated, and the hydrogen escapes, potentially leaving large abiotic O₂ inventories — a biosignature false positive.
explanations.c: Mass is not the driver here; the desiccation is driven by the star’s early high luminosity and XUV output.
explanations.d: Tidal heating can matter for some worlds, but the specific Luger & Barnes mechanism is early stellar superluminosity plus XUV-driven water loss.

questions.prompt: What did JWST observations of TRAPPIST-1 b (Greene et al. 2023) suggest about that planet?

options.text: It has a thick, water-rich atmosphere
Its dayside temperature (~500 K) is consistent with a bare rock and little or no atmosphere
It shows clear signs of life
It is a gas giant

explanations.a: The measured dayside was too hot and un-redistributed for a thick atmosphere; the data pointed away from a substantial atmosphere.
explanations.b: Correct — the ~500 K dayside brightness temperature matched a dark bare rock with little heat redistribution, suggesting TRAPPIST-1 b has little or no atmosphere, an early data point that close-in M-dwarf worlds may struggle to keep their air.
explanations.c: TRAPPIST-1 b is the innermost, hottest planet, well inside the habitable zone, and the result was about the absence of an atmosphere, not biosignatures.
explanations.d: TRAPPIST-1 b is an Earth-sized rocky planet, not a gas giant.

lessons.label: Biosignatures and Their False Positives: Oxygen, Methane, and the Disequilibrium Argument

sections.heading: What a biosignature is — and why oxygen was the first candidate
sections.body: A biosignature is a feature of a planet’s atmosphere or surface that is best explained by life. The classic candidate is molecular oxygen, O₂, and its photochemical product ozone, O₃. Earth’s atmosphere is 21% O₂, an extraordinary state of affairs: oxygen is highly reactive and would combine with surface rocks and volcanic gases on geologically short timescales if it were not continuously replenished. On Earth that replenishment is oxygenic photosynthesis. The reasoning that a heavily out-of-balance, oxygen-rich atmosphere points to a biological source goes back to James Lovelock in the 1960s, and O₂/O₃ remains the most-discussed biosignature because ozone in particular has a strong feature (near 9.6 μm in the mid-infrared, plus UV bands) that a future telescope could plausibly detect on an Earth-like planet.

sections.heading: The disequilibrium argument: no single gas is enough
sections.body: The deeper and more robust idea is chemical disequilibrium. Lovelock’s insight was that life betrays itself not by any one gas but by maintaining an atmosphere far from chemical equilibrium — holding together gases that should rapidly react with each other. The gold-standard pair is oxygen and methane. In an oxygen-rich atmosphere methane is oxidized in only about a decade, so finding O₂ and CH₄ together in abundance means both are being replenished fast enough to outrun that reaction — a continuous source that, on Earth, is biology (photosynthesis making O₂, microbes making CH₄). This is why the pair is far more convincing than either alone.
