The most striking demonstration is real: Carl Sagan and collaborators (1993, Nature) used the Galileo spacecraft’s flyby of Earth as a controlled experiment, detecting Earth’s life through the simultaneous O₂–CH₄ disequilibrium and the red edge of vegetation — a "detection of life on Earth" from a passing spacecraft that set the logic for how we would recognize it elsewhere.

sections.heading: False positives and why context is everything
sections.body: The hard lesson of the last decade is that individual biosignature gases have abiotic false positives, and interpreting them demands context. Oxygen can build up without life: on M-dwarf planets, early water loss (photodissociation plus hydrogen escape) can leave massive abiotic O₂ atmospheres — the Luger & Barnes (2015) mechanism — and CO₂ photolysis can also generate O₂ abiotically. Victoria Meadows and collaborators catalogued these O₂ false positives and, importantly, the discriminants that break them: for instance, an abiotic O₂ atmosphere from CO₂ photolysis is typically accompanied by carbon monoxide (CO), whose presence argues against a biological explanation. Methane too has abiotic sources — volcanic outgassing and water-rock serpentinization can make it without life. The community consensus, laid out in reviews such as Schwieterman et al. (2018), is that no single gas is a robust biosignature. A convincing detection requires a disequilibrium pair (O₂ with CH₄) plus contextual gases (CO₂ present, CO absent) and knowledge of the host star and planet — the whole atmospheric picture, not one line.

lessons.workedExample: Quantify why O₂ and CH₄ together are so telling. In an oxygen-rich atmosphere like Earth’s, methane has a photochemical lifetime of only about a decade before it is oxidized. Yet Earth’s atmosphere sustains methane at ~1.8 parts per million. To hold a species at steady abundance against a ~10-year destruction time, its source must resupply the entire standing inventory every ~10 years — on Earth a methane flux of roughly 500 teragrams per year, overwhelmingly biological (wetlands, microbes, and now agriculture). No plausible abiotic geology supplies methane at that rate in the simultaneous presence of 21% O₂. That is the disequilibrium argument made concrete: it is not that either gas is impossible abiotically, but that maintaining both at once demands fluxes that, taken together and in context (abundant CO₂, negligible CO), point to biology. It is exactly the signal Sagan et al. (1993) read off Earth from the Galileo flyby.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing biosignature reasoning will ask "if you saw oxygen on an exoplanet, would you announce life?" — and the disciplined answer is no, not from oxygen alone. The sophisticated response invokes false positives (abiotic O₂ from water loss on M dwarfs or from CO₂ photolysis) and the disequilibrium argument: the convincing signal is a pair of gases that should not coexist, like O₂ and CH₄, together with context (CO₂ present, CO absent) and knowledge of the star. A student who frames biosignatures as a weight-of-evidence, context-dependent inference — citing the Sagan 1993 Galileo detection of Earth and the O₂ false-positive literature — shows the scientific caution that judges specifically reward on so consequential a claim.

questions.prompt: Why is molecular oxygen (O₂) considered a candidate biosignature on Earth?

options.text: Oxygen is chemically inert and therefore accumulates naturally without life
Oxygen is highly reactive and would be removed by rocks and volcanic gases on short timescales, so its persistence at 21% requires continuous replenishment — on Earth, by photosynthesis
Oxygen is the most common element in the universe
Oxygen can only be produced by living organisms

explanations.a: The opposite is true — oxygen is very reactive, which is exactly why its high, sustained abundance is surprising and needs a source.
explanations.b: Correct — free O₂ would react away with surface and volcanic reservoirs on geological timescales; maintaining 21% requires a large, continuous source, which on Earth is oxygenic photosynthesis.
explanations.c: Hydrogen is the most common element; abundance in the universe is not why O₂ is a biosignature.
explanations.d: Oxygen can also form abiotically (e.g., water or CO₂ photolysis), which is precisely why O₂ alone is not a definitive biosignature.

questions.prompt: What is the "disequilibrium argument" for detecting life?

options.text: Life is detected by finding a single gas at high abundance
Life maintains an atmosphere far from chemical equilibrium, holding together gases that should rapidly react — e.g., O₂ and CH₄, which coexist only if both are continuously replenished
Life is detected by measuring the planet’s temperature
Disequilibrium means the atmosphere is at perfect chemical balance

explanations.a: A single gas is weak evidence because most have abiotic sources; the disequilibrium argument is specifically about combinations that should not coexist.
explanations.b: Correct — Lovelock’s insight is that life sustains chemical disequilibrium; O₂ and CH₄ together are the gold standard because methane is oxidized within ~a decade in an O₂ atmosphere, so their coexistence demands ongoing replenishment.
explanations.c: Temperature constrains habitability, not the presence of life; the disequilibrium argument is about atmospheric chemistry.
explanations.d: Disequilibrium is the opposite of balance — it is the persistence of gases that thermodynamics says should react away.

questions.prompt: Match each biosignature-gas scenario to the correct interpretation or discriminant.

left.text: Abundant O₂ AND CH₄ together, with CO₂ present and CO absent
O₂ accompanied by significant carbon monoxide (CO)

right.text: Strong disequilibrium biosignature — hard to explain without biology
Likely abiotic O₂ from CO₂ photolysis — the CO is a false-positive flag
Possible abiotic methane from geology — not a biosignature on its own

questions.explanation: O₂ and CH₄ together with CO₂ present and CO absent is the strong disequilibrium case pointing to biology; O₂ accompanied by CO flags abiotic O₂ from CO₂ photolysis (Meadows and colleagues’ discriminant); and methane alone near volcanic or serpentinizing rock can be abiotic geology, so it is not a biosignature by itself.

questions.prompt: Sagan et al. (1993) used the Galileo spacecraft’s flyby to make what point?

options.text: That Mars has life
That Earth’s life is detectable from a passing spacecraft via O₂–CH₄ disequilibrium and the red edge of vegetation — a controlled test of how we would recognize life elsewhere
That biosignatures are impossible to detect
That oxygen alone is a definitive proof of life

explanations.a: The Galileo flyby observed Earth, not Mars; the study was about detecting Earth’s own life as a benchmark.
explanations.b: Correct — Sagan and colleagues treated the Galileo Earth flyby as a controlled experiment, detecting life through the simultaneous O₂–CH₄ disequilibrium and the vegetation red edge, establishing the logic for remote biosignature detection.
explanations.c: The paper demonstrated the opposite: that life IS remotely detectable, given the right combination of signals.
explanations.d: The study emphasized disequilibrium (a combination of signals), not oxygen alone, which has abiotic false positives.

units.label: Landmark Studies and Open Debates

lessons.label: 51 Pegasi b (Mayor & Queloz 1995): The Wobble That Founded a Field and Won a Nobel

sections.heading: A star that wobbles: the radial-velocity method
sections.body: A planet does not orbit a fixed star — both bodies orbit their common center of mass (the barycenter), so the star traces a small mirror-image ellipse and its line-of-sight velocity oscillates. That periodic velocity shows up as a Doppler shift of the star’s spectral lines: blueshifted as the star swings toward us, redshifted as it swings away. Measuring this reflex velocity is the radial-velocity (RV) method. The key observable is the semi-amplitude K — the peak line-of-sight speed of the star. For scale, Jupiter tugs the Sun by only about 12.5 m/s over its 12-year orbit, and Earth by a mere 0.09 m/s. In 1995 the best spectrographs were only just reaching the ~10 m/s precision needed to see a giant planet at all.

sections.heading: October 1995: Mayor & Queloz and the ELODIE spectrograph
sections.body: Michel Mayor and his doctoral student Didier Queloz, using the ELODIE spectrograph at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence in France, announced in Nature (Mayor & Queloz 1995) a planet orbiting 51 Pegasi, an ordinary Sun-like (G-type) star about 50 light-years away. It was the first planet confirmed around a normal main-sequence star (the 1992 Wolszczan & Frail pulsar planets orbited a neutron star, a very different environment). The signal was a clean 4.23-day sinusoid with a semi-amplitude of roughly 59 m/s. Geoff Marcy and Paul Butler confirmed it within days from Lick Observatory in California, turning a startling single result into an established discovery. Mayor and Queloz shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics (with cosmologist James Peebles) for this work.

sections.heading: Minimum mass, not mass: the sin i degeneracy
sections.body: RV gives only a lower bound on the planet’s mass, because the Doppler shift measures only the line-of-sight component of the star’s motion. If the orbit is tilted by inclination i to our line of sight, the measured K scales with sin i, so the mass you derive is M_p·sin i — the true mass could be larger if the orbit is nearly face-on (small i). For 51 Peg b, M_p·sin i ≈ 0.47 M_Jupiter, so it is at least about half a Jupiter mass. This sin i degeneracy is exactly why a later transit detection (which pins i near 90°) or an astrometric measurement is so valuable: it removes the ambiguity and yields the true mass.

lessons.workedExample: Recover 51 Peg b’s minimum mass from the raw numbers. A convenient practical form of the RV equation is K = 28.4 m/s · (M_p·sin i / M_Jup) · (M_star/M_sun)^(-2/3) · (P/1 yr)^(-1/3). Rearranged: M_p·sin i / M_Jup = (K / 28.4) · (M_star/M_sun)^(2/3) · (P/1 yr)^(1/3). Plug in K = 59 m/s, M_star = 1.0 M_sun, and P = 4.23 days = 4.23/365.25 = 0.01158 yr. Then (P/1 yr)^(1/3) = 0.01158^(1/3) ≈ 0.226, and K/28.4 = 2.08. So M_p·sin i ≈ 2.08 × 1 × 0.226 ≈ 0.47 M_Jup — matching the published value. The short 4.23-day period also forces a tiny orbit: Kepler’s third law gives a = (M_star · P²)^(1/3) ≈ (1 · 0.01158²)^(1/3) ≈ 0.052 AU, one-eighth of Mercury’s distance from the Sun.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe 51 Peg b because it is the field’s origin story AND its cleanest teaching case for what RV can and cannot claim. A student who says "we detected the planet’s mass" has missed the sin i degeneracy; one who says "RV gives a minimum mass, M_p·sin i, and you need a transit or astrometry to break it" shows they understand the geometry behind the measurement. Being able to name Mayor & Queloz (1995), the ELODIE spectrograph, and the 2019 Nobel — accurately — signals the student read the primary history rather than a vague summary.

questions.prompt: Why does the radial-velocity method yield only M_p·sin i rather than the planet’s true mass?

options.text: Because spectrographs cannot measure velocities smaller than 1 km/s
Because the Doppler shift measures only the line-of-sight component of the star’s reflex motion, which scales with sin i
Because the planet’s own light contaminates the star’s spectrum
Because stellar mass is never known well enough

explanations.a: Modern spectrographs reach ~1 m/s or better; the limit is not a coarse velocity floor but the orbital geometry.
explanations.b: Correct — RV senses only the velocity component along our sight line, so an orbit inclined at i contributes K ∝ sin i, and the derived mass is the product M_p·sin i (a lower bound).
explanations.c: Planet light is utterly negligible next to the star in RV work; the degeneracy is geometric, not a contamination issue.
explanations.d: Stellar mass enters the calculation but is usually known to ~5–10%; the fundamental floor is the unknown inclination, not stellar mass.

questions.prompt: What made 51 Pegasi b specifically a landmark, as opposed to the 1992 pulsar planets?

options.text: It was the first exoplanet ever detected by any method
It was the first planet confirmed around a normal, Sun-like main-sequence star
It was the first exoplanet imaged directly
It was the first Earth-mass planet found

explanations.a: The 1992 Wolszczan & Frail pulsar planets predate it; 51 Peg b was not the first exoplanet overall.
explanations.b: Correct — the pulsar planets orbit a neutron star, an exotic remnant; 51 Peg b was the first around an ordinary G-type main-sequence star, opening the search around Sun-like stars.
explanations.c: It was found by radial velocity, not direct imaging; the first directly imaged planets came over a decade later.
explanations.d: At M_p·sin i ≈ 0.47 M_Jup it is a giant planet, not an Earth-mass world.

questions.prompt: The reflex velocity Jupiter induces on the Sun is about 12.5 m/s. What does 51 Peg b’s ~59 m/s semi-amplitude, at ~0.47 M_Jup, tell you compared to Jupiter?

options.text: A less-massive planet produced a larger wobble because it orbits far closer in (short period, small orbit)
The measurement must be an error, since a lighter planet cannot cause a bigger signal
51 Peg b must actually be more massive than Jupiter
The two signals are unrelated because they use different spectrographs

explanations.a: Correct — K grows as P decreases (K ∝ P^(-1/3)) and with proximity; 51 Peg b’s 4.23-day, ~0.05 AU orbit produces a much larger wobble than Jupiter’s 12-year orbit despite its smaller mass.
explanations.b: It is not an error — K depends on both mass and orbital period, so a close-in lighter planet can out-wobble a distant heavier one.
explanations.c: Its minimum mass ~0.47 M_Jup is below Jupiter’s; the larger K comes from the short period, not greater mass.
explanations.d: The instruments differ but both measure the same physical reflex velocity; the comparison is valid.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history of exoplanet detection from earliest to latest.

items.text: Wolszczan & Frail detect planets around a pulsar (neutron star)
Mayor & Queloz announce 51 Pegasi b around a Sun-like star
Marcy & Butler independently confirm 51 Peg b from Lick
Mayor & Queloz share the Nobel Prize in Physics

questions.explanation: The pulsar planets came in 1992; Mayor & Queloz announced 51 Peg b in 1995; Marcy & Butler confirmed it within days that same autumn; and the Nobel Prize followed much later, in 2019.

lessons.label: The Hot-Jupiter Surprise: In-Situ Formation vs. Disk Migration

sections.heading: Why a Jupiter at 0.05 AU broke the textbooks
sections.body: 51 Peg b was not just a planet — it was a planet in the wrong place. The core-accretion picture of giant-planet formation says you first build a solid core of several Earth masses, then runaway-accrete a massive hydrogen–helium envelope. Building that solid core needs abundant ices, which only condense beyond the "snow line" — the distance where the disk is cold enough (roughly 150–170 K) for water to freeze, about 2.7 AU in the young Solar System. Right next to the star, at 0.05 AU, the disk is far too hot and starved of solids to grow a giant in place. So a Jupiter-mass planet on a 4-day orbit demanded an explanation: either our formation theory was wrong, or the planet did not form where we found it.

sections.heading: Disk migration: born far, dragged in
sections.body: The leading explanation is orbital migration. A young giant planet embedded in the gaseous protoplanetary disk exerts gravitational torques on the gas (through spiral density waves at Lindblad resonances, the mechanism Goldreich & Tremaine worked out for rings in the 1970s–80s). The net torque removes orbital angular momentum from the planet, and it spirals inward — "Type II" migration once the planet is massive enough to open a gap in the disk. Lin, Bodenheimer & Richardson (1996) applied exactly this to 51 Peg b, arguing it formed beyond the snow line and migrated in, halting near the star. Disk migration is smooth and keeps orbits nearly circular and aligned with the star’s spin.

sections.heading: High-eccentricity migration and the alignment test
sections.body: A rival channel is high-eccentricity migration: a giant is thrown onto a very elongated, tilted orbit by planet–planet scattering or by Kozai–Lidov cycles from a distant companion, then tides raised on the planet at each close pass drain orbital energy and shrink-and-circularize the orbit. The two channels make a testable prediction about the angle between the planet’s orbit and the star’s spin axis. Disk migration should leave orbits well-aligned; violent high-e migration should produce many tilted, even retrograde, orbits. That spin–orbit angle is measured with the Rossiter–McLaughlin effect — the tiny RV distortion as a transiting planet successively blocks the approaching (blueshifted) and receding (redshifted) halves of the rotating stellar disk. The data are messy: many hot Jupiters are aligned, but a substantial fraction are strongly misaligned, so the field’s consensus is that BOTH channels operate, and the open debate is their relative importance.

lessons.workedExample: Show quantitatively why "hot Jupiter" is literal. A planet’s equilibrium temperature (for zero albedo, efficient heat redistribution) is T_eq = T_star · sqrt(R_star / 2a). For 51 Peg b: T_star ≈ 5800 K, R_star ≈ 1 R_sun = 0.00465 AU, a = 0.052 AU. Then R_star/2a = 0.00465 / (2 × 0.052) = 0.0447, sqrt(0.0447) = 0.211, so T_eq ≈ 5800 × 0.211 ≈ 1230 K. (This uses R_star ≈ 1 R_sun for a round number; 51 Peg is actually a slightly evolved subgiant with R ≈ 1.2 R_sun, and since T_eq ∝ sqrt(R_star) the true value is somewhat higher, ~1350 K. Either way the planet is well over 1000 K.) Contrast the snow-line temperature of ~170 K where the planet’s ices could originally condense: the planet now sits where it is roughly 1200 K, about seven times hotter than the environment its core needed to form. That gulf between the ~2.7 AU birthplace and the 0.05 AU present orbit is precisely the distance migration (of one kind or another) has to explain.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use hot Jupiters to see whether a student can separate an observation (a giant planet at 0.05 AU) from the competing interpretations (disk migration vs. high-eccentricity migration vs. rare in-situ formation). The mark of depth is naming a discriminating test — the Rossiter–McLaughlin spin–orbit angle — and stating honestly that the evidence supports a mix of channels rather than a single winner. A student who declares migration "solved" one way has overclaimed; the real science is in the still-open partition between mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Why is in-situ formation of a Jupiter-mass planet at 0.05 AU difficult under core accretion?

options.text: Because the star’s gravity is too weak that close in to hold a planet
Because so close to the star the disk is too hot for ices to condense, starving the region of the solids needed to build a giant core
Because planets cannot orbit faster than the star rotates
Because hydrogen and helium do not exist that close to a star

explanations.a: Stellar gravity is stronger close in, not weaker; that is not the obstacle.
explanations.b: Correct — core accretion needs abundant ices that only condense beyond the snow line (~2.7 AU, ~170 K); at 0.05 AU the disk is far too hot and solid-poor to grow a giant core in place.
explanations.c: Orbital speed is set by gravity, not the star’s spin; a close-in planet routinely orbits faster than the star rotates and that poses no problem.
explanations.d: H and He are abundant in the inner disk gas; the shortage is solid ices for the core, not the envelope gas.

questions.prompt: The Rossiter–McLaughlin effect is used to constrain hot-Jupiter formation because it measures:

options.text: The planet’s exact mass, breaking the sin i degeneracy
The angle between the planet’s orbital plane and the star’s spin axis (spin–orbit alignment)
The chemical composition of the planet’s atmosphere
The age of the host star

explanations.a: It does not give the mass; that comes from the RV amplitude plus a known inclination.
explanations.b: Correct — as a transiting planet crosses the rotating star it blocks first the blueshifted then the redshifted limb, distorting the RV curve in a way that reveals the sky-projected spin–orbit angle; alignment favors disk migration, misalignment favors high-eccentricity migration.
explanations.c: Atmospheric composition comes from transmission/emission spectroscopy, not the Rossiter–McLaughlin effect.
explanations.d: Stellar age comes from other diagnostics (rotation, isochrones); the Rossiter–McLaughlin effect measures orbital geometry.

questions.prompt: Match each migration/formation channel to its characteristic signature or claim.

right.text: Smooth inward drift via disk torques; leaves near-circular, well-aligned orbits
Scattering or Kozai–Lidov + tidal circularization; produces many tilted/retrograde orbits
The giant assembles near the star with little or no radial migration

questions.explanation: Disk migration drifts the planet inward through gas torques and tends to preserve circular, aligned orbits; high-eccentricity migration flings the planet onto a tilted, eccentric orbit that tides later shrink, leaving frequent misalignments; in-situ formation posits assembly near the star with little migration — the minority position.

questions.prompt: What is the current consensus reading of hot-Jupiter spin–orbit data?

options.text: All hot Jupiters are aligned, proving disk migration alone
All hot Jupiters are misaligned, proving high-eccentricity migration alone
Many are aligned but a substantial fraction are misaligned, so both channels appear to operate and their relative importance is still debated
Spin–orbit angles are unmeasurable, so the question is unanswerable

explanations.a: A real subset of hot Jupiters is strongly misaligned or retrograde, so alignment alone does not hold.
explanations.b: Many hot Jupiters are in fact well-aligned, so universal misalignment is false.
explanations.c: Correct — the observed mix of aligned and misaligned systems points to both disk and high-eccentricity migration contributing, with the open debate being their relative fractions.
explanations.d: Spin–orbit angles are routinely measured via the Rossiter–McLaughlin effect (and other methods); the question is very much answerable in part.

lessons.label: The Kepler Mission, Completeness Corrections, and the Contested eta-Earth Estimate

sections.heading: Kepler: staring at one patch of sky for planets in transit
sections.body: NASA’s Kepler mission (launched 2009, PI William Borucki) stared almost continuously at a single ~115 square-degree field in Cygnus–Lyra, monitoring the brightness of about 150,000 stars for the tiny periodic dips caused by planets transiting across their stars. A transit dims the star by the fraction of its disk the planet covers: the transit depth equals (R_p/R_star)². Kepler transformed the field from dozens of planets to thousands, and its statistical power — many similar stars watched uniformly — made it the instrument for asking not just "do planets exist?" but "how COMMON are they?"

sections.heading: From a catalog of detections to an occurrence rate
sections.body: You cannot read planet frequency straight off the catalog, because Kepler did not detect every planet that was there. Two big selection effects intervene. First, geometry: a transit is only visible if the orbit is edge-on enough, with probability roughly R_star/a — for an Earth at 1 AU around the Sun that is only about 0.5%. Second, detection completeness: small planets make shallow dips, and long-period planets transit rarely (fewer events to stack), so both push the signal below the detection threshold. The true occurrence rate is the detected count divided by the product of the geometric probability and the completeness — corrections that can multiply the raw counts by large, uncertain factors precisely in the regime of small, long-period planets.

sections.heading: eta-Earth: an extrapolation, not a measurement
sections.body: eta-Earth (η⊕) is the fraction of Sun-like stars hosting a roughly Earth-size planet in the habitable zone. It matters enormously — it sets how densely future missions must search for a habitable-zone Earth analog. But it sits in the worst possible corner of Kepler’s sensitivity: small radius (shallow transit, ~84 ppm for an Earth across the Sun) and long period (~1 year, so only a few transits in the data), where completeness is lowest and the correction factor is largest. Different teams making different completeness and habitable-zone assumptions got wildly different answers — Petigura, Howard & Marcy (2013) reported roughly 22% of Sun-like stars with a near-Earth-size planet in a broadly defined habitable zone, while other analyses (e.g., Foreman-Mackey et al. 2014, and later Bryson et al. 2021) landed lower or attached very wide uncertainties. The honest statement is that η⊕ is dominated by an extrapolation into Kepler’s incompleteness, so it is a contested estimate, not a settled number.

lessons.workedExample: Work the two selection effects for an Earth analog. Transit depth: (R_earth/R_sun)² = (6371 km / 696,000 km)² = (0.00916)² = 8.4×10⁻⁵ ≈ 84 parts per million — an 84 ppm dip, far shallower than a Jupiter’s (R_Jup/R_sun)² = (69,911/696,000)² = (0.1004)² ≈ 0.0101 = 1%, i.e. a full percent. Geometric probability: p ≈ R_sun/a = 0.00465 AU / 1 AU ≈ 0.0047, about 0.47%. So even before any noise, only ~1 in 210 Earth-analog systems is oriented to transit, and the transit it produces dims the star by under a hundredth of a percent across only ~4 events in the mission — the combination that makes η⊕ hinge on how you extrapolate completeness rather than on direct detections.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges lean on Kepler and η⊕ to test whether a student understands that a catalog is not an occurrence rate. The tell is whether they invoke completeness and geometric corrections — and admit that η⊕ is an extrapolation into Kepler’s least-sensitive regime, which is why published values disagree by an order of magnitude. A student who quotes a single η⊕ as fact has missed the debate; one who says "it depends on the completeness model and the habitable-zone definition" has grasped why it is contested.

questions.prompt: The transit depth of a planet crossing its star is given by which expression?

options.text: R_p / R_star
(R_p / R_star)²
(R_p / a)²
R_star / a

explanations.a: A linear ratio of radii is not the depth; the dimming is set by area, not radius directly.
explanations.b: Correct — the fractional dip equals the ratio of the planet’s disk area to the star’s, (πR_p²)/(πR_star²) = (R_p/R_star)².
explanations.c: The orbital distance a does not enter the depth; it enters the geometric transit probability instead.
explanations.d: R_star/a is the geometric probability that a transit occurs, not how deep it is.

questions.prompt: Why must a raw Kepler planet catalog be corrected before it gives an occurrence rate?

options.text: Because Kepler observed every star in the whole sky, so the sample is too large
Because only a small fraction of orbits are geometrically aligned to transit, and detection completeness drops for small, long-period planets — both must be divided out
Because transit depths are always overestimated by the pipeline
Because occurrence rates are fixed at 100% for Sun-like stars

explanations.a: Kepler watched one ~115 sq-deg field of ~150,000 stars, not the whole sky; the issue is missed planets, not too many stars.
explanations.b: Correct — the true rate = detected / (geometric probability × completeness); the geometric factor (~R_star/a) and the completeness (worst for small, long-period planets) both suppress the raw counts and must be corrected.
explanations.c: Depths are not systematically overestimated; the corrections are for missed detections, not biased depths.
explanations.d: Occurrence rates are the quantity being measured, not a fixed constant.

questions.prompt: Why is eta-Earth specifically the hardest occurrence rate to pin down from Kepler data?

options.text: Because Earth-size habitable-zone planets are too bright to observe
Because such planets are small (shallow ~84 ppm transits) and long-period (few transits to stack), landing in Kepler’s least-complete regime where the correction is largest and most uncertain
Because habitable-zone planets do not transit at all
Because Sun-like stars are extremely rare in the Kepler field

explanations.a: These planets are hard because their signals are faint, not because they are too bright.
explanations.b: Correct — an Earth analog gives a ~84 ppm dip only a few times over the mission, the corner of parameter space where completeness is lowest, so η⊕ hinges on extrapolating that correction rather than on secure detections.
explanations.c: Habitable-zone planets do transit when geometrically aligned; the difficulty is detecting the shallow, infrequent signal.
explanations.d: Sun-like (FGK) stars are plentiful in the Kepler sample; rarity of hosts is not the issue.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of turning Kepler photometry into an eta-Earth estimate, from first to last.

items.text: Detect periodic transit dips in the light curves and build a planet catalog
Correct each detection for geometric transit probability (~R_star/a)
Correct for detection completeness (sensitivity to small, long-period planets)
Extrapolate the corrected occurrence into the Earth-size, habitable-zone bin to get η⊕

questions.explanation: You first detect transits and build the catalog, then divide out the geometric alignment probability and the pipeline’s completeness, and only then extrapolate the corrected occurrence into the Earth-size habitable-zone bin — the extrapolation step where the answer becomes model-dependent and contested.

lessons.label: What Carved the Radius Valley? Photoevaporation vs. Core-Powered Mass Loss

sections.heading: The Fulton gap: a dip in the small-planet radius distribution
sections.body: When Fulton et al. (2017), using precise California-Kepler Survey radii, plotted the number of small close-in planets against their size, they found not a smooth spread but a bimodal distribution with a deficit — the "radius valley" or Fulton gap — near 1.5–2.0 Earth radii. On one side sit super-Earths peaking around 1.3 R_earth (dense, essentially bare rock); on the other sit sub-Neptunes peaking around 2.4 R_earth (rocky cores wrapped in a few-percent hydrogen–helium envelope that puffs them up). The gap is a genuine feature of planet demographics, and the question is what physical process empties the middle.

sections.heading: Photoevaporation: the young star strips the envelope
sections.body: One mechanism is photoevaporation (Owen & Wu 2013, 2017). In its first ~100 million years a star pours out high-energy X-ray and ultraviolet (XUV) radiation, which heats and inflates a close-in planet’s H/He envelope until it escapes. A planet with a small enough core cannot hold its atmosphere and is stripped to bare rock (landing on the super-Earth peak); a planet with a big enough core keeps its envelope (staying a sub-Neptune). Because the process is driven by stellar high-energy output early on, photoevaporation predicts the valley’s location should depend on the star’s XUV history and on the planet’s insolation, and it operates on short (~10⁸ yr) timescales.

sections.heading: Core-powered mass loss: the planet strips itself
sections.body: A competing mechanism is core-powered mass loss (Ginzburg, Schlichting & Sari 2018). Here the escape is driven not by the star’s XUV but by the planet’s OWN internal heat: the leftover heat of formation stored in the cooling rocky core slowly leaks out through the envelope over ~billion-year timescales, powering a gradual atmospheric escape (regulated near the bolometric-driven energy limit). It predicts a very similar valley near ~1.8 R_earth — which is the problem: both mechanisms reproduce the gap’s location. The debate is settled only by second-order clues, chiefly how the valley’s position depends on stellar age, stellar mass, and orbital period, because photoevaporation (fast, XUV-driven, early) and core-powered loss (slow, internally driven, late) predict subtly different dependences. The origin of the radius valley remains an active, unresolved dispute.

lessons.workedExample: See why the gap is a "fossil of atmospheres" by how little gas moves a planet across it. Take a rocky core of about 5 M_earth. Bare, its radius is roughly 1.5 R_earth (rock is dense). Now add a hydrogen–helium envelope of just 1% of the planet’s mass. Because H/He is so low in density and so extended, that tiny mass fraction inflates the observed radius to roughly 2.4 R_earth — nearly doubling the planet’s size while barely changing its mass. So two planets with essentially identical ~5 M_earth cores can sit on opposite sides of the valley purely by whether they kept or lost that ~1% gas skin. That is exactly what makes the gap diagnostic: it separates atmosphere-keepers from atmosphere-losers, and the argument is over which loss process — external XUV or internal heat — does the stripping.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the radius valley to test whether a student can hold two viable mechanisms in mind that predict the SAME headline feature. The depth signal is naming both photoevaporation (fast, XUV-driven, ~10⁸ yr) and core-powered mass loss (slow, internally driven, ~10⁹ yr), and then citing the discriminator — the valley’s dependence on stellar age, mass, or insolation — rather than asserting one has "won." A student who treats the gap’s existence as proof of a single mechanism has skipped the actual open question.

questions.prompt: What does the "radius valley" (Fulton gap) refer to?

options.text: A gap in orbital distances where no planets are found
A deficit of close-in planets near 1.5–2.0 Earth radii, separating rocky super-Earths from sub-Neptunes with H/He envelopes
A gap in stellar masses that host planets
A range of temperatures at which no planets can survive

explanations.a: The valley is in planet RADIUS, not orbital distance.
explanations.b: Correct — Fulton et al. (2017) found a bimodal radius distribution with a deficit near 1.5–2.0 R_earth, splitting bare rocky super-Earths (~1.3 R_earth) from envelope-bearing sub-Neptunes (~2.4 R_earth).
explanations.c: It is a feature of planet radii, not of host-star masses.
explanations.d: It is a radius gap, not a forbidden temperature band.

questions.prompt: The core difference between photoevaporation and core-powered mass loss is:

options.text: Photoevaporation adds atmosphere while core-powered mass loss removes it
Photoevaporation is driven by the star’s early XUV radiation on ~10⁸-yr timescales, while core-powered mass loss is driven by the planet’s own internal heat on ~10⁹-yr timescales
Photoevaporation applies only to gas giants, core-powered only to rocky planets
They predict completely different valley locations, so the data already settle it

explanations.a: Both processes REMOVE atmosphere; neither adds it.
explanations.b: Correct — photoevaporation strips the envelope using the young star’s high-energy XUV output early (~100 Myr), whereas core-powered mass loss uses the leftover heat of the cooling core over billions of years.
explanations.c: Both act on the same class of small close-in planets with H/He envelopes, not on disjoint planet types.
explanations.d: The crux of the debate is that they predict a NEARLY IDENTICAL valley location, so the data do not trivially settle it.

questions.prompt: Why can a planet cross from the sub-Neptune peak to the super-Earth peak by losing only ~1% of its mass in gas?

options.text: Because losing 1% of the mass halves the core’s density
Because a low-density, extended H/He envelope of just ~1% by mass can nearly double the observed radius, so stripping it collapses the planet onto the bare-rock size
Because the orbital distance changes when gas is lost
Because the core turns to gas as the atmosphere escapes

explanations.a: The rocky core’s density is essentially unchanged; what changes is the puffy gas layer on top.
explanations.b: Correct — hydrogen–helium is so light and extended that a ~1% mass envelope inflates the radius from ~1.5 to ~2.4 R_earth; removing it drops the planet to the bare-rock size, moving it across the valley.
explanations.c: Atmospheric loss does not appreciably change the orbit; the radius changes, not a.
explanations.d: The solid core does not vaporize; only the gaseous envelope escapes.

questions.prompt: Match each mass-loss mechanism to the correct property.

right.text: Driven by the young star’s XUV radiation, acting within ~100 Myr
Driven by the planet’s own leftover internal heat, acting over ~Gyr
How the valley’s location depends on stellar age, stellar mass, and insolation

questions.explanation: Photoevaporation is external and early, powered by stellar XUV within ~100 Myr; core-powered mass loss is internal and slow, powered by the cooling core over billions of years; because both reproduce the same gap location, the way the valley shifts with stellar age, mass, and insolation is the discriminator observers use.

lessons.label: Phosphine at Venus (Greaves 2020): Anatomy of a Contested Detection

sections.heading: The claim: a single line, an extraordinary conclusion
sections.body: In September 2020, Jane Greaves and collaborators reported in Nature Astronomy the apparent detection of phosphine (PH₃) in the atmosphere of Venus, at an abundance of about 20 parts per billion, based on a single absorption feature near 1.123 mm (about 266.94 GHz) seen first with the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) and then with the ALMA array. Their argument was not that phosphine IS life, but that they could not identify any known abiotic chemistry able to sustain it in Venus’s clouds — and phosphine on rocky worlds had been floated as a possible biosignature — so the temperate cloud deck around 50 km became a target of intense interest. The claim illustrates a recurring hazard: an extraordinary interpretation resting on one spectral line.

sections.heading: The baseline problem and the SO₂ confusion
sections.body: The detection quickly drew scrutiny on two fronts. First, the spectral baseline: extracting a faint line requires subtracting the instrument-and-atmosphere continuum, and the original analysis used a high-order (up to 12th-order) polynomial fit. Critics (e.g., Snellen et al. 2020) argued that fitting so many free parameters to a noisy spectrum can manufacture spurious dips at roughly the claimed significance, so the ~15-sigma headline was not robust. Second, chemistry: sulfur dioxide (SO₂), which Venus has in abundance, has a transition very close in frequency, and Villanueva et al. (2020) argued the feature could be largely or entirely SO₂ rather than PH₃ — mis-attributing an SO₂ line to phosphine would inflate a biosignature story out of ordinary Venusian sulfur chemistry.

sections.heading: Reprocessing, retraction pressure, and the lesson
sections.body: When the ALMA data were recalibrated (an issue with the array’s bandpass processing was found and the archive corrected), the reprocessed spectrum showed a far weaker or absent feature; several independent reanalyses reported no significant detection, or an upper limit near ~1 ppb rather than ~20 ppb. The original team reanalyzed and maintained a marginal (~1 ppb) signal, and the debate did not fully close. The scientific value of the episode is methodological: it is a clean case study in separating data from interpretation — a single-line detection, a flexible baseline that can create features, a plausible mundane alternative (SO₂), and a calibration error all conspired to turn a bold biosignature claim into a cautionary tale about statistical significance and confirmation.

lessons.workedExample: Trace how the headline number collapsed. The original paper quoted the feature at roughly 15 standard deviations (15-sigma), which sounds unassailable — a 15-sigma excursion has a chance probability far below one in a trillion IF the noise is Gaussian and the baseline is correct. But the significance is only as trustworthy as those two assumptions. Allowing a 12th-order polynomial baseline injects up to a dozen extra degrees of freedom that can soak up real structure and sculpt an apparent dip; refitting with a more conservative baseline, and then using the corrected ALMA calibration, dropped the significance below the ~3-sigma level where reasonable people call it a detection — and revised the implied abundance from ~20 ppb down toward ~1 ppb or an upper limit. The physics lesson: a stated sigma is not a fixed property of the data; it is conditional on the baseline and calibration model, and an extraordinary claim needs those held to an extraordinary standard.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges raise the Venus phosphine saga to see whether a student can dissect WHY a headline detection failed to hold, not just repeat that it was "debunked." The depth markers are concrete: a single-line detection, a high-order polynomial baseline that can fabricate features, an overlapping SO₂ line offering a mundane explanation, and an ALMA calibration error that shrank the signal on reprocessing. A student who names these — and frames the whole thing as separating data from interpretation — demonstrates exactly the skeptical rigor a judge wants when a project makes a bold claim from a marginal signal.

questions.prompt: What was the primary statistical criticism of the original phosphine detection?

options.text: The telescopes were pointed at the wrong planet
A high-order (up to 12th-order) polynomial baseline fit has enough free parameters to manufacture a spurious feature at roughly the claimed significance
Phosphine cannot exist as a molecule
The observation used visible light, which cannot see molecules

explanations.a: The pointing was correct; the dispute was about data reduction, not the target.
explanations.b: Correct — critics argued the flexible high-order baseline could absorb noise structure and create an apparent dip, so the ~15-sigma significance was not robust to the baseline choice.
explanations.c: Phosphine (PH₃) is a well-known stable molecule; its existence was never in question.
explanations.d: The detection was at millimeter (radio) wavelengths where molecular rotational lines appear, not in the visible.

questions.prompt: Why did sulfur dioxide (SO₂) become central to the debate?

options.text: SO₂ is a known biosignature that competes with phosphine
SO₂ is abundant on Venus and has a transition close in frequency to the phosphine line, so the feature might be ordinary SO₂ rather than PH₃
SO₂ destroys all phosphine instantly, so none could be present
SO₂ was used to calibrate the telescope

explanations.a: SO₂ is common volcanic/atmospheric sulfur chemistry, not a biosignature.
explanations.b: Correct — Venus has abundant SO₂, which has a nearby transition; Villanueva et al. (2020) argued the observed feature could be largely SO₂, giving a mundane explanation for what was claimed as phosphine.
explanations.c: The point was spectral confusion between the two, not that SO₂ chemically eliminates phosphine.
explanations.d: SO₂ was not the calibrator; the calibration issue was a separate ALMA bandpass problem.

questions.prompt: What happened to the claimed abundance after the ALMA data were recalibrated and reanalyzed?

options.text: It rose from ~20 ppb to ~200 ppb, strengthening the claim
It fell to a far weaker or absent signal, with reanalyses reporting no significant detection or an upper limit near ~1 ppb
It stayed exactly at 20 ppb, fully confirmed
The planet was found to have no atmosphere at all

explanations.a: The signal weakened, not strengthened, after reprocessing.
explanations.b: Correct — corrected ALMA calibration and more conservative baselines yielded a much weaker or absent feature; several teams found no significant detection or an upper limit around ~1 ppb versus the original ~20 ppb.
explanations.c: The ~20 ppb value did not survive reanalysis intact; the significance dropped substantially.
explanations.d: Venus has a thick atmosphere; the dispute was about one trace molecule, not the atmosphere’s existence.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of the Venus phosphine episode from first to last.

items.text: Greaves et al. report a ~20 ppb phosphine feature near 1.123 mm (JCMT, then ALMA)
Critics challenge the high-order polynomial baseline and its inflated significance
Others argue the feature could be an overlapping SO₂ line, not PH₃
ALMA data are recalibrated and reanalyses find a far weaker or absent signal

questions.explanation: The sequence ran from the original ~20 ppb claim, to the statistical challenge over the flexible baseline, to the chemical alternative that SO₂ could mimic the line, and finally to the ALMA recalibration and reanalyses that reduced the signal to weak-or-absent.

lessons.label: DMS on K2-18b and the Biosignature Wars: What Counts as Evidence for Life?

sections.heading: K2-18b and the Hycean hypothesis
sections.body: K2-18b is a sub-Neptune — about 8.6 Earth masses and 2.6 Earth radii — orbiting in the habitable zone of the cool M dwarf K2-18, roughly 120 light-years away. Water vapor was reported in its atmosphere in 2019. Madhusudhan and collaborators proposed it might be a "Hycean" world (Madhusudhan et al. 2021): a planet with a deep liquid-water ocean beneath a thick hydrogen atmosphere, a potentially habitable class quite unlike Earth. Because K2-18 is a small, cool star, the planet’s transmission spectrum is comparatively accessible, making it a prime target for JWST atmospheric spectroscopy.

sections.heading: JWST detections — and a contested molecule
sections.body: In 2023, JWST transmission spectra (Madhusudhan et al. 2023) showed methane (CH₄) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) with an apparent lack of ammonia and carbon monoxide — a pattern consistent with, though not unique to, a Hycean interpretation. The same work reported a TENTATIVE hint of dimethyl sulfide (DMS), a molecule that on Earth is produced almost entirely by marine phytoplankton, hence its interest as a possible biosignature. A 2025 follow-up (Madhusudhan et al. 2025, using JWST’s mid-infrared MIRI) reported a stronger DMS/DMDS signal at roughly the 3-sigma level. Crucially, 3-sigma is NOT a discovery: it corresponds to a chance probability of about 0.3% (~1 in 370), well short of the 5-sigma (~1 in 3.5 million) threshold physics conventionally demands for a claim of this magnitude.

sections.heading: The biosignature wars: alternatives and false positives
sections.body: The DMS claim triggered exactly the scrutiny a life claim should. Independent reanalyses of the same JWST data found that DMS was not statistically required — other molecules or a featureless model could fit comparably — so the significance is model-dependent and fragile. Chemically, DMS is not an airtight biosignature: it has been reported on comet 67P and in the interstellar medium, showing abiotic routes exist. And the planet’s very nature is disputed — instead of a Hycean ocean world, K2-18b could be a gas-rich mini-Neptune with no habitable surface, or even harbor a magma ocean. This is the heart of the "biosignature wars": a candidate molecule is not evidence for life until you have (1) a robust detection above threshold, (2) confidence the molecule is really present and correctly identified, and (3) exclusion of abiotic sources — the false-positive problem. The consensus is that K2-18b is a fascinating target, not a detection of life.

lessons.workedExample: Put the "3-sigma DMS" claim in context two ways. First, the signal size: K2-18b’s transit depth is (R_p/R_star)² = (2.6 × 6371 km) / (0.41 × 696,000 km), squared = (16,565 / 285,360)² = (0.0581)² ≈ 0.00337 ≈ 0.34% (about 3400 ppm) — but the atmospheric absorption features that carry molecular fingerprints sit only at the level of tens of ppm on TOP of that dip, so DMS lives in a signal a hundred-plus times smaller than the transit itself. Second, the statistics: 3-sigma means roughly a 0.3% chance of arising from noise (~1 in 370). That feels convincing until you recall the 5-sigma standard (~1 in 3.5 million) used for extraordinary claims, and that scanning many possible molecules inflates the chance of a spurious 3-sigma "hit" (a look-elsewhere effect). A ~1-in-370 fluke, searched across a spectrum, is exactly the kind of marginal result that history — see Venus phosphine — warns against over-reading.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use K2-18b to test the single most important habit in astrobiology: refusing to equate a candidate molecule with life. The depth markers are the significance gap (3-sigma is ~1 in 370, not the 5-sigma discovery bar), the false-positive problem (DMS has abiotic sources on comet 67P and in the interstellar medium), the model-dependence (independent reanalyses found DMS not statistically required), and disputed planet nature (Hycean vs. mini-Neptune vs. magma ocean). A student who says "they found life on K2-18b" fails; one who lays out what would have to be true — robust detection, correct identification, abiotic sources excluded — before life is on the table has grasped what counts as evidence.

questions.prompt: A reported DMS signal at 3-sigma corresponds to roughly what chance probability, and how does it compare to the discovery standard?

options.text: About a 30% chance of noise — well above any threshold
About a 0.3% chance (~1 in 370) of noise — suggestive but well short of the 5-sigma (~1 in 3.5 million) discovery standard
Effectively zero chance of noise — a confirmed discovery
About a 5% chance — exactly the discovery threshold

explanations.a: 3-sigma is far more stringent than 30%; that value badly understates the significance.
explanations.b: Correct — 3-sigma is about a 0.3% chance probability (~1 in 370), which is suggestive but far below the conventional 5-sigma (~1 in 3.5 million) bar for an extraordinary claim.
explanations.c: 3-sigma is not "effectively zero"; a ~1-in-370 fluke is entirely plausible, especially after searching many molecules.
explanations.d: The ~5% figure is a 2-sigma-ish level, not the discovery threshold; 5-sigma is the standard for claims like this.

questions.prompt: Why is DMS not, by itself, an airtight biosignature?

options.text: Because DMS is never produced by living things
Because DMS has known abiotic sources — it has been reported on comet 67P and in the interstellar medium — so a detection does not uniquely imply life (the false-positive problem)
Because DMS cannot survive in any atmosphere
Because DMS is too heavy to detect by spectroscopy

explanations.a: On Earth DMS is overwhelmingly biological (marine phytoplankton), which is exactly why it was proposed as a biosignature.
explanations.b: Correct — abiotic DMS has been reported on comet 67P and in the interstellar medium, so its presence does not by itself prove biology; ruling out abiotic sources is the false-positive problem central to biosignature claims.
explanations.c: DMS can persist in atmospheres; survivability is not the objection.
explanations.d: DMS is readily targeted spectroscopically; molecular weight is not the barrier.

questions.prompt: What did independent reanalyses of the JWST K2-18b data conclude about the DMS signal?

options.text: They confirmed DMS at 5-sigma, settling the question
They found DMS was not statistically required — comparable fits exist without it — so the significance is model-dependent and fragile
They found the planet does not exist
They detected chlorophyll instead of DMS

explanations.a: No reanalysis pushed DMS to a robust 5-sigma; the reverse happened.
explanations.b: Correct — independent teams showed the data could be fit comparably well without DMS, so its detection depends on modeling choices and is not secure.
explanations.c: K2-18b is a well-established transiting planet; its existence was never in doubt.
explanations.d: Chlorophyll was not detected; the contested molecule was DMS.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement for a credible biosignature claim to why the K2-18b DMS case fell short of it.

left.text: Correct, unambiguous identification of the molecule

right.text: The signal was only ~3-sigma (~1 in 370), short of the 5-sigma discovery bar
Independent reanalyses fit the data comparably well without DMS, so the identification is model-dependent
DMS has abiotic sources (comet 67P, interstellar medium), so its presence need not imply life

questions.explanation: A credible biosignature needs a detection above threshold (the ~3-sigma DMS signal is below the 5-sigma bar), a secure identification (reanalyses fit the data without DMS, so it is model-dependent), and exclusion of abiotic sources (DMS occurs abiotically on comet 67P and in the interstellar medium) — K2-18b’s DMS claim fell short on all three.

units.label: Populations, Rarer Methods, and Designing an Exoplanet Study

lessons.label: Occurrence Rates: Turning a Pile of Detections into Planets-Per-Star

sections.heading: From a catalog of finds to a statement about nature
sections.body: A survey like Kepler hands you a list of detected planets, but that list is not the answer to the question people actually care about — "how many planets does a typical star have?" A raw catalog is a biased sample: it is stuffed with the planets that are easy to find (big, close-in) and nearly empty of the ones that are hard (small, long-period), even if the hard ones are far more numerous in reality. An OCCURRENCE RATE converts detections into a physical statement: the average number of planets per star within a defined box of planet radius and orbital period. Computing it means answering, for every detected planet, "how many planets like this one did the survey MISS for each one it caught?" — then adding those corrected counts and dividing by the number of stars searched.

sections.heading: Two corrections: geometry and completeness
sections.body: Every transit detection must be up-weighted by two independent factors. The first is the GEOMETRIC TRANSIT PROBABILITY: only planets whose orbit happens to be edge-on enough to cross the stellar disk transit at all. For a circular orbit that probability is simply p_tr = Rs/a — the stellar radius over the orbital semi-major axis. A hot Jupiter at a/Rs ≈ 10 transits about 10% of the time; an Earth analogue at a/Rs ≈ 215 transits only ~0.5% of the time. So for every transiting Earth analogue you see, roughly 200 non-transiting ones are hidden by geometry alone. The second factor is DETECTION COMPLETENESS: even among planets that DO transit, the pipeline misses some because their signal is too weak or falls in a data gap. Each detected planet therefore counts as 1/(p_tr × completeness) planets. The landmark Kepler analyses — Howard et al. (2012) and Petigura, Howard & Marcy (2013) — built exactly this kind of inverse-weighted census.

sections.heading: What the census revealed: small planets are the rule
sections.body: Once corrected, the Kepler population overturned the picture that the early radial-velocity surveys (dominated by hot Jupiters) had suggested. Small planets — super-Earths and sub-Neptunes between roughly 1 and 4 Earth radii — turned out to be the most common kind of planet around Sun-like stars, vastly outnumbering giants. Petigura, Howard & Marcy (2013) estimated that about 22% (±8%) of Sun-like stars host an Earth-size to twice-Earth-size planet receiving Earth-like light — the much-cited "eta-Earth" figure, with famously large error bars driven by the extrapolation to long periods and small sizes where completeness is worst. A later refinement of the same population, Fulton et al. (2017), found the RADIUS VALLEY (or "Fulton gap"): a deficit of planets right around 1.5–2.0 Earth radii, splitting the small planets into rocky super-Earths below the gap and gas-enveloped sub-Neptunes above it — a feature that only emerged after careful completeness correction and precise stellar radii.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a survey of 40,000 Sun-like stars detects a single planet in a bin around 1 Earth radius and a 1-year period. The star has radius R_Sun and the orbit has a = 1 AU, so a/Rs ≈ (1.496×10⁸ km)/(696,000 km) ≈ 215, giving a geometric transit probability p_tr = Rs/a ≈ 1/215 ≈ 0.0047 (about 0.47%). Injection-recovery tests say the pipeline would have caught only 50% of such shallow, long-period signals, so completeness c = 0.5. This one detection therefore represents 1/(p_tr × c) = 1/(0.0047 × 0.5) ≈ 425 planets among the searched stars. The occurrence rate in that bin is 425 / 40,000 ≈ 0.011, i.e. roughly 1 such planet per 100 stars — from just one detection. The example makes the leverage vivid: a single Earth analogue stands in for hundreds of unseen ones, so the answer is dominated by how well you know p_tr and c, not by how many raw detections you have.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges press on occurrence rates because it is where students confuse "what I detected" with "what is out there." A weak project reports "I found 3 giant planets and 1 small one, so giants are more common" — reading the bias straight off the catalog. A strong one says "raw counts are the detection function, not the true population; I up-weighted each planet by 1/(transit probability × completeness) before comparing bins." If a student can explain why one detected Earth analogue implies hundreds of hidden ones (geometry alone hides ~99.5% of them), they have understood that a survey measures nature only after you invert its selection function.

questions.prompt: For a planet on a circular orbit with semi-major axis a around a star of radius Rs, the geometric probability that the orbit is oriented to produce a transit is approximately:

options.text: (Rp/Rs)²
Rs/a
a/Rs
Independent of the orbit — every planet transits

explanations.a: That is the transit DEPTH (the area ratio), not the probability that the orbit is aligned to transit at all.
explanations.b: Correct — for a circular orbit the fraction of random orientations that yield a transit is Rs/a, so close-in planets (small a) transit far more often than distant ones.
explanations.c: This is the inverse; a/Rs is a large number (tens to hundreds), and a probability cannot exceed 1. The probability is its reciprocal, Rs/a.
explanations.d: Only orbits sufficiently edge-on transit; most orientations do not, which is exactly why a geometric correction is needed.

questions.prompt: Why did corrected Kepler occurrence rates overturn the hot-Jupiter-heavy picture from early radial-velocity surveys?

options.text: Radial-velocity surveys had been fabricating detections
After correcting for geometry and completeness, small planets (≈1–4 R_Earth) proved to be by far the most common, though individually the hardest to detect
Hot Jupiters were shown not to exist
Kepler could only detect small planets, so it saw a different sky

explanations.a: The RV detections were real; the issue was selection bias toward easy-to-find giants, not fraud.
explanations.b: Correct — giants are over-represented in raw catalogs because they are easy to detect, but once each detection is up-weighted for its transit probability and completeness, small super-Earths and sub-Neptunes dominate the true population.
explanations.c: Hot Jupiters are real and were confirmed by Kepler too; they are simply rare (well under 1% of stars), not nonexistent.
explanations.d: Kepler detected planets across a wide size range, including giants; the shift came from bias correction, not from a size-limited instrument.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of computing a transit-survey occurrence rate, from raw data to a planets-per-star number.

items.text: Detect planets and bin them by radius and orbital period
For each bin, estimate the geometric transit probability (Rs/a) for those orbits
Run injection-recovery to estimate the pipeline completeness in each bin
Up-weight each detection by 1/(transit probability × completeness) and sum
Divide the summed weighted count by the number of stars searched

questions.explanation: You first bin the raw detections, then quantify the two things the survey missed — geometry (Rs/a) and pipeline completeness (from injection-recovery) — then correct each detection by the product of those factors, and finally normalize by the number of stars searched to get a planets-per-star occurrence rate.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning in an occurrence-rate calculation.

right.text: Average number of planets per star in a radius–period box
Rs/a — fraction of orbit orientations that produce a transit
Fraction of present planets the pipeline would recover if they transited
A deficit of planets near 1.5–2.0 R_Earth splitting rocky super-Earths from sub-Neptunes

questions.explanation: Occurrence is planets per star in a bin; transit probability is the geometric factor Rs/a; completeness is the recovered fraction from injection-recovery tests; and the radius valley (Fulton et al. 2017) is the gap near 1.5–2.0 R_Earth that emerged only after careful correction and precise stellar radii.

lessons.label: Survey Completeness and Detection Bias: Correcting for What You Cannot See

sections.heading: Completeness is measured, not assumed: injection and recovery
sections.body: Completeness is the probability that a planet of a given radius and period, if it were present AND transiting, would actually be flagged by the detection pipeline. You cannot derive it from theory because it depends on the messy specifics of the data — stellar noise, observation gaps, the detection threshold, the vetting cuts. The standard tool is INJECTION-RECOVERY: you inject a large number of synthetic transit signals of known depth and period directly into the real light curves, run the unchanged pipeline, and count what fraction come back out. Christiansen and collaborators ran exactly this exercise for Kepler, injecting hundreds of thousands of fake transits to map the completeness across the radius–period plane. The result is a "detection efficiency" surface that is near 100% for deep, short-period signals and falls toward zero for shallow, long-period ones — precisely the corner (Earth-like planets in wide orbits) where the science is most interesting and the correction is largest and most uncertain.

sections.heading: The detection threshold and reliability
sections.body: Kepler declared a signal a candidate only above a statistical threshold: the Multiple Event Statistic (MES), roughly the combined signal-to-noise of all the stacked transits, had to exceed about 7.1σ. That cut was tuned to keep the expected number of pure-noise false alarms low across the ~150,000 stars. But there is a symmetric danger: near the threshold, statistical fluctuations and instrumental artifacts can masquerade as planets, so a catalog also needs a RELIABILITY estimate — the fraction of candidates that are real rather than false alarms. Completeness (did I catch the real ones?) and reliability (are my catches real?) are two different corrections, and a defensible occurrence rate needs both. Ignoring reliability inflates the count of long-period planets, because that is exactly where noise fluctuations pile up near the threshold.

sections.heading: Every method has its own bias — know your instrument’s blind spots
sections.body: Detection bias is not unique to transits; each technique sees a skewed slice of parameter space. The TRANSIT method is biased toward large planets (deeper dips) on short-period orbits (higher transit probability and more repeats to stack). The RADIAL-VELOCITY method is biased toward massive planets (the reflex velocity K scales with planet mass) on short-period orbits (larger K and more completed cycles), and it measures only M·sin i, a minimum mass. DIRECT IMAGING is biased toward young, hot, massive planets on WIDE orbits (the opposite corner from transits). MICROLENSING is biased toward planets near the Einstein radius, a few AU out, and is essentially blind to short-period ones. This is why a full picture of planet populations requires stitching methods together: each is a differently-shaped window, and the truth lives in their union, not in any single survey. A classic historical caution is the reverse error — reading a bias-shaped catalog as if it were the true population, which is exactly what made hot Jupiters look "typical" in the mid-1990s.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to compare giant-planet occurrence found by transits versus radial velocity and naively notes that RV surveys report more long-period giants. Before concluding "RV finds more distant giants because they are more common there," they lay out the biases. Transits require Rs/a alignment, so a giant at 5 AU around a Sun-like star transits with probability Rs/a ≈ 696,000 km / (5 × 1.496×10⁸ km) ≈ 0.0009, under 0.1% — geometry alone hides 99.9% of them, and you also need several years of data to catch repeats. RV instead measures the reflex wobble, whose amplitude for that same Jupiter is K ≈ 12.5 m/s regardless of inclination (up to sin i), and only needs to sample the orbit, not catch an alignment. So RV’s apparent "excess" of cold giants is largely the transit method’s geometric blindness, not a real difference in the sky. The correct move is to convert both to bias-corrected occurrence rates before comparing — the same 1/(probability × completeness) machinery, with each method’s own selection function.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use completeness to separate students who understand that a null result is not the same as an absence. If your project "found no small planets," a judge will ask: would your method have detected one if it were there? A student who ran even a simple injection-recovery — adding a synthetic transit of known depth to their data and checking whether their own pipeline recovers it — can defend the claim "my non-detection rules out planets above X size," which is a real, quantitative result. A student who cannot state their detection efficiency has measured only their own instrument, not the sky, and a sharp judge will say so.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an injection-recovery test?

options.text: To increase the sensitivity of the telescope hardware
To measure completeness by injecting synthetic transits of known properties into real data and counting what fraction the unchanged pipeline recovers
To remove real planets from the data so only noise remains
To calibrate the star’s radius

explanations.a: Injection-recovery is a data-analysis procedure; it changes nothing about the hardware and adds no real sensitivity.
explanations.b: Correct — you inject fake signals of known depth and period, rerun the same detection pipeline, and the recovered fraction directly measures the completeness across the radius–period plane.
explanations.c: It adds synthetic signals; it does not subtract real planets. Recovered fake signals reveal how many real ones the pipeline would catch.
explanations.d: Stellar radius comes from spectroscopy, asteroseismology, or Gaia parallax, not from injecting synthetic transits.

questions.prompt: A student’s survey detects no planets smaller than 2 R_Earth. What must they check before claiming small planets are rare in their sample?

options.text: Nothing — a non-detection directly proves the planets are absent
Whether their pipeline would have detected such small planets if present (its completeness at that size)
Whether the star’s color changed during observation
Whether the planets are tidally locked

explanations.a: A non-detection with unknown sensitivity is uninformative — you might simply be blind to small planets.
explanations.b: Correct — only after establishing that the pipeline recovers small-planet signals (via injection-recovery or an SNR estimate) can a non-detection be turned into a real upper limit on occurrence.
explanations.c: Stellar color is unrelated to whether the pipeline could detect a shallow transit.
explanations.d: Tidal locking has no bearing on transit detectability; the question is signal strength versus the detection threshold.

questions.prompt: Match each detection method to the region of parameter space it is biased toward.

right.text: Large planets on short-period orbits (deep dips, high transit probability)
Massive planets on short-period orbits; yields only M·sin i
Young, hot, massive planets on wide orbits
Planets near the Einstein radius, a few AU out; blind to short periods

questions.explanation: Transits favor big, close-in planets; radial velocity favors massive, close-in planets and gives only a minimum mass M·sin i; direct imaging favors young, self-luminous giants far from their stars; microlensing favors planets near the Einstein radius a few AU out. Each is a differently-shaped window on the true population.

questions.prompt: Kepler required a Multiple Event Statistic (MES) above roughly 7.1σ. Why is a second correction — reliability — also needed near this threshold?

options.text: Because the threshold makes the telescope physically less sensitive over time
Because near the threshold, noise fluctuations and instrumental artifacts can imitate weak transits, so some candidates are false alarms rather than real planets
Because reliability is just another name for completeness
Because bright stars always produce false planets

explanations.a: The threshold is a statistical cut on the data, not a change to the hardware’s sensitivity.
explanations.b: Correct — completeness asks "did I catch the real ones?" while reliability asks "are my catches real?"; near the 7.1σ cut, noise piles up, so long-period candidates especially need a reliability correction to avoid over-counting.
explanations.c: They are distinct: completeness is the recovered fraction of true planets; reliability is the true fraction among candidates. Both are needed.
explanations.d: Bright stars actually have lower noise; false alarms cluster in noisier data and near the detection threshold, not simply on bright targets.

lessons.label: Gravitational Microlensing: Finding Cold, Distant, and Free-Floating Planets

sections.heading: A planet betrayed by gravity, not by light or wobble
sections.body: Microlensing exploits a prediction of general relativity: mass bends light. When a foreground star (the LENS) passes almost exactly in front of a more distant background star (the SOURCE), the lens’s gravity focuses and magnifies the source’s light, producing a smooth, symmetric brightening and fading over days to weeks as the alignment comes and goes. Crucially, the method does not require any light from the lens itself — it works even if the lens is faint, dark, or a planet with no star at all. The technique was proposed for planet-finding by Bohdan Paczyński (who revived stellar microlensing in 1986) and, for planets specifically, by Shude Mao & Paczyński (1991) and Andy Gould & Abraham Loeb (1992). Because the required alignment is so rare, surveys such as OGLE and MOA monitor tens of millions of bulge stars nightly to catch the handful that light up.

sections.heading: The Einstein radius and the planetary blip
sections.body: The natural scale of a lensing event is the EINSTEIN RADIUS, the angular radius of the ring into which a perfectly aligned point source would be smeared: θ_E = √[ (4GM/c²) · (D_S − D_L)/(D_S D_L) ], where M is the lens mass and D_L, D_S are the observer-to-lens and observer-to-source distances. For a typical bulge lens of a few tenths of a solar mass, θ_E is of order a milliarcsecond and the event timescale (the time to cross θ_E) is weeks. A PLANET orbiting the lens star adds its own tiny lens right where one of the source’s magnified images passes, producing a brief secondary spike — a "blip" lasting hours to a couple of days superimposed on the smooth stellar event. The strength and duration of that blip encode the planet-to-star MASS RATIO q and the projected separation in units of θ_E. The first planet found this way, OGLE-2003-BLG-235/MOA-2003-BLG-53 b, was announced by Ian Bond and collaborators (2004): a giant planet about 3–4 AU from a low-mass lens star several kiloparsecs away, with a well-determined mass ratio (q ≈ 0.0039) and an initial mass estimate of ~1.5 Jupiter masses — later refined by a HST-based reanalysis (Bennett et al. 2006) to ~2.6 Jupiter masses around a heavier lens near the K/M boundary.

sections.heading: The unique niche: cold planets and free-floaters
sections.body: Microlensing is sensitive precisely where the other methods are weakest. Its peak sensitivity is to planets at a few AU — near and beyond the snow line, the cold outer region where giant planets are thought to assemble — and it can reach planets thousands of parsecs away, sampling the whole Milky Way rather than just the solar neighborhood. Most strikingly, because it needs no host-star light, it can detect FREE-FLOATING (rogue) planets that are gravitationally unbound to any star: an isolated planetary-mass lens produces a short, star-less microlensing event with a timescale of only a day or two. Surveys have found such candidates, and careful analyses (e.g. Mróz et al. 2017) have used them to place limits on how common Jupiter-mass rogues are — constraining them to well under one per main-sequence star. A major limitation is that microlensing events are essentially one-shot: the alignment never repeats, so a given planet can rarely be re-observed or confirmed by a second method, which is why NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope was designed with a dedicated microlensing survey to build a statistical census of cold and free-floating planets.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a lens star of mass M = 0.3 M_Sun at D_L = 4 kpc, with the source at D_S = 8 kpc. The Einstein radius works out to θ_E = √[ (4GM/c²)·(D_S − D_L)/(D_S D_L) ] ≈ √[ (4 × 6.674×10⁻¹¹ × 0.3 × 1.99×10³⁰ / (3×10⁸)²) × (4 kpc)/(8 kpc × 4 kpc) ] . The mass term 4GM/c² gives a length of ≈ 1.77×10³ m per this mass, and folding in the distance factor yields θ_E of order a few tenths of a milliarcsecond and a physical Einstein radius at the lens of a few AU — so a planet orbiting a few AU out sits right where the images pass and is maximally detectable. A planet of mass ratio q = Mp/M = 10⁻³ (a Jupiter around an M-dwarf) produces a blip whose duration scales roughly as √q × t_E: if the stellar event lasts t_E ≈ 30 days, the planetary perturbation lasts about √(10⁻³) × 30 d ≈ 0.03 × 30 d ≈ 1 day. The takeaways: (1) the method’s sensitivity peaks at a few AU because that is where θ_E projects, and (2) you must sample the light curve at least hourly, because the whole planetary signal can come and go within a day and will never recur.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up microlensing to test whether a student grasps that different methods populate different, non-overlapping regions of parameter space — and that this is a feature, not a redundancy. The revealing question is "which planets can microlensing find that transits and radial velocity essentially cannot?" A student who answers "cold planets a few AU out, planets across the whole Galaxy, and free-floating planets with no star at all — because the method needs the lens’s gravity, not its light" understands why a complete demographic census must combine methods. A student who thinks microlensing is just "another way to see transits" has missed that it probes the outer, colder, and unbound population the transit surveys are blind to.

questions.prompt: What physical effect makes gravitational microlensing possible?

options.text: A planet reflecting starlight back toward Earth
A foreground mass bending and magnifying the light of a background source, as predicted by general relativity
The Doppler shift of the lens star’s spectral lines
The transit of the planet across the lens star’s disk

explanations.a: Reflected light is the basis of some direct-imaging phase measurements, not microlensing, which needs no light from the lens at all.
explanations.b: Correct — the lens’s gravity focuses the source’s light (general relativity’s light-bending), briefly magnifying it; a planet around the lens adds a short secondary spike.
explanations.c: That is radial velocity; microlensing is a photometric magnification effect, not a spectroscopic shift.
explanations.d: A transit requires the planet to cross a star’s disk; microlensing works via gravitational magnification of a separate, distant background star.

questions.prompt: Why is microlensing uniquely able to detect free-floating (rogue) planets?

options.text: Rogue planets are unusually bright and easy to image
The method relies on the planet’s gravity to magnify a background star, so it needs no host-star light and works even for unbound planets
Rogue planets have especially deep transits
Rogue planets emit strong radio signals

explanations.a: Rogue planets are extremely faint; they emit essentially no reflected light and are not detectable by imaging at such distances.
explanations.b: Correct — because microlensing detects the gravitational magnification of a background source rather than any light from the lens, an isolated planet with no star produces a short, star-less lensing event.
explanations.c: A free-floating planet has no star to transit, so transit depth is irrelevant.
explanations.d: Planets do not emit detectable radio signals of this kind; the detection is purely gravitational lensing.

questions.prompt: Match each microlensing quantity or milestone to its correct description.

right.text: The angular ring scale set by lens mass and the observer–lens–source distances
Planet mass divided by lens-star mass, read from the perturbation
A brief secondary spike (hours to ~a day) on the smooth stellar light curve
The first exoplanet discovered by microlensing, a giant planet (~1.5 M_Jup as first estimated, later refined to ~2.6 M_Jup) around a low-mass lens star

questions.explanation: θ_E is the angular Einstein-ring scale set by mass and distances; q = Mp/M_lens is the mass ratio read from the perturbation; the planetary blip is a short secondary spike on the stellar event; and OGLE-2003-BLG-235/MOA-2003-BLG-53 b (Bond et al. 2004) was the first microlensing planet, a giant body first estimated at ~1.5 M_Jup (later refined to ~2.6 M_Jup by Bennett et al. 2006) around a low-mass lens star.

questions.prompt: A major limitation of microlensing planet discoveries, compared with transits or radial velocity, is that:

options.text: The planet can be re-observed nightly for years to refine its orbit
The alignment is a one-time event that never repeats, so the planet usually cannot be re-observed or confirmed by a second method
It only works for planets closer than 0.1 AU
It requires the lens and source to be in our own solar neighborhood

explanations.a: The opposite is true — the chance alignment does not recur, so follow-up on the same event is generally impossible.
explanations.b: Correct — a microlensing event is a unique, non-repeating alignment, which is why the planets it finds are rarely confirmable by other techniques and why statistical surveys (like Roman) are the path forward.
explanations.c: Microlensing is most sensitive at a few AU, near the snow line, not at ultra-short periods.
explanations.d: Microlensing typically probes lenses thousands of parsecs away across the Galaxy, not just the solar neighborhood.
