The conceptual leap is the same one the winding dilemma forces on you: a wave crest on the ocean moves across the water without carrying the water bodily along, so it is not wound up by the currents beneath it.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate how badly a material arm winds up at the Sun's position. The orbital period is T = 2piR / v. With R = 8 kpc = 8 x 3.086e16 km = 2.47e17 km and v = 220 km/s: circumference 2piR = 1.55e18 km, so T = 1.55e18 / 220 = 7.05e15 s. Converting, 7.05e15 s / 3.156e7 s per year = 2.2e8 yr, about 230 million years per orbit. Over the Galaxy's 13.6-Gyr life that is 13.6e9 / 2.2e8 = 62 orbits at the solar radius. Now compare an inner ring at 4 kpc, where the flat 220 km/s curve gives T = 115 Myr — HALF the solar period. In one solar orbit the inner ring laps the Sun once; after sixty orbits the two are wound around each other ~60 times. That runaway coiling is exactly what a real, open two-arm spiral does NOT show, which is the whole point.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the winding dilemma because it separates students who memorized "galaxies have spiral arms" from those who understand WHY the arms are surprising. If a student can state that a flat rotation curve implies differential rotation, and that differential rotation would wind a material arm into a tight coil within a few orbits, they have identified the actual scientific problem that density-wave theory exists to solve. A judge who hears "the arms would wind up but they don't, so the arms can't be fixed stars" knows the student grasps arms as dynamical patterns, not painted-on decorations.

questions.prompt: A flat galactic rotation curve (constant orbital SPEED with radius) implies what about the ANGULAR speed of the disk?

options.text: Angular speed is constant, so the disk rotates rigidly
Angular speed decreases with radius, so inner material laps outer material
Angular speed increases with radius, so outer material orbits fastest
Angular speed is undefined because speed is constant

explanations.a: Rigid rotation would require angular speed to be constant, which needs orbital speed to RISE linearly with radius (v = OmegaR) — not a flat curve.
explanations.b: Correct — with v roughly constant, Omega = v/R falls as 1/R, so inner annuli complete orbits faster and progressively lap the outer disk. This differential rotation is what winds up any material feature.
explanations.c: A flat speed curve means angular speed FALLS with radius, not rises; outer material has the same speed but a longer path, so it lags.
explanations.d: Angular speed Omega = v/R is perfectly well-defined; it simply varies with R when v is fixed.

questions.prompt: About how long does one orbit take at the Sun's galactocentric radius (~8 kpc, v ~ 220 km/s), and what does the Galaxy's age imply?

options.text: ~2 million years, so the Galaxy has made thousands of turns
~230 million years, so the Galaxy has made roughly 60 turns
~13 billion years, so the Galaxy has made only about one turn
~1 billion years, so the Galaxy has made about 13 turns

explanations.a: 2 Myr is far too short; the Sun moves at 220 km/s over a ~50,000 light-year circumference, which takes hundreds of millions of years, not a couple million.
explanations.b: Correct — T = 2piR/v gives about 2.3e8 yr, and 13.6 Gyr / 0.23 Gyr is roughly 60 orbits, which is why a material arm would be catastrophically wound up.
explanations.c: 13 Gyr is the Galaxy's AGE, not one orbital period; the disk turns far faster than that at the solar radius.
explanations.d: 1 Gyr overestimates the period by about a factor of four; the correct value is ~230 Myr.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of the winding dilemma argument, from premise to conclusion.

items.text: Rotation curves are observed to be roughly flat (constant speed)
Constant speed means angular speed falls with radius (differential rotation)
A fixed group of stars/gas would wind into a tight coil within a few orbits
But real arms stay open over many orbits
Therefore arms cannot be a fixed material feature — they must be a pattern

questions.explanation: The argument runs: observe flat curves -> infer differential rotation -> note that material arms would wind up quickly -> confront the fact that observed arms stay open -> conclude arms are patterns (waves), not fixed material.

lessons.label: Density-Wave Theory: Lin, Shu, and the Standing Pattern

sections.heading: The quasi-stationary spiral structure hypothesis
sections.body: In 1964, C. C. Lin and Frank Shu published the theory that still frames the modern picture: spiral arms are a DENSITY WAVE — a self-sustaining, quasi-stationary pattern of enhanced density that rotates rigidly at a single PATTERN SPEED, Omega_p, independent of the material orbiting through it. Their "quasi-stationary spiral structure" (QSSS) hypothesis treated the arms as a standing wave in the disk's density, analogous to a mode of vibration. Crucially, the pattern speed is a single number for the whole disk, so the pattern does NOT wind up even though the stars do — sidestepping the winding dilemma entirely. Lin and Shu solved the linearized equations for a rotating, self-gravitating disk and found that trailing spiral density waves are natural, long-lived solutions.

sections.heading: The traffic-jam picture
sections.body: The intuition is a traffic jam on a highway. Cars (stars and gas clouds) stream along at their own orbital speed; the JAM (the density enhancement) sits at a spot on the road and drifts slowly, at a different speed from any individual car. Each car slows as it enters the crowded region, spends extra time there, then speeds up and leaves — so at any instant the jam contains a crowd, but not the SAME cars minute to minute. In the galaxy, stars on slightly elliptical orbits, with their orbital orientations organized so the ellipses crowd together along a spiral locus, pile up where orbits converge. The density in the arm is only modestly enhanced — typically 10-20% above the smooth disk in the old-star population — yet that is enough to organize the disk into arms.

sections.heading: Why the gas response is dramatic
sections.body: A 10-20% bump in the old stars would be an unremarkable feature on its own. What makes arms so striking in images is the GAS. The interstellar gas is cold and highly compressible, so as it flows into the arm's deeper gravitational potential it is shocked and compressed by a much larger factor — a galactic shock front, worked out by W. W. Roberts in 1969 as a natural consequence of the Lin-Shu wave. The shock triggers the collapse of molecular clouds, lighting up the arm with bright, short-lived O and B stars and glowing HII regions. This is why arms appear blue and knotty in visible light even though the underlying stellar density contrast is gentle: the young luminous tracers are born AT the arm and die before drifting far from it.

lessons.workedExample: Contrast the pattern speed with the material speed at the Sun's radius to see why the pattern does not wind up. At R = 8 kpc the material's angular speed is Omega = v/R = 220 km/s / 8 kpc = 27.5 km/s/kpc. Estimates for the Milky Way's spiral pattern speed cluster around Omega_p = 20-25 km/s/kpc; take Omega_p = 20 km/s/kpc. Because Omega (27.5) exceeds Omega_p (20) here, the Sun and its neighbors OVERTAKE the spiral pattern from behind. The SYNODIC period — the time to catch up to and return to the SAME arm — is (2pi)/(Omega - Omega_p) = (2pi)/(7.5 km/s/kpc). Converting 7.5 km/s/kpc to inverse time (1 km/s/kpc = 1.023 per Gyr) gives 7.7 per Gyr, so 2pi/7.7 ~ 0.8 Gyr to return to the same arm. But a canonical two-armed spiral has TWO arms per turn, so the Sun actually crosses an arm every HALF synodic period, pi/(Omega - Omega_p) ~ 0.4 Gyr — consistent with published Milky Way solar arm-crossing estimates of ~0.1-0.5 Gyr. The key point: Omega varies with radius but Omega_p is a single fixed number, so the PATTERN keeps its open shape while the stars stream through it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about density-wave theory wants to hear the distinction between the pattern speed Omega_p and the material orbital speed Omega — because that single distinction is what resolves the winding dilemma and is the most common thing students get wrong. Students often say arms "are" regions of star formation; the sharper answer is that arms are a density wave, and star formation is a CONSEQUENCE of gas being shocked as it flows through the wave. Naming Lin and Shu (1964) and the traffic-jam analogy, and knowing the old-star density contrast is only ~10-20%, signals a student who understands mechanism rather than picture.

questions.prompt: In Lin and Shu's density-wave theory, what is the "pattern speed" Omega_p?

options.text: The orbital speed of the stars currently inside an arm
The single, radius-independent angular speed at which the spiral pattern rotates
The speed of light in the interstellar medium
The speed at which arms wind up over time

explanations.a: The stars' orbital speed varies with radius and is generally different from Omega_p; stars flow THROUGH the pattern rather than moving with it.
explanations.b: Correct — the pattern rotates as a rigid figure at one Omega_p for the whole disk, which is precisely why it does not wind up even though the material rotates differentially.
explanations.c: Density waves are dynamical gravitational features, unrelated to the propagation of light.
explanations.d: The whole point of a fixed Omega_p is that the pattern does NOT wind up; there is no winding rate.

questions.prompt: Why do spiral arms appear so much more prominent in blue light than the ~10-20% old-star density contrast would suggest?

options.text: Blue light penetrates dust better, revealing the true stellar density
Compressible gas is shocked at the arm, triggering bright, short-lived O and B stars that outline it
The arms are genuinely 100x denser in stars than the disk between them
Blue stars are older and have drifted far from where they formed

explanations.a: Blue light is actually scattered and absorbed MORE by dust than red light; it does not preferentially reveal stellar density.
explanations.b: Correct — the galactic shock (Roberts 1969) compresses gas far more than the 10-20% stellar bump, igniting luminous but short-lived massive stars and HII regions right at the arm.
explanations.c: The old-star density contrast is modest (~10-20%), not a factor of 100; the visual drama comes from young tracers, not stellar density.
explanations.d: O and B stars are the YOUNGEST, most short-lived stars; they die before drifting far, which is exactly why they trace the arm.

questions.prompt: Match each element of the density-wave picture to the correct description.

left.text: Old-star density contrast in an arm

right.text: A single fixed rotation rate for the whole pattern, so it never winds up
The same crowded spot persists while different cars flow through it
Compression of infalling gas that triggers star formation at the arm
A modest enhancement, roughly 10-20% above the smooth disk

questions.explanation: Omega_p is one fixed pattern rotation rate; the traffic jam persists while cars stream through; the galactic shock compresses gas and triggers star formation; and the old-star density enhancement in an arm is only ~10-20%.

questions.prompt: How does density-wave theory escape the winding dilemma?

options.text: It assumes the rotation curve is rigid, so nothing winds up
The arm is a wave pattern with a single Omega_p, not a fixed set of stars that would shear
It claims arms are re-created from scratch every orbit
It shows stars orbit slowly enough that winding never matters

explanations.a: Real rotation curves are flat, not rigid; density-wave theory works WITH differential rotation, it does not assume it away.
explanations.b: Correct — because the pattern rotates as one figure at Omega_p while stars merely pass through, the open shape is preserved indefinitely despite differential material motion.
explanations.c: The QSSS hypothesis holds the pattern is quasi-stationary and self-sustaining, not destroyed and rebuilt each orbit.
explanations.d: Stars orbit fast (~60 times over the Galaxy's life); winding absolutely would matter for material arms, which is why a pattern is needed.

lessons.label: Corotation, Resonances, and Self-Propagating Star Formation

sections.heading: Corotation and the Lindblad resonances
sections.body: A density wave cannot fill the disk at every radius. At the COROTATION radius the material's angular speed equals the pattern speed (Omega(R) = Omega_p); there the stars drift with the pattern rather than through it. Inside corotation stars overtake the arms; outside, the arms overtake the stars. Bracketing corotation are the LINDBLAD RESONANCES, named for Bertil Lindblad: the Inner Lindblad Resonance (ILR) where Omega_p = Omega - kappa/2, and the Outer Lindblad Resonance (OLR) where Omega_p = Omega + kappa/2. Here kappa is the epicyclic frequency — the rate at which a star oscillates radially about its guiding circle. The self-consistent Lin-Shu density wave lives in the annulus BETWEEN the ILR and OLR; near the resonances the wave is absorbed or reflected, which is one reason real arms have finite radial extent.

sections.heading: Where the shock sits relative to corotation
sections.body: The offset between old stars, gas, and young stars flips across corotation, and this is a testable prediction. Inside the corotation radius, gas and stars catch up to the arm from behind, are shocked on the trailing (upstream) edge, and the newborn star clusters then age as they drift downstream — producing an ordered color gradient ACROSS the arm. Several studies of grand-design spirals have looked for exactly this age gradient (younger clusters on one side of the arm, older on the other) as a fingerprint of a steady density wave, and its presence or absence is used to argue whether a given galaxy's arms are wave-driven or transient. The corotation radius in the Milky Way is thought to lie not far from the Sun's orbit, though its exact value remains debated.

sections.heading: Stochastic self-propagating star formation
sections.body: Not every spiral is a clean, two-armed grand design. Many galaxies are FLOCCULENT — patchy, feathery, many short arm segments with no global symmetry. Mueller and Arnett (1976) and then Gerola and Seiden (1978) proposed a very different mechanism for these: stochastic self-propagating star formation (SSPSF). A burst of massive-star formation drives supernovae and expanding shells that compress neighboring gas and trigger the NEXT burst nearby; differential rotation then shears these chains of induced star formation into trailing spiral arclets. SSPSF needs no global density wave at all — it is a local, self-exciting, sheared chain reaction. The modern synthesis is that grand-design arms (often driven by a bar or a companion's tidal tug, as in M51 and its companion NGC 5195) are density waves, while flocculent arms are largely SSPSF; many real galaxies show a blend of both.

lessons.workedExample: Locate the corotation radius for a simple Milky Way-like disk. Take a flat rotation curve v = 220 km/s, so the material angular speed is Omega(R) = 220/R (in km/s/kpc when R is in kpc). Adopt a pattern speed Omega_p = 20 km/s/kpc. Corotation is where Omega(R) = Omega_p: 220/R = 20, giving R_CR = 220/20 = 11 kpc. So stars inside 11 kpc (including the Sun at 8 kpc, where Omega = 27.5 > 20) overtake the pattern, while stars beyond 11 kpc lag behind it. If instead Omega_p were 25 km/s/kpc, corotation would fall to R_CR = 220/25 = 8.8 kpc — much closer to the Sun. This sensitivity is why measuring Omega_p precisely (and thus locating corotation) is a live observational problem: a 25% change in Omega_p moves corotation by ~2 kpc.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use corotation and resonances to test whether a student understands that a density wave occupies a bounded annulus rather than the whole disk — and that its position relative to material orbits (inside vs. outside corotation) makes a falsifiable prediction: an age gradient of star clusters across the arm. A student who can also distinguish grand-design (density-wave, often bar- or companion-driven) from flocculent (SSPSF) spirals, and cite that M51's grand design is tied to its interaction with NGC 5195, shows they know that "spiral" is not one mechanism but a family of them — exactly the nuance a judge rewards.

questions.prompt: At the corotation radius of a spiral galaxy, what is true?

options.text: The material's angular speed equals the pattern speed, so stars drift WITH the arm
The rotation curve reaches its maximum value
The disk's density is exactly zero
The arm winds up fastest

explanations.a: Correct — corotation is defined by Omega(R) = Omega_p, so locally the stars and the pattern rotate together; inside they overtake the arm, outside they lag it.
explanations.b: Corotation is set by matching angular speeds, not by any feature of the rotation-curve maximum.
explanations.c: Density does not vanish at corotation; the disk is fully populated there.
explanations.d: A density wave has a fixed pattern speed and does not "wind up" at corotation or anywhere else.

questions.prompt: What mechanism best explains FLOCCULENT (patchy, many-armed) spiral structure?

options.text: A single global Lin-Shu density wave with a clean pattern speed
Stochastic self-propagating star formation sheared by differential rotation
A perfectly rigid disk with no differential rotation
The 2175-angstrom dust bump lighting up random regions

explanations.a: A clean global density wave produces GRAND-DESIGN (two-armed, symmetric) structure, not the patchy flocculent pattern.
explanations.b: Correct — SSPSF (Mueller & Arnett 1976; Gerola & Seiden 1978) has supernova shells triggering neighboring bursts, which shear into short trailing arclets without any global wave.
explanations.c: A rigid disk would not shear at all and could not produce trailing arclets; differential rotation is essential to SSPSF.
explanations.d: The 2175-angstrom feature is an extinction property of dust grains, unrelated to the origin of flocculent arms.

questions.prompt: Inside corotation, order what happens to gas and the stars it forms as they encounter a density-wave arm.

items.text: Gas catches up to the arm from behind (it orbits faster than the pattern)
Gas is shocked and compressed on the arm's upstream edge
Compressed molecular clouds collapse into new O and B stars
The young clusters age as they drift downstream out of the arm
An age/color gradient appears across the arm

questions.explanation: Inside corotation the faster-orbiting gas overtakes the arm, is shocked on the upstream edge, forms massive stars, which then age while drifting downstream — leaving a systematic age gradient across the arm that is a signature of a steady density wave.

questions.prompt: Match each resonance/radius to its defining condition or role.

right.text: Omega(R) = Omega_p
Omega_p = Omega - kappa/2
Omega_p = Omega + kappa/2
The rate a star oscillates radially about its guiding circle

questions.explanation: Corotation is Omega = Omega_p; the ILR is Omega_p = Omega - kappa/2 and the OLR is Omega_p = Omega + kappa/2, with kappa the epicyclic (radial oscillation) frequency. The Lin-Shu wave lives between the ILR and OLR.

lessons.label: The Multiphase ISM: Molecular, Neutral, Ionized, and Hot Gas

sections.heading: Why the ISM has distinct phases
sections.body: The interstellar medium is not a uniform fog. It sorts itself into several PHASES that can coexist because they sit at nearly the same PRESSURE while spanning enormous ranges in density and temperature. The key physics is thermal instability: at fixed pressure, gas at intermediate temperatures cools or heats until it lands in one of a few stable states, because the balance of heating (starlight, cosmic rays) and radiative cooling has multiple stable solutions. George Field, David Goldsmith, and Harm Habing (1969) worked out the classic TWO-PHASE model — a cold dense phase in pressure balance with a warm diffuse phase. Christopher McKee and Jeremiah Ostriker (1977) then added the crucial THIRD phase created by supernovae, giving the three-phase model that still anchors the modern picture.

sections.heading: The phases, from coldest to hottest
sections.body: Working up in temperature: MOLECULAR clouds (H2) are the coldest and densest, roughly 10-20 K with number densities from ~100 up to 1e6 cm^-3 in dense cores — the sites of all star formation. The COLD NEUTRAL MEDIUM (CNM) is atomic hydrogen (HI) at about 100 K and n ~ 30 cm^-3, appearing as sheets and filaments. The WARM NEUTRAL MEDIUM (WNM) is diffuse atomic gas near 8000 K at n ~ 0.5 cm^-3. The WARM IONIZED MEDIUM (WIM) is similar in temperature (~8000 K) but ionized, n ~ 0.1 cm^-3, seen in diffuse Hα. Finally the HOT IONIZED MEDIUM (HIM) is supernova-shocked coronal gas at ~1e6 K and n ~ 3e-3 cm^-3, filling large low-density bubbles. Separately, HII regions — small, dense pockets of gas photoionized to ~10,000 K around O stars — are transient signposts of very recent star formation.

sections.heading: Rough pressure balance holds the picture together
sections.body: What makes a MULTIPHASE medium (rather than a single well-mixed gas) is that these very different phases share a comparable thermal pressure P/k = n x T (in units of K cm^-3). A cold cloud at n ~ 30, T ~ 100 gives P/k ~ 3000; a warm diffuse cloud at n ~ 0.5, T ~ 8000 gives P/k ~ 4000; the hot medium at n ~ 3e-3, T ~ 1e6 gives P/k ~ 3000. Because the pressures roughly match, a cold cloud and its warm envelope can sit in mechanical equilibrium, with density and temperature trading off inversely. This pressure-balance logic is why you can have 10 K molecular gas and 1e6 K coronal gas in the same galaxy at the same time — they are not mixing to some average, they are distinct stable phases sharing a pressure.

lessons.workedExample: Check pressure balance across three ISM phases using P/k = n x T (K cm^-3). Cold Neutral Medium: n = 30 cm^-3, T = 100 K -> P/k = 30 x 100 = 3000 K cm^-3. Warm Neutral Medium: n = 0.5 cm^-3, T = 8000 K -> P/k = 0.5 x 8000 = 4000 K cm^-3. Hot Ionized Medium: n = 3e-3 cm^-3, T = 1e6 K -> P/k = 3e-3 x 1e6 = 3000 K cm^-3. All three land within a factor of ~1.3 of each other (~3000-4000 K cm^-3), which is why they coexist in pressure balance despite densities spanning 30 / 3e-3 = 1e4 and temperatures spanning 1e6 / 100 = 1e4. Contrast a dense molecular core, n = 1e4 cm^-3, T = 15 K -> P/k = 1.5e5 K cm^-3 — far ABOVE the diffuse phases, which is why such cores are gravitationally bound and collapsing rather than in equilibrium with their surroundings.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the multiphase ISM to see whether a student understands that "gas" in a galaxy is really several distinct populations that a single observation cannot capture. The insight worth demonstrating is pressure balance: cold dense clouds and hot rarefied bubbles coexist because P/k = nT is comparable across phases, so density and temperature trade off. Naming the McKee-Ostriker (1977) three-phase model and knowing which phase forms stars (cold molecular) versus which traces recent supernovae (hot ionized) tells a judge the student can reason about WHICH tracer to observe for their science question, rather than treating the ISM as one thing.

questions.prompt: What allows a cold, dense HI cloud and a warm, diffuse HI envelope to coexist as distinct ISM phases?

options.text: They have the same temperature
They share a comparable thermal pressure P/k = nT, with density and temperature trading off inversely
They have the same number density
They are constantly mixing to a single average state

explanations.a: The phases differ in temperature by a large factor (e.g., 100 K vs 8000 K); equal temperature is not what balances them.
explanations.b: Correct — the phases sit near a common pressure P/k = nT, so a low-T high-n cloud and a high-T low-n envelope can be in mechanical equilibrium; that shared pressure defines a multiphase medium.
explanations.c: The densities differ by large factors between phases; equal density is not the reason they coexist.
explanations.d: If they mixed to one average state there would be no distinct phases; thermal instability keeps them separate at fixed pressure.

questions.prompt: Which ISM phase did McKee and Ostriker (1977) add to the earlier two-phase model, and what creates it?

options.text: The molecular phase, created by starlight
The hot ionized medium (~1e6 K), created by supernova shocks
The cold neutral medium, created by cosmic rays
The warm ionized medium, created by planetary nebulae

explanations.a: Molecular gas was already recognized; the McKee-Ostriker addition was the hot coronal phase, and it is heated by supernovae, not ordinary starlight.
explanations.b: Correct — McKee & Ostriker (1977) added the ~1e6 K hot ionized medium produced by supernova blast waves, completing the three-phase model alongside the Field-Goldsmith-Habing (1969) cold and warm phases.
explanations.c: The CNM was part of the earlier two-phase picture, not the new McKee-Ostriker addition.
explanations.d: The WIM is real but is not the phase McKee & Ostriker introduced; their contribution was the supernova-driven HOT phase.

questions.prompt: Match each ISM phase to its characteristic temperature and role.

right.text: ~10-20 K; densest phase; the site of all star formation
~100 K; dense atomic sheets and filaments
~8000 K; diffuse atomic gas filling much of the disk
~1e6 K; supernova-shocked coronal gas in large bubbles

questions.explanation: Molecular gas is coldest (~10-20 K) and forms stars; the CNM is ~100 K atomic gas; the WNM is ~8000 K diffuse atomic gas; the HIM is ~1e6 K supernova-heated coronal gas.

lessons.label: Tracing the Gas: 21-cm Hydrogen, CO, and H-alpha Maps

sections.heading: 21-cm HI: mapping the neutral atomic disk
sections.body: Neutral atomic hydrogen is nearly invisible optically, but it radiates a faint radio line from the hyperfine SPIN-FLIP transition of its ground state: when the proton and electron spins go from parallel to antiparallel, the atom emits a photon at 1420.4 MHz — a wavelength of 21.1 cm. Hendrik van de Hulst predicted the line in 1944 while the Netherlands was under wartime occupation; Harold Ewen and Edward Purcell first detected it at Harvard in 1951. The transition is forbidden with a spontaneous rate so low that a given atom waits ~10 million years to emit — but interstellar hydrogen is so abundant that the line is easy to see. Because radio waves pass through dust, 21-cm surveys trace the WHOLE atomic disk, and the line's Doppler shift gives the gas velocity, which — combined with a rotation model — yields kinematic distances and reveals the Galaxy's spiral arms in position-velocity space.

sections.heading: CO: the proxy for cold molecular H2
sections.body: Stars form from molecular hydrogen (H2), but H2 is a symmetric molecule with no permanent dipole moment and it is far too cold (~10-20 K) to excite its weak quadrupole lines — so the star-forming gas is essentially invisible in H2 itself. Astronomers instead trace it with CARBON MONOXIDE (CO), the next most abundant molecule, whose J = 1 -> 0 rotational line at 115 GHz (2.6 mm) is easily excited by collisions with H2 even at 10 K. The CO line brightness is converted to an H2 column density using the empirical X-FACTOR, X_CO ~ 2e20 cm^-2 per (K km/s), calibrated from virial masses, gamma-rays, and dust. CO surveys (pioneered by Nick Scoville, Phil Solomon, Tom Dame, and collaborators from the 1970s onward) reveal that molecular gas is strongly concentrated into giant molecular clouds strung ALONG the spiral arms.

sections.heading: H-alpha: lighting up ionized, star-forming gas
sections.body: Where hot young O and B stars have formed, their ultraviolet photons ionize the surrounding hydrogen, and as protons and electrons recombine they cascade down the energy levels, emitting the Balmer H-alpha line at 656.3 nm — the red glow of HII regions and diffuse ionized gas. Because only massive, short-lived (< ~10 Myr) stars produce enough ionizing photons, H-alpha luminosity is a direct tracer of the very RECENT, massive star-formation rate. In a spiral galaxy, an H-alpha image lights up beads of HII regions strung along the arms, marking exactly where the density-wave shock has just triggered star birth. Comparing the three tracers side by side — 21-cm (atomic reservoir), CO (molecular fuel), and H-alpha (active star formation) — lets you watch gas flow through its life cycle across an arm.

lessons.workedExample: Use the CO X-factor to turn an observation into a molecular gas mass. Suppose a patch of a spiral arm is mapped in CO(1-0) with an integrated line intensity W_CO = 20 K km/s. The H2 column density is N(H2) = X_CO x W_CO = (2e20 cm^-2 per K km/s) x 20 K km/s = 4e21 cm^-2. To get a mass surface density, multiply by the mass per hydrogen molecule (allowing ~1.36x for helium): Sigma ~ 1.36 x 2 x m_p x N(H2) = 1.36 x 2 x 1.67e-24 g x 4e21 cm^-2 = 1.8e-2 g/cm^2. Converting to solar masses per square parsec (1 g/cm^2 = 4788 M_sun/pc^2) gives Sigma ~ 87 M_sun/pc^2 — a typical molecular surface density in an active arm. Separately, the 21-cm line at 1420.4 MHz has rest wavelength c/nu = 3e8 / 1.4204e9 = 0.2111 m = 21.11 cm, confirming the "21-cm" name.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "how did you trace the gas?" because the answer reveals whether a student picked the RIGHT observable for their question. A student who knows that H2 is essentially invisible and that CO is a proxy calibrated by the X-factor — not a direct measurement — understands a real subtlety that trips up beginners. Likewise, knowing that 21-cm traces the atomic reservoir through dust, while H-alpha traces only the last ~10 Myr of massive star formation, shows the student can match a tracer to a timescale and a phase. Naming van de Hulst's 1944 prediction and the Ewen-Purcell 1951 detection grounds the answer in real history.

questions.prompt: The 21-cm hydrogen line arises from which physical process?

options.text: The n=3 to n=2 electron transition in hydrogen
The hyperfine spin-flip of the electron relative to the proton in ground-state HI
Ionized hydrogen recombining in an HII region
A rotational transition of the H2 molecule

explanations.a: The n=3->2 transition is H-alpha at 656.3 nm (visible red light), not the 21-cm radio line.
explanations.b: Correct — 21-cm (1420.4 MHz) comes from the hyperfine spin-flip (parallel to antiparallel spins) in the ground state of neutral atomic hydrogen, predicted by van de Hulst (1944) and detected by Ewen & Purcell (1951).
explanations.c: Recombination in HII regions produces optical/UV lines like H-alpha, not the 21-cm hyperfine line, which comes from NEUTRAL atomic hydrogen.
explanations.d: H2 rotational lines are a different tracer entirely; 21-cm is atomic hydrogen, and H2 is nearly invisible, which is why CO is used as its proxy.

questions.prompt: Why is CO, rather than H2 itself, used to trace cold molecular star-forming gas?

options.text: CO is more abundant than H2 in molecular clouds
H2 has no permanent dipole and is too cold to excite; CO(1-0) at 115 GHz is easily excited and calibrated via the X-factor
H2 only exists in ionized regions where it cannot be seen
CO emits at 21 cm, the same as neutral hydrogen

explanations.a: H2 is vastly MORE abundant than CO; CO is used despite being a trace species because it actually radiates at cloud temperatures.
explanations.b: Correct — symmetric H2 lacks a dipole moment and its lines need high temperatures, so cold H2 is invisible; CO(1-0) at 115 GHz (2.6 mm) is collisionally excited even at 10 K and is converted to N(H2) with the empirical X-factor (~2e20).
explanations.c: H2 exists precisely in cold neutral molecular clouds, not ionized regions; the problem is that it does not radiate, not where it lives.
explanations.d: CO(1-0) is at 115 GHz / 2.6 mm, not 21 cm; the 21-cm line is atomic hydrogen.

questions.prompt: Match each gas tracer to what it reveals.

right.text: The neutral ATOMIC hydrogen reservoir across the whole dusty disk
The cold MOLECULAR (H2) fuel in giant clouds along the arms
Ionized gas marking star formation in the last ~10 Myr

questions.explanation: 21-cm maps the atomic HI reservoir through dust; CO is the proxy for cold molecular H2 fuel; H-alpha marks ionized gas around young massive stars, tracing the most recent (< ~10 Myr) star formation.

questions.prompt: An H-alpha image of a spiral galaxy primarily traces which population?

options.text: The old, low-mass stars that make up most of the disk mass
Very recent (< ~10 Myr) massive star formation in HII regions along the arms
Cold molecular clouds before any stars have formed
The hot ~1e6 K coronal gas from supernovae

explanations.a: Old low-mass stars do not emit enough ionizing photons to power H-alpha; they are traced in red/near-IR continuum, not H-alpha.
explanations.b: Correct — H-alpha comes from hydrogen ionized by short-lived O and B stars, so it tracks star formation within roughly the last 10 Myr, appearing as HII-region beads along the arms.
explanations.c: Pre-stellar molecular clouds are cold and neutral; they are traced by CO, not H-alpha, which requires ionizing radiation from stars that have already formed.
explanations.d: The ~1e6 K HIM is traced in X-rays and UV absorption lines, not the 656.3 nm H-alpha recombination line.

lessons.label: Star Formation and the Kennicutt-Schmidt Law in the Arms

sections.heading: From Schmidt's density law to a surface-density law
sections.body: In 1959 Maarten Schmidt proposed that the star-formation rate per unit volume scales as a power of the gas density: rho_SFR proportional to rho_gas^n, with n ~ 2 from the Milky Way data he had. Because galaxy disks are thin and we usually measure gas and star formation projected on the sky, the modern, practical form is a SURFACE-density law: Sigma_SFR proportional to Sigma_gas^N, relating the star-formation-rate surface density to the gas surface density. This is the Kennicutt-Schmidt (KS) law, and it turns "where does a galaxy make stars" into a single empirical scaling that any student can test with a gas map and a star-formation map.

sections.heading: Kennicutt 1998: N ~ 1.4
sections.body: Robert Kennicutt's landmark 1998 study measured Sigma_SFR (from H-alpha) and Sigma_gas (atomic plus molecular) across the disks of dozens of normal and starburst galaxies and found a tight power law spanning several orders of magnitude, with slope N = 1.4 +/- 0.15. His best fit is Sigma_SFR ~ 2.5e-4 x (Sigma_gas / 1 M_sun pc^-2)^1.4 M_sun per year per kpc^2. The super-linear slope (N > 1) means gas-rich regions form stars DISPROPORTIONATELY fast — doubling the gas surface density more than doubles the star-formation rate. Later work using CO (e.g., the THINGS survey, Bigiel et al. 2008) found that when you isolate the MOLECULAR gas, the relation with H2 is closer to linear (N ~ 1), suggesting a roughly constant star-formation efficiency per molecular cloud, with the steeper global slope arising from how atomic gas converts to molecular.

sections.heading: Why star formation concentrates in the arms
sections.body: The KS law explains why arms glow. The density-wave shock (Lesson 2) piles gas up, RAISING Sigma_gas along the arm; because Sigma_SFR climbs faster than linearly with Sigma_gas, even a modest gas enhancement drives a large boost in star formation right at the arm. Whether arms actually raise the total star-formation rate of a galaxy, or merely ORGANIZE where existing star formation happens, is a genuine open debate: many studies find that arm and inter-arm regions lie on the SAME KS relation once you account for their gas, implying arms concentrate but do not greatly increase overall efficiency. This is exactly the kind of question a well-designed student project can probe: compare Sigma_SFR versus Sigma_gas on the arm and between the arms and see whether they fall on one line.

lessons.workedExample: Apply the Kennicutt 1998 law to two regions of a spiral. In an arm, the gas surface density is Sigma_gas = 50 M_sun/pc^2. Then Sigma_SFR = 2.5e-4 x (50)^1.4. Compute (50)^1.4: log10(50) = 1.699, times 1.4 = 2.379, so 10^2.379 = 239. Thus Sigma_SFR = 2.5e-4 x 239 = 6.0e-2 M_sun/yr/kpc^2. Between the arms, Sigma_gas = 10 M_sun/pc^2: (10)^1.4 = 10^1.4 = 25.1, so Sigma_SFR = 2.5e-4 x 25.1 = 6.3e-3 M_sun/yr/kpc^2. The gas went up by a factor of 5 (10 -> 50) but the star-formation rate went up by 6.0e-2 / 6.3e-3 = 9.5 — nearly a factor of 10, because the slope 1.4 makes the response super-linear (5^1.4 = 9.5). That disproportionate boost is why the arm outshines the inter-arm disk in H-alpha far more than its gas contrast alone would suggest.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges like the Kennicutt-Schmidt law because it is a rare astrophysics relation a student can actually TEST with public data: overlay a star-formation map on a gas map and fit a power law. A student who states the slope (N ~ 1.4 from Kennicutt 1998), knows it is super-linear, and can explain that the molecular-gas relation is closer to linear (Bigiel et al. 2008) demonstrates command of a real, quantitative result and its refinements. Even better is a student who frames the open question — do arms increase star formation or just concentrate it? — because that is a genuine debate their own arm-versus-inter-arm comparison could address, which is precisely the kind of testable design judges reward.

questions.prompt: The Kennicutt-Schmidt law relates which two quantities, and with roughly what slope from Kennicutt (1998)?

options.text: Sigma_SFR proportional to Sigma_gas^1.4 (star-formation surface density vs gas surface density)
Luminosity proportional to temperature^4 (the blackbody law)
Velocity proportional to distance (Hubble's law)
Sigma_SFR proportional to Sigma_gas^0.5 (a sub-linear relation)

explanations.a: Correct — Kennicutt (1998) found Sigma_SFR proportional to Sigma_gas^N with N = 1.4 +/- 0.15 across many galaxies, a super-linear surface-density scaling.
explanations.b: That is the Stefan-Boltzmann relation for blackbody flux, not the star-formation law.
explanations.c: Hubble's law v = H0 d relates recession velocity to distance for the cosmic expansion, unrelated to the KS star-formation law.
explanations.d: The slope is 1.4 (super-linear), not 0.5; gas-rich regions form stars DISPROPORTIONATELY fast, the opposite of sub-linear.

questions.prompt: A super-linear KS slope (N ~ 1.4) means that if a region's gas surface density is 5x higher, its star-formation surface density is about:

options.text: 5x higher (linear)
About 9-10x higher (5^1.4 ~ 9.5)
2.5x higher (sub-linear)
Unchanged, because SFR does not depend on gas

explanations.a: Linear scaling (N = 1) would give 5x; the measured slope is steeper, so the response exceeds the gas ratio.
explanations.b: Correct — with N = 1.4, the SFR ratio is 5^1.4 = 9.5, so a 5x gas enhancement drives a nearly 10x star-formation boost, which is why arms outshine inter-arm gas contrast.
explanations.c: 2.5x would require a sub-linear slope below 1; the KS slope of 1.4 is super-linear.
explanations.d: The whole KS law says SFR depends strongly on gas; it is far from unchanged.

questions.prompt: Order the historical/logical development of the star-formation law.

items.text: Schmidt (1959): SFR per volume scales as a power of gas density
Recast as a surface-density law for thin, projected disks
Kennicutt (1998): measures N ~ 1.4 across many galaxies
Bigiel et al. (2008): molecular-gas relation is closer to linear (N ~ 1)

questions.explanation: Schmidt (1959) proposed the volumetric power law; it was recast as a surface-density relation; Kennicutt (1998) measured the global slope N ~ 1.4; and later molecular-gas studies (Bigiel et al. 2008) found a near-linear relation with H2 specifically.

lessons.label: Interstellar Dust: Extinction, Reddening, and Grand-Design Structure

sections.heading: Extinction: dust dims starlight
sections.body: Interstellar dust — sub-micron grains of silicates and carbonaceous material — absorbs and scatters starlight, dimming distant stars by an amount called the EXTINCTION, A (in magnitudes) at a given wavelength. Robert Trumpler established that this dimming is real and pervasive in 1930: studying open star clusters, he found that more distant clusters appeared systematically too faint AND too large for the distances implied by their brightness, which only made sense if an intervening medium were absorbing their light. Ignoring extinction makes stars look farther away than they are, so it is not a minor correction — a line of sight through the Galactic plane can suffer many magnitudes of visual extinction, and toward the Galactic center A_V exceeds ~30 magnitudes, which is why we cannot see the center in visible light at all.

sections.heading: Reddening and the extinction curve
sections.body: Dust does not dim all colors equally: grains scatter and absorb BLUE light more efficiently than RED, so starlight passing through dust is REDDENED as well as dimmed — the same physics that makes sunsets red. The color change is the color excess E(B-V) = (B-V)_observed - (B-V)_intrinsic. The ratio of total to selective extinction, R_V = A_V / E(B-V), captures the shape of the extinction curve; for diffuse interstellar dust in the Milky Way it averages R_V ~ 3.1, though it rises toward ~5 in dense clouds where grains have grown larger. The full extinction curve rises from the infrared into the ultraviolet and shows a distinctive bump at 2175 angstroms, generally attributed to small carbonaceous (graphitic/PAH) grains — a feature that constrains what interstellar dust is actually made of.

sections.heading: Dust lanes and grand-design arms
sections.body: Because dust is mixed with the cold, dense gas that flows into the density-wave shock, it collects on the UPSTREAM (concave, trailing) edge of a spiral arm as a dark DUST LANE — the crisp, narrow dark bands seen threading the arms of grand-design spirals like M51 and M81. Their position matters: the dust lane sits just inside the ridge of newborn blue stars, tracing exactly where gas is being compressed BEFORE it forms stars, so the sequence dust lane -> HII regions -> aging clusters across the arm is a direct picture of the density-wave shock at work. Dust thus does double duty: it obscures and reddens (a nuisance to be corrected) and it maps the shock front (a signpost of the star-formation mechanism), tying this whole unit together — arms are dynamical patterns whose gas, dust, and young stars line up in a predictable order.

lessons.workedExample: Correct a reddened star for extinction. A main-sequence B star has an intrinsic color (B-V)_0 = -0.10, but is observed at (B-V)_obs = +0.40. The color excess is E(B-V) = 0.40 - (-0.10) = 0.50 mag. Using the standard diffuse-ISM ratio R_V = 3.1, the visual extinction is A_V = R_V x E(B-V) = 3.1 x 0.50 = 1.55 mag — the star is dimmed by 1.55 magnitudes in V, a flux factor of 10^(1.55/2.5) = 4.2x fainter than it would appear without dust. If you had ignored extinction and used the distance modulus m - M = 5 log10(d) - 5 with the reddened apparent magnitude, you would place the star 10^(1.55/5) = 2.0x too FAR away. Correcting first (subtract A_V = 1.55 from the apparent V magnitude) is essential before any distance or luminosity is trusted.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe dust because forgetting extinction is one of the most common and consequential mistakes in observational projects: uncorrected reddening biases colors, temperatures, and distances, often by factors of two. A student who distinguishes extinction (dimming, A_V) from reddening (color change, E(B-V)), knows the average R_V ~ 3.1, and can correct a distance for A_V demonstrates they will not fool themselves. Bonus credit for connecting dust to structure: knowing that dust lanes sit on the upstream edge of arms and trace the density-wave shock shows the student sees dust not just as noise to remove but as a physical tracer — the through-line of this whole unit.

questions.prompt: Interstellar reddening occurs because dust grains:

options.text: Emit red light of their own that adds to the star's spectrum
Scatter and absorb blue light more efficiently than red, so transmitted starlight is shifted redward
Doppler-shift the starlight through the expansion of the Galaxy
Convert red photons into blue ones

explanations.a: Cold dust does emit (in the far-infrared), but REDDENING of a background star is caused by preferential removal of blue light along the line of sight, not by added red emission.
explanations.b: Correct — grains scatter/absorb short (blue) wavelengths more than long (red) ones, so the star that reaches us is both dimmed and reddened; this is measured as the color excess E(B-V).
explanations.c: Reddening from dust is a wavelength-dependent EXTINCTION effect, not a Doppler shift; it changes colors, not line positions in the cosmological sense.
explanations.d: Dust removes blue light; it does not up-convert red photons into blue ones.

questions.prompt: For a star with intrinsic color (B-V)_0 = 0.0 observed at (B-V) = 0.4, using R_V = 3.1, what is the visual extinction A_V?

options.text: A_V = 0.4 mag
A_V = 1.24 mag
A_V = 3.1 mag
A_V = 0.13 mag

explanations.a: 0.4 is the color excess E(B-V), not A_V; you still must multiply by R_V to get the total visual extinction.
explanations.b: Correct — E(B-V) = 0.4 - 0.0 = 0.4, and A_V = R_V x E(B-V) = 3.1 x 0.4 = 1.24 mag.
explanations.c: 3.1 is R_V itself (the ratio), not the extinction; A_V = R_V x E(B-V) = 3.1 x 0.4.
explanations.d: 0.13 inverts the relation (0.4/3.1); the correct operation is R_V TIMES E(B-V), giving 1.24.

questions.prompt: What does Robert Trumpler's 1930 study of open clusters establish?

options.text: That interstellar dust exists and systematically dims (extinguishes) starlight
That the Milky Way rotates differentially
That spiral nebulae are separate galaxies
That hydrogen is the most abundant element in stars

explanations.a: Correct — Trumpler (1930) found distant open clusters were too faint (and apparently too large) for their brightness-based distances, revealing pervasive interstellar extinction by dust.
explanations.b: Differential rotation of the Galaxy was quantified by Oort (1927), a separate result from Trumpler's extinction work.
explanations.c: The extragalactic nature of spiral nebulae was settled by Hubble (1925) using Cepheids, not by Trumpler's cluster study.
explanations.d: Hydrogen's dominance in stellar composition was Cecilia Payne's 1925 result, unrelated to interstellar extinction.

questions.prompt: Match each dust-related quantity or feature to its meaning.

right.text: Total extinction (dimming) in the V band, in magnitudes
Color excess: how much redder the star appears than its intrinsic color
Ratio A_V / E(B-V), ~3.1 for diffuse Milky Way dust
A UV extinction feature attributed to small carbonaceous grains

questions.explanation: A_V is the total V-band dimming; E(B-V) is the reddening (color excess); R_V = A_V/E(B-V) ~ 3.1 characterizes the extinction-curve shape; and the 2175-angstrom bump is a UV feature attributed to small carbonaceous (graphitic/PAH) grains.

units.label: The Extragalactic Zoo: Morphology and Classification

lessons.label: The Hubble Tuning Fork: Ellipticals, Lenticulars, and Spirals

sections.heading: One diagram that organized the whole sky
sections.body: By the mid-1920s Edwin Hubble had just settled the “island universe” debate — spiral nebulae are separate galaxies far outside the Milky Way — and immediately faced a new problem: those galaxies come in wildly different shapes. In his 1926 paper and later his 1936 book “The Realm of the Nebulae,” Hubble proposed a classification that is still the field’s backbone. Drawn as a tuning fork, it places smooth, featureless ellipticals on the handle, graded E0 through E7 by how flattened they look; a transitional class of lenticulars (S0) sits at the fork junction; and two prongs of disk galaxies branch off — ordinary spirals Sa–Sb–Sc on one tine and barred spirals SBa–SBb–SBc on the other. The power of the scheme is that a single glance at a galaxy image places it on a one-dimensional-ish sequence that turns out to correlate with a great deal of physics.

sections.heading: Ellipticity is a projection, not a shape
sections.body: An elliptical galaxy’s type number is defined purely by apparent flattening: E_n where n = 10·(1 − b/a), with a and b the observed major and minor axis lengths. An E0 looks round (b/a = 1); the flattest observed ellipticals are about E7 (b/a ≈ 0.3), and more extreme flattening appears to be suppressed — most likely because such anisotropic, pressure-supported stellar systems become dynamically unstable to bar and bending-mode instabilities when pushed flatter. Crucially this is the PROJECTED shape on the sky, not the true 3D shape: a genuinely football-shaped (prolate) or discus-shaped (oblate) galaxy viewed end-on looks E0 and side-on looks flattened, so the Hubble type of one elliptical mixes intrinsic shape with viewing angle. This is a caution that recurs throughout morphology — you classify what you can measure, not necessarily what is physically there.

sections.heading: The “early/late” misnomer and what the sequence really tracks
sections.body: Hubble borrowed the terms “early-type” for ellipticals and lenticulars and “late-type” for spirals, purely as a naming convenience — and he explicitly warned they imply NO evolutionary sequence. Galaxies do not slide down the tuning fork from E0 to Sc (or the reverse) as they age; the language is a historical trap that still confuses students. What the sequence genuinely tracks is a bundle of correlated physical properties. Toward the elliptical/S0 end: old, red stellar populations, little cold gas, negligible ongoing star formation, and pressure-supported (random-orbit) dynamics. Toward the Sc/spiral end: prominent gas-and-dust disks, young blue stars in spiral arms, active star formation, and rotation-supported dynamics. So a “late-type spiral” is not old — it is typically the more actively star-forming, gas-rich system, despite the name.

lessons.workedExample: You image an elliptical galaxy and fit an ellipse to an outer isophote (a contour of constant surface brightness), measuring a major axis a = 40 arcsec and minor axis b = 24 arcsec. The axis ratio is b/a = 24/40 = 0.60, so the Hubble type number is n = 10·(1 − 0.60) = 4 — an E4. A classmate re-measures a fainter isophote farther out and gets b/a = 0.52, i.e. E5, illustrating that ellipticals often show “isophote twisting” and changing ellipticity with radius, so you must state WHICH isophote you classified on. Neither of you can conclude the galaxy is “really” a flattened oblate spheroid rather than a round one seen edge-on — the single number E4 is consistent with both, and only stellar kinematics (does it rotate, or is it pressure-supported?) would break that degeneracy.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the tuning fork to see whether a student treats it as a naming exercise or a physical hypothesis. The tell of real understanding is (1) knowing E_n = 10(1 − b/a) is projected flattening, not intrinsic shape, and (2) rejecting the evolutionary reading of “early” and “late.” A student who says “ellipticals are old, gas-poor, pressure-supported; spirals are gas-rich, star-forming, rotation-supported — and the labels early/late carry no age meaning” has grasped that morphology encodes formation history. One who says “galaxies evolve from ellipticals into spirals” has fallen for the exact trap Hubble warned against.

questions.prompt: An elliptical galaxy has an observed axis ratio b/a = 0.30. What is its Hubble type?

options.text: E3
E7
E0

explanations.a: E3 would correspond to b/a = 0.70, not 0.30 — this reverses the formula.
explanations.b: Correct — n = 10·(1 − b/a) = 10·(1 − 0.30) = 7, so E7, which is also about the flattest elliptical actually observed.
explanations.c: E0 is a round galaxy with b/a = 1.0, the opposite extreme.
explanations.d: The type number caps near 7; “E30” is not on the scale — the formula gives 10·(1 − 0.30) = 7, not 30.

questions.prompt: Why did Hubble caution against reading his “early-type” and “late-type” labels literally?

options.text: Because ellipticals are actually younger than spirals
Because the terms are naming conventions and imply no evolutionary sequence from one type to another
Because galaxies were later found not to have types at all
Because the labels only apply to barred galaxies

explanations.a: The stellar populations of ellipticals are typically OLD and red, not young; the point is not a reversed age order but that the sequence is not an age sequence at all.
explanations.b: Correct — Hubble adopted “early/late” as convenient labels and explicitly warned they do not mean galaxies evolve along the tuning fork with time.
explanations.c: Galaxies very much do have reproducible morphological types; that is what the scheme captures.
explanations.d: The terms apply across the whole sequence (E, S0, spirals, barred and unbarred), not just to bars.

questions.prompt: Match each morphological class to its characteristic physical properties.

right.text: Old red stars, little cold gas, pressure-supported by random orbits
Gas-rich disk with young blue stars and active star formation, rotation-supported
Has a disk but is largely gas-poor with little star formation — transitional at the fork junction

questions.explanation: Ellipticals are old, gas-poor and pressure-supported; late-type spirals like Sc are gas-rich, blue, star-forming and rotation-supported; lenticulars (S0) sit at the junction — they have a disk like a spiral but are gas-poor and passive like an elliptical.

questions.prompt: A galaxy is classified E1 from its image, but a colleague argues it might intrinsically be quite flattened. How is that possible?

options.text: It is not — E1 means the galaxy is definitely round in 3D
The Hubble type is the projected (apparent) flattening; a flattened galaxy seen near face-on can look nearly round
E1 galaxies always change type over a few years
The colleague is confusing surface brightness with shape

explanations.a: E_n encodes the apparent axis ratio on the sky, which mixes true shape with viewing angle — it does not pin down the 3D shape.
explanations.b: Correct — because n = 10(1 − b/a) uses the projected b/a, an intrinsically oblate or prolate galaxy viewed near end-on projects to a rounder image, so E1 is consistent with a genuinely flattened system seen at a favorable angle.
explanations.c: Galaxy morphology does not change on human timescales; this is unrelated to the projection point.
explanations.d: The colleague’s point is exactly correct and is about projection, not a surface-brightness confusion.

lessons.label: Reading the Notation: Sa–Sc, Bars, and de Vaucouleurs’ T-Types

sections.heading: What separates an Sa from an Sc: three correlated criteria
sections.body: Along the spiral prong, the letter a→b→c encodes three visual criteria that Hubble found tend to change together. First, the bulge-to-disk ratio: an Sa has a large, dominant central bulge, while an Sc has a small bulge and a disk that dominates the light. Second, how tightly the spiral arms wind: Sa arms are tightly wrapped and smooth, Sc arms are open and loosely wound. Third, how “resolved” the arms are into knots: Sa arms look continuous, while Sc arms break up into bright clumps of star-forming regions and individual bright stars. These three do not have to move in lockstep, but on average they do, which is what makes a→c a usable one-parameter sequence. Allan Sandage codified the visual standards in the “Hubble Atlas of Galaxies” (1961), which for decades was the reference set of example images.

sections.heading: Bars are common — including in the Milky Way
sections.body: Hubble split the disk galaxies into unbarred (S) and barred (SB) prongs, where a bar is a straight, elongated stellar structure running through the center from which the spiral arms spring. Bars are not rare curiosities: in near-infrared imaging (which sees the old stellar mass and pierces dust), roughly two-thirds of disk galaxies show a bar, with the exact fraction depending on wavelength and how strong a bar you require. Our own Milky Way is a barred spiral, classified about SBbc. Physically, a bar is a rotating instability of the stellar disk that funnels gas inward toward the center — driving nuclear star formation and helping build a central concentration — so a bar is not just a label but a mechanism that reshapes its host over time.

sections.heading: De Vaucouleurs turned letters into a number (the T-type)
sections.body: Gérard de Vaucouleurs (1959) extended and quantified Hubble’s scheme into a three-dimensional classification volume: the STAGE along the sequence (E → S0 → Sa → Sb → Sc → Sd → Sm → Irr), the FAMILY (SA unbarred, SB barred, and the intermediate SAB), and the VARIETY (s = pure spiral, r = inner ring, and intermediate rs). Most usefully for data work, he assigned each stage a numerical Hubble stage T so morphology can be plotted and averaged: roughly T = −5 for ellipticals, −2 for S0, 0 for S0/a, +1 for Sa, +3 for Sb, +5 for Sc, +7 for Sd, +9 for Sm, and +10 for irregulars. The Third Reference Catalogue (RC3, de Vaucouleurs et al. 1991) tabulated T-types for thousands of galaxies. The numeric T is what lets a researcher ask, e.g., “does gas fraction correlate with T?” instead of arguing over verbal labels.

lessons.workedExample: You are handed an image to classify. It shows: a moderate central bulge (not dominant, not tiny), spiral arms of intermediate openness that are partly resolved into star-forming knots, and a short bar through the nucleus with a faint inner ring where the arms begin. Working the de Vaucouleurs volume: the moderate bulge + intermediate arms put the STAGE near Sb, so T ≈ 3; the clear-but-modest bar makes the FAMILY intermediate, SAB rather than a strong SB; and the inner ring makes the VARIETY “rs.” Combining gives a classification of SAB(rs)b, T ≈ 3. Notice you did not need a single number off the image — you read three semi-independent visual axes and reported all three, which is exactly what makes de Vaucouleurs’ scheme richer (and more reproducible between classifiers) than a bare “Sb.”
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use classification notation to test whether a student can read the data language of their own field. If a project bins galaxies “by type,” a judge will ask what Sa-versus-Sc actually means — and the strong answer names the criteria (bulge-to-disk ratio, arm winding, arm resolution) rather than saying “Sa is prettier.” Bringing in the T-type shows you understand why researchers convert morphology to a NUMBER: so it can be correlated and averaged. Correctly stating that the Milky Way is a barred spiral (SBbc), and that bars are common (~two-thirds in the near-IR), signals you know morphology is quantitative and physically consequential, not decorative.

questions.prompt: Order these disk galaxies by de Vaucouleurs T-type, from smallest (most bulge-dominated, earliest stage) to largest (most disk-dominated, latest stage).

items.text: S0 (lenticular)
Sa
Sc
Sm (Magellanic spiral)

questions.explanation: On the numeric scale S0 ≈ −2, Sa ≈ +1, Sc ≈ +5, and Sm ≈ +9, so ascending T runs S0 → Sa → Sc → Sm — equivalently, from large-bulge/tightly-wound toward small-bulge/loose-and-clumpy.

questions.prompt: Which set of features best distinguishes an Sa from an Sc spiral?

options.text: Sa has a small bulge and open, clumpy arms; Sc has a large bulge and tight, smooth arms
Sa has a large bulge with tight, smooth arms; Sc has a small bulge with open, resolved (clumpy) arms
Sa is barred and Sc is unbarred, by definition
Sa is red and Sc is blue solely because of distance

explanations.a: This is exactly backwards — it swaps the Sa and Sc descriptions.
explanations.b: Correct — moving a→c the bulge-to-disk ratio drops, the arms open up, and the arms resolve into star-forming knots, all together.
explanations.c: Bar presence is a separate axis (S vs SB / the family), not what the a→c stage encodes; both Sa and Sc can be barred or unbarred.
explanations.d: Any color difference reflects real stellar populations (older/redder bulge-dominated vs younger/bluer disk), not distance; distance does not change intrinsic color this way.

questions.prompt: Match each axis of the de Vaucouleurs classification volume to what it describes.

right.text: Position along E → S0 → Sa → Sb → Sc → Sd → Sm → Irr
Degree of central bar: none, intermediate, or strong
Presence of an inner ring vs pure spiral arms

questions.explanation: De Vaucouleurs classifies on three semi-independent axes: the STAGE is the Hubble-sequence position (numeric T), the FAMILY is how barred it is (SA unbarred, SB barred, SAB intermediate), and the VARIETY is whether it has an inner ring (r), pure spiral (s), or an intermediate (rs).

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of disk galaxies host a bar when imaged in the near-infrared, and what does the Milky Way’s classification tell us?

options.text: Under 5%, and the Milky Way is unbarred (SA)
About two-thirds, and the Milky Way is itself a barred spiral (about SBbc)
Essentially 100%, and the Milky Way is an elliptical
Exactly 50%, and the Milky Way has no measurable type

explanations.a: Bars are far more common than 5%, and the Milky Way is in fact barred, not SA.
explanations.b: Correct — near-IR imaging (which traces old stellar mass through dust) shows roughly two-thirds of disks are barred, and our own Galaxy is a barred spiral classified about SBbc.
explanations.c: The Milky Way is a disk galaxy, not an elliptical, and the bar fraction is not 100%.
explanations.d: The fraction is closer to two-thirds than a clean 50%, and the Milky Way has a well-established SBbc-type classification.

lessons.label: Elliptical Galaxies: the r¹ᐟ⁴ Law and the Fundamental Plane

sections.heading: The de Vaucouleurs r^(1/4) profile
sections.body: Morphology becomes a measurement the moment you plot how brightness falls off with radius — the surface-brightness profile I(r). For elliptical galaxies, Gérard de Vaucouleurs (1948) found that light does NOT fall off exponentially (as spiral disks do) but follows the “r-to-the-one-quarter” law: I(r) = I_e · exp{−7.669·[(r/r_e)^(1/4) − 1]}. Here r_e is the effective radius — the radius of the isophote enclosing exactly half the galaxy’s total light — and I_e is the surface brightness at that radius. The constant 7.669 is chosen precisely so that r_e is the half-light radius. Plotted as surface brightness (in magnitudes, i.e. a log scale) against r^(1/4), this profile becomes a straight line, which is why the r^(1/4) law is such a convenient diagnostic: a true elliptical “straightens out” on that axis, whereas a disk does not.

sections.heading: Faber–Jackson: luminosity from a single velocity
sections.body: Ellipticals are pressure-supported: their stars are on randomly oriented orbits, and the spread of line-of-sight stellar velocities, the velocity dispersion σ, measures how deep the potential well is. In 1976 Sandra Faber and Robert Jackson discovered a tight scaling: L ∝ σ⁴, i.e. luminosity rises as roughly the fourth power of the velocity dispersion. This means σ — measurable from the width of absorption lines in a single spectrum, with no distance needed — predicts luminosity, so comparing predicted L to observed apparent brightness yields a distance. The Faber–Jackson relation was the elliptical-galaxy analogue of the Tully–Fisher relation for spirals (which ties spiral luminosity to rotation speed), and it hinted that ellipticals are not a random zoo but a structured family obeying scaling laws rooted in the virial theorem.

sections.heading: The Fundamental Plane and its “tilt”
sections.body: Faber–Jackson is actually a shadow of a tighter relation. In 1987 two teams — Djorgovski & Davis, and Dressler, Lynden-Bell and collaborators (the “Seven Samurai”) — showed that ellipticals occupy a thin two-dimensional PLANE in the three-dimensional space of effective radius r_e, velocity dispersion σ, and mean surface brightness within r_e. Written as a scaling, r_e ∝ σ^a · ⟨I⟩_e^b, with observed exponents near a ≈ 1.24 and b ≈ −0.82. The virial theorem alone predicts a “pure” plane with a = 2, b = −1; the fact that the OBSERVED exponents differ is called the “tilt” of the Fundamental Plane, and it tells us the mass-to-light ratio of ellipticals varies systematically with mass (more massive ellipticals are slightly more dark-matter-dominated or have older/redder populations). The Fundamental Plane is one of the best distance indicators for elliptical galaxies precisely because its scatter is so small.

lessons.workedExample: You measure the stellar velocity dispersion of an elliptical from its absorption-line widths and get σ = 300 km/s. A reference elliptical of the same type has σ_ref = 150 km/s and luminosity L_ref = 3×10¹⁰ L_⊙. Using Faber–Jackson, L ∝ σ⁴: the dispersion is doubled (300/150 = 2), so the luminosity should scale by 2⁴ = 16, giving L ≈ 16 × 3×10¹⁰ = 4.8×10¹¹ L_⊙. Now use that as a standard candle: if the target’s apparent brightness implies you receive far less flux than a 4.8×10¹¹ L_⊙ galaxy at, say, 20 Mpc would deliver, you solve the inverse-square law for the larger distance. The whole chain — line width → σ → L → distance — needed no Cepheids and no redshift, which is exactly why scaling relations like Faber–Jackson (and the tighter Fundamental Plane) are prized rungs on the distance ladder for early-type galaxies.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges test the r^(1/4) law and Fundamental Plane to see whether a student understands that “elliptical” is a quantitative, predictive category, not just a smooth blob. A strong answer notes that ellipticals follow a de Vaucouleurs (n = 4) profile that straightens on an r^(1/4) axis, and that they obey scaling laws (Faber–Jackson L ∝ σ⁴; the Fundamental Plane) rooted in the virial theorem. The sharpest students mention the “tilt” — that the observed Fundamental-Plane exponents differ from the virial prediction because the mass-to-light ratio varies with mass — showing they grasp that a small deviation from a theoretical law is itself a physical measurement, not an error.

questions.prompt: In the de Vaucouleurs profile I(r) = I_e·exp{−7.669·[(r/r_e)^(1/4) − 1]}, what is r_e?

options.text: The radius where the galaxy’s light drops to zero
The effective radius — the isophote enclosing half of the galaxy’s total light
The radius of the central black hole’s influence
The distance to the galaxy

explanations.a: The profile falls off smoothly and never truly reaches zero; r_e is not an edge.
explanations.b: Correct — r_e is the half-light (effective) radius, and the constant 7.669 is set precisely so that half the total light falls within r_e.
explanations.c: The black-hole sphere of influence is a much smaller, unrelated scale; r_e characterizes the whole stellar light distribution.
explanations.d: r_e is an intrinsic size of the galaxy’s light profile, not a distance.

questions.prompt: An elliptical’s velocity dispersion is measured to be three times larger than a reference elliptical. Using Faber–Jackson, how much brighter is it (to leading order)?

options.text: 3 times
9 times
81 times
12 times

explanations.a: That would be L ∝ σ, but Faber–Jackson is a fourth-power relation.
explanations.b: That would be L ∝ σ², not the observed fourth power.
explanations.c: Correct — L ∝ σ⁴, so tripling σ multiplies luminosity by 3⁴ = 81.
explanations.d: This does not correspond to any power of 3; the fourth power gives 81, not 12.

questions.prompt: What does the “tilt” of the Fundamental Plane refer to?

options.text: A measurement error that adds scatter to the relation
The fact that the observed exponents (a ≈ 1.24, b ≈ −0.82) differ from the pure virial prediction (a = 2, b = −1), implying the mass-to-light ratio varies with mass
The inclination angle at which an elliptical is viewed
The bar in a barred elliptical

explanations.a: The tilt is a real, systematic offset from the virial expectation, not random measurement scatter — the plane itself is remarkably thin.
explanations.b: Correct — the observed FP exponents depart from what a constant mass-to-light-ratio virial system would give, and that departure (the tilt) encodes a systematic variation of M/L with galaxy mass.
explanations.c: Viewing inclination affects an individual measurement, not the intrinsic exponents of the plane.
explanations.d: Ellipticals are not bars; the tilt is about the scaling exponents, unrelated to bars.

questions.prompt: Match each scaling relation to the quantities it links.

right.text: Surface brightness I(r) vs radius for an elliptical (straight line on an r^(1/4) axis)
Luminosity vs velocity dispersion, L ∝ σ⁴
Effective radius, velocity dispersion, and mean surface brightness lying on one thin plane

questions.explanation: The r^(1/4) law describes how surface brightness falls with radius in an elliptical; Faber–Jackson links luminosity to velocity dispersion (L ∝ σ⁴); the Fundamental Plane ties three variables — r_e, σ, and mean surface brightness — into one thin plane, of which Faber–Jackson is a projection.

lessons.label: Disk Decomposition: Exponential Disks, Bulge-to-Disk Ratio, and Sérsic Index

sections.heading: Disks fall off exponentially
sections.body: Where ellipticals follow an r^(1/4) law, the DISK of a spiral obeys a much gentler exponential profile: I(r) = I_0 · exp(−r/h), where I_0 is the central surface brightness of the disk (extrapolated inward) and h is the disk scale length — the radius over which the brightness drops by a factor of e (≈ 2.72). Ken Freeman established this in his landmark 1970 study of spiral and lenticular disks, and along the way noted “Freeman’s law”: the extrapolated central surface brightness of disks clustered near a nearly constant value, about μ_0 ≈ 21.65 B-mag/arcsec². (That apparent constancy later turned out to be partly a SELECTION effect — a warning we return to next lesson.) A handy consequence of the exponential form: the total luminosity of a pure exponential disk is L = 2π·I_0·h², so measuring I_0 and h alone fixes the disk’s brightness.

sections.heading: The Sérsic index unifies both profiles
sections.body: José Luis Sérsic (1963, 1968) generalized both laws into one formula: I(r) = I_e · exp{−b_n·[(r/r_e)^(1/n) − 1]}, where n is the Sérsic index and b_n ≈ 2n − 1/3. The magic is in n: setting n = 1 recovers the pure EXPONENTIAL disk (with b_1 ≈ 1.678), while n = 4 recovers the de Vaucouleurs r^(1/4) law for ellipticals (with b_4 ≈ 7.669). So a single fitted number n places a galaxy’s light profile on a continuum from disk-like (low n, shallow core, sharp truncation) to spheroid-like (high n, steep core, extended wings). Modern surveys fit n automatically, and n has become a quantitative proxy for morphology: n ≲ 2.5 is broadly “disk-dominated / late-type” and n ≳ 2.5 “bulge-dominated / early-type,” far more reproducible than eyeballing arms.

sections.heading: Two-component fits, B/T, and classical vs pseudobulges
sections.body: Real spirals are two things at once — an inner bulge plus an outer disk — so serious morphology fits a two-component model: an n = 4 (or free-n) bulge PLUS an n = 1 exponential disk, using codes like GALFIT (Peng et al. 2002). The key output is the bulge-to-total light ratio B/T (or bulge-to-disk ratio B/D), which decreases along the Hubble sequence — high B/T for Sa, low for Sc — turning the qualitative “big bulge vs small bulge” criterion of Lesson 2 into a measured number. A deeper twist: not all bulges are alike. “Classical” bulges have high Sérsic index (n ≈ 3–4), are pressure-supported, and look like little ellipticals grown by mergers; “pseudobulges” have low index (n ≈ 1–2), are flattened and rotating, and are thought to be built slowly (secularly) by disk instabilities and bars funneling gas inward. Kormendy & Kennicutt (2004) crystallized this distinction, which matters because it says a “bulge” can be a merger relic OR a disk-grown structure — two very different formation histories hiding behind the same word.

lessons.workedExample: You fit a spiral’s disk and read off central surface brightness I_0 corresponding to μ_0 = 21.0 mag/arcsec² and a scale length h = 4.0 kpc, then a separate bulge component with an r^(1/4) (n = 4) profile. Two quick results follow. (1) The disk brightness at one scale length is I(h) = I_0·e^(−1) = 0.37·I_0 — i.e. 1.0 magnitude fainter than the center (since Δμ = 2.5·log₁₀(e) ≈ 1.086 mag per scale length), a useful sanity check on any disk fit. (2) You compare the fitted bulge and disk integrated luminosities and find L_bulge/L_disk = 0.25, so the bulge-to-total ratio is B/T = 0.25/(1 + 0.25) = 0.20. A B/T of 0.2 with a low-Sérsic-index bulge is consistent with a middling spiral around Sb–Sc with a possible pseudobulge — a specific, defensible classification from numbers rather than a glance.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on profile fitting because it is where “I looked at the picture” becomes “I measured the structure.” A strong student can say that disks are exponential (scale length h) while ellipticals are r^(1/4), and that the Sérsic index n unifies them — n = 1 for a disk, n = 4 for an elliptical — so a fitted n is a reproducible stand-in for morphology. The best answers reach the bulge-to-total ratio B/T as the quantitative version of “bulge dominance,” and know the classical-vs-pseudobulge distinction, because that shows the student understands a single fitted number can encode a whole formation history (merger-built vs secularly grown).

questions.prompt: Match each Sérsic index value to the profile it reproduces.

right.text: Pure exponential disk, I(r) = I_0·exp(−r/h)
de Vaucouleurs r^(1/4) law for an elliptical

questions.explanation: The Sérsic law I(r) = I_e·exp{−b_n[(r/r_e)^(1/n) − 1]} reduces to a pure exponential disk when n = 1 and to the de Vaucouleurs r^(1/4) elliptical profile when n = 4 — one formula spanning disk-like to spheroid-like light.

questions.prompt: The disk scale length h is defined as the radius over which the disk surface brightness drops by what factor?

options.text: A factor of 2
A factor of e ≈ 2.72
A factor of 10
To exactly zero

explanations.a: A factor of 2 corresponds to a “half-light” style radius, not the e-folding scale length of an exponential.
explanations.b: Correct — for I(r) = I_0·exp(−r/h), at r = h the brightness is I_0/e, a drop by the factor e ≈ 2.72; that e-folding radius IS the scale length.
explanations.c: A factor of 10 is a decade in brightness, not the definition of h.
explanations.d: The exponential never reaches zero at finite radius; h is where it drops by e, not to nothing.

questions.prompt: A galaxy is fit with a bulge whose L_bulge/L_disk = 1.0. What is its bulge-to-total ratio B/T, and how does B/T trend along the Hubble sequence?

options.text: B/T = 1.0; it increases from Sa to Sc
B/T = 0.5; it decreases from Sa (high) to Sc (low)
B/T = 0.0; it is constant along the sequence
B/T = 2.0; it is undefined for spirals

explanations.a: B/T = L_bulge/(L_bulge + L_disk) = 1/(1+1) = 0.5, not 1.0, and B/T DECREASES toward late types, not increases.
explanations.b: Correct — with equal bulge and disk light, B/T = 1/(1+1) = 0.5, and B/T falls from bulge-dominated Sa down to disk-dominated Sc.
explanations.c: B/T is not zero here (the bulge equals the disk), and it is definitely not constant along the sequence.
explanations.d: B/T is a fraction bounded between 0 and 1 by construction; 2.0 is impossible.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a “pseudobulge” from a “classical” bulge?

options.text: Pseudobulges have high Sérsic index (n ≈ 4) and formed in mergers
Pseudobulges have low Sérsic index (n ≈ 1–2), are flattened and rotating, and are thought to form secularly via disk instabilities and bars
Pseudobulges are just poorly measured classical bulges
Pseudobulges are found only in elliptical galaxies

explanations.a: That description (high n, merger-built) is the CLASSICAL bulge, not the pseudobulge.
explanations.b: Correct — pseudobulges are disky (low n ≈ 1–2), rotation-supported, and built slowly by internal secular processes such as bar-driven gas inflow, unlike merger-built classical bulges.
explanations.c: The distinction is physical (formation and kinematics), not a measurement artifact; Kormendy & Kennicutt (2004) laid out real diagnostic criteria.
explanations.d: Pseudobulges live in the centers of disk galaxies, not in ellipticals.

lessons.label: Dwarfs, Irregulars, and Low-Surface-Brightness Galaxies

sections.heading: The tuning fork misses the most common galaxies
sections.body: Hubble’s tuning fork was built from bright, nearby, well-resolved “grand design” galaxies — but by NUMBER, the universe is dominated by faint dwarfs the scheme barely addresses. Dwarfs split into families: dwarf ellipticals (dE) and the even fainter dwarf spheroidals (dSph), smooth and gas-poor; dwarf irregulars (dIrr), gas-rich and lumpy with patchy star formation; and blue compact dwarfs. The Milky Way is orbited by dozens of dSph satellites — Draco, Fornax, Sculptor, Carina, and many more — and irregulars have no ordered spiral structure at all, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds being the classic nearby examples (the LMC shows a stub of a bar, hence “Magellanic” type Sm/Im at the very end of the sequence). The lesson: a classification scheme calibrated on the brightest objects systematically under-represents the numerically dominant population.

sections.heading: Dwarf spheroidals are dark-matter dominated
sections.body: Dwarf spheroidals are among the most dark-matter-dominated objects known. They are so faint (some with only ~10⁵–10⁶ solar luminosities) that their measured internal stellar motions vastly exceed what their visible stars could hold together gravitationally. Estimating the mass within the half-light radius from the stellar velocity dispersion σ and comparing to the light gives mass-to-light ratios of tens to several hundred in solar units — versus M/L ≈ 1–3 for the stars alone — the excess being dark matter. The wave of “ultra-faint dwarfs” discovered in Sloan Digital Sky Survey data from 2005 onward (Willman 1 in 2005, Segue 1 around 2007, and others) pushed this further: some have M/L in the hundreds to thousands, making them prime targets for dark-matter and dark-matter-annihilation searches. Dwarf kinematics are therefore not a footnote — they are a central line of evidence for dark matter on small scales.

sections.heading: Low-surface-brightness galaxies and a selection blind spot
sections.body: A whole population hides below the sky-brightness detection threshold: low-surface-brightness (LSB) galaxies. The extreme case is Malin 1 (identified by Bothun and collaborators in 1987), a GIANT LSB spiral with a disk scale length of tens of kiloparsecs yet a central surface brightness far fainter than an ordinary spiral — it stayed hidden until deliberately deep imaging found it. More recently, ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) — as large as the Milky Way but with the star count of a dwarf — were found in bulk in the Coma cluster by van Dokkum and collaborators (2015) using the Dragonfly Telephoto Array. One UDG, NGC 1052-DF2 (van Dokkum et al. 2018), was reported to contain almost NO dark matter, an actively debated result that would be surprising if confirmed.
