The overarching point, argued forcefully by Mike Disney (1976): magnitude- and surface-brightness-limited surveys preferentially catch high-surface-brightness galaxies, so “Freeman’s law” of nearly constant disk central brightness was partly a SELECTION EFFECT — we were blind to the faint disks. Classification is only as complete as your survey’s detection limits.

lessons.workedExample: You want to test whether a Milky Way dwarf spheroidal is dark-matter dominated. For Draco you measure a line-of-sight stellar velocity dispersion σ ≈ 9 km/s and a half-light radius r₁/₂ ≈ 220 pc. A standard dynamical estimator gives the mass within the half-light radius as roughly M₁/₂ ≈ 930·σ²·r₁/₂ (M in solar masses, σ in km/s, r in pc): M₁/₂ ≈ 930 × 9² × 220 ≈ 930 × 81 × 220 ≈ 1.7×10⁷ M_⊙. Draco’s total luminosity is only ~3×10⁵ L_⊙, so about half its light, ~1.5×10⁵ L_⊙, lies inside r₁/₂. The dynamical mass-to-light ratio within the half-light radius is then M/L ≈ 1.7×10⁷ / 1.5×10⁵ ≈ 110 in solar units. Since the stars alone should give M/L ≈ 1–3, a value near 110 means Draco is roughly two orders of magnitude more massive than its stars can explain — direct evidence of a dominant dark-matter halo in a galaxy the tuning fork does not even chart.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges raise dwarfs and LSB galaxies to check whether a student mistakes “the galaxies in the textbook diagram” for “all galaxies.” The strong move is to point out that dwarfs are the most NUMEROUS type yet nearly absent from the tuning fork, and that dwarf spheroidals’ huge dynamical mass-to-light ratios (tens to hundreds) are frontline evidence for dark matter. Even sharper is naming the SELECTION EFFECT — Disney’s argument that surface-brightness-limited surveys miss LSB systems, so any census (including a student’s own sample) is biased toward bright objects unless the detection limits are stated. That awareness of what a survey cannot see is exactly the methodological maturity judges reward.

questions.prompt: A dwarf spheroidal shows a dynamical mass-to-light ratio of about 100 (solar units) within its half-light radius, while its stars alone should give M/L ≈ 1–3. What does this imply?

options.text: The distance was measured wrong by a factor of 100
The galaxy is dominated by dark matter — its gravitating mass far exceeds its stellar mass
The stars are unusually bright, lowering the ratio
Dwarf spheroidals have no dark matter

explanations.a: The high M/L comes from comparing dynamical mass (from stellar motions) to light within the same radius; it is not an artifact of a distance error of that size.
explanations.b: Correct — a dynamical M/L of ~100 against a stellar expectation of 1–3 means roughly 97–99% of the mass is non-luminous, i.e. dark-matter dominated.
explanations.c: Unusually bright stars would LOWER M/L, the opposite of what is observed; the high ratio needs extra unseen mass, not brighter stars.
explanations.d: A high M/L is the signature of ABUNDANT dark matter, not its absence.

questions.prompt: What is the significance of “Freeman’s law” of nearly constant disk central surface brightness being partly a selection effect?

options.text: It proves all disks truly have identical central brightness
Surveys with surface-brightness limits preferentially detect bright disks, so low-surface-brightness galaxies were systematically missed (Disney 1976)
It means the exponential disk profile is wrong
It applies only to elliptical galaxies

explanations.a: The point is the OPPOSITE — the apparent constancy was inflated by only detecting the bright end; genuinely faint disks exist.
explanations.b: Correct — Mike Disney (1976) argued surface-brightness-limited catalogues miss LSB systems, so the near-constant central brightness partly reflected the detection threshold, not a law of nature.
explanations.c: The exponential form of disks is well established; the selection point is about which disks get INTO the sample, not the profile shape.
explanations.d: Freeman’s law concerns disks (spirals and lenticulars), not ellipticals.

questions.prompt: Match each object or class to its defining description.

right.text: Very faint, smooth, gas-poor satellite with a huge dark-matter mass-to-light ratio
A giant low-surface-brightness spiral with a tens-of-kpc disk, found in deep imaging (Bothun et al. 1987)
Milky-Way-sized in extent but with the star count of a dwarf; found in bulk in Coma (van Dokkum et al. 2015)
Gas-rich, lumpy, actively star-forming dwarf with no ordered spiral structure

questions.explanation: Dwarf spheroidals are faint, smooth, dark-matter-dominated satellites; Malin 1 is the archetypal giant low-surface-brightness spiral; ultra-diffuse galaxies are as extended as big galaxies but hold as few stars as dwarfs; dwarf irregulars are gas-rich, clumpy, star-forming systems with no spiral order.

questions.prompt: Which discovery channel produced the wave of “ultra-faint” dwarf galaxies around the Milky Way starting in 2005?

options.text: Radio pulsar timing arrays
Deep, wide-field digital imaging from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS)
Gravitational-wave detectors
Solar neutrino experiments

explanations.a: Pulsar timing arrays search for nanohertz gravitational waves, not faint stellar overdensities.
explanations.b: Correct — SDSS’s deep, uniform, wide-field digital imaging let astronomers pick out sparse stellar overdensities (Segue 1, Willman 1, and others) as new ultra-faint dwarfs from 2005 onward.
explanations.c: Gravitational-wave detectors (e.g., LIGO) observe merging compact objects, not resolved dwarf galaxies.
explanations.d: Solar neutrino experiments study the Sun’s core, entirely unrelated to Local Group dwarfs.

lessons.label: The Galaxy Color–Magnitude Diagram: Red Sequence, Blue Cloud, Green Valley

sections.heading: From morphology to color: a quantitative axis
sections.body: Classifying galaxies by eye is subjective; classifying them by COLOR is a measurement any survey can make automatically. A galaxy’s integrated color — for example u − r, the difference between ultraviolet-ish and red broadband magnitudes — encodes the mix of its stellar populations: hot, short-lived blue stars make a galaxy blue and signal RECENT star formation, while a population of only old, cool stars makes it red. Plot color on the vertical axis against absolute magnitude (or stellar mass) on the horizontal axis and you get the galaxy color–magnitude diagram (CMD), the extragalactic cousin of the stellar Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. Its great virtue is objectivity: no judgment call about arm winding, just two numbers per galaxy from calibrated photometry.

sections.heading: A bimodal population: red sequence and blue cloud
sections.body: When Strateva and collaborators (2001) plotted hundreds of thousands of Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxies this way, and Baldry et al. (2004) fit the distribution, a striking result emerged: galaxy colors are BIMODAL. Most galaxies pile into one of two groups. The RED SEQUENCE is a tight, slightly tilted band of red galaxies — mostly ellipticals and lenticulars, passively evolving with old stars and little star formation. The BLUE CLOUD is a broader scatter of bluer galaxies — mostly star-forming spirals and irregulars. The red sequence’s tilt (more luminous/massive galaxies are slightly redder) reflects the mass–metallicity relation: bigger galaxies retain more metals, and metal-rich stars are redder. The bimodality is a clue that galaxies do not drift smoothly through all colors — something moves them relatively quickly from one group to the other.

sections.heading: The green valley and quenching
sections.body: Between the two peaks lies a sparsely populated GREEN VALLEY. Its underpopulation is the physically interesting part: if galaxies transitioned slowly from blue to red, the valley would be crowded; its emptiness implies the crossing is FAST — galaxies quench their star formation relatively quickly (roughly a Gyr or so), then redden onto the red sequence. What does the quenching? The leading mechanisms fall into two broad channels, which Peng et al. (2010) showed act nearly independently: “mass quenching,” internal to a galaxy and tied to its stellar mass (with AGN feedback — energy from a central supermassive black hole heating or expelling gas — a leading culprit in massive galaxies), and “environment quenching,” which acts on satellites in dense groups and clusters via processes like ram-pressure stripping (the cluster’s hot gas sweeping cold gas out of an infalling galaxy) and strangulation (cutting off the fresh-gas supply). Crucially, color and morphology are correlated but NOT identical: there are dusty red spirals and rejuvenated blue ellipticals, so the CMD and the tuning fork are complementary lenses, not the same measurement twice.

lessons.workedExample: You have SDSS photometry for a galaxy: rest-frame absolute magnitudes M_u = −18.5 and M_r = −21.0, so its color is u − r = M_u − M_r = (−18.5) − (−21.0) = +2.5. A common empirical divider between the two populations sits near u − r ≈ 2.2, so at 2.5 this galaxy lies on the RED SEQUENCE — consistent with a passive, old population. To confirm it is genuinely quenched rather than just dust-reddened, you check its specific star-formation rate (star-formation rate per unit stellar mass): a widely used threshold for “quenched” is sSFR ≲ 10⁻¹¹ yr⁻¹, meaning it would take more than ~100 Gyr to double its stellar mass at the current rate. If the galaxy’s sSFR comes in at ~10⁻¹² yr⁻¹, both diagnostics agree: red color AND negligible ongoing star formation place it firmly on the red sequence, not merely a reddened blue-cloud galaxy hiding behind dust.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the color–magnitude diagram to test whether a student can turn a qualitative “type” into a reproducible measurement and then reason about MECHANISM. The strong answer explains that the CMD is objective (two photometric numbers) and bimodal — red sequence (passive) versus blue cloud (star-forming) — and that the sparse green valley implies quenching is fast. Naming a real mechanism (AGN feedback for mass quenching; ram-pressure stripping or strangulation for environment quenching, following Peng et al. 2010) shows physical depth. The subtlest point, which separates the best students, is that color and morphology are correlated but not identical — red spirals and blue ellipticals exist — so the two classification axes carry complementary information rather than being redundant.

questions.prompt: On the galaxy color–magnitude diagram, what characterizes the “red sequence”?

options.text: A band of actively star-forming, gas-rich spirals
A tight, slightly tilted band of passively evolving red galaxies, mostly ellipticals and lenticulars with old stars and little star formation
The reddest galaxies purely because they are the most distant
A random scatter of galaxies with no structure

explanations.a: Star-forming gas-rich spirals occupy the BLUE cloud, not the red sequence.
explanations.b: Correct — the red sequence is a narrow, slightly tilted band of quiescent red galaxies (mostly early types) whose colors come from old stellar populations, not ongoing star formation.
explanations.c: These are rest-frame colors of intrinsic populations; distance/redshift effects are corrected out, so the redness is physical, not a distance artifact.
explanations.d: The whole point of the CMD is that the distribution is highly structured (bimodal), with the red sequence being one tight peak.

questions.prompt: Why is the sparsely populated “green valley” between the red sequence and blue cloud physically important?

options.text: It shows galaxies never change color
Its underpopulation implies galaxies cross it quickly, i.e. star formation quenches relatively fast (~1 Gyr)
It is an instrumental gap where telescopes cannot measure color
It contains only foreground stars, not galaxies

explanations.a: The valley’s existence between two peaks is precisely evidence that galaxies DO change color, moving from blue to red.
explanations.b: Correct — if the transition were slow the valley would be crowded; its emptiness means galaxies pass through fast, implying rapid quenching of star formation.
explanations.c: There is no instrumental blind spot at green colors; the underdensity is astrophysical, reflecting a short residence time.
explanations.d: The green valley is populated by real transitioning galaxies, not foreground stars.

questions.prompt: Match each quenching mechanism to its description.

right.text: Energy from a central supermassive black hole heats or expels the galaxy’s gas, mainly in massive galaxies
A cluster’s hot intracluster gas sweeps cold gas out of an infalling satellite
The supply of fresh cold gas is cut off, so the galaxy slowly exhausts its remaining fuel

questions.explanation: AGN feedback is internal “mass quenching” — the central black hole’s energy removes or heats gas in massive galaxies; ram-pressure stripping and strangulation are “environment quenching” of satellites — the former violently sweeps out existing cold gas, the latter cuts off the resupply so the galaxy quietly runs out.

questions.prompt: A galaxy has rest-frame color u − r = 2.5 (above the ~2.2 divider) and a specific star-formation rate of ~10⁻¹² yr⁻¹. What is the safest classification, and why check both?

options.text: Blue cloud, because its color is above 2.2
Red sequence and genuinely quenched — the red color plus a very low sSFR rules out a merely dust-reddened star-forming galaxy
Green valley, because sSFR is nonzero
Cannot classify without its morphology

explanations.a: A color of 2.5 is ABOVE the ~2.2 divider, which places it on the red sequence, not the blue cloud.
explanations.b: Correct — the red color could in principle come from dust, but a very low sSFR (~10⁻¹² yr⁻¹, well below the ~10⁻¹¹ quenched threshold) confirms little ongoing star formation, so the two diagnostics together nail it as a genuinely quenched red-sequence galaxy.
explanations.c: A sSFR of 10⁻¹² yr⁻¹ is far below the quenched threshold, indicating an already-red galaxy, not a transitioning green-valley one.
explanations.d: Color plus sSFR already give a robust, quantitative classification; morphology adds complementary information but is not required to place it on the CMD.

units.label: Measuring Galaxies: Kinematics, Mass, and Scaling Laws

lessons.label: Building a Rotation Curve: Long-Slit Spectra and 21-cm Line Widths

sections.heading: What a rotation curve is, and why it weighs a galaxy
sections.body: A rotation curve is the plot of circular orbital speed v against galactocentric radius R for a disk galaxy. It matters because, for material on a near-circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: v(R)^2 / R = G·M(<R) / R^2, which rearranges to the enclosed-mass estimator M(<R) = v(R)^2·R / G. Every point on the curve is therefore a weighing of all the mass (stars, gas, and dark matter) interior to that radius. If light traced mass, the curve would rise in the star-rich inner disk and then fall off in a Keplerian v ∝ R^(−1/2) decline once you passed most of the visible stars — the way planet speeds drop with distance from the Sun. Real spiral galaxies do not do this: their rotation curves stay flat out to the last measured point, which is one of the cleanest, and historically the first, galaxy-scale pieces of evidence for dark matter halos.

sections.heading: Long-slit spectroscopy: reading velocity off a tilted emission line
sections.body: The optical technique places a spectrograph slit along the galaxy's major axis. Ionized gas in HII regions emits bright narrow lines — Hα at 6563 Å, the [NII] doublet, [OIII] 5007 Å — and at each point along the slit that line is Doppler-shifted by the local line-of-sight velocity. One side of the disk approaches (blueshift), the other recedes (redshift), so on the two-dimensional spectrum the emission line appears tilted or S-shaped: its wavelength offset versus slit position IS the rotation curve, once you subtract the galaxy's systemic (whole-galaxy) recession velocity. The catch is projection: you measure only v_obs = v_rot·sin(i), where i is the inclination (i = 90° is edge-on, i = 0° is face-on and shows no rotation at all). You must deproject by dividing by sin(i), and a nearly face-on galaxy gives a badly amplified, noisy correction.

sections.heading: The 21-cm line: neutral hydrogen reaches past the stars
sections.body: Neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) emits the 21-cm line (rest frequency 1420.4 MHz) from the hyperfine spin-flip transition. HI disks typically extend well beyond the optical edge of a galaxy, so radio observations trace the rotation curve to radii where there are almost no stars — exactly where a Keplerian falloff should appear if there were no dark matter. A single-dish radio telescope that cannot resolve the disk still records the integrated HI profile as a characteristic double-horned shape whose full width W (often quoted as W20 at 20% of peak, or W50 at 50%) measures twice the projected rotation speed, W ≈ 2·v_rot·sin(i). That single number — a line width — is the input to the Tully–Fisher relation two lessons from now.

sections.heading: Vera Rubin, Kent Ford, and the flat-curve revolution
sections.body: In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford used a sensitive image-tube spectrograph to build optical rotation curves for Andromeda (M31) and then dozens of spirals, finding curve after curve that stayed flat rather than declining. Radio astronomers (including work by Morton Roberts and later Albert Bosma's 1978 thesis mapping HI curves) confirmed the flatness extended even farther in HI. A flat curve, v ≈ constant, forces M(<R) ∝ R — mass keeps growing linearly with radius even where the light has faded away, implying a dark halo with density ρ ∝ R^(−2). This built on Zwicky's 1933 dynamical evidence for missing mass in the Coma cluster and turned dark matter from a cluster-scale curiosity into a property of individual galaxies.

lessons.workedExample: Weigh the Milky Way inside the Sun's orbit. The Sun sits at R0 ≈ 8.0 kpc and the local circular speed is v ≈ 220 km/s. Convert to SI: v = 2.20×10^5 m/s, R = 8.0 kpc × 3.086×10^19 m/kpc = 2.47×10^20 m, G = 6.674×10^−11. Then M(<R0) = v^2·R / G = (2.20×10^5)^2 × 2.47×10^20 / 6.674×10^−11 = (4.84×10^10 × 2.47×10^20) / 6.674×10^−11 = 1.20×10^31 / 6.674×10^−11 ≈ 1.79×10^41 kg. Dividing by the solar mass 1.989×10^30 kg gives ≈ 9×10^10 M_sun — about 90 billion solar masses interior to the Sun. Because the curve stays near 220 km/s well beyond 8 kpc, the enclosed mass keeps climbing linearly outward, the signature of the dark halo.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe rotation curves because "we saw the curve was flat" is where students either show or fake understanding of dark matter. The tell is whether a student can state WHY flatness is surprising — that a Keplerian v ∝ R^(−1/2) decline is the naive expectation once you pass the visible stars — and can name the deprojection by sin(i) and the enclosed-mass formula M = v^2R/G. A student who says "the 21-cm line lets us measure rotation past the optical disk, and it stays flat, so M ∝ R out there" has connected an observation to a mass, which is the whole point of the method.

questions.prompt: A spiral galaxy rotation curve stays flat (v ≈ constant) far beyond the visible stars. What does this imply about the enclosed mass M(<R)?

options.text: M(<R) is constant, so no mass is added at large radius
M(<R) grows linearly with R, implying unseen (dark) mass at large radius
M(<R) falls with R in a Keplerian decline
M(<R) cannot be inferred from a rotation curve

explanations.a: If M were constant beyond the stars, v would fall as R^(−1/2) (Keplerian); a flat curve is exactly what a constant mass does NOT produce.
explanations.b: Correct — from v^2 = G·M(<R)/R, a constant v forces M(<R) ∝ R, so mass keeps accumulating where there is little light: the dark-halo signature.
explanations.c: A Keplerian decline is the naive expectation past the stars; the observed flatness is the surprise that motivates dark matter.
explanations.d: Mass is precisely what a rotation curve infers, via M(<R) = v^2·R/G for circular orbits.

questions.prompt: Why is neutral-hydrogen 21-cm mapping so valuable for rotation curves?

options.text: The 21-cm line is brighter than any optical emission line
HI disks extend beyond the optical disk, tracing rotation where there are almost no stars
Radio observations are immune to the inclination projection effect
21-cm emission only comes from the galactic center

explanations.a: Brightness is not the point; in fact HI emission is faint. Its value is spatial extent, not intensity.
explanations.b: Correct — HI reaches well past the stellar edge, so it samples the rotation curve exactly where a Keplerian falloff would appear if there were no dark halo, and it stays flat instead.
explanations.c: All line-of-sight velocity measurements, radio or optical, still measure v_rot·sin(i) and need deprojection by inclination.
explanations.d: HI is distributed across the extended disk, not confined to the center — the opposite of what makes it useful here.

questions.prompt: A galaxy is observed nearly face-on (inclination i ≈ 10°). Why is its rotation curve hard to measure?

options.text: Face-on galaxies do not rotate
The observed velocity is v_rot·sin(i), so a small sin(i) makes the deprojection large and noisy
Emission lines vanish at low inclination
The systemic velocity cannot be measured face-on

explanations.a: They rotate the same; the disk plane is just nearly perpendicular to the line of sight, so little of the rotation projects onto it.
explanations.b: Correct — with i ≈ 10°, sin(i) ≈ 0.17, so recovering v_rot means dividing the tiny observed shift by 0.17, amplifying every measurement error.
explanations.c: The lines are still present; it is the line-of-sight Doppler projection of rotation that shrinks, not the emission itself.
explanations.d: Systemic velocity (the whole-galaxy redshift) is easy at any inclination; it is the rotational component that projects poorly.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to turn a long-slit spectrum into an enclosed-mass estimate at a given radius.

items.text: Align the slit along the major axis and record the tilted emission line
Convert each line-of-sight wavelength shift to a velocity and subtract the systemic velocity
Deproject by dividing by sin(i) to get the true rotation speed v_rot(R)
Apply M(<R) = v_rot^2·R / G at the chosen radius

questions.explanation: You first capture the tilted line along the major axis, convert wavelength shift to velocity and remove the galaxy-wide systemic recession, deproject for inclination to recover the true circular speed, and only then plug v_rot and R into M(<R) = v^2R/G.

lessons.label: Velocity Dispersion and Mass in Pressure-Supported Ellipticals

sections.heading: Ellipticals are held up by random motion, not spin
sections.body: A spiral disk is rotation-supported: stars and gas orbit in a plane, and the ordered speed v balances gravity. An elliptical galaxy is mostly pressure-supported: its stars swarm on randomly oriented orbits like molecules in a hot gas, and it is the spread of those velocities — the velocity dispersion σ — that resists collapse. There is no single rotation speed to measure; instead you characterize the width of the stellar velocity distribution. The dividing quantity is the ratio v/σ of ordered rotation to random dispersion: disks have v/σ well above 1, while classical ellipticals have v/σ below ~1, meaning random motions dominate. This distinction sets which mass estimator you are allowed to use.

sections.heading: Measuring σ from absorption-line broadening
sections.body: Ellipticals are gas-poor and old, so their spectra show stellar ABSORPTION lines, not the emission lines of star-forming disks — strong features like the Ca II H and K lines, the Mg b triplet near 5175 Å, and the Ca II near-infrared triplet. Each star contributes lines Doppler-shifted by its own velocity; summed over millions of stars with a spread of velocities, the galaxy's composite absorption lines are BROADENED relative to a single narrow-lined template star. In practice you cross-correlate the galaxy spectrum against a stellar template: the width of the correlation peak gives the line-of-sight velocity dispersion σ. Giant ellipticals reach σ ≈ 250–350 km/s; ordinary ellipticals sit around 150–250 km/s; low-mass ellipticals and dwarfs drop below 100 km/s.

sections.heading: The virial theorem turns σ into a mass
sections.body: For a self-gravitating system in equilibrium, the virial theorem states 2K + U = 0, where K is total kinetic energy and U is gravitational potential energy. This yields a mass estimate M ≈ k·σ^2·R_e / G, where R_e is the effective (half-light) radius and k is a dimensionless virial coefficient — of order 5 for realistic light and orbit distributions — that absorbs the galaxy's structure and the projection from three-dimensional to line-of-sight dispersion. The estimator is powerful because both σ (from line width) and R_e (from imaging) are directly observable, but it assumes dynamical equilibrium and a mass-follows-light geometry, so it is a virial mass, not an exact one. This same reasoning, applied to whole clusters, is what led Fritz Zwicky in 1933 to infer missing mass in the Coma cluster.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate the virial mass of a typical giant elliptical. Suppose absorption-line broadening gives σ = 200 km/s and imaging gives an effective radius R_e = 3 kpc. Using M ≈ 5·σ^2·R_e / G: σ = 2.0×10^5 m/s so σ^2 = 4.0×10^10 m^2/s^2; R_e = 3 kpc × 3.086×10^19 = 9.26×10^19 m; G = 6.674×10^−11. Then M ≈ 5 × 4.0×10^10 × 9.26×10^19 / 6.674×10^−11 = (1.85×10^31) / 6.674×10^−11 ≈ 2.8×10^41 kg. Dividing by 1.989×10^30 kg gives ≈ 1.4×10^11 M_sun — roughly a hundred billion solar masses, comparable to the Milky Way but assembled and measured through random stellar motions rather than a rotation curve.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "how do you weigh a galaxy that does not rotate?" to see whether a student understands support mechanisms, not just formulas. The insight worth showing is that ellipticals are pressure-supported, so you measure the SPREAD of stellar velocities (σ) via absorption-line broadening and feed it into a virial estimate M ≈ 5σ^2R_e/G — and that this rests on an equilibrium assumption. A student who reaches for a rotation curve on an elliptical, or who cannot say why v/σ distinguishes the two cases, reveals they memorized one method without knowing when it applies.

questions.prompt: What physically supports a classical elliptical galaxy against gravitational collapse?

options.text: Ordered rotation of stars in a thin disk
The random (dispersion) velocities of stars on differently oriented orbits
Radiation pressure from ongoing star formation
Magnetic fields threading the interstellar gas

explanations.a: Ordered rotation supports spiral disks (high v/σ); classical ellipticals have v/σ below ~1, so rotation is not the primary support.
explanations.b: Correct — ellipticals are pressure-supported: the spread of random stellar velocities (σ) provides the dynamical pressure balancing gravity.
explanations.c: Ellipticals are old and gas-poor with little ongoing star formation, so radiation pressure is negligible for their support.
explanations.d: Magnetic fields are dynamically unimportant for the stellar orbits that dominate an elliptical's mass budget.

questions.prompt: How is the velocity dispersion σ of an elliptical actually measured from its spectrum?

options.text: From the Doppler shift of a single bright emission line
From the broadening of stellar absorption lines relative to a narrow-lined template star
From the total brightness of the galaxy
From the 21-cm neutral-hydrogen line width

explanations.a: Ellipticals are gas-poor and show absorption, not bright emission lines; and dispersion is about line WIDTH, not a single shift.
explanations.b: Correct — millions of stars with a spread of velocities broaden the composite absorption lines; cross-correlating against a narrow-lined template recovers σ from the width.
explanations.c: Brightness relates to luminosity/mass scaling laws but does not by itself yield the internal velocity dispersion.
explanations.d: Gas-poor ellipticals have little HI, so 21-cm is generally unavailable; dispersion comes from stellar absorption features.

questions.prompt: The virial mass estimator M ≈ 5·σ^2·R_e / G rests on which key assumption?

options.text: The galaxy is expanding freely, far from equilibrium
The galaxy is in dynamical equilibrium (2K + U = 0)
The galaxy is rotationally supported with v ≫ σ
All the mass is concentrated at the center as a point source

explanations.a: The virial theorem applies to bound, relaxed systems, not to freely expanding ones.
explanations.b: Correct — the estimator descends directly from the virial theorem 2K + U = 0, which holds for a self-gravitating system in equilibrium.
explanations.c: That describes a rotation-supported disk; the virial-σ estimator is precisely for the pressure-supported (dispersion-dominated) case.
explanations.d: The coefficient k ≈ 5 encodes an extended mass distribution tracking the light, not a central point mass.

questions.prompt: Match each galaxy type or quantity to its correct description.

right.text: Rotation-supported; measured with a rotation curve
Pressure-supported; weighed with the virial estimator
The spread of stellar velocities, from absorption-line broadening
Diagnostic of ordered vs. random support (high for disks, ~1 for ellipticals)

questions.explanation: Spirals are rotation-supported and read out through a rotation curve; classical ellipticals are pressure-supported and weighed with M ≈ 5σ^2R_e/G; σ is the velocity spread from absorption-line broadening; and v/σ diagnoses whether ordered rotation (high) or random motion (~1) dominates.

lessons.label: The Tully–Fisher Relation as a Distance and Mass Tool

sections.heading: An empirical law: faster spirals are more luminous
sections.body: In 1977 R. Brent Tully and J. Richard Fisher published a tight empirical correlation between a spiral galaxy's luminosity and its rotation: L ∝ v_rot^α, with the slope α ≈ 4 in red/infrared bands (and shallower, ~3, in the blue where dust and young stars scatter the relation). Equivalently, absolute magnitude is linear in log of the rotation width: M = a·log(W) + b. The rotation input is exactly the 21-cm line width W from Lesson 1 (or an optical rotation-curve amplitude), corrected for inclination via W/sin(i). Physically the relation ties together two facts — more massive halos rotate faster (v^2 ∝ M/R), and more massive galaxies host more stars — so luminosity climbs steeply with rotation speed.

sections.heading: Why it is a distance indicator: a redshift-independent standard candle
sections.body: The power of Tully–Fisher is that rotation speed is DISTANCE-INDEPENDENT: a line width in km/s does not care how far away the galaxy is. So you measure W (giving the intrinsic luminosity L, hence absolute magnitude M) entirely from the galaxy's own kinematics, then compare with the observed apparent magnitude m, which DOES fade with distance. The distance modulus μ = m − M then yields distance through μ = 5·log10(d/10 pc). This makes Tully–Fisher a secondary distance rung on the cosmic distance ladder, calibrated by Cepheids in nearby spirals and reaching out to ~100 Mpc — historically one of the routes to the Hubble constant H0 (which itself sets distance from redshift via Hubble's law v = H0·d).

sections.heading: The Baryonic Tully–Fisher relation and the MOND debate
sections.body: The classic relation scatters and even breaks for small, gas-rich galaxies whose stars are outshone by their gas mass. Stacy McGaugh and collaborators (2000) fixed this by plotting TOTAL baryonic mass (stars plus cold gas, M_b = M_star + M_gas) instead of luminosity: the Baryonic Tully–Fisher Relation, M_b ∝ v_flat^4, is strikingly tight over five decades of mass and uses the flat rotation speed as the velocity. Its tightness is a live theoretical battleground: a fixed slope of 4 with tiny scatter is exactly what Mordehai Milgrom's MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics, 1983) predicts as a law, whereas in the standard dark-matter (ΛCDM) picture it must emerge from the messy interplay of halo assembly and feedback. Both camps cite the BTFR; how naturally each explains its tightness is genuinely debated.

lessons.workedExample: Use Tully–Fisher to find a spiral's distance. A galaxy's 21-cm profile gives a width that, corrected for its inclination, implies a flat rotation speed v_rot = 200 km/s. Read off the calibrated I-band relation (roughly M_I ≈ −21.0 for v_rot = 200 km/s). Now measure its apparent I-band magnitude: m_I = 12.0. The distance modulus is μ = m − M = 12.0 − (−21.0) = 33.0. Invert μ = 5·log10(d/10 pc): log10(d/10 pc) = 33.0/5 = 6.6, so d = 10 pc × 10^6.6 = 10 × 3.98×10^6 = 3.98×10^7 pc ≈ 40 Mpc. As a cross-check, at ~40 Mpc Hubble's law with H0 ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc predicts a recession velocity v ≈ 70 × 40 ≈ 2800 km/s — the redshift you would expect to observe for this galaxy.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about Tully–Fisher to test whether a student grasps how a purely kinematic measurement becomes a distance. The clinching idea is that line width is distance-independent, so it fixes intrinsic luminosity; the apparent brightness then reveals distance through the distance modulus. A student who can also name the Baryonic version (M_b ∝ v^4) and note that its tightness fuels the MOND-vs-dark-matter debate shows they see the relation as both a practical tool AND a probe of galaxy physics, not just a plotted line.

questions.prompt: What makes the Tully–Fisher relation usable as a distance indicator?

options.text: Rotation speed (line width) is distance-independent, so it fixes intrinsic luminosity before you know the distance
Apparent magnitude is the same for all spirals
All spirals rotate at exactly 220 km/s
Line width directly measures distance in megaparsecs

explanations.a: Correct — a rotation width in km/s does not depend on distance, so it yields the intrinsic luminosity/absolute magnitude; comparing that to the (distance-dependent) apparent magnitude then gives distance via the distance modulus.
explanations.b: Apparent magnitude fades with distance and differs greatly between spirals; that variation is what encodes distance.
explanations.c: Rotation speeds range widely (roughly 50–300 km/s); a universal speed would make the relation useless.
explanations.d: Line width gives luminosity, not distance directly; distance follows only after comparing intrinsic to apparent brightness.

questions.prompt: In the infrared, the Tully–Fisher relation goes roughly as L ∝ v_rot^4. Physically, why does luminosity rise so steeply with rotation speed?

options.text: Faster rotation heats the stars, making them intrinsically bluer and brighter
More massive galaxies both rotate faster and contain more stars, so luminosity climbs steeply with rotation
The Doppler effect amplifies the light of fast-rotating galaxies
Rotation speed sets the galaxy's distance, which sets its brightness

explanations.a: Rotation does not heat individual stars; stellar colors are set by their masses and ages, not the galaxy's spin.
explanations.b: Correct — greater total mass means both a faster rotation (v^2 ∝ M/R) and more stars (more light), coupling luminosity to rotation with a steep slope near 4.
explanations.c: Doppler shifting moves light in wavelength but does not systematically brighten a galaxy by its rotation speed.
explanations.d: Rotation speed is distance-independent; that is exactly why it can serve as a standard candle rather than a distance itself.

questions.prompt: The Baryonic Tully–Fisher Relation (McGaugh 2000) improves on the classic version by plotting rotation speed against what?

options.text: Stellar luminosity alone
Total baryonic mass (stars plus cold gas)
Dark-halo mass measured from lensing
Central black-hole mass

explanations.a: Using luminosity (starlight) alone is exactly what breaks down for small gas-rich galaxies whose gas outweighs their stars.
explanations.b: Correct — summing stars and cold gas into total baryonic mass M_b restores a tight M_b ∝ v^4 relation across five decades of mass.
explanations.c: The BTFR uses directly observed baryons (stars + gas), not a lensing-derived dark-halo mass.
explanations.d: Black-hole mass relates to σ (the M–σ relation), not to the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to estimate a spiral galaxy's distance with the Tully–Fisher relation.

items.text: Measure the 21-cm line width and correct it for inclination
Use the calibrated relation to convert rotation speed to absolute magnitude M
Measure the apparent magnitude m from imaging
Form the distance modulus μ = m − M and solve μ = 5·log10(d/10 pc) for d

questions.explanation: You first get the inclination-corrected rotation width, map it to an intrinsic absolute magnitude via the calibrated relation, separately measure the apparent magnitude, and finally combine them in the distance modulus to solve for distance.

lessons.label: Faber–Jackson, the Dₙ–σ Relation, and the Fundamental Plane

sections.heading: Faber–Jackson: the ellipticals' answer to Tully–Fisher
sections.body: In 1976 Sandra Faber and Robert Jackson found that an elliptical galaxy's luminosity scales with its velocity dispersion as L ∝ σ^4 — the pressure-supported analog of Tully–Fisher, and expected from the virial reasoning of Lesson 2 (combine M ∝ σ^2·R_e with a roughly constant surface brightness and mass-to-light ratio). So a bigger dispersion means a brighter galaxy. But Faber–Jackson has substantial scatter: at a fixed σ, ellipticals show a real spread in luminosity, which limits it as a distance tool. That scatter is not random noise — it is telling us the two-parameter relation is a projection of something higher-dimensional.

sections.heading: The Fundamental Plane: three parameters, one flat sheet
sections.body: The scatter shrinks dramatically when you add a third variable. Ellipticals do not scatter through the three-dimensional space of effective radius R_e, central velocity dispersion σ, and mean effective surface brightness I_e — they lie on a thin two-dimensional sheet, the Fundamental Plane, discovered in 1987 by two teams (Djorgovski & Davis; and Dressler, Lynden-Bell and collaborators). Its form is roughly R_e ∝ σ^1.24·I_e^(−0.82). The virial theorem alone predicts exponents of σ^2·I_e^(−1); the observed "tilt" away from those values (the 1.24 instead of 2) is a real physics result, usually attributed to a systematic variation of mass-to-light ratio with galaxy mass — more massive ellipticals are slightly "heavier" per unit light. Faber–Jackson is just the edge-on shadow of this plane.

sections.heading: Dₙ–σ, the Seven Samurai, and peculiar velocities
sections.body: To exploit the plane as a distance tool, Dressler and collaborators (1987) defined Dₙ, the angular diameter within which the mean surface brightness reaches a fixed threshold; Dₙ correlates tightly and nearly linearly with σ (Dₙ ∝ σ^1.2-ish). Since σ is distance-independent, the relation predicts a galaxy's physical diameter, and comparing to its angular size gives distance — with only ~10–20% scatter per galaxy, better than Faber–Jackson. The collaboration behind this — Dressler, Faber, Burstein, Davies, Lynden-Bell, Terlevich, and Wegner, nicknamed the "Seven Samurai" — used Dₙ–σ distances to map deviations from smooth Hubble flow and inferred a large-scale bulk streaming of galaxies toward the "Great Attractor," an early demonstration that scaling relations could measure peculiar velocities and hence the mass distribution of the local universe.

lessons.workedExample: Use Faber–Jackson to estimate an elliptical's luminosity, then see why the Fundamental Plane does better. Take a reference L* elliptical with σ* = 200 km/s and luminosity L* ≈ 2×10^10 L_sun. For a galaxy with σ = 250 km/s, Faber–Jackson L ∝ σ^4 gives L = L*·(250/200)^4 = L*·(1.25)^4 = L*·2.44 ≈ 4.9×10^10 L_sun. But if the target actually has an unusually large effective radius and low surface brightness, its true luminosity could sit well off this single-σ prediction — the ~0.4–0.5 mag scatter of Faber–Jackson. Feeding all three of (σ = 250 km/s, R_e, I_e) into R_e ∝ σ^1.24·I_e^(−0.82) instead places the galaxy on the thin Fundamental Plane, cutting the scatter roughly in half and giving a far more reliable distance.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use these scaling relations to test whether a student understands the difference between a correlation and a physical law. The key point to articulate is that Faber–Jackson (L ∝ σ^4) is a noisy two-parameter projection, while the Fundamental Plane resolves that scatter by adding surface brightness — and that the plane's "tilt" away from the naive virial exponents encodes real mass-to-light variation. A student who names Dₙ–σ as the low-scatter distance tool and knows the Seven Samurai used it to find bulk flows toward the Great Attractor shows they see scaling relations as cosmological instruments, not just tidy plots.

questions.prompt: The Faber–Jackson relation L ∝ σ^4 is best described as:

options.text: The pressure-supported (elliptical) analog of the Tully–Fisher relation, but with larger scatter
A relation between rotation speed and luminosity for spiral disks
A perfectly tight law with essentially no scatter
A relation between galaxy color and star-formation rate

explanations.a: Correct — it links elliptical luminosity to velocity dispersion σ, mirroring Tully–Fisher for disks, but its scatter is large because it is a two-parameter projection of the Fundamental Plane.
explanations.b: That is Tully–Fisher; Faber–Jackson applies to pressure-supported ellipticals using σ, not disk rotation.
explanations.c: It is notably scattered (~0.4–0.5 mag); the tighter relation is the three-parameter Fundamental Plane.
explanations.d: Faber–Jackson concerns luminosity and dynamics (σ), not color or star-formation rate.

questions.prompt: What is the Fundamental Plane of elliptical galaxies?

options.text: The physical mid-plane of a disk galaxy where most stars orbit
A thin 2D relation among effective radius, velocity dispersion, and surface brightness that ellipticals occupy
The plane of the sky onto which galaxies are projected
A relation between black-hole mass and bulge mass

explanations.a: That describes a spiral's disk plane, a spatial structure, not the parameter-space relation meant here.
explanations.b: Correct — ellipticals lie on a thin sheet in the space of R_e, σ, and mean surface brightness I_e, roughly R_e ∝ σ^1.24·I_e^(−0.82).
explanations.c: The plane of the sky is a projection geometry, unrelated to this scaling relation among structural parameters.
explanations.d: That is the M–σ / black-hole–bulge relation, a different correlation entirely.

questions.prompt: The Fundamental Plane's exponents (R_e ∝ σ^1.24·I_e^(−0.82)) differ from the naive virial prediction (σ^2·I_e^(−1)). This "tilt" is usually attributed to:

options.text: Measurement error in σ that cannot be reduced
A systematic variation of mass-to-light ratio with galaxy mass
The expansion of the universe stretching the galaxies
Dust extinction randomizing the surface brightness

explanations.a: The tilt is a systematic, reproducible offset from virial exponents, not random measurement scatter.
explanations.b: Correct — more massive ellipticals have a slightly higher mass-to-light ratio, which tilts the observed plane away from the constant-M/L virial expectation.
explanations.c: Cosmic expansion does not distort the internal structural scaling of individual ellipticals in this way.
explanations.d: Dust is minor in old gas-poor ellipticals and would add scatter, not a systematic tilt in the exponents.

questions.prompt: Match each scaling relation or team to what it is known for.

right.text: Spiral luminosity vs. rotation speed (L ∝ v^4)
Elliptical luminosity vs. dispersion (L ∝ σ^4), high scatter
Thin 2D sheet in R_e, σ, I_e that reduces the scatter
Low-scatter distances used to find bulk flow toward the Great Attractor

questions.explanation: Tully–Fisher ties spiral luminosity to rotation; Faber–Jackson ties elliptical luminosity to σ with large scatter; the Fundamental Plane adds surface brightness to make a thin low-scatter sheet; and the Seven Samurai used the Dₙ–σ distance relation to detect bulk streaming toward the Great Attractor.

lessons.label: Weighing Galaxies with Gravitational Lensing

sections.heading: Light bends around mass — a direct, dynamics-free scale
sections.body: General relativity predicts that mass deflects light: a ray grazing a point mass M at impact parameter b bends by α = 4GM/(c^2·b), twice the Newtonian value. Arthur Eddington's 1919 solar-eclipse expedition measured the Sun's predicted 1.75-arcsecond deflection of background stars, confirming Einstein's 1915 theory. Fritz Zwicky argued in 1937 that galaxies and clusters would act as gravitational lenses and could be "weighed" this way. The appeal for mass measurement is profound: lensing responds to ALL the mass along the line of sight — dark or luminous, relaxed or not — with no assumption of dynamical equilibrium, unlike rotation curves or virial estimates.

sections.heading: Strong lensing: Einstein rings and the mass inside θ_E
sections.body: When a massive galaxy sits almost exactly in front of a distant source, the source can appear as multiple images, giant arcs, or a complete Einstein ring of angular radius θ_E. The Einstein radius encodes the mass projected within it: θ_E = sqrt[ (4GM/c^2)·(D_LS)/(D_L·D_S) ], where D_L, D_S, and D_LS are the (angular-diameter) observer–lens, observer–source, and lens–source distances. Inverting gives the mass inside the Einstein radius essentially model-independently — one of the cleanest mass measurements in astronomy. The first confirmed lens was the "Twin Quasar" Q0957+561, two images of one quasar split by a foreground galaxy, found by Walsh, Carswell, and Weymann in 1979. Galaxy-scale strong lenses today routinely pin down the total (baryonic + dark) mass within a few kiloparsecs of the lens center.

sections.heading: Weak lensing and the Bullet Cluster: mapping unseen mass
sections.body: Far more common than rings is weak lensing: mass gently shears the shapes of thousands of faint background galaxies, stretching them tangentially by a percent or two. No single galaxy shows an obvious distortion, but averaging the shapes over many sources reconstructs the foreground mass map statistically — the basis of galaxy–galaxy lensing (stacking many lenses to weigh average halos) and cluster mass mapping. The landmark case is the Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-558), where Douglas Clowe and collaborators (2006) showed the weak-lensing mass peaks are spatially OFFSET from the X-ray-emitting hot gas (most of the ordinary baryons): during the collision the collisionless dark matter passed straight through while the gas was slowed, separating mass from light. It is often cited as direct empirical evidence that most of the mass is dark and non-baryonic.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate the mass inside a galaxy's Einstein radius. Suppose a lens galaxy produces an Einstein ring of radius θ_E = 1.0 arcsec, with angular-diameter distances D_L = 1.0 Gpc, D_S = 2.0 Gpc, and D_LS = 1.3 Gpc. Rearrange the Einstein-radius formula to M = θ_E^2·(c^2/4G)·(D_L·D_S/D_LS). Convert θ_E = 1.0 arcsec = 1/206265 rad = 4.85×10^−6 rad, so θ_E^2 = 2.35×10^−11. The prefactor c^2/(4G) = (9.0×10^16)/(4×6.674×10^−11) = 3.37×10^26 kg/m. The distance combination D_L·D_S/D_LS = (1.0×2.0/1.3) Gpc = 1.54 Gpc = 1.54×10^3 Mpc × 3.086×10^22 m/Mpc = 4.75×10^25 m. Multiply: M = 2.35×10^−11 × 3.37×10^26 × 4.75×10^25 ≈ 3.8×10^41 kg ≈ 1.9×10^11 M_sun — roughly two hundred billion solar masses projected within the ring, measured without any assumption about the galaxy's internal motions.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges favor lensing questions because they separate students who understand WHY a mass measurement is trustworthy from those who just cite a number. The decisive insight is that lensing weighs all mass along the line of sight with no equilibrium assumption — so it cross-checks rotation curves and virial masses that DO assume equilibrium. A student who explains that the mass inside an Einstein ring is nearly model-independent, and who cites the Bullet Cluster as lensing mass offset from the X-ray gas, demonstrates that they can marshal an independent line of evidence for dark matter rather than leaning on a single method.

questions.prompt: What is the chief advantage of gravitational lensing over rotation curves or virial estimates for measuring galaxy mass?

options.text: It only responds to luminous (baryonic) matter, so it is easier to interpret
It measures all mass along the line of sight with no assumption of dynamical equilibrium
It requires no knowledge of distances to the lens or source
It works only for galaxies that are perfectly relaxed

explanations.a: The opposite — lensing responds to ALL mass, dark and luminous alike, which is exactly why it is powerful.
explanations.b: Correct — lensing depends only on gravity along the sightline and needs no equilibrium assumption, unlike rotation-curve or virial masses.
explanations.c: Lensing masses DO depend on the angular-diameter distances D_L, D_S, D_LS; those enter the Einstein-radius formula.
explanations.d: A key strength is that lensing does NOT require the system to be relaxed, so it works even for merging or disturbed systems.

questions.prompt: A complete Einstein ring of angular radius θ_E lets you measure:

options.text: The mass projected within the Einstein radius, nearly model-independently
The exact three-dimensional density profile of the lens
The rotation speed of the source galaxy
The lens galaxy's star-formation rate

explanations.a: Correct — θ_E fixes the mass enclosed within the Einstein radius via θ_E^2 ∝ M·(D_LS/D_L·D_S), one of the cleanest, most assumption-free mass measurements available.
explanations.b: A single ring pins the enclosed mass, not the full 3D profile; that requires extra modeling and more constraints.
explanations.c: The ring measures the LENS mass, not the source's internal rotation.
explanations.d: Lensing is a gravitational effect and says nothing directly about the lens's star-formation rate.

questions.prompt: In the Bullet Cluster (Clowe et al. 2006), why is the weak-lensing mass being offset from the X-ray gas taken as evidence for dark matter?

options.text: The gas is where all the mass is, so lensing and X-rays should agree but do not because of measurement error
During the collision, collisionless dark matter passed through while the gas was slowed, so the bulk of the mass (traced by lensing) separated from most of the baryons (the gas)
The offset shows there is no dark matter, only modified gravity
Lensing measures the gas directly and finds it more massive than expected

explanations.a: Most of the ordinary baryons ARE in the hot gas, yet the lensing mass sits elsewhere — that mismatch is the signal, not an error.
explanations.b: Correct — the collisionless dark matter sailed through the collision while the X-ray gas (most of the baryons) was ram-pressure slowed, so the lensing mass peaks are displaced from the gas, directly separating mass from light.
explanations.c: The offset is generally read as favoring dark matter over modified-gravity-only models, since the mass does not track the dominant baryonic component.
explanations.d: Lensing traces total mass, and it finds that mass displaced FROM the gas, not that the gas itself is the mass.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the history of gravitational lensing.

items.text: Einstein publishes general relativity, predicting light deflection by mass (1915)
Eddington's eclipse expedition measures the Sun's 1.75-arcsec deflection (1919)
The Twin Quasar Q0957+561, the first confirmed lens, is discovered (1979)
The Bullet Cluster shows lensing mass offset from the X-ray gas (2006)

questions.explanation: General relativity (1915) predicted deflection; Eddington confirmed it at the 1919 eclipse; the first galaxy-scale lens (the Twin Quasar) was found in 1979; and the Bullet Cluster provided the dark-matter offset result in 2006.

lessons.label: Surface Photometry, Isophotes, and Petrosian/Kron Magnitudes

sections.heading: Surface brightness profiles: how light falls off with radius
sections.body: Surface photometry measures how a galaxy's surface brightness — flux per unit solid angle, in magnitudes per square arcsecond — declines from center to edge. Two classic laws bracket the morphologies. Gérard de Vaucouleurs (1948) found elliptical galaxies follow the R^(1/4) law, I(R) = I_e·exp{−7.67[(R/R_e)^(1/4) − 1]}, a steeply centrally concentrated profile. Ken Freeman (1970) showed spiral DISKS follow an exponential, I(R) = I_0·exp(−R/h), with scale length h. Both are special cases of the general Sérsic profile I(R) = I_e·exp{−b_n[(R/R_e)^(1/n) − 1]}: index n = 4 recovers de Vaucouleurs, n = 1 recovers the exponential disk, and fitting n itself measures how concentrated a galaxy is. A crucial property: surface brightness is distance-INDEPENDENT in a static universe (a galaxy moved farther has less flux but proportionally smaller angular area), which is why it is such a robust structural descriptor, though at high redshift cosmological (1+z)^4 dimming does set in.

sections.heading: Isophotes: the shapes of constant-brightness contours
sections.body: An isophote is a contour of constant surface brightness. Fitting ellipses to a galaxy's isophotes yields, at each radius, the center, ellipticity, position angle, and — from higher-order Fourier terms — deviations from a perfect ellipse. The fourth cosine coefficient a4 is diagnostic: a4 > 0 marks "disky" isophotes (pointed, hinting at an embedded disk), a4 < 0 marks "boxy" isophotes. Ralf Bender and collaborators (late 1980s) showed this split correlates with real physics — boxy ellipticals tend to be more massive, slower-rotating, and radio/X-ray loud, while disky ones rotate faster — so a purely geometric measurement of isophote shape carries information about a galaxy's formation and dynamics.

sections.heading: The total-magnitude problem: Petrosian and Kron apertures
sections.body: Because these profiles formally extend to infinity, "the total magnitude" is ambiguous — a bigger aperture always catches a little more light, and how much depends on depth and noise. Two adaptive, distance-robust aperture definitions solve this. The Kron radius (Robert Kron, 1980) sets the aperture to a multiple (typically ~2.5×) of the flux-weighted mean radius (the first moment of the light profile), capturing a nearly fixed fraction of the light regardless of the profile. The Petrosian radius (Vahé Petrosian, 1976) is defined where the LOCAL surface brightness drops to a fixed fraction (0.2 in SDSS) of the mean surface brightness interior to that radius; the flux within a fixed multiple of that radius is the Petrosian magnitude. Because the Petrosian aperture is set by a surface-brightness RATIO, it is independent of distance and of cosmological dimming — which is exactly why the Sloan Digital Sky Survey adopted Petrosian magnitudes to compare galaxies across a wide range of redshifts on an equal footing.

lessons.workedExample: Compute an elliptical's effective surface brightness from its total magnitude and half-light radius. Suppose a galaxy has total apparent magnitude m = 14.0 and effective (half-light) radius R_e = 5.0 arcsec, so half the total light falls within R_e. Half the flux is fainter by −2.5·log10(0.5) = +0.75 mag, so the light within R_e corresponds to m_half = 14.0 + 0.75 = 14.75. That light is spread over the area A = π·R_e^2 = π·(5.0)^2 = 78.5 arcsec^2. The mean effective surface brightness is μ_e = m_half + 2.5·log10(A) = 14.75 + 2.5·log10(78.5) = 14.75 + 2.5×1.895 = 14.75 + 4.74 ≈ 19.5 mag/arcsec^2 — a typical value for the bright inner region of an elliptical, and, crucially, a number that does not change if you place the same galaxy twice as far away.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe surface photometry to check whether a student measured a galaxy's structure honestly or just cited a catalog magnitude. The revealing point is understanding WHY "total magnitude" is ambiguous — profiles run to infinity — and how Petrosian or Kron apertures give a reproducible, distance-independent answer. A student who can say "I used a Sérsic fit to get the index and effective radius, and Petrosian magnitudes so my brightnesses are comparable across redshift" shows command of the difference between a raw number and a well-defined, comparable measurement, which is exactly the rigor a judge rewards.

questions.prompt: The Sérsic profile with index n = 4 and n = 1 recovers which two classic laws?

options.text: n = 4 gives the exponential disk; n = 1 gives the de Vaucouleurs law
n = 4 gives the de Vaucouleurs R^(1/4) law (ellipticals); n = 1 gives the exponential disk (spirals)
Both indices give the same exponential profile
n = 4 gives a flat (constant) surface brightness; n = 1 gives a point source

explanations.a: The assignment is reversed: n = 4 is de Vaucouleurs (ellipticals), n = 1 is the exponential disk.
explanations.b: Correct — the Sérsic index n = 4 reproduces de Vaucouleurs' R^(1/4) law for ellipticals, and n = 1 reproduces Freeman's exponential disk for spirals.
explanations.c: Different n values give distinctly different concentration; only n = 1 is exponential.
explanations.d: Neither index gives a flat profile or a point source; both are smoothly declining profiles of different concentration.

questions.prompt: Why did the Sloan Digital Sky Survey adopt Petrosian magnitudes?

options.text: They capture 100% of a galaxy's light exactly
The Petrosian aperture is set by a surface-brightness ratio, making it independent of distance and cosmological dimming
They are the brightest possible magnitude definition
They require no imaging, only a spectrum

explanations.a: No finite aperture captures 100% of an infinitely extended profile; Petrosian magnitudes deliberately capture a fixed, reproducible FRACTION.
explanations.b: Correct — because the Petrosian radius is defined by the ratio of local to interior mean surface brightness, it does not depend on distance or (1+z)^4 dimming, so galaxies at different redshifts are measured consistently.
explanations.c: The goal is consistency and reproducibility, not maximizing measured brightness.
explanations.d: Petrosian magnitudes are photometric measurements from imaging, not derived from spectra.

questions.prompt: An elliptical galaxy shows "boxy" isophotes (fourth Fourier coefficient a4 < 0). Based on the Bender-era correlations, this galaxy is more likely to be:

options.text: A low-mass, fast-rotating galaxy
A more massive, slowly-rotating galaxy, often radio/X-ray loud
A gas-rich, actively star-forming spiral
A galaxy with a perfectly circular light distribution

explanations.a: Fast-rotating, less massive ellipticals tend to be DISKY (a4 > 0), the opposite of boxy.
explanations.b: Correct — boxy isophotes correlate with more massive, slowly rotating ellipticals that are more often radio- and X-ray-loud.
explanations.c: Isophote boxiness/diskiness is a property of ellipticals, not a marker of star-forming spirals.
explanations.d: A4 measures DEVIATION from an ellipse; a nonzero a4 means the isophote is specifically not a simple ellipse.

questions.prompt: Match each photometric concept to its correct definition.

right.text: The R^(1/4) surface-brightness profile of elliptical galaxies
A fitted parameter measuring how centrally concentrated the light is
Where local surface brightness falls to a fixed fraction (0.2 in SDSS) of the interior mean
A multiple (~2.5×) of the flux-weighted mean (first-moment) radius

questions.explanation: The de Vaucouleurs law is the R^(1/4) profile for ellipticals; the Sérsic index n quantifies concentration (n=4 de Vaucouleurs, n=1 exponential); the Petrosian radius is set by a surface-brightness ratio (0.2 in SDSS); and the Kron radius is ~2.5 times the flux-weighted first-moment radius.

units.label: Dark Matter and the Dynamics of Galaxies

lessons.label: The Mass Discrepancy: From Flat Curves to Missing Mass

sections.heading: What a Keplerian galaxy would look like
sections.body: If a spiral galaxy's mass were concentrated where its light is — in the bright inner disk and bulge — then a star orbiting well beyond that light would feel the gravity of essentially all the galaxy's mass acting as a central point. For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: GM(<r)/r² = v²/r, so the orbital speed is v = √(GM(<r)/r). Once you are outside the bulk of the mass, M(<r) stops growing, and v should fall off as r^(−1/2) — the same "Keplerian decline" that makes Neptune orbit the Sun slower than Mercury. Double the radius past the edge of the mass and the speed should drop by a factor of √2. This is a hard, quantitative prediction: the outer rotation curve of a light-traces-mass galaxy must turn over and decline.

sections.heading: What rotation curves actually do
sections.body: They do not decline. Vera Rubin and Kent Ford, using their sensitive image-tube spectrograph, measured the rotation of the Andromeda galaxy (M31) around 1970 and then a large sample of spirals through the late 1970s; the rotation curves stayed flat — v roughly constant at ~150–300 km/s — out to the farthest measurable radius, far beyond where the starlight had faded to nothing. Radio observations of the 21 cm hydrogen line pushed the curves even farther out and confirmed the flatness. A flat curve is not a small anomaly. If v is constant, then v² = GM(<r)/r demands M(<r) ∝ r — the enclosed mass keeps rising linearly with radius in a region where there is almost no light to account for it. Something with mass but no appreciable luminosity extends far past the visible galaxy.

sections.heading: Naming the discrepancy, not yet the culprit
sections.body: The quantity astronomers actually measure is a discrepancy, not a particle: the dynamical mass inferred from motion vastly exceeds the baryonic mass inferred from light (plus gas). The ratio grows with radius, reaching factors of ~5–10 for a whole galaxy and higher in the outskirts. Fritz Zwicky had already flagged the same disease at cluster scales in 1933 (next lessons), and he coined "dunkle Materie" — dark matter — for it. But the flat rotation curve alone does not tell you whether the missing mass is a new particle, faint ordinary matter (dead stars, gas, planets — collectively MACHOs), or a failure of gravity itself (MOND, Lesson 3). Rubin herself was famously cautious about the interpretation. The honest statement of the 1970s result is: galaxies contain far more gravitating mass, distributed far more extendedly, than their light reveals.

lessons.workedExample: A spiral shows a flat rotation curve with v ≈ 220 km/s that is still flat at r = 20 kpc, well past the visible disk. The enclosed dynamical mass is M(<r) = v²r/G. Convert: v = 2.2×10⁵ m/s, so v² = 4.84×10¹⁰ m²/s²; r = 20 kpc = 20 × 3.086×10¹⁹ m = 6.17×10²⁰ m. Then M = (4.84×10¹⁰ × 6.17×10²⁰)/(6.674×10⁻¹¹) ≈ 4.5×10⁴¹ kg ≈ 2.3×10¹¹ M_sun. Now compare to expectation from light: the stellar+gas mass inside 20 kpc for such a galaxy is only a few ×10¹⁰ M_sun. The dynamical mass exceeds the luminous mass by roughly a factor of 5–10 — and because the curve is still flat, pushing to 40 kpc would double M again while adding essentially no light. The "missing mass" is real, growing, and not where the stars are.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the flat rotation curve because it is the entry point to the entire dark-matter case, and it separates students who can state a falsifiable prediction from those who just recite "galaxies have dark matter." The tell of understanding is naming the Keplerian expectation (v ∝ r^(−1/2) once you are outside the mass) and contrasting it with the observed flatness that forces M(<r) ∝ r — plus the discipline to call the result a mass discrepancy rather than jumping straight to "a particle," since the curve alone cannot distinguish unseen matter from modified gravity.

questions.prompt: If a galaxy's mass were concentrated where its light is, how should the orbital speed of a star well outside that mass behave with radius?

options.text: Stay constant (flat) at all radii
Decline as r^(−1/2), the Keplerian falloff
Rise linearly with radius
Rise as r², steeper than any solid-body region

explanations.a: A flat curve is precisely what is OBSERVED and is the anomaly; a light-traces-mass galaxy would NOT stay flat outside its mass.
explanations.b: Correct — outside the bulk of the mass M(<r) is constant, so v = √(GM/r) ∝ r^(−1/2), the same decline that makes outer planets orbit slower than inner ones.
explanations.c: Linearly rising v would require M(<r) ∝ r³; that is not the expectation once you are beyond the luminous mass.
explanations.d: No mass distribution gives v ∝ r² in the outskirts; even a constant-density inner region produces only v ∝ r (solid-body rotation), never r².

questions.prompt: A rotation curve that stays flat (v ≈ constant) far beyond the visible disk directly implies that:

options.text: The enclosed mass M(<r) stays constant with radius
The enclosed mass M(<r) grows in proportion to r, even where there is little light
The galaxy has stopped rotating
The starlight also stays constant with radius

explanations.a: Constant M would give a Keplerian decline, not a flat curve — the opposite of what is observed.
explanations.b: Correct — setting v = √(GM(<r)/r) constant requires M(<r) ∝ r, so mass keeps accumulating with radius in a region that is nearly dark.
explanations.c: A flat curve means constant orbital SPEED, not zero rotation; the galaxy is very much rotating.
explanations.d: The starlight falls off steeply (roughly exponentially); it is precisely because light drops while mass keeps rising that the discrepancy exists.

questions.prompt: Whose 1970s rotation-curve measurements of Andromeda and many spirals established that flat curves are the norm?

options.text: Edwin Hubble and Milton Humason
Vera Rubin and Kent Ford
Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson
Mordehai Milgrom

explanations.a: Hubble established the velocity–distance (expansion) relation in 1929 using Humason's velocities (their joint paper followed in 1931), not galaxy rotation curves.
explanations.b: Correct — Rubin and Ford, using their image-tube spectrograph, measured M31 around 1970 and a large spiral sample through the late 1970s, finding curves that stayed flat far beyond the light.
explanations.c: Penzias and Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background in 1965; unrelated to rotation curves.
explanations.d: Milgrom proposed MOND in 1983 as an interpretation; he did not do the founding rotation-curve surveys.

questions.prompt: Why is "the flat rotation curve proves dark matter is a new particle" an overstatement of the 1970s result?

options.text: Because the curves actually decline, so there is no discrepancy to explain
Because the curve measures only a mass discrepancy; unseen ordinary matter or modified gravity could in principle also produce it
Because rotation curves cannot be measured beyond the visible disk
Because Rubin proved the missing mass was ordinary gas

explanations.a: The curves stay flat, not decline; the discrepancy is real, so this is factually wrong.
explanations.b: Correct — the rotation curve constrains the gravitating mass and its distribution, but by itself cannot distinguish a new particle from faint baryons (MACHOs) or a modification of gravity like MOND.
explanations.c: They can and were — 21 cm hydrogen observations extend the curves well past the starlight; that reach is what made the flatness undeniable.
explanations.d: Rubin did not prove the culprit; she was notably cautious, and gas alone falls far short of the required mass.

lessons.label: Modeling the Halo: NFW Profiles, Cores, and Cusps

sections.heading: From a flat curve to a 3-D density law
sections.body: A rotation curve tells you M(<r), the mass inside each radius, but to model a halo you want ρ(r), its three-dimensional density. The simplest halo that produces a flat curve is the pseudo-isothermal sphere: a constant-density inner "core" that transitions to ρ ∝ r^(−2) outside, which gives exactly v = constant. For decades this cored model was fit to rotation curves by hand. The revolution came from simulations: when you evolve cold dark matter (CDM) — slow-moving, collisionless particles — under gravity in an expanding universe, the halos that collapse out of the initial fluctuations do not look isothermal. Their structure is set by the physics of hierarchical merging, not chosen by the modeler.

sections.heading: The NFW profile and its cusp
sections.body: Julio Navarro, Carlos Frenk, and Simon White, in a pair of landmark papers in 1996–1997, found that CDM halos across an enormous range of masses share a nearly universal density profile, now called the NFW profile: ρ(r) = ρ_s / [ (r/r_s)(1 + r/r_s)² ]. It has a single characteristic radius r_s (the scale radius). Inside r_s the density rises as ρ ∝ r^(−1) — a "cusp" that formally diverges toward the center — and outside r_s it steepens to ρ ∝ r^(−3). A halo is then described by just two numbers: a mass and a "concentration" c = r_vir/r_s, with lower-mass halos typically more concentrated because they collapsed earlier when the universe was denser. The NFW form is the standard prediction of the CDM paradigm against which real galaxies are tested.

sections.heading: The core–cusp problem, in one profile comparison
sections.body: Here is the tension that has driven a thousand papers: NFW predicts a central cusp (ρ ∝ r^(−1), density climbing all the way in), but the rotation curves of many dark-matter-dominated dwarf and low-surface-brightness (LSB) galaxies rise more gently, implying a flat-density CORE (ρ ≈ constant near the center). W. J. G. de Blok and collaborators, analyzing high-resolution LSB rotation curves through the 2000s, argued the data prefer cored profiles like the Burkert profile (Andreas Burkert, 1995) over cuspy NFW. The disagreement is a factor-of-a-few in central density but it is a direct, quantitative clash between the cleanest CDM prediction and observation. Two escape routes dominate the modern debate: (1) baryonic feedback — repeated gas blowouts from supernovae can gravitationally "heat" and flatten a cusp into a core; and (2) the dark matter is not perfectly cold or collisionless (e.g. self-interacting dark matter, which naturally makes cores). Distinguishing these is an active research frontier, revisited in Lesson 5.

lessons.workedExample: Take an NFW halo and probe its inner logarithmic slope. Deep inside the scale radius, r ≪ r_s means (1 + r/r_s) ≈ 1, so ρ(r) ≈ ρ_s /(r/r_s) = ρ_s (r_s/r) ∝ r^(−1). Compare density at r = 0.1 r_s versus r = 0.01 r_s: the radius dropped by a factor of 10, and ρ ∝ r^(−1) means the density ROSE by a factor of 10 — the cusp. Now do the same for a cored halo with ρ ≈ ρ_0 = constant inside the core: from 0.1 r_s to 0.01 r_s the density barely changes. That single contrast — a tenfold density rise versus a flat plateau over the same inner decade of radius — is exactly the observable the core–cusp debate turns on, and it shows up in the rotation curve as a steeply rising (cuspy) versus a gently rising (cored) inner v(r).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about halo profiles to see whether a student can connect a simulation prediction to a measurable curve, rather than treating "dark matter halo" as a shapeless cloud. The mark of depth is naming the NFW form and its ρ ∝ r^(−1) cusp, contrasting it with the cored profiles observed in dwarfs/LSBs, and — crucially — knowing the core–cusp discrepancy is unresolved, with baryonic feedback and non-cold/self-interacting dark matter as the live competing explanations. A student who says "the halo is just NFW, problem solved" has missed the actual scientific controversy.

questions.prompt: In the NFW profile ρ(r) = ρ_s / [(r/r_s)(1 + r/r_s)²], how does the density behave deep inside the scale radius (r ≪ r_s)?

options.text: It flattens to a constant-density core
It rises as a cusp, ρ ∝ r^(−1)
It falls as ρ ∝ r^(−3)
It drops to zero at the center

explanations.a: A constant-density core is the OBSERVED behavior in many dwarfs — it is what NFW fails to predict, not what NFW predicts.
explanations.b: Correct — with (1 + r/r_s) ≈ 1 for small r, ρ ≈ ρ_s(r_s/r) ∝ r^(−1), the diverging central cusp that defines the NFW form.
explanations.c: ρ ∝ r^(−3) is the OUTER slope of NFW (r ≫ r_s), not the inner behavior.
explanations.d: The cusp density rises toward the center rather than dropping to zero.

questions.prompt: The core–cusp problem is the tension that:

options.text: CDM simulations predict cored halos but observations show cusps
CDM simulations predict cuspy (NFW) halos but many dwarf/LSB rotation curves prefer constant-density cores
Rotation curves decline while simulations predict them flat
Halos are more massive than their host galaxies

explanations.a: This reverses the problem — CDM predicts CUSPS, and the data favor cores, not the other way around.
explanations.b: Correct — the cleanest CDM prediction (NFW ρ ∝ r^(−1) cusp) clashes with the gently rising inner rotation curves of dark-matter-dominated dwarfs and LSB galaxies, which imply flat-density cores.
explanations.c: Both theory and observation agree curves are roughly flat at large radius; the tension is about the INNER density shape.
explanations.d: Halos being more massive than the luminous galaxy is just dark matter existing — not the core–cusp problem.

questions.prompt: Match each proposed resolution or model to its description.

right.text: Universal CDM-simulation form with a central ρ ∝ r^(−1) cusp
Constant-density inner region that better fits many dwarf/LSB curves
Repeated supernova-driven gas outflows gravitationally heat and flatten the cusp
Dark-matter self-scattering redistributes particles and naturally produces cores

questions.explanation: NFW is the cuspy universal profile from CDM simulations; the Burkert profile is a cored alternative that fits dwarf/LSB data better; baryonic feedback flattens cusps via repeated supernova-driven outflows within standard CDM; self-interacting dark matter makes cores by letting particles scatter and redistribute — the two live escape routes from the core–cusp tension.

questions.prompt: What is the "concentration" c of an NFW halo?

options.text: The ratio of dark to luminous mass
The ratio c = r_vir/r_s of the virial radius to the scale radius
The central density ρ_s in solar masses per parsec³
The fraction of the halo that is baryonic

explanations.a: The dark-to-luminous mass ratio is a different quantity; concentration is purely a shape parameter of the dark halo.
explanations.b: Correct — concentration is c = r_vir/r_s, so together with a mass it fully specifies an NFW halo; lower-mass halos tend to be more concentrated because they collapsed earlier when the universe was denser.
explanations.c: ρ_s is the characteristic density, a separate parameter, not the concentration ratio.
explanations.d: The baryon fraction is unrelated to the geometric concentration of the dark halo.

lessons.label: The Baryonic Tully–Fisher Relation and the MOND Challenge

sections.heading: From Tully–Fisher to its baryonic form
sections.body: In 1977 R. Brent Tully and J. Richard Fisher found that a spiral galaxy's luminosity correlates tightly with the width of its 21 cm hydrogen line — a proxy for its flat rotation speed v_flat. Brighter galaxies spin faster, following roughly L ∝ v_flat⁴. The relation was immediately useful as a distance indicator (measure the line width, infer the luminosity, compare to apparent brightness). But it also carries physics. When Stacy McGaugh and collaborators (around 2000) replaced luminosity with total BARYONIC mass — stars plus atomic and molecular gas — the scatter shrank and the relation tightened into the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation (BTFR): M_baryon ∝ v_flat⁴, holding over roughly five decades in mass, from giant spirals down to gas-rich dwarfs. The gas correction is what straightens it: low-mass galaxies are gas-dominated, so counting only starlight biased the original relation.

sections.heading: Why a tight slope-4 law is surprising in ΛCDM
sections.body: The BTFR is a puzzle for the standard dark-matter picture. In ΛCDM, the rotation speed is set by the total (mostly dark) halo mass, while the baryonic mass is set by how efficiently that halo turned gas into stars — a messy, feedback-regulated process that varies galaxy to galaxy. There is no obvious reason the two should lock into a razor-thin power law with almost no scatter across five decades of mass. ΛCDM can reproduce the BTFR, but it requires the galaxy-formation "efficiency" and halo properties to conspire; the tightness is an outcome that has to be arranged, not an inevitability. The relation therefore became a favorite battleground: its very existence, slope, and small scatter are exactly what a competing theory can try to predict from first principles.

sections.heading: MOND: a rival that predicts the BTFR outright
sections.body: Mordehai Milgrom proposed Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) in 1983: below a universal acceleration scale a₀ ≈ 1.2×10⁻¹⁰ m/s², gravity is stronger than Newton predicts, with the effective acceleration approaching g = √(g_N a₀) where g_N = GM/r² is the usual Newtonian value. For a circular orbit in this deep-MOND regime, g = v²/r, so v²/r = √(GM a₀)/r, giving v⁴ = G M a₀. That is the BTFR — with slope exactly 4 and a normalization fixed by the single constant a₀ — derived, not fitted. MOND thereby "predicts" the flat rotation curves and the tight BTFR that dark matter must accommodate after the fact. Its weaknesses are equally real: MOND struggles badly at cluster scales (Lesson 4), has no natural relativistic completion that also explains the cosmic microwave background and structure growth, and the Bullet Cluster is widely read as evidence against it. The mainstream view remains particle dark matter — but a serious student states the MOND challenge honestly: on galaxy rotation curves and the BTFR, MOND is not a strawman, it is a genuinely successful phenomenology that any dark-matter model must match.

lessons.workedExample: Test MOND's BTFR prediction on a galaxy with baryonic mass M_b = 1×10¹⁰ M_sun. MOND predicts v_flat⁴ = G M_b a₀. Plug in: M_b = 1×10¹⁰ × 1.989×10³⁰ kg = 1.989×10⁴⁰ kg; G = 6.674×10⁻¹¹; a₀ = 1.2×10⁻¹⁰ m/s². Then v⁴ = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ × 1.989×10⁴⁰ × 1.2×10⁻¹⁰ ≈ 1.59×10²⁰ (m/s)⁴. Take the fourth root: √(1.59×10²⁰) = 1.26×10¹⁰, and √(1.26×10¹⁰) = 1.12×10⁵ m/s ≈ 112 km/s. So MOND says a 10¹⁰-M_sun galaxy should spin at ~110 km/s — right in the observed range for such galaxies, with no free parameters beyond the universal a₀. Repeat for a galaxy 16× more massive (1.6×10¹¹ M_sun): v scales as M^(1/4), so v rises by 16^(1/4) = 2×, to ~224 km/s. The slope-4 law means a 16-fold mass jump is just a doubling of rotation speed — exactly the tight scaling the data show.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges raise the BTFR and MOND to test intellectual honesty: can the student describe a serious challenge to the mainstream without either dismissing it or overselling it?
