Short exposures plus software de-rotation (rotating and stacking frames) is the budget alternative.

sections.heading: Pointing models: correcting for a mount that is never perfect
sections.body: No mount points perfectly: the polar (or azimuth) axis is slightly misaligned, the optical axis is not exactly perpendicular to the mechanical axes, the tube flexes under gravity differently at different elevations, and the encoders have zero-point offsets. A pointing model measures these errors empirically — the operator slews to and centres dozens of stars spread across the sky, and software fits a model of the systematic terms (index errors, non-perpendicularity, tube flexure, and more) so the mount can be told to "go to these coordinates" and land the target on the chip. The de-facto standard package, TPoint (written by Patrick Wallace and used on observatory telescopes worldwide as well as by serious amateurs), reduces blind-pointing errors from arcminutes to a handful of arcseconds. A pointing model is open-loop correction (a fixed map applied to commanded coordinates); autoguiding, from the previous lesson, is the closed-loop complement that cleans up whatever the model misses during the exposure.

lessons.workedExample: You are imaging from latitude 34 degrees N with an alt-az mount, and your target is near the meridian, due south, at altitude 56 degrees (so azimuth ~180 degrees). The field-rotation rate is 15.04 * cos(34) * cos(180) / cos(56) = 15.04 * 0.829 * (-1) / 0.559 = -22.3 degrees per hour. Over a modest 5-minute exposure (1/12 hour) the field rotates 22.3 / 12 = 1.86 degrees. That sounds tiny until you convert it to smear at the edge of the frame: a star 500 pixels from the rotation centre traces an arc of length 500 * 1.86 * (pi/180) = 500 * 0.0325 = 16 pixels. Sixteen pixels of arc turns pinpoint edge stars into little curved streaks, ruining photometry and astrometry for everything off-centre. This is precisely why the same object on an equatorial mount needs no de-rotator (its field orientation is fixed), while the alt-az rig must either run an instrument rotator or fall back to short sub-exposures that are de-rotated in software before stacking.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges raise field rotation to test whether a student understands their mount as a system, not a black box. If a project used an alt-az telescope (or an unguided camera-tripod setup) and shows clean long-exposure images, a judge will ask how field rotation was handled — a de-rotator, short subs plus software de-rotation, or an equatorial wedge. A student who says "equatorial mounts do not rotate the field because the drive axis is aligned with Earth spin, and my alt-az rig needed a de-rotator near the zenith where the rate peaks" has demonstrated real command of the geometry; a student who never noticed arced stars at the frame edge has not.

questions.prompt: Why can an equatorial mount track a star with a single constant-rate motor while an alt-az mount cannot?

options.text: Its polar axis is parallel to Earth rotation axis, so one axis turning at the sidereal rate follows any star
Equatorial mounts have larger apertures
Alt-az mounts cannot track the sky at all
Equatorial mounts do not experience Earth rotation

explanations.a: Correct — aligning the polar axis with Earth spin axis means a single sidereal-rate rotation about that one axis follows a star along its constant-declination circle.
explanations.b: Aperture is unrelated to mount type; both types exist at all sizes.
explanations.c: Alt-az mounts track fine, but they must drive both axes at continuously varying rates computed by a controller.
explanations.d: Every ground mount experiences Earth rotation; the equatorial simply aligns one axis with it.

questions.prompt: Field rotation on an alt-az mount is worst when the target is:

options.text: Near the horizon due east or west
High overhead near the zenith (small cos(altitude) in the denominator)
Exactly on the celestial pole
Below the horizon

explanations.a: The rate actually vanishes for an object due east or west at the horizon; that is the calmest case, not the worst.
explanations.b: Correct — the rate goes as 1/cos(altitude), which blows up as the target approaches the zenith, so high-overhead objects rotate fastest.
explanations.c: The pole is a fixed point in the sky; the extreme field-rotation case for an alt-az target is the zenith, not the pole.
explanations.d: You cannot image a target below the horizon; the worst observable case is near the zenith.

questions.prompt: A pointing model (e.g., TPoint by Patrick Wallace) improves a telescope how?

options.text: It fits the mount systematic errors from many star observations so commanded coordinates land on the chip
It increases the sidereal tracking rate
It replaces the need for a camera
It removes atmospheric seeing

explanations.a: Correct — by centring dozens of stars across the sky and fitting terms like axis misalignment, non-perpendicularity, and tube flexure, a pointing model cuts blind-pointing error from arcminutes to arcseconds.
explanations.b: The tracking rate is fixed by physics; a pointing model corrects where the mount points, not how fast it tracks.
explanations.c: The camera is needed to record images and to build the model in the first place.
explanations.d: Seeing is atmospheric and is not affected by a mechanical pointing model.

questions.prompt: Match each mount characteristic to the correct mount type.

left.text: Tracks with one constant-rate axis; no field rotation
Mechanically simpler/stiffer; favored for the largest modern telescopes
Requires a de-rotator (or short subs) for long exposures
Design of the classic 200-inch Hale telescope

right.text: Equatorial mount (tracking geometry)
Alt-az mount (build advantage)
Alt-az mount (field-rotation drawback)
Equatorial mount (historical example)

questions.explanation: Equatorial mounts track on one aligned axis with no field rotation and describe the classic Hale 200-inch; alt-az mounts win on stiffness/cost for the largest telescopes but pay for it with field rotation that demands a de-rotator or de-rotated short exposures.

lessons.label: Filters and Photometric Systems: Johnson-Cousins, SDSS ugriz, and Narrowband

sections.heading: A magnitude means nothing without a passband
sections.body: You never measure "brightness" in the abstract — you measure the light that survives a filter of defined shape, so a magnitude is meaningless until you name its passband. A photometric system is a standardised set of filters plus the rules for calibrating them, so that a "V magnitude" measured in Chile can be compared with one measured in Arizona. The oldest broadband standard still in heavy use is the Johnson-Cousins UBVRI system: Harold Johnson and William Morgan defined U (ultraviolet, ~365 nm), B (blue, ~445 nm), and V (visual, ~551 nm) in 1953, and A.W.J. Cousins extended it to R (red) and I (near-infrared) in the 1970s. It is a Vega-based system: the bright star Vega is defined to have a magnitude near zero in every band, so its colours (differences of magnitudes) are near zero by construction.

sections.heading: Colour index encodes temperature
sections.body: The difference between two magnitudes of the same star is a colour index — B-V being the workhorse. Because a hotter blackbody peaks bluer (Wien law), a hot star is relatively brighter in B than in V, giving a small or negative B-V, while a cool star is brighter in V than B, giving a large positive B-V. Concretely, hot O and B stars have B-V near -0.3, Vega (an A0 star) has B-V = 0.00 by definition, the Sun (a G2 star) has B-V ~= 0.65, and cool M dwarfs run past +1.5. Colour index is thus a cheap thermometer: two calibrated magnitudes give an estimate of surface temperature without a spectrograph, which is why colour-magnitude diagrams (the observational cousin of the HR diagram) are built from exactly these indices. This is the same physics that lets a colour-magnitude diagram date a star cluster by its main-sequence turnoff.

sections.heading: ugriz and the AB system; narrowband for emission lines
sections.body: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey introduced the ugriz system (u ~354 nm, g ~477 nm, r ~623 nm, i ~763 nm, z ~913 nm), a set of five contiguous, nearly non-overlapping filters that tile the optical band more cleanly than the older overlapping UBVRI curves — now the default for most modern digital surveys. ugriz is usually reported in the AB magnitude system (Oke and Gunn, 1983), defined so a source with constant flux density f_nu = 3631 janskys has AB magnitude 0 in every band, tying magnitudes directly to physical flux rather than to Vega. Distinct from these broadband systems are narrowband filters, only a few nanometres wide, tuned to specific emission lines: H-alpha at 656.3 nm, doubly-ionised oxygen [O III] at 500.7 nm, and singly-ionised sulphur [S II] at ~671.6 nm. Narrowband isolates the glowing gas of emission nebulae and, because it passes only a sliver of the spectrum, it powerfully rejects broadband light pollution, letting city-bound observers image nebulae that would otherwise be washed out.

lessons.workedExample: You do aperture photometry on a field star and, after calibrating against standard stars, get B = 11.00 and V = 10.20. Its colour index is B-V = 11.00 - 10.20 = 0.80. That is redder (larger) than the Sun (0.65) and much redder than Vega (0.00), so this is a cooler, roughly K-type star with a surface temperature around 5200-5300 K — a conclusion drawn from two broadband magnitudes and no spectrograph at all. Now suppose you want to image a faint emission nebula in that same field from a light-polluted suburb. Through a broad V filter the sky glow swamps it; through a 5-nm H-alpha narrowband filter centred on 656.3 nm you pass the nebula redshifted-negligibly H-alpha emission while blocking almost all of the broadband streetlight continuum, and the nebula emerges against a dark background. Same telescope, same sky — the filter choice decides whether you measured a stellar temperature or revealed ionised hydrogen.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges press on filters because "how bright is it?" is not a real measurement until the passband and system are named. A student who reports "V = 10.2 and B = 11.0 on the Johnson-Cousins system, calibrated to standard stars, giving B-V = 0.8" has made a comparable, defensible measurement; one who reports "magnitude 10.5" with no filter has reported a number no one can reproduce. Judges also test whether a student knows why they chose narrowband (line isolation and light-pollution rejection) versus broadband (color and total flux), because the right filter is dictated by the science question, not by what came in the box.

questions.prompt: Who defined the original UBV system and its RI extension, and on what magnitude standard is Johnson-Cousins based?

options.text: Johnson and Morgan defined UBV (1953); Cousins added RI (1970s); it is a Vega-based system
Oke and Gunn defined it in 1983 on the AB system
Edwin Hubble defined it in 1929 on the redshift scale
Annie Cannon defined it on the OBAFGKM scale

explanations.a: Correct — Harold Johnson and William Morgan set up UBV in 1953, A.W.J. Cousins extended it to R and I in the 1970s, and Vega anchors the zero points (a Vega-based system).
explanations.b: Oke and Gunn (1983) defined the AB magnitude system used with ugriz, not the Vega-based Johnson-Cousins UBVRI.
explanations.c: Hubble law relates recession velocity to distance; it has nothing to do with defining photometric passbands.
explanations.d: Cannon organised stellar spectral classification (OBAFGKM), a separate scheme from broadband photometric systems.

questions.prompt: A star has B-V = -0.2. What does that imply, and why?

options.text: It is hot — a negative B-V means it is relatively brighter in blue (B) than visual (V), as for a hot blackbody peaking bluer
It is cool, because negative numbers mean low temperature
It is the same temperature as the Sun
The measurement must be an error; B-V cannot be negative

explanations.a: Correct — a hotter blackbody peaks at bluer wavelengths (Wien), so it is relatively brighter in B, driving B-V negative; hot O/B stars sit near -0.3.
explanations.b: This inverts the physics: larger (more positive) B-V means cooler, and negative means hotter.
explanations.c: The Sun has B-V ~= 0.65; a star at -0.2 is far hotter than the Sun.
explanations.d: Negative B-V is perfectly real for hot stars; Vega is 0.00 by definition and hotter stars go negative.

questions.prompt: Why is a narrowband H-alpha filter effective against light pollution?

options.text: It passes only a few nanometres around 656.3 nm, so most broadband streetlight continuum is blocked while nebular H-alpha gets through
It makes the telescope aperture larger
It shifts the wavelength of the light pollution
It works by increasing exposure time automatically

explanations.a: Correct — passing only a ~few-nm slice at the H-alpha line transmits the nebula emission while rejecting nearly all of the broadband continuum that makes up light pollution.
explanations.b: A filter cannot change aperture; it only selects wavelengths.
explanations.c: Filters block or transmit light; they do not shift its wavelength.
explanations.d: A filter does not set exposure time; the rejection is purely spectral selection.

questions.prompt: Match each object to the approximate B-V colour index it would show.

right.text: About -0.3
0.00 (defined)
About +0.65
Greater than +1.5

questions.explanation: B-V rises with decreasing temperature: hot O/B stars near -0.3, Vega defined at 0.00, the Sun near +0.65, and cool M dwarfs past +1.5 — the colour index acts as a broadband thermometer.

lessons.label: Atmospheric Extinction, Airmass, and Planning a Real Observing Run

sections.heading: Airmass: how much atmosphere you look through
sections.body: Every ground-based photon is dimmed by the air it crosses, and the amount of air scales with how far from the zenith you look. Airmass X quantifies this: it is 1.0 straight overhead (looking through the minimum column of atmosphere) and grows as you tilt toward the horizon. To good approximation X = sec(z), the secant of the zenith angle z (z = 90 degrees minus altitude), so at 60 degrees from the zenith the airmass is sec(60) = 2.0 — twice the overhead air. The plain secant formula breaks down near the horizon (beyond z ~ 70 degrees) because it pretends the atmosphere is a flat slab rather than a curved shell; more accurate formulae (Hardie 1962, and Kasten and Young 1989) tame the runaway, but for most work above ~2 airmasses the simple secant is fine and is what you should quote.

sections.heading: Bouguer law: extinction is linear in airmass
sections.body: Because absorption and scattering are multiplicative per unit path, magnitudes (a logarithmic measure) dim linearly with airmass. This is the Bouguer relation: m_observed = m_0 + k * X, where m_0 is the magnitude the star would have above the atmosphere (X = 0), X is the airmass, and k is the extinction coefficient in magnitudes per airmass for that filter. Crucially k is strongly wavelength-dependent: Rayleigh scattering goes as roughly 1/wavelength^4, so blue light is extinguished far more than red. At a good dark site typical coefficients run about k_V ~ 0.15, k_B ~ 0.25, and k_U ~ 0.5 mag per airmass; at a hazy low site they are worse. The practical consequence is that a star measured near the horizon is not only fainter but reddened (blue dimmed more than red), so uncorrected extinction biases both magnitudes and colours.

sections.heading: Measuring k and planning the night around airmass
sections.body: You can measure your own extinction coefficient by observing the same star repeatedly as it rises or sets across a range of airmasses and plotting instrumental magnitude against X — the slope is k and the intercept extrapolated to X = 0 is the above-atmosphere magnitude (a "Bouguer line"). This is why observers do differential photometry against comparison stars in the SAME frame, at essentially the SAME airmass, so the extinction terms cancel to first order. Planning a real run is largely airmass logistics: pick targets that transit (cross the meridian, their lowest airmass) during your observing window, cap work at some airmass limit (often X < 2, i.e. altitude above ~30 degrees) to keep extinction and seeing manageable, avoid pointing near the Moon for faint targets, and schedule photometric standard-star fields at several airmasses to pin down k. A defensible observing plan is a timeline of who is at low airmass when — not just a wish-list of pretty objects.

lessons.workedExample: You want the true (above-atmosphere) V magnitude of a star. You measure it twice on a photometric night: V = 12.00 when it is overhead at airmass X = 1.0, and V = 12.15 when it has sunk to airmass X = 2.0. Applying Bouguer, m_obs = m_0 + k*X: the two equations 12.00 = m_0 + k(1.0) and 12.15 = m_0 + k(2.0) subtract to give 0.15 = k(1.0), so k = 0.15 mag per airmass — a textbook V-band coefficient. Back-substituting, m_0 = 12.00 - 0.15(1.0) = 11.85, the extinction-corrected magnitude above the atmosphere. Notice the payoff for planning: if you had instead observed this star only at X = 2.5 (near your 30-degree altitude limit), it would read 12.00 + 0.15(1.5) = 12.22 raw, and any comparison against a catalogue value measured near the zenith would be off by nearly a quarter magnitude purely from air you forgot to account for. In the blue (k_B ~ 0.25) the same 1.5-airmass difference costs ~0.38 mag — which is why serious teams observe comparison stars at matched airmass so these terms cancel.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe extinction and airmass because it separates students who understood that the atmosphere is part of the instrument from those who treated raw counts as truth. A team that says "I corrected for extinction using k_V = 0.15 measured from a Bouguer line, and I did differential photometry against comparison stars at the same airmass so the extinction cancels" has shown a professional-grade grasp of the error budget. A team whose light curve drifts over the night as the target sinks in altitude, with no airmass correction, has an artefact masquerading as a signal — and a judge will ask exactly why the star "got fainter" as the night went on.

questions.prompt: A target is at zenith angle z = 60 degrees (altitude 30 degrees). What is its approximate airmass, and via what relation?

options.text: About 2.0, from X = sec(z) = sec(60 deg) = 2.0
About 0.5, because it is halfway to the horizon
Exactly 1.0, the same as overhead
About 60, one per degree of zenith angle

explanations.a: Correct — X ~= sec(z), and sec(60 deg) = 1/cos(60 deg) = 1/0.5 = 2.0, so you look through twice the overhead air column.
explanations.b: Airmass increases away from the zenith; it never drops below 1.0, so 0.5 is impossible.
explanations.c: Airmass is 1.0 only at the zenith (z = 0); at z = 60 it is larger.
explanations.d: Airmass is not linear in degrees; it follows the secant of the zenith angle.

questions.prompt: In m_observed = m_0 + k*X, why is the extinction coefficient k larger in B than in V?

options.text: Blue light is scattered/absorbed more than red (Rayleigh scattering ~ 1/wavelength^4), so shorter wavelengths are extinguished more per airmass
Blue stars are intrinsically fainter
The B filter is physically thicker
k is the same in every band; the claim is false

explanations.a: Correct — Rayleigh scattering rises steeply toward the blue (~1/wavelength^4), so blue light suffers more extinction per airmass, giving k_B > k_V (roughly 0.25 vs 0.15 at a good site).
explanations.b: Extinction is a property of the atmosphere and wavelength, not of how bright blue stars are.
explanations.c: Filter thickness does not set atmospheric extinction; wavelength does.
explanations.d: k is strongly wavelength-dependent, larger toward the blue, so it is not the same in every band.

questions.prompt: A star reads V = 13.00 at airmass 1.2 and V = 13.30 at airmass 2.2 on a photometric night. What is k, and the above-atmosphere magnitude m_0?

options.text: k = 0.30 mag/airmass and m_0 = 12.64
k = 0.15 mag/airmass and m_0 = 13.00
k = 0.30 mag/airmass and m_0 = 13.30
k cannot be found from two measurements

explanations.a: Correct — the airmass difference is 1.0 and the magnitude difference is 0.30, so k = 0.30; then m_0 = 13.00 - 0.30(1.2) = 13.00 - 0.36 = 12.64.
explanations.b: That k comes from a 0.15 mag change over one airmass, but here the star dimmed 0.30 mag over one airmass.
explanations.c: The slope k = 0.30 is right, but m_0 is the intercept at X = 0, not the reading at X = 2.2.
explanations.d: Two points on a Bouguer line are exactly enough to fit the slope k and intercept m_0.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to build a Bouguer line and extract the above-atmosphere magnitude.

items.text: Observe the same star repeatedly as it rises or sets, spanning a range of airmass
Compute each airmass X ~= sec(z) from the zenith angle at each observation
Plot instrumental magnitude versus airmass X
Read the slope as k and extrapolate the intercept to X = 0 for m_0

questions.explanation: You gather the same star across a range of airmasses, convert each zenith angle to an airmass, plot magnitude against airmass, and read the extinction coefficient off the slope while extrapolating to X = 0 for the above-atmosphere magnitude.

lessons.label: The Observatory Data Chain: From Shutter to FITS Header

sections.heading: FITS: the format that survived forty years
sections.body: When the shutter opens, photons become electrons in the detector, electrons become digital counts (ADU) via the analog-to-digital converter, and those counts are written to disk almost universally as FITS — the Flexible Image Transport System, first defined by Don Wells, Eric Greisen, and Ron Harten in 1981 (A&AS 44, 363) and endorsed by the IAU. FITS has outlasted nearly every other scientific data format because of one design choice: every file carries a human-readable ASCII header of keyword = value cards (80 characters each, in 2880-byte blocks) describing exactly how the data were taken, ahead of the binary image itself. A FITS file is self-documenting: the pixels and their provenance travel together, so a frame taken today is still fully interpretable decades later.

sections.heading: The header is the metadata that makes pixels science
sections.body: The header keywords are what turn an anonymous grid of counts into a measurement. Structural keywords (SIMPLE, BITPIX for the data type, NAXIS1/NAXIS2 for dimensions) let any reader parse the array. Observational keywords record the conditions the analysis depends on: EXPTIME (exposure seconds), FILTER (which passband, from Lesson 4), OBJECT, DATE-OBS (the UTC start time in ISO 8601), plus detector terms like GAIN (electrons per ADU) and read noise that the noise model needs. A second layer, the World Coordinate System (WCS) keywords — CRPIX1/CRPIX2 (a reference pixel), CRVAL1/CRVAL2 (its sky coordinates), and the CD or PC matrix (pixel-to-sky scale and rotation) — encodes the plate solution so software can translate any pixel to a right ascension and declination. Miss or corrupt these and the image is just a picture; get them right and it is data anyone can reduce.

sections.heading: Calibration and the timestamp that time-domain work lives on
sections.body: Raw frames are not yet science: they carry an electronic offset (bias), thermally generated signal (dark current, scaling with exposure and temperature), and pixel-to-pixel and optical sensitivity variations (flat field). The standard reduction is science = (raw - bias - dark) / flat, applied per pixel, which removes the instrument signature so the remaining counts are proportional to real sky flux (the raw-frames-to-calibrated chain from Core photometry). For time-domain science the single most abused header value is the timestamp. DATE-OBS is usually UTC at the START of the exposure, so you must add half the EXPTIME to get the mid-exposure epoch, then convert to a Julian Date. And because Earth orbits the Sun, the light-travel-time across Earth orbit shifts arrival times by up to +/-8.3 minutes (one astronomical unit / speed of light ~= 499 s) over a year — so precise transit and variable-star timing is reported in Barycentric Julian Date in the Barycentric Dynamical Time standard (BJD_TDB), which refers every event to the Solar System barycentre and removes that annual wobble.

lessons.workedExample: You are timing an exoplanet transit — a hot Jupiter whose depth (Rp/Rs)^2 = (69911 km / 696000 km)^2 = (0.1005)^2 = 0.0101, about a 1% (roughly 10000 ppm) dip, easily within reach of a backyard scope. A single frame carries DATE-OBS = 2026-03-14T08:32:00 (UTC start) and EXPTIME = 120 s. First you find the mid-exposure time by adding half the exposure: 08:32:00 + 60 s = 08:33:00 UTC, which converts to a Julian Date. But if you plotted your mid-transit time in plain UTC-based JD and compared it to a published ephemeris in BJD_TDB, you could be wrong by up to 8.3 minutes depending on where Earth sat in its orbit that night — enough to wreck an observed-minus-calculated (O-C) timing analysis looking for transit-timing variations of only a minute or two. Converting your mid-exposure JD to BJD_TDB (applying the light-travel-time correction to the barycentre) puts your timing on the same clock as everyone else and lets your one-percent dip contribute to a real ephemeris. The moral: the shutter-to-FITS chain is only trustworthy if the header time is understood and corrected, not copied blindly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges open a project data chain by asking what actually sits in the FITS header, because that is where reproducibility lives. A student who can explain "DATE-OBS is UTC at exposure start, so I added half the EXPTIME and converted to BJD_TDB to remove the up-to-8.3-minute light-travel effect" has shown their timing is on the same clock as the professional literature — decisive for any transit or variable-star result. Likewise, being able to name the calibration chain science = (raw - bias - dark) / flat, and the WCS keywords that plate-solve an image, signals that a team knows their pixels became measurements through a documented process rather than by magic.

questions.prompt: Who defined the FITS format and when, and what makes it self-documenting?

options.text: Wells, Greisen, and Harten (1981); each file carries a human-readable ASCII header of keyword=value cards describing how the data were taken
Oke and Gunn (1983); it stores AB magnitudes directly
Johnson and Morgan (1953); it encodes the UBV passbands
It has no header; the pixels stand alone

explanations.a: Correct — Don Wells, Eric Greisen, and Ron Harten defined FITS in 1981, and its ASCII keyword=value header travels with the pixels, making each file self-documenting.
explanations.b: Oke and Gunn (1983) defined the AB magnitude system, not the FITS file format.
explanations.c: Johnson and Morgan (1953) defined the UBV photometric system, unrelated to the FITS format.
explanations.d: The defining feature of FITS is precisely that it has a rich header ahead of the data.

questions.prompt: DATE-OBS in a FITS header reads 08:32:00 UTC (exposure start) with EXPTIME = 120 s. What is the mid-exposure time, and why does it matter?

options.text: 08:33:00 UTC — you add half the exposure (60 s) to get the epoch a time-series measurement should be tagged with
08:32:00 UTC — the start time is already the correct epoch
08:34:00 UTC — you add the full exposure time
08:30:00 UTC — you subtract one minute for detector lag

explanations.a: Correct — DATE-OBS is the start, so the representative epoch is the midpoint, start plus half of EXPTIME (60 s), giving 08:33:00 UTC.
explanations.b: Using the start time biases the epoch by half the exposure, which matters for precise timing.
explanations.c: Adding the full 120 s gives the END of the exposure, not the midpoint.
explanations.d: There is no generic one-minute detector-lag subtraction; the correction is to add half the exposure.

questions.prompt: Why do time-domain observers convert timestamps to Barycentric Julian Date (BJD_TDB)?

options.text: Light-travel time across Earth orbit shifts arrival times by up to +/-8.3 minutes over a year; BJD_TDB refers events to the Solar System barycentre to remove that wobble
Because Julian Dates are too large to store otherwise
To convert magnitudes into fluxes
Because UTC does not exist at night

explanations.a: Correct — Earth position in its orbit changes the light path to a target by up to one AU (~499 light-seconds, ~8.3 minutes), so BJD_TDB moves the clock to the barycentre and removes the annual timing shift.
explanations.b: Storage size is not the reason; the barycentric correction fixes a real physical timing offset.
explanations.c: BJD_TDB is a time standard; it has nothing to do with the magnitude-to-flux conversion.
explanations.d: UTC is a continuous time standard used day and night; the issue is orbital light-travel time, not UTC availability.

questions.prompt: Match each FITS header item or calibration frame to what it provides.

right.text: The exposure duration in seconds
The pixel-to-sky mapping (plate solution) so any pixel yields an RA/Dec
The electronic zero-level offset subtracted from every raw frame
Pixel-to-pixel and optical sensitivity variations you divide out

questions.explanation: EXPTIME gives the exposure length; the WCS keywords encode the plate solution mapping pixels to sky coordinates; the bias frame captures the electronic offset to subtract; and the flat field captures sensitivity variations to divide out, following science = (raw - bias - dark) / flat.

units.label: The CCD Reduction Pipeline

lessons.label: Overscan, Bias Structure, and Building a Master Bias

sections.heading: The bias level, and why the electronics add it on purpose
sections.body: A CCD counts photo-electrons, but the analog-to-digital converter cannot represent negative numbers, and read noise scatters some pixels below zero. To keep every readout positive, the electronics add a fixed positive offset — the bias, or pedestal — to every pixel before digitization. On a typical amateur camera the bias sits at a few hundred ADU (analog-to-digital units, also called counts); on many research CCDs it is set near 300–1000 ADU. This offset carries no sky information, so it must be removed before the counts mean anything. The bias is not a single number, though: it has a faint two-dimensional structure — gradients, amplifier glow near a corner, and column-to-column patterns — that repeats every readout. That repeatable pattern is exactly what a calibration frame can capture and subtract.

sections.heading: Overscan: virtual pixels that measure the bias every exposure
sections.body: The bias level drifts slowly with temperature and time, so measuring it once is not enough for precise work. CCDs solve this by clocking out extra "virtual" pixels beyond the physical light-sensitive array — the overscan region. These pixels were never exposed to light, so they read out pure bias plus read noise, giving a live measurement of the pedestal for that specific frame. The serial (horizontal) overscan is appended to each row; a parallel (vertical) overscan adds extra rows. In reduction you collapse the overscan columns to a robust per-row estimate (a median, or a low-order polynomial fit down the columns to track a gentle gradient) and subtract it. Overscan handles the frame-to-frame drift of the *level*; the master bias, built separately, handles the fixed two-dimensional *structure* that overscan alone cannot see.

sections.heading: Building a master bias — and why you stack many
sections.body: A single bias frame (a zero-second exposure with the shutter closed) is dominated by read noise: subtracting one bias from your science frame would inject that full read noise into your data. Instead you take many bias frames — commonly 25 to 50 — and combine them, usually with a median or a sigma-clipped average, into a master bias. Averaging N frames reduces the random read-noise contribution by roughly √N: a master from 25 frames carries about 1/5 the read noise of a single bias, so its structure is well-measured while adding almost no noise to the science data. The median (or sigma-clip) also rejects the occasional cosmic-ray hit that lands even in a zero-second frame. Read noise is quoted in electrons (typical research CCDs: 3–10 e- RMS), converted to ADU through the gain (e- per ADU), and it is the one noise source you can never subtract away — only average down.

lessons.workedExample: Your science frame reads 4,820 ADU at a star pixel. First, overscan: the overscan columns for that row median to 512 ADU, so the live bias level is 512. Next, structure: your master bias — median of 30 zero-second frames — reads 6 ADU above the overscan level at that pixel (a bit of fixed amplifier structure). A clean bias removal subtracts the overscan level and the residual structure: 4,820 − 512 − 6 = 4,302 ADU. Note the noise bookkeeping: a single bias frame has, say, 7 e- read noise, but the master of 30 frames contributes only about 7/√30 ≈ 1.3 e- — so you get the full fixed-pattern correction while adding negligible noise. Had you subtracted one raw bias instead, you would have added the full 7 e- back into every science pixel.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe bias handling to see whether a student knows the difference between a level and a structure. A team that says "I used the overscan to track the pedestal drift each frame and a 30-frame master bias for the fixed two-dimensional pattern" demonstrates they understand two distinct problems and two distinct tools. The tell of a shallow reduction is subtracting a single bias frame — it shows the student treated calibration as a checkbox and unknowingly injected read noise into their science data, exactly the kind of unforced error a judge will press on.

questions.prompt: Why do CCD electronics add a positive bias offset to every pixel before digitizing?

options.text: To make faint stars appear brighter
So that read noise and small fluctuations do not push pixels below zero, which the analog-to-digital converter cannot represent
To correct for atmospheric extinction
To increase the exposure time automatically

explanations.a: The bias is a constant offset on every pixel; it does not change the relative brightness of stars and carries no sky signal.
explanations.b: Correct — the ADC outputs only non-negative numbers, and read noise scatters some pixels below zero, so a positive pedestal keeps every readout representable.
explanations.c: Atmospheric extinction is corrected photometrically, not by the detector electronics; the bias is an internal electronic offset.
explanations.d: Bias has nothing to do with exposure timing; it is added at readout regardless of exposure length.

questions.prompt: What does the overscan region of a CCD frame measure that a master bias alone cannot?

options.text: The frame-to-frame drift of the bias level for that specific exposure
The total dark current in the science exposure
The color of the star being observed
The atmospheric seeing at the time of exposure

explanations.a: Correct — overscan pixels are clocked out but never exposed to light, giving a live per-frame reading of the pedestal that tracks its slow drift with time and temperature.
explanations.b: Dark current accumulates only in light-sensitive pixels over the exposure; overscan pixels are never integrated on-sky, so they contain no dark signal.
explanations.c: Overscan contains no sky light at all, so it says nothing about any star.
explanations.d: Seeing is an atmospheric effect on the image; overscan is a purely electronic measurement.

questions.prompt: A team combines 25 bias frames into a master bias rather than using one. The read-noise contribution of the master, relative to a single bias, is about:

options.text: The same — combining frames does not change noise
25 times larger
About 1/5 as large, because random read noise averages down by roughly √25 = 5
Exactly zero read noise

explanations.a: Averaging independent frames does reduce random noise; the master is not the same as a single frame.
explanations.b: Combining reduces, not increases, the random noise; the master is quieter than one frame.
explanations.c: Correct — averaging N independent frames reduces random read noise by √N, so 25 frames give roughly a 5× reduction (about 1/5 the noise).
explanations.d: Averaging lowers noise toward zero only in the limit of infinite frames; 25 frames leaves a small but nonzero residual.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to what it corrects in bias removal.

right.text: The slowly drifting overall bias level, per frame
The fixed two-dimensional bias pattern (gradients, amplifier glow)
Rejection of stray cosmic-ray hits in the calibration frames

questions.explanation: Overscan tracks the per-frame drift of the bias level; the master bias captures the fixed 2D structure that overscan cannot see; a median or sigma-clip during combination rejects transient cosmic-ray spikes so they do not pollute the master.

lessons.label: Dark Current, Master Darks, and Thermal Scaling

sections.heading: Where dark current comes from and why cooling is everything
sections.body: Even with the shutter closed, a CCD pixel slowly fills with electrons generated thermally in the silicon — thermal agitation kicks electrons into the conduction band with no photon involved. This dark current accumulates linearly with exposure time and depends steeply on temperature. As a rule of thumb it roughly doubles for every 6–7 °C of warming (an Arrhenius dependence on the silicon bandgap), which is why research cameras are cooled hard: professional CCDs run at −100 °C or colder with liquid nitrogen, where dark current is essentially negligible, while amateur thermoelectric cameras cool to −10 to −20 °C and still contend with measurable dark. Dark current is quoted in electrons per pixel per second; a good cooled sensor might sit at 0.01–0.1 e-/pixel/s, so a 5-minute exposure accumulates only a few to a few tens of electrons of dark — but hot pixels, defects with anomalously high dark current, can saturate.

sections.heading: Master darks: the same recipe, matched conditions
sections.body: A dark frame is a shutter-closed exposure that captures bias plus accumulated dark current. As with bias, one dark frame is noisy, so you take many (typically 10–20) at the *same temperature* and *same exposure time* as your science frames and combine them (median or sigma-clip) into a master dark. Matching matters because dark current depends on both temperature and time: a dark taken at a different sensor temperature carries the wrong dark level, and a mismatched exposure time carries the wrong amount of accumulated dark. When the master dark is taken with the same exposure time as the science frame, it already contains the bias, so subtracting it removes bias and dark in one step. Median combining rejects cosmic rays (which strike even closed-shutter frames) and beats the dark-frame read noise down by roughly √N.

sections.heading: Thermal scaling when you cannot match exposure time
sections.body: Sometimes you have darks of one duration but science frames of another. Because dark current accumulates linearly with time, you can scale a dark — but only if you first remove the bias, since bias is a fixed offset that does NOT scale with time while dark current does. The correct procedure is: subtract the master bias from the master dark to isolate the pure thermal signal, multiply that thermal-only frame by the exposure-time ratio (t_science / t_dark), then subtract it together with the bias from the science frame. Scaling a bias-included dark by the time ratio would wrongly multiply the fixed pedestal and corrupt the result. Thermal scaling also assumes the sensor temperature is identical for darks and science; if the temperature differs, the doubling-per-6-to-7-°C dependence breaks the simple linear scaling and the correction fails. This is why matched darks are always preferred and scaling is a fallback.

lessons.workedExample: Your sensor runs at −15 °C with a measured dark current of 0.08 e-/pixel/s and a gain of 1.5 e-/ADU. A 300-second science exposure therefore accumulates 0.08 × 300 = 24 e- of dark per normal pixel, which is 24 / 1.5 = 16 ADU on top of the bias. Ideally you have matched 300-s darks. Suppose instead you only have a master dark taken at 600 s (same −15 °C). First isolate the thermal part: subtract the master bias so the dark holds pure thermal signal (600 s × 0.08 = 48 e-, i.e. 32 ADU). Then scale by the time ratio 300/600 = 0.5, giving 16 ADU of thermal signal to subtract — matching the true 300-s value. Had you scaled a bias-included dark (bias 512 + 32 = 544 ADU) by 0.5, you would subtract 272 ADU, wrongly halving the 512-ADU pedestal instead of removing it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use dark-current questions to test whether a student understands that different artifacts obey different math. A team that can explain "dark current scales linearly with time and doubles about every 6–7 °C, but bias is a fixed offset, so I bias-subtract before scaling a dark" shows real command of the physics. The classic failure a judge listens for is a student who scaled a raw dark by the exposure ratio and unknowingly scaled the pedestal too — a subtle bug that silently biases every measurement and reveals the reduction was run without understanding.

questions.prompt: Dark current in a CCD roughly doubles for every 6–7 °C of warming. This temperature dependence is why:

options.text: Research CCDs are cooled to around −100 °C to make dark current negligible
Telescopes are placed on mountaintops
Longer focal lengths reduce dark current
Dark frames must be taken during the daytime

explanations.a: Correct — because dark current falls steeply as the sensor cools, aggressive cooling (liquid nitrogen near −100 °C) drives it to negligible levels for precise work.
explanations.b: Mountaintop siting reduces atmospheric turbulence and absorption, not the thermally generated dark current inside the detector.
explanations.c: Focal length changes the plate scale and image brightness distribution, not the thermal generation of electrons in the silicon.
explanations.d: Darks are taken with the shutter closed and can be taken any time; timing does not set the dark level — temperature and exposure time do.

questions.prompt: Why must you subtract the bias from a master dark BEFORE scaling it to a different exposure time?

options.text: Because bias increases with exposure time and dark current does not
Because dark current scales linearly with time but the bias is a fixed offset that does not, so scaling a bias-included dark would wrongly multiply the pedestal
Because the bias must always be larger than the dark current
Scaling order does not matter; the result is the same either way

explanations.a: This is backwards: bias is fixed and time-independent, while dark current is the quantity that grows with exposure time.
explanations.b: Correct — only the thermal (dark) component scales with time; multiplying a frame that still contains the fixed bias would incorrectly rescale the pedestal and corrupt the subtraction.
explanations.c: Relative magnitude is irrelevant; the issue is that bias and dark scale differently with time.
explanations.d: Order matters critically: scaling before removing bias multiplies a quantity that should be constant, producing a wrong result.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to apply a mismatched-duration master dark to a science frame via thermal scaling.

items.text: Median-combine many dark frames into a master dark
Subtract the master bias to isolate the pure thermal signal
Multiply the thermal-only dark by the exposure-time ratio (t_science / t_dark)
Subtract the scaled thermal dark and the bias from the science frame

questions.explanation: Build a low-noise master dark, remove the fixed bias so only time-scaling thermal current remains, scale that by the exposure-time ratio, then subtract it (together with bias) from the science frame.

questions.prompt: A cooled CCD has a dark current of 0.05 e-/pixel/s. How much dark charge accumulates in a normal pixel over a 200-second exposure?

options.text: 0.05 electrons
10 electrons
200 electrons
4,000 electrons

explanations.a: This ignores the exposure time entirely; dark current accumulates over the full integration.
explanations.b: Correct — dark charge = rate × time = 0.05 e-/pixel/s × 200 s = 10 electrons.
explanations.c: This uses the time in seconds directly without multiplying by the 0.05 e-/s rate.
explanations.d: This multiplies by an extra factor of 20 with no basis; the correct product is 0.05 × 200 = 10 e-.

lessons.label: Flat Fields: Dome, Twilight, and Sky Flats and What Each Actually Corrects

sections.heading: The three problems a flat field corrects at once
sections.body: A flat field is an image of a uniformly illuminated source, and dividing by a normalized flat corrects three distinct multiplicative effects at once. First, pixel-to-pixel quantum-efficiency variations: no two pixels convert photons to electrons at exactly the same rate, and the scatter is typically a few percent. Second, vignetting: the optical system delivers less light to the edges and corners of the field than to the center, producing a smooth large-scale gradient that can reach 10–30% dimming at the corners of a wide field. Third, dust: motes on the filter or dewar window sit out of focus and cast soft doughnut-shaped shadows ("dust donuts") a few percent deep. Because all three scale the detected signal multiplicatively, they are removed by dividing the science frame by a flat normalized to a mean of 1.0.

sections.heading: Dome, twilight, and sky flats — the trade-offs
sections.body: There are three common ways to obtain that uniform illumination, each with a real weakness. Dome flats image an illuminated white screen inside the dome: convenient, repeatable, and available any time, but the screen's illumination is rarely perfectly uniform and its color (a warm incandescent or LED source) does not match the night sky, so dome flats can leave low-order gradients and mis-correct color-dependent features. Twilight flats image the blank dusk or dawn sky: far more uniform in illumination and closer to the sky spectrum, but the sky brightness changes by orders of magnitude within minutes, forcing you to adjust exposures on the fly and work in a short window, and a residual brightness gradient across the twilight sky can remain. Sky flats (also called dark-sky or super-flats) are built by median-combining many dithered science frames of sparse fields so stars fall on different pixels and cancel: these match the true night-sky spectrum and illumination best — ideal for removing fringing and illumination gradients — but the sky is faint, so you need many frames and good dithering to build one.

sections.heading: Flats are filter-specific, and pixel vs illumination correction
sections.body: A flat is only valid for the exact optical configuration it was taken in. Dust shadows and, especially, fringing and vignetting are wavelength-dependent, so you need a separate flat for every filter — a V-band flat cannot correct an I-band image. Flats must also be bias- and dark-subtracted before normalization, exactly like science frames, or they carry additive contamination into a step that should be purely multiplicative. Practitioners often split the correction: a high-frequency "pixel flat" (from dome or lamp flats) captures the fast pixel-to-pixel structure, while a low-frequency "illumination correction" (from a super-sky flat) fixes the large-scale gradient that dome flats get wrong. Getting the flat right is often the limiting factor in precision photometry — a 1% flat-field error translates directly into a 1% (about 0.01 mag) systematic brightness error across the field.

lessons.workedExample: A star lands in a vignetted corner of your wide-field image where the optics deliver only 82% of the central illumination, and it happens to sit on the edge of a dust donut that removes another 3%, so the local flat value (after normalizing the master flat to mean 1.0) is 0.82 × 0.97 ≈ 0.795. Your bias/dark-subtracted science frame reads 3,180 ADU there. Dividing by the flat restores the true signal: 3,180 / 0.795 = 4,000 ADU. If you had skipped the flat entirely, you would have under-counted this star by about 20% — a 0.25-magnitude error (since Δm = 2.5·log10(4000/3180) = 2.5·log10(1.258) ≈ 0.25 mag), enough to ruin any photometric measurement or transit depth you were trying to extract from that corner of the field.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask which kind of flat a team used because the choice reveals whether they thought about their specific systematic. A student who says "I used twilight flats because my science was in V and I needed the illumination gradient corrected, and I took a separate flat for each filter" shows they understand a flat is filter- and configuration-specific, not a generic cleanup. The revealing mistake is a team that reused one flat across filters, or divided by a flat that was never bias-subtracted — both are silent errors that a judge can expose by simply asking "what does your flat actually correct, and how do you know it matches your data?"

questions.prompt: Match each flat-field type to its principal trade-off.

right.text: Convenient and repeatable, but non-uniform screen illumination and wrong color leave low-order gradients
Uniform and near-sky-color, but usable only in a short, rapidly changing brightness window
Best match to true night-sky spectrum and illumination, but faint — needs many dithered frames to build

questions.explanation: Dome flats are always available but have imperfect, wrongly colored screen illumination; twilight flats are uniform and sky-colored but only work in a brief, fast-changing window; sky/super-flats best match the real sky but require many dithered exposures because the sky is faint.

questions.prompt: Dividing a science frame by a normalized flat corrects all of the following EXCEPT:

options.text: Pixel-to-pixel quantum-efficiency variations
Vignetting (dimming toward the field edges)
Out-of-focus dust doughnuts on the filter or window
Cosmic-ray hits in the science exposure

explanations.a: Pixel-to-pixel QE variation is multiplicative and is exactly what the flat corrects.
explanations.b: Vignetting is a smooth multiplicative loss toward the edges, corrected by the flat.
explanations.c: Dust donuts are multiplicative shadows captured and removed by the flat.
explanations.d: Correct — cosmic rays are transient additive spikes unique to each frame; they are removed by masking/sigma-clipping, not by flat-fielding.

questions.prompt: Why must you use a separate flat field for each filter?

options.text: Because exposure time is always different for each filter
Because dust shadows, fringing, and vignetting are wavelength-dependent, so a flat taken in one band does not correctly describe the response in another
Because the bias level changes with filter
Because filters change the read noise of the CCD

explanations.a: Exposure time may differ, but that is not the reason; even at equal exposure the response pattern differs by wavelength.
explanations.b: Correct — the multiplicative response pattern (dust, fringing, and some vignetting) depends on wavelength, so each filter needs its own flat.
explanations.c: The bias is an electronic offset set by the readout, independent of which filter is in the beam.
explanations.d: Read noise is a property of the readout electronics, not of the filter installed.

questions.prompt: A star sits where the normalized flat reads 0.80. A 1% error in that flat value translates to roughly what error in the measured brightness?

options.text: About 1% (roughly 0.01 mag) — flat errors propagate directly into photometry
Zero — flat errors cancel out
About 100%, because you divide by the flat
Exactly 0.80 magnitudes

explanations.a: Correct — because the correction is a division, a 1% error in the flat produces a 1% (about 0.01 mag) systematic error in the derived flux.
explanations.b: Flat errors do not cancel; they are systematic and propagate directly into the measurement.
explanations.c: Dividing by ~0.8 rescales the value but a 1% *error* in the flat gives a 1% error in the result, not 100%.
explanations.d: 0.80 is the flat value, not the magnitude error; the fractional error carries through as a ~1% (0.01 mag) effect.

lessons.label: Bad Pixels, Cosmic Rays, and Fringing: Masking and Removing the Ugly

sections.heading: Bad-pixel masks: mapping the defects you cannot fix
sections.body: Every CCD has permanent defects: hot pixels with anomalously high dark current that saturate quickly, dead or "cold" pixels with near-zero sensitivity, and sometimes entire bad columns from a charge-transfer defect that bleeds down a column. These are not correctable by bias/dark/flat arithmetic because their response is nonlinear or simply broken. The standard approach is to build a bad-pixel mask: hot pixels are identified from a long dark frame (they stand far above the normal dark level), dead pixels from a flat (they respond far below the mean), and the mask is stored alongside the data. Masked pixels are then either flagged and ignored in analysis or interpolated over from their neighbors for display. The mask is a permanent property of the chip and is reused across many nights — unlike cosmic rays, which are different in every single frame.

sections.heading: Cosmic rays: sharp, random, and not shaped like a star
sections.body: Cosmic rays are high-energy particles (from space and from radioactive decay in the instrument) that dump charge directly into pixels, producing sharp, bright spikes covering just one to a few pixels. Their key signature is that they are NOT convolved with the telescope's point-spread function: a real star is spread over several pixels by the optics and atmosphere, giving a smooth rounded profile, while a cosmic ray has razor-sharp edges. There are two removal strategies. When you have many dithered exposures of the same field, a sigma-clipped combine rejects any pixel that is anomalously high in one frame — the cosmic ray appears in only one exposure, so the stack median ignores it. For a single frame you use an algorithm that exploits the sharpness: L.A.Cosmic, introduced by Pieter van Dokkum in 2001 (PASP), applies a Laplacian edge-detection filter to flag the sharp cosmic-ray edges while leaving the smoother, PSF-broadened stars untouched.

sections.heading: Fringing: interference from the night sky in the red
sections.body: Fringing is a wavy, ripple-like pattern that appears in red and near-infrared images (I-band, z-band) taken with thinned CCDs. Its cause is thin-film interference: the CCD's silicon layer acts like a thin etalon, and near-monochromatic night-sky emission lines — principally the atmospheric OH airglow bands (which fall mostly at wavelengths beyond ~7000 Å) and the red [O I] 6300 Å line — interfere within the chip, brightening and dimming across the field in a pattern set by tiny thickness variations. Fringe amplitudes can reach 5–10% of the sky in the I-band, easily swamping faint sources. Because fringing comes from additive sky-line emission (not the continuum that flats correct), it is NOT removed by an ordinary flat. Instead you build a fringe frame — median-combine many dithered, object-masked science frames so only the additive fringe pattern survives — then scale it to each science frame's sky level and subtract it. Front-illuminated and thicker/deep-depletion CCDs suppress fringing, which is one reason modern survey detectors are built that way.

lessons.workedExample: You are imaging in the I-band, where your thinned CCD shows a fringe pattern with peak-to-peak amplitude of about 6% of the sky. Your sky level is 2,500 ADU, so the fringes swing roughly ±150 ADU across the field — and your target, a faint variable, adds only ~200 ADU above sky. Without defringing, a fringe crest under the star would inflate its measured brightness by up to ~75% (150/200), and a trough would deflate it: uncorrected fringing would masquerade as spurious variability. You median-combine 20 dithered, object-masked I-band frames to build a fringe frame carrying the ±150-ADU pattern with the stars washed out. Scaling it to match each frame's sky and subtracting removes the ripple. Separately, a cosmic ray had struck three pixels 4,000 ADU above sky right beside the star; because it is razor-sharp (unlike the PSF-broadened star), L.A.Cosmic's Laplacian filter flags and removes it before photometry.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe cosmic-ray and fringe handling because both are places where a naive pipeline silently invents a signal. A team studying variability that says "my target is in the I-band, so I built a fringe frame and subtracted it, and I ran L.A.Cosmic so a cosmic ray next to my star could not be read as a brightening" has anticipated the exact artifacts that produce false detections. The damaging tell is a student who reports a variable or transient without having cleaned cosmic rays or fringing — a judge knows a single unremoved cosmic-ray hit can fabricate a "flare," and will ask precisely how the team ruled that out.

questions.prompt: What is the key signature that distinguishes a cosmic-ray hit from a real star in a single CCD frame?

options.text: Cosmic rays are always green in color
Cosmic rays are sharp — not spread by the point-spread function — whereas a real star has a smooth, PSF-broadened profile over several pixels
Cosmic rays are always fainter than stars
Cosmic rays appear in exactly the same place in every frame

explanations.a: CCD frames are monochrome within a filter; cosmic rays have no intrinsic color, and color is not the discriminator.
explanations.b: Correct — the optics/atmosphere spread real stars into a smooth PSF over several pixels, while a cosmic ray dumps charge directly, giving razor-sharp edges that edge-detection algorithms exploit.
explanations.c: Cosmic rays are often very bright, sometimes brighter than nearby stars; brightness is not the discriminator.
explanations.d: Cosmic rays strike random pixels differently in every frame — that randomness is exactly why stacking rejects them; fixed-location defects are bad pixels, not cosmic rays.

questions.prompt: The L.A.Cosmic algorithm (van Dokkum 2001) detects cosmic rays in a single frame by:

options.text: Comparing many dithered frames and rejecting outliers
Applying a Laplacian edge-detection filter that flags the sharp edges of cosmic rays while leaving smoother PSF-broadened stars
Dividing by a flat field
Subtracting a scaled dark frame

explanations.a: That describes sigma-clipped stacking of multiple frames; L.A.Cosmic works on a single image, which is its whole purpose.
explanations.b: Correct — van Dokkum's method uses a Laplacian filter to detect the sharp intensity edges of cosmic rays, distinguishing them from the smooth PSF of real sources in one frame.
explanations.c: Flat-fielding corrects multiplicative response, not transient cosmic-ray spikes.
explanations.d: Dark subtraction removes thermal current, not cosmic rays.

questions.prompt: Why is fringing NOT removed by an ordinary flat field?

options.text: Because fringing is an additive pattern from night-sky emission-line interference, not a multiplicative response, so it must be modeled and subtracted separately
Because fringing only occurs in blue light where flats are not taken
Because flats are taken with the shutter closed
Because fringing changes the bias level

explanations.a: Correct — fringing is additive light from interfering sky emission lines; flats correct multiplicative response, so a fringe frame is built and subtracted instead.
explanations.b: Fringing is a red/near-IR phenomenon (I- and z-band), the opposite of blue; and flats are taken in the same band as the science.
explanations.c: Flats are taken with the shutter open on a uniformly illuminated source; that is unrelated to why fringing survives flat-fielding.
explanations.d: Fringing is a spatial sky-emission pattern on the science frame, not a shift in the electronic bias pedestal.

questions.prompt: Match each artifact to how it is handled in reduction.

right.text: Permanent bad-pixel mask, reused across nights (from long darks and flats)
Sigma-clipped stacking or a Laplacian single-frame filter (L.A.Cosmic)
A scaled fringe frame built from object-masked dithered images, then subtracted

questions.explanation: Permanent chip defects go into a reusable bad-pixel mask; transient cosmic rays are rejected by stacking or a Laplacian single-frame algorithm; additive fringing is removed with a scaled fringe frame subtracted from each image.

lessons.label: Astrometric Calibration: Plate-Solving and the World Coordinate System (WCS)

sections.heading: From pixels to the sky: the World Coordinate System
sections.body: A reduced image is still just a grid of pixel values; astrometric calibration is what pins each pixel (x, y) to a celestial coordinate (RA, Dec). The mapping is encoded in the FITS header as a World Coordinate System (WCS). The core keywords are CRPIX1/CRPIX2 (a chosen reference pixel), CRVAL1/CRVAL2 (the RA and Dec at that reference pixel), and a CD matrix (CD1_1, CD1_2, CD2_1, CD2_2) that sets the plate scale and rotation — how many degrees of sky each pixel step spans and how the frame is rotated relative to north. The CTYPE keywords name the projection, most commonly the tangent-plane (gnomonic) projection written "RA---TAN" and "DEC--TAN," which projects the curved sky onto the flat detector. With a valid WCS, any software can convert a pixel position to sky coordinates and back — essential for identifying your target, cross-matching catalogs, and stacking frames taken at different pointings.

sections.heading: Plate scale and field of view from first principles
sections.body: Before solving, you can predict the geometry from the optics. The plate scale — arcseconds of sky per pixel — follows from the small-angle relation: plate scale (arcsec/pixel) = 206,265 × (pixel size / focal length), where 206,265 is the number of arcseconds in a radian and pixel size and focal length are in the same units. A camera with 9-micron pixels on a telescope of 2,000 mm focal length gives 206,265 × (0.009 / 2000) ≈ 0.93 arcsec/pixel. Multiply by the number of pixels to get the field of view: a 4,000-pixel-wide detector at 0.93 arcsec/pixel spans about 3,700 arcsec ≈ 62 arcminutes ≈ 1 degree. Knowing the expected scale and field lets you sanity-check a solve and choose the right catalog density: too fine a scale over-resolves and needs a deep catalog, too coarse blends stars.

sections.heading: Blind plate-solving and higher-order distortion
sections.body: You rarely know the pointing precisely, so modern practice is "blind" plate-solving: hand the software a list of detected star positions and let it find where on the sky they belong with no prior guess. The landmark tool is Astrometry.net, described by Dustin Lang, David Hogg, Keir Mierle, Michael Blanton, and Sam Roweis in 2010 (Astronomical Journal). It builds geometric "hash codes" from groups of four stars (quads) — quantities invariant under position, rotation, and scale — and matches them against a pre-indexed catalog (built from sources like the USNO/2MASS, and today Gaia) to recognize the field like a fingerprint. Once matched, it fits the WCS. Real optics also introduce field distortion that a linear CD matrix cannot capture, so the solution is refined with polynomial terms — the SIP (Simple Imaging Polynomial) convention of Shupe et al. (2005) adds distortion coefficients to the header. The astrometric reference frame itself is now anchored to the Gaia catalog, whose sub-milliarcsecond positions from the ESA Gaia mission set the modern standard for star coordinates.

lessons.workedExample: You image with 9-micron pixels on a 2,000-mm focal-length telescope. Plate scale = 206,265 × (0.009 mm / 2,000 mm) = 206,265 × 4.5×10⁻⁶ = 0.928 arcsec/pixel. Your detector is 3,000 × 2,000 pixels, so the field of view is 3,000 × 0.928 ≈ 2,784 arcsec ≈ 46.4 arcmin wide by 2,000 × 0.928 ≈ 1,856 arcsec ≈ 30.9 arcmin tall. You feed the detected star list to Astrometry.net; it forms quads, matches their hash codes against its Gaia-based index, and recognizes the field. It writes a WCS header with CRPIX at the frame center, CRVAL at the solved RA/Dec of that pixel, a CD matrix encoding 0.928 arcsec/pixel and the frame's rotation, CTYPE = "RA---TAN"/"DEC--TAN," and SIP polynomial terms for the few-pixel edge distortion. Now any pixel converts to sky coordinates — your target at pixel (1520, 985) resolves to a specific RA and Dec you can cross-match against a catalog.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "how do you know that is your target and not a look-alike star?" and a WCS is the defensible answer. A student who says "I plate-solved with Astrometry.net, so every pixel has an RA and Dec anchored to Gaia, and my target sits at the catalog coordinates" has turned an image into measured sky positions rather than a pretty picture. It also shows they can predict their plate scale from pixel size and focal length — a quick calculation a judge can pose on the spot, where fumbling the 206,265 arcsec-per-radian conversion reveals the geometry was never really understood.

questions.prompt: A camera has 6-micron pixels on a telescope with 1,200-mm focal length. What is the approximate plate scale?

options.text: About 1.03 arcsec/pixel
About 0.10 arcsec/pixel
About 10.3 arcsec/pixel
About 206 arcsec/pixel

explanations.b: This is off by 10×; check the arithmetic — 0.006/1200 = 5×10⁻⁶, times 206,265 gives ~1.03, not ~0.10.
explanations.c: This is 10× too large; it likely misplaces a decimal in the pixel-size-to-focal-length ratio.
explanations.d: This mistakes the 206,265 conversion constant itself for the answer instead of multiplying it by the (pixel/focal) ratio.

questions.prompt: In a FITS WCS, what do the CRVAL1/CRVAL2 keywords specify?

options.text: The RA and Dec of the reference pixel
The exposure time and filter
The bias and dark levels
The number of pixels on each axis

explanations.a: Correct — CRVAL1/CRVAL2 give the world coordinates (RA, Dec) at the reference pixel named by CRPIX1/CRPIX2.
explanations.b: Exposure and filter live in other header keywords (e.g. EXPTIME, FILTER), not CRVAL.
explanations.c: Bias and dark levels are calibration quantities, not part of the WCS coordinate keywords.
explanations.d: Axis dimensions are given by NAXIS1/NAXIS2, not by CRVAL.

questions.prompt: How does the Astrometry.net "blind" solver (Lang et al. 2010) recognize a field without a prior pointing guess?

options.text: It requires the telescope to report exact coordinates first
It builds rotation- and scale-invariant geometric hash codes from groups of four stars (quads) and matches them against a pre-indexed reference catalog
It compares the raw pixel brightness histogram to a template
It measures the redshift of each star

explanations.a: The whole point of blind solving is that it needs no prior pointing; requiring exact coordinates would defeat its purpose.
explanations.b: Correct — it forms quads of stars, computes hash codes invariant to position, rotation, and scale, and matches them against an indexed catalog to identify the field.
explanations.c: A brightness histogram carries no geometric fingerprint of the star pattern and cannot localize a field.
explanations.d: Stars in a normal field have negligible redshift and it is not measured from an image; this is unrelated to astrometry.

questions.prompt: Match each WCS/astrometry element to what it provides.

right.text: The reference pixel and its RA/Dec anchor point
The plate scale and rotation of the linear pixel-to-sky mapping
Higher-order optical distortion beyond the linear mapping
The sub-milliarcsecond reference positions the solution is anchored to

questions.explanation: CRPIX/CRVAL set the reference pixel and its sky coordinates; the CD matrix encodes the linear plate scale and rotation; SIP polynomials capture field distortion the linear term misses; and the Gaia catalog supplies the ultra-precise reference positions the whole solution is tied to.

lessons.label: Assembling the Pipeline: Order of Operations and Propagating the Errors

sections.heading: The canonical order, and why each step sits where it does
sections.body: A defensible reduction runs the steps in a fixed order dictated by the physics of each artifact. The canonical sequence is: (1) overscan-correct to remove the per-frame bias level; (2) subtract the master bias to remove the fixed 2D pedestal structure; (3) subtract the master dark (scaled if necessary) to remove thermal current; (4) divide by the normalized master flat to correct multiplicative response; (5) mask bad pixels and reject cosmic rays; (6) subtract a scaled fringe frame in the red bands; (7) plate-solve to attach a WCS; and (8) align and stack the calibrated frames. The order is not arbitrary: additive contaminants (bias, dark) must be subtracted before the multiplicative flat division, because dividing first would propagate the un-removed dark through the flat. Cosmic-ray and fringe cleaning come after flat-fielding so the frame is already on a uniform response scale, and astrometry comes before stacking so frames at slightly different pointings can be registered onto a common grid.

sections.heading: Propagating errors: the variance image travels with the data
sections.body: Every arithmetic step changes not just the signal but its uncertainty, and a rigorous pipeline carries a variance (or uncertainty) image alongside the science frame. Noise adds in quadrature: independent sources combine as σ_total = √(σ₁² + σ₂² + …). Subtracting a master bias or dark adds that frame's (small, √N-reduced) noise in quadrature — a reason master frames are stacked, so they add little. Dividing by the flat is the subtle one: division scales both the signal and its noise, so the fractional flat-field uncertainty adds in quadrature to the fractional source noise. The dominant noise floor is set by the CCD equation: for a source measured in an aperture of n_pix pixels, the noise in electrons is σ = √(N_source + n_pix·(N_sky + N_dark + RON²)), combining Poisson (shot) noise from the source, sky, and dark with the read noise RON added per pixel. Gain (electrons per ADU) converts measured counts to electrons so Poisson statistics apply — you must work in electrons, since shot noise is √N only for electron counts, not raw ADU.

sections.heading: Why the whole chain has to be internally consistent
sections.body: The reason to treat reduction as one pipeline rather than a bag of steps is that errors compound. A bias-including dark scaled by exposure time, a flat that was never bias-subtracted, or working in ADU instead of electrons each corrupts everything downstream — and because the steps multiply and divide, a systematic introduced early cannot be recovered later. This is the through-line of the whole unit: overscan and bias (Lesson 1), darks and thermal scaling (Lesson 2), flats (Lesson 3), and cosmic-ray/fringe cleaning (Lesson 4) each remove one artifact with the correct operation, and astrometry (Lesson 5) ties the result to the sky — but only if they are done in the right order with the uncertainties tracked. A reduction whose final answer comes with a propagated error bar, derived from the CCD equation and every calibration step, is what separates a measurement a judge can trust from a number pulled off a screen.

lessons.workedExample: You measure a star in an aperture of n_pix = 20 pixels with a gain of 1.5 e-/ADU. The sky-subtracted source collects N_source = 10,000 e-. Per pixel: sky = 100 e-, dark = 5 e-, and read noise RON = 8 e- (so RON² = 64 e-²). Apply the CCD equation: noise = √(N_source + n_pix·(N_sky + N_dark + RON²)) = √(10,000 + 20·(100 + 5 + 64)) = √(10,000 + 20·169) = √(10,000 + 3,380) = √13,380 ≈ 115.7 e-. The signal-to-noise ratio is SNR = 10,000 / 115.7 ≈ 86, which corresponds to a photometric precision of about 1.086/SNR ≈ 0.013 magnitudes. Notice that if you had forgotten the gain and treated the raw ADU (10,000/1.5 ≈ 6,667 ADU) as electrons, √6,667 ≈ 82 "ADU" would give a wrong, inflated fractional error — the shot-noise √N law holds only for the electron count, which is why converting through the gain is not optional.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the capstone question a judge saves for last: "walk me through your pipeline, in order, and where does your error bar come from?" A team that recites the order — subtract additives before dividing by the flat, clean cosmic rays and fringes, plate-solve, then stack — and then derives its uncertainty from the CCD equation in electrons has demonstrated that its final number is a defensible measurement. The fatal tell is a student who has a beautiful stacked image but no propagated uncertainty, or who did the steps out of order; a judge knows an unpropagated error bar means the team cannot actually say whether its result is significant, which undercuts every claim built on it.

questions.prompt: Order the full CCD reduction pipeline from raw frame to stacked, sky-referenced science image.

items.text: Overscan-correct (remove per-frame bias level)
Subtract the master bias (fixed 2D pedestal structure)
Subtract the master dark (scaled if needed)
Divide by the normalized master flat
Mask bad pixels, reject cosmic rays, subtract fringes
Plate-solve to attach a WCS
Align and stack the calibrated frames

questions.explanation: Remove additive contaminants (overscan level, bias structure, dark) first, then divide by the multiplicative flat; clean cosmic rays and fringes on the flattened frame; plate-solve to a WCS so frames can be registered; finally align and stack.

questions.prompt: Why must additive corrections (bias, dark) be applied BEFORE dividing by the flat?

options.text: It is only a software convention with no consequence
Because dividing by the flat first would propagate the un-removed additive dark/bias through the multiplicative flat, corrupting the result
Because the flat is always taken after the darks
Because bias and dark are multiplicative like the flat

explanations.a: The order is dictated by the math of additive versus multiplicative artifacts, not by convention; getting it wrong changes the answer.
explanations.b: Correct — the flat is a division, so any residual additive signal left in the frame gets scaled by the flat and spread through the data; you must subtract additives first.
explanations.c: The acquisition order of calibration frames does not determine the reduction order; the physics does.
explanations.d: Bias and dark are additive (extra counts), not multiplicative; that is exactly why they are subtracted, not divided.

questions.prompt: Using the CCD equation, a source of 10,000 e- measured over 20 pixels with per-pixel sky 100 e-, dark 5 e-, and read noise 8 e- has a noise of about:

options.text: 100 e- (just the square root of the source counts)
About 13,380 e-
8 e- (the read noise alone)

explanations.a: This omits the sky, dark, and read-noise contributions summed over the 20-pixel aperture, which are substantial here.
explanations.c: This is the variance (the quantity under the square root), not the noise; the noise is its square root, ~116 e-.
explanations.d: Read noise is only one term added per pixel; the total noise combines source, sky, dark, and read noise in quadrature.

questions.prompt: Why must you convert measured counts (ADU) to electrons using the gain before computing shot noise?

options.text: Because the gain changes the exposure time
Because Poisson shot noise equals √N only for the actual electron count, so the √N law does not hold on raw ADU
Because electrons are always fewer than ADU
Because the gain removes the bias offset

explanations.a: Gain (electrons per ADU) is a fixed conversion factor of the electronics; it has nothing to do with exposure time.
explanations.b: Correct — shot noise follows Poisson statistics on the physical electron count (σ = √N electrons); applying √N to raw ADU gives the wrong noise unless the gain is 1.
explanations.c: Whether electrons outnumber ADU depends on the gain value (typically >1 e-/ADU means more electrons than ADU); count relationship is not the reason.
explanations.d: The gain is a scaling factor for photon-to-count conversion; the bias offset is removed separately by bias subtraction.

units.label: Photometry in Depth

lessons.label: Aperture Photometry Revisited: Growth Curves and the Aperture Correction

sections.heading: What an aperture actually sums, and the instrumental magnitude
sections.body: The Core introduced aperture photometry as "add up the light in a circle." In depth, the operation is: for a circular aperture of radius r centred on a star, sum the counts (in ADU, analog-to-digital units) of every pixel inside, subtract the local sky per pixel, and convert to a brightness. Multiplying ADU by the detector gain g (electrons per ADU, typically ~1–2 e⁻/ADU on a research CCD) gives the number of photoelectrons — the physically meaningful quantity, because Poisson noise scales with electrons, not ADU. The instrumental magnitude is m_inst = −2.5·log₁₀(net_counts / exposure_time) + constant. The −2.5 and the log are the definition of the magnitude system (a factor of 100 in flux = 5 magnitudes; Pogson, 1856). "Instrumental" means it is uncalibrated — tied to this telescope, filter, and night — and says nothing yet about a standard system. Everything in this unit is about making that one number trustworthy at the millimagnitude (0.001 mag) level.

sections.heading: The curve of growth: how flux accumulates with aperture radius
sections.body: A star is not a point on the detector — it is a blurred profile, the point-spread function (PSF), broadened by the atmosphere (seeing), the telescope optics, and the detector. Its width is quoted as the FWHM (full width at half maximum), typically 1–4 arcsec from the ground. The curve of growth (or "encircled-energy curve") plots the summed flux of a bright, isolated star against aperture radius. It rises steeply through the PSF core, then flattens as it collects the faint wings, asymptoting to the total flux at large r. A pure 2-D Gaussian of the same FWHM encircles ~94% of its light within one FWHM radius and essentially 100% within ~1.5 FWHM — but real stellar PSFs have broader wings (better described by a Moffat profile), so they approach the asymptote more slowly, often needing 3–4 FWHM to reach 99%. The curve of growth is how you decide, empirically, how much light any given aperture is throwing away.

sections.heading: The small-aperture trade-off and the aperture correction
sections.body: Why not just use a huge aperture and capture 100%? Because every extra pixel adds sky noise and read noise while adding almost no starlight in the wings, so the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) peaks at a fairly small aperture — often near r ≈ 1–1.5 FWHM. Faint stars are best measured with these tight apertures, which deliberately miss a few percent of the flux. The fix is the aperture correction: measure a handful of bright, isolated stars in BOTH a small aperture and a large "total-light" aperture from the same frame, and the constant offset between the two is the correction Δm you add to every small-aperture measurement.
