If the small aperture captures 92% of the light, Δm = +2.5·log₁₀(0.92) = −0.091 mag (negative because you are brightening a too-faint measurement toward its true value). This differential approach — pioneered in the crowded-field photometry of Peter Stetson's DAOPHOT (1987) — lets you enjoy the high SNR of a small aperture while recovering the total flux of a large one.

lessons.workedExample: You measure a bright, isolated calibration star and build its curve of growth: aperture radius r = 3 px sums 46,000 ADU (net of sky), while a large r = 12 px aperture sums 50,000 ADU (the asymptote, taken as "total light"). The 3-px aperture therefore captures 46,000 / 50,000 = 92.0% of the flux. Its instrumental magnitude in a 30 s exposure is m₃ = −2.5·log₁₀(46,000 / 30) = −2.5·log₁₀(1533) = −7.97 (plus the arbitrary constant, here 0). The large aperture gives m₁₂ = −2.5·log₁₀(50,000 / 30) = −8.06. The aperture correction is Δm = m₁₂ − m₃ = −0.091 mag. Now for a FAINT program star, where the big aperture would be too noisy, you measure only the 3-px aperture and apply the SAME correction: m_faint,total = m_faint,3px + (−0.091). With a gain of 1.5 e⁻/ADU, that 46,000 ADU is 69,000 e⁻, whose Poisson noise is √69,000 ≈ 263 e⁻ — an SNR of ~262 and a photometric precision of about 1.086/262 ≈ 0.004 mag, i.e. 4 millimag.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the aperture correction because it is the cleanest test of whether a student understands that a measured number is not automatically the true number. A student who says "I used a 3-pixel aperture because it maximized SNR, then corrected the −0.09 mag it was missing using a growth curve from bright stars" has grasped the small-aperture trade-off; one who says "I made the aperture big enough to get all the light" has quietly thrown away SNR on every faint star and cannot defend their choice of radius.

questions.prompt: Why is the optimal photometric aperture usually SMALLER than the radius that would capture 100% of a star’s light?

options.text: A smaller aperture captures more starlight per pixel
Beyond the PSF core, extra pixels add sky and read noise while adding almost no starlight, so SNR peaks at a small radius
CCDs cannot read out large apertures accurately
The magnitude system only works for small apertures

explanations.a: A smaller aperture captures LESS total starlight, not more per pixel; the point is about noise, not signal density.
explanations.b: Correct — in the faint wings each added pixel contributes noise (sky + read noise) but negligible starlight, so signal-to-noise is maximized at a tight aperture (~1–1.5 FWHM), which is then aperture-corrected.
explanations.c: Read-out accuracy does not depend on aperture size; the aperture is defined in software after read-out.
explanations.d: The magnitude definition (−2.5·log₁₀ of flux) is independent of aperture size.

questions.prompt: A small aperture captures 90% of a star’s total flux. What is the aperture correction you add to its instrumental magnitude?

options.text: +2.5·log₁₀(0.90) = −0.114 mag (a brightening)
−2.5·log₁₀(0.90) = +0.114 mag (a dimming)
0.90 mag
No correction is needed if the same aperture is used for all stars

explanations.a: Correct — measuring only 90% of the flux makes the star appear too faint, so the correction +2.5·log₁₀(0.90) = −0.114 mag is negative, brightening the measurement toward the true total.
explanations.b: The sign is wrong: a missing 10% of light makes the star measure too FAINT, so the correction must brighten (be negative), not dim it.
explanations.c: The correction is a logarithmic magnitude offset, not the linear fraction 0.90.
explanations.d: Even with a consistent aperture, transforming to a standard system requires knowing the total flux; the missing light is a real systematic offset that the aperture correction removes.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to derive and apply an aperture correction to a faint star.

items.text: Build a curve of growth from bright, isolated stars
Choose a small aperture that maximizes SNR
Measure the offset between the small aperture and the large “total-light” aperture
Add that offset to the faint star’s small-aperture magnitude

questions.explanation: You first characterize how flux grows with radius using bright stars, pick the SNR-optimal small aperture, measure the small-vs-large offset (the correction), then apply that same offset to faint stars measured only in the small aperture.

questions.prompt: On a research CCD with gain 2.0 e⁻/ADU, a star nets 40,000 ADU. Roughly what Poisson-limited SNR (ignoring sky and read noise) does this give?

explanations.a: 200 would be √40,000 — but you must convert to electrons first (40,000 × 2.0 = 80,000 e⁻) before taking the square root.
explanations.b: Correct — 40,000 ADU × 2.0 e⁻/ADU = 80,000 e⁻; Poisson noise is √80,000 ≈ 283 e⁻, so SNR = 80,000 / 283 ≈ 283.
explanations.c: That is the raw ADU count, not an SNR; SNR is signal divided by its noise.
explanations.d: This mistakes the SNR for half the count; SNR of a Poisson signal N is √N in electrons.

lessons.label: Estimating the Sky: Annuli, Backgrounds, and Crowded Fields

sections.heading: Why the sky is the enemy, and how the annulus estimates it
sections.body: Every pixel in a star's aperture contains not only starlight but the night-sky background: airglow, scattered moonlight, zodiacal light, unresolved faint stars, and light pollution. A dark, moonless site reads roughly V ≈ 21.5 mag per square arcsecond; a suburban sky can be several magnitudes brighter (each magnitude is 2.512× more light). For a faint star, this diffuse background can outweigh the star itself, and subtracting it correctly is often the single largest source of photometric error. The standard estimator is the sky annulus: a ring around the star (say inner radius 4×FWHM, outer 6×FWHM) placed far enough out to avoid the star's wings but close enough to sample the local background. You compute a per-pixel sky value from the annulus and subtract it from every pixel inside the aperture: net = Σ(aperture pixels) − n_pix × sky_per_pixel.

sections.heading: Mean, median, and the robust mode estimator
sections.body: The naive choice — the mean of the annulus pixels — is badly biased whenever a faint contaminating star, a cosmic ray, or a hot pixel falls in the ring, because the mean is dragged toward those bright outliers. Real photometry packages instead use a robust estimator. The median is far more resistant to outliers. Better still is an estimate of the MODE (the peak of the pixel-value histogram), because contaminants only ever add light — they skew the distribution to the bright side, so the mode sits below the mean and median and best represents the true "empty sky." DAOPHOT and IRAF use the classic approximation mode ≈ 3×median − 2×mean, often combined with iterative sigma-clipping (reject pixels more than ~3σ from the current estimate, then recompute). Choosing mean vs. median vs. mode can shift a faint star's magnitude by several hundredths — a real, defensible methods decision.

sections.heading: When the annulus fails: crowded fields
sections.body: The annulus assumes the ring samples empty sky. In a crowded field — a globular cluster core, a rich Galactic-plane field, a nebula with structured background — that assumption collapses: neighboring stars sit inside the annulus and inflate the sky estimate, causing you to over-subtract and systematically UNDER-measure your target's flux. Sigma-clipping helps for a few contaminants but not for genuine crowding where there is no empty sky. This is precisely the regime where aperture photometry breaks down and PSF-fitting photometry (next lesson) takes over, because a fitted PSF can model overlapping stars and a smoothly varying background simultaneously rather than assuming a single flat sky level in a ring.

lessons.workedExample: A faint variable star is measured in a circular aperture of area 28 pixels; the raw sum inside is 51,240 ADU. The surrounding sky annulus contains 950 pixels. Their mean is 186 ADU/pixel, but the histogram is skewed by two faint field stars clipped in the ring, so you use the robust mode ≈ 3×median − 2×mean. With median = 180 and mean = 186, mode ≈ 3(180) − 2(186) = 540 − 372 = 168 ADU/pixel. Net star flux = 51,240 − 28 × 168 = 51,240 − 4,704 = 46,536 ADU. Had you naively used the mean (186), you would have subtracted 28 × 186 = 5,208 ADU, netting only 46,032 — a difference of 504 ADU, about 1.1% of the flux, or ≈ 0.012 mag. For a millimagnitude time-series, that 12-mmag systematic from the wrong sky estimator would swamp the very signal you are hunting.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "how did you handle the background?" because sky subtraction is where faint-object projects quietly go wrong. A student who explains they used a median or mode from an annulus, sigma-clipped contaminants, and checked that the annulus wasn't sitting on a neighboring star shows they understand the largest error term for faint stars. "The software subtracted the sky automatically" is a red flag that they never inspected whether the estimate was corrupted by crowding.

questions.prompt: Why is the MODE (or median) of the sky annulus preferred over the mean?

options.text: The mode is always exactly equal to the true sky level
Contaminants (faint stars, cosmic rays) only ADD light, skewing the histogram bright, so the mode/median resist that bias while the mean is dragged up
The mean cannot be computed for a ring-shaped region
The mode uses fewer pixels, so it is faster

explanations.a: The mode is a robust ESTIMATE, not a guaranteed exact value; it is preferred because it resists outliers, not because it is exact.
explanations.b: Correct — sky contaminants can only brighten pixels, skewing the distribution to the bright side; the mode/median are outlier-resistant while the mean is pulled upward, causing over-subtraction.
explanations.c: The mean is perfectly well defined for any set of pixels, including a ring.
explanations.d: Robustness, not speed, is the reason; computing the mode/median is generally MORE work than a mean.

questions.prompt: In a crowded globular-cluster field, using a sky annulus tends to make your target star measure:

options.text: Too BRIGHT, because neighbors add flux to the aperture
Too FAINT, because neighbors inflate the sky estimate and you over-subtract
Exactly correct, because the annulus averages the neighbors out
Unaffected, since crowding only matters for spectroscopy

explanations.a: While neighbors can leak into the aperture, the dominant crowded-field effect on the SKY step is an inflated background estimate, which over-subtracts and dims the target.
explanations.b: Correct — stars in the annulus raise the estimated sky per pixel, so you subtract too much and systematically under-measure the target’s flux; this is why PSF fitting replaces apertures here.
explanations.c: Averaging does not remove the bias; the neighbors systematically raise the estimate, they do not cancel.
explanations.d: Crowding is a central problem for photometry, not just spectroscopy.

questions.prompt: An aperture of 30 pixels sums 60,000 ADU; the robust sky is 150 ADU/pixel. What is the net stellar flux?

explanations.a: That is the raw sum with no sky removed; the background must be subtracted per pixel.
explanations.c: This subtracts only a single pixel’s worth of sky (150), not n_pix × sky (30 × 150).
explanations.d: This subtracts 15,000, as if the sky were 500 ADU/pixel; the given sky is 150.

questions.prompt: Match each sky-estimation choice to its main consequence.

left.text: PSF fitting with a fitted background

right.text: Biased upward by bright outliers → over-subtraction
Robust to contaminants → least-biased sky
No empty sky exists → target measured too faint
Models overlapping stars + background instead of a flat ring

questions.explanation: The mean is dragged up by outliers; the mode/clipped-median resist them; an annulus in a crowded field has no empty sky and over-subtracts; PSF fitting sidesteps the ring entirely by modeling the scene.

lessons.label: PSF-Fitting Photometry: DAOPHOT and When Fitting Beats Apertures

sections.heading: The idea: fit a shared PSF model, don’t just sum pixels
sections.body: In PSF-fitting photometry, instead of summing counts in a circle you assume every star on the frame is the SAME point-spread function — the same normalized shape — differing only in position (x, y) and brightness (a scale factor). You build a model of that shared PSF from bright, isolated stars, then find, for each program star, the scale factor and centroid that best reproduce its pixels in a least-squares sense. The star's flux is then that fitted scale factor, not a raw pixel sum. Because the fit weights each pixel by its expected noise, PSF fitting extracts near-optimal SNR from faint stars, and because it models the light as a specific shape, it can pull apart two stars whose apertures would overlap. This is the foundation of Peter Stetson's DAOPHOT (1987, Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific), still the reference algorithm decades later, and of its many descendants (ALLSTAR, ALLFRAME, DoPHOT, and the modern Python photutils).

sections.heading: Modeling the PSF: analytic core plus empirical wings
sections.body: A real stellar profile is not a Gaussian — Gaussians fall off too fast and underpredict the wings. The workhorse analytic form is the Moffat profile (Moffat, 1969), I(r) ∝ [1 + (r/α)²]^(−β), whose power-law wings match seeing-limited stars far better; as β → ∞ it reduces to a Gaussian. DAOPHOT's practical PSF is a hybrid: an analytic function (Gaussian, Moffat, or similar) for the core, PLUS an empirical look-up table of residuals that captures the messy, real deviations the analytic form misses, and it can let the PSF vary across the field to handle optical distortions. The PSF is built iteratively — pick candidate PSF stars, subtract their neighbors, re-derive the model — because you need clean, uncontaminated stars to define a shape you will then impose on everything else.

sections.heading: When fitting beats apertures — and when it doesn’t
sections.body: PSF fitting wins decisively in two regimes. First, CROWDED fields: in a globular-cluster core where stellar images overlap, ALLSTAR fits many stars simultaneously, apportioning the blended light between them — something an aperture, which cannot tell whose photons are whose, simply cannot do. Second, FAINT stars near the sky limit, where the noise-weighted fit beats a fixed circle. But fitting is not free: it assumes the PSF model is correct, so a poorly characterized or spatially variable PSF injects systematic errors, and for a bright, isolated star on an uncrowded frame a simple aperture is more robust and requires no model. The professional workflow uses BOTH: PSF fitting for the science, tied back to an aperture-photometry scale via the aperture correction (Lesson 1), because the standard-star calibration ultimately rests on aperture measurements of bright standards.

lessons.workedExample: Two stars sit 2.0 arcsec apart in 1.8-arcsec-FWHM seeing — their images visibly overlap, and no aperture can enclose one without catching the wings of the other. You measure the PSF from several bright, isolated stars elsewhere on the frame, fitting a Moffat core (β ≈ 3, α set by the 1.8-arcsec FWHM) plus a residual table. ALLSTAR then fits the blend as two PSFs at fixed relative shape, solving for two centroids and two scale factors at once. Say it returns fluxes of 12,000 and 3,000 e⁻: the fit has cleanly apportioned the blended light 4:1, giving the fainter companion (Δm = −2.5·log₁₀(3,000/12,000) = 1.51 mag fainter than its neighbor) a magnitude an aperture could never isolate. Cross-check: the two fitted PSFs, added back and subtracted from the image, should leave only sky-level noise — a flat residual is the acceptance test that the fit was valid.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "why PSF fitting instead of apertures?" to see whether a student chose a method for a reason or ran whatever the tutorial defaulted to. The winning answer names the regime: "my field was crowded, so overlapping stars made apertures over-subtract; DAOPHOT-style PSF fitting deblends them and I checked the subtracted residual was flat." A student who used PSF fitting on a sparse field of bright isolated stars — where an aperture is simpler and more robust — reveals they were pattern-matching, not reasoning about their data.

questions.prompt: What is the core assumption that makes PSF-fitting photometry possible?

options.text: Every star is a mathematical point with no width
All stars on a frame share the same PSF shape, differing only in position and brightness (scale)
The sky background is exactly zero
Brighter stars have intrinsically wider profiles

explanations.a: The whole point is that stars are NOT points on the detector — they are blurred into the PSF, which is precisely what you model.
explanations.b: Correct — a single shared, normalized PSF is fit to every star, solving only for each star’s centroid and flux scale; this is what lets the method deblend and noise-weight.
explanations.c: PSF fitting explicitly includes a background term; it does not assume zero sky.
explanations.d: To first order all stars share the same PSF regardless of brightness (saturation aside); brighter stars are scaled-up copies of the same shape, not wider.

questions.prompt: Why is a Moffat profile often preferred over a Gaussian for modeling a seeing-limited PSF?

options.text: The Moffat profile is easier to integrate analytically
Its power-law wings match real stellar profiles, which a Gaussian underpredicts by falling off too fast
The Moffat profile has no free parameters to fit
Gaussians cannot represent a peaked profile

explanations.a: Ease of integration is not the reason; if anything the Gaussian is analytically simpler. The Moffat is chosen for FIDELITY to real wings.
explanations.b: Correct — the Moffat form [1 + (r/α)²]^(−β) has extended power-law wings that fit atmospheric seeing profiles, whereas a Gaussian decays too steeply and misses the wing flux (as β→∞ the Moffat becomes a Gaussian).
explanations.c: The Moffat has free parameters (α, β) that are fit to the data.
explanations.d: Gaussians are perfectly peaked; the issue is the WINGS, not the peak.

questions.prompt: In which situation does PSF fitting give the LEAST advantage over simple aperture photometry?

options.text: The dense core of a globular cluster with overlapping images
A sparse field of bright, well-isolated stars
Very faint stars near the sky-noise limit
A rich Galactic-plane field with many blends

explanations.a: Crowded cores are exactly where PSF fitting is essential — it deblends overlapping stars an aperture cannot separate.
explanations.b: Correct — for bright, isolated stars a simple aperture is robust and needs no PSF model, so fitting adds complexity (and PSF-model systematics) for little gain.
explanations.c: Near the sky limit the noise-weighted PSF fit meaningfully beats a fixed aperture, so fitting helps here.
explanations.d: Many blends are precisely where simultaneous PSF fitting pays off.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a DAOPHOT-style PSF-fitting reduction.

items.text: Select bright, isolated candidate PSF stars
Build the PSF model (analytic core + empirical residual table)
Fit the scaled PSF to every program star (simultaneously for blends)
Subtract the fitted models and check the residual image is flat

questions.explanation: You choose clean stars to define the shared shape, build the hybrid PSF model, fit that model’s scale/position to all stars (jointly where they overlap), then verify by confirming the star-subtracted residuals are at sky level.

lessons.label: Differential Photometry and the Comparison-Star Method

sections.heading: Measure the difference, not the absolute brightness
sections.body: Absolute (all-sky) photometry — pinning a star's brightness to a standard system on any given night — is limited by the atmosphere: clouds, haze, and changing transparency alter how much light reaches the detector minute to minute, and the extinction grows with airmass as the target sinks toward the horizon. Differential photometry sidesteps all of this. Instead of asking "how bright is the target?", you ask "how much brighter or fainter is the target than a nearby comparison star, measured in the SAME image?" Because both stars sit in the same frame and see the same atmosphere at nearly the same airmass, a passing thin cloud dims BOTH by the same factor, and the DIFFERENCE Δm = m_target − m_comp is unchanged. This is why differential photometry routinely reaches millimagnitude precision from the ground even when the night is not photometric — it cancels the atmosphere by construction.

sections.heading: Choosing a good comparison star
sections.body: The method only works if the comparison star is trustworthy, which imposes real requirements. It must be genuinely constant (not itself variable), or your target's "variation" is really the comparison's — a classic false detection. It should be similar in BRIGHTNESS to the target, so both have comparable SNR and neither saturates. And crucially it should be similar in COLOR (spectral type): the atmosphere's extinction depends on wavelength (blue light is scattered more), so a red target and a blue comparison drift apart in brightness as airmass changes — the "second-order extinction" and differential color-extinction effects. Matching colors makes the residual atmospheric term nearly cancel. Observers historically vet a candidate comparison by "check stars" — a third star whose differential magnitude against the comparison should stay flat all night; if it wobbles, the comparison is suspect.

sections.heading: The killer application: exoplanet transits
sections.body: Differential photometry is the engine of ground-based transit detection. When a planet crosses its star, it blocks a fraction of the light equal to the ratio of areas: transit depth = (R_p / R_s)², where R_p and R_s are the planet and star radii. For a Jupiter-sized planet (R_p ≈ 0.10 R_sun) transiting a Sun-like star, the depth is (0.10)² ≈ 0.01 = 1% ≈ 11 millimag — small, but reachable differentially. This is exactly how the first transiting exoplanet, HD 209458 b, was caught in 1999 (Charbonneau, Brown, Latham & Mayor 2000; independently Henry, Marcy, Butler & Vogt 2000), showing a ~1.5% dip that confirmed the radial-velocity planet was a genuine, eclipsing world. The same differential technique, scaled up, drives the transit surveys and the light-curve science of missions like Kepler and TESS.

lessons.workedExample: You observe a candidate hot-Jupiter host, V ≈ 11, and select a comparison star of similar brightness and color 3 arcmin away in the same field. Over the night, thin cirrus dims the whole field by up to 30%, yet the differential magnitude Δm = m_target − m_comp holds flat to a few millimag — until, mid-run, Δm dips by 15 mmag for about 3 hours, then recovers: a transit. Interpreting the depth: 15 mmag corresponds to a flux drop of 1 − 10^(−0.015/2.5) = 1 − 10^(−0.006) = 1.37%, so (R_p/R_s)² = 0.0137, giving R_p/R_s = 0.117. If the host is a G star with R_s = 1.1 R_sun = 1.1 × 696,000 km, then R_p = 0.117 × 1.1 × 696,000 ≈ 89,600 km ≈ 1.25 R_Jupiter — a bona-fide inflated hot Jupiter. A check star measured against the same comparison stays flat throughout, confirming the dip is the target's and not a variable comparison.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love the comparison-star question because it exposes whether a student understands WHY their ground-based light curve is even possible. The strong answer: "differential photometry cancels clouds and airmass because the comparison sees the same atmosphere, so I could detect a 15-mmag transit on a non-photometric night — and I matched the comparison's color and used a check star to be sure it wasn't itself variable." A student who measured only the target's raw brightness, with no comparison, cannot explain how they beat the atmosphere, and a judge will press exactly there.

questions.prompt: Why can differential photometry reach millimagnitude precision even on a slightly cloudy (non-photometric) night?

options.text: Clouds do not affect starlight at optical wavelengths
The target and comparison share the same frame and atmosphere, so transparency changes divide out of the DIFFERENCE in magnitude
The comparison star is brighter, so it overwhelms the clouds
Differential photometry uses infrared light that penetrates clouds

explanations.a: Clouds strongly attenuate optical starlight; the method survives them by cancellation, not because they have no effect.
explanations.b: Correct — a cloud dims both stars by the same factor, so it cancels in m_target − m_comp, leaving the true differential signal intact.
explanations.c: Relative brightness is not the mechanism; the cancellation works because both stars see the same atmosphere, regardless of which is brighter.
explanations.d: The technique is generally done in the same optical band as the science; it does not rely on infrared cloud penetration.

questions.prompt: A planet with radius 0.1 R_sun transits a star of radius 1.0 R_sun. What is the approximate transit depth?

explanations.a: 10% is the RADIUS ratio R_p/R_s, not the depth; the depth is the ratio of AREAS, i.e. the radius ratio squared.
explanations.b: Correct — depth = (R_p/R_s)² = (0.1/1.0)² = 0.01 = 1% ≈ 11 millimag, because the blocked light equals the ratio of the disk areas.
explanations.c: This doubles the radius ratio; depth is the square of the ratio, not twice it.
explanations.d: This squares 0.1 twice or otherwise mis-scales; (0.1)² = 0.01, not 0.001.

questions.prompt: Why should a comparison star be similar in COLOR to the target?

options.text: So the two stars have the same distance from Earth
Atmospheric extinction is wavelength-dependent, so mismatched colors drift apart in brightness as airmass changes
Color matching guarantees the comparison is non-variable
Detectors can only measure two stars of identical color

explanations.a: Color says nothing about distance; comparison stars need not be at the target’s distance.
explanations.b: Correct — blue light is extinguished more than red, so a color mismatch produces a differential trend with airmass (second-order/color extinction) that a matched color largely cancels.
explanations.c: Color similarity does not ensure constancy; that requires separately vetting the comparison (e.g., with a check star).
explanations.d: Detectors measure stars of any color; the requirement is about extinction physics, not detector capability.

questions.prompt: What was the significance of HD 209458 b (Charbonneau et al. 2000; Henry et al. 2000)?

options.text: It was the first exoplanet ever discovered
It was the first exoplanet observed to TRANSIT its star, confirming via a ~1.5% photometric dip a planet already found by radial velocity
It was the first Earth-mass planet found
It was discovered purely by differential photometry with no other data

explanations.a: The first exoplanet around a Sun-like star was 51 Pegasi b (Mayor & Queloz 1995); HD 209458 b was the first to be seen transiting.
explanations.b: Correct — the ~1.5% transit dip confirmed a radial-velocity planet as a genuine eclipsing world and opened transit science (radii, atmospheres).
explanations.c: HD 209458 b is a hot Jupiter, not an Earth-mass planet.
explanations.d: It was first identified by radial velocity; the transit photometry then confirmed and characterized it.

lessons.label: Ensemble Photometry: Building a Stable Reference from Many Stars

sections.heading: From one comparison star to many
sections.body: A single comparison star has two weaknesses: its own photon noise limits the precision floor, and if it turns out to be even slightly variable, that variability leaks straight into every measurement of the target. Ensemble photometry generalizes the comparison-star method by using MANY stars in the field as a collective reference. Averaging N comparison stars beats down the reference's random noise as roughly 1/√N — ten good comparisons give a reference about √10 ≈ 3.2× more stable than any one of them — while also letting you spot and reject a rogue variable among them, because a single misbehaving star stands out against the consensus of the rest. The target is then measured differentially against this stable, low-noise "artificial standard" built from the ensemble.

sections.heading: Honeycutt’s self-calibrating algorithm
sections.body: The elegant formulation is R. Kent Honeycutt's ensemble photometry (1992, Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific). The problem is circular: to get each star's true magnitude you need each frame's zero-point (its transparency/exposure offset), but to get each frame's zero-point you need the stars' magnitudes. Honeycutt solved it as one big least-squares system over ALL stars and ALL frames simultaneously, solving jointly for every star's mean instrumental magnitude and every frame's zero-point, weighting each measurement by its uncertainty. Crucially it needs no designated "standard" comparison and tolerates missing data (a star off the edge, or lost to a cosmic ray, in some frames) — the whole dataset self-calibrates. This is the intellectual ancestor of the systematics-removal used in modern survey pipelines.

sections.heading: Detrending: SysRem, TFA, and the survey era
sections.body: Ensemble thinking scales into the algorithms that clean wide-field time-domain surveys. Techniques like SysRem (Tamuz, Mazeh & Zucker 2005) and the Trend Filtering Algorithm (TFA; Kovács, Bakos & Noyes 2005) learn the systematic trends SHARED across thousands of light curves — trends from airmass, detector temperature, focus drift, flat-field errors — and subtract them from each star, because a true astrophysical signal (a transit, a flare) is unique to one star while instrumental systematics are common to many. This is how surveys such as HATNet, WASP, Kepler, and TESS pushed toward the sub-millimagnitude precision needed to detect shallow transits, using the many stars in the field as a self-referencing model of everything that is NOT the signal.

lessons.workedExample: You are chasing a 3-mmag brightness variation, but your single best comparison star delivers only ~5 mmag of scatter — the target signal is buried. You instead build an ensemble of 10 comparison stars of similar brightness and color. Assuming their errors are independent, the ensemble reference scatter drops by √10 ≈ 3.16×, from 5 mmag to about 1.6 mmag — now below your 3-mmag target signal, which becomes detectable. Running Honeycutt's least-squares solution over all 10 stars across all 200 frames flags star #7: its residuals against the ensemble show a slow 8-mmag drift, marking it as a low-amplitude variable. You drop star #7, re-solve with the remaining 9 (reference scatter √9 = 3× improvement, ~1.7 mmag), and the target's 3-mmag oscillation now stands clean above the noise. This is the difference between "one comparison" and "an ensemble": you both lowered the floor and caught a contaminant that would have injected a false signal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the reference because a lone comparison star is a single point of failure, and knowing that separates a careful time-series project from a lucky one. The strong answer: "I used an ensemble of comparison stars, so my reference noise fell as 1/√N and I could reject one that turned out to be variable." A student who relied on a single comparison and never checked it against others cannot rule out that their headline signal is actually their comparison star varying — exactly the failure mode ensemble photometry exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: Using an ensemble of N independent comparison stars improves the reference precision by approximately what factor?

options.text: A factor of N
A factor of √N
No improvement — more stars only add noise
A factor of N²

explanations.a: Averaging independent random errors reduces noise as 1/√N, not 1/N; a factor of N would overstate the gain.
explanations.b: Correct — averaging N stars with independent errors beats down the random noise by √N (e.g., 10 stars ≈ 3.2× more stable), the standard error-of-the-mean scaling.
explanations.c: More stars REDUCE random noise (and let you catch variables); they do not simply add noise.
explanations.d: N² is far too strong; the square-root law governs averaging of independent noise.

questions.prompt: What circular problem does Honeycutt’s (1992) ensemble algorithm solve?

options.text: You need star magnitudes to get frame zero-points, but need frame zero-points to get star magnitudes — solved jointly by least squares
Stars are too faint to measure without a larger telescope
The sky background cannot be estimated in crowded fields
PSF models vary across the detector

explanations.a: Correct — the mutual dependence of stellar magnitudes and per-frame zero-points is solved as one big weighted least-squares system over all stars and all frames simultaneously, with no designated standard.
explanations.b: Telescope aperture is unrelated; the algorithm is about self-calibrating an existing dataset.
explanations.c: Crowded-field sky estimation is a different problem (Lesson 2), not what Honeycutt’s method addresses.
explanations.d: Spatially varying PSFs are a PSF-fitting concern (Lesson 3), not the zero-point/magnitude circularity Honeycutt solves.

questions.prompt: Why do detrending algorithms like SysRem and TFA work by finding trends SHARED across many light curves?

options.text: Astrophysical signals are also shared identically by all stars
Instrumental systematics (airmass, focus, temperature) are common to many stars, while a real signal is unique to one star — so shared trends can be removed as systematics
Sharing trends increases the number of detectable planets by duplication
It is the only way to measure a star’s color

explanations.a: The opposite — a true transit or flare is unique to one star; only systematics are shared, which is precisely what lets you separate them.
explanations.b: Correct — systematics from the instrument/atmosphere affect many stars together, so a model of the common trends can be subtracted, leaving each star’s unique astrophysical signal.
explanations.c: Detrending does not duplicate planets; it cleans noise so real, unique signals emerge.
explanations.d: These algorithms remove systematics from time series; they are not color-measurement tools.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building and using an ensemble reference to detect a small signal.

items.text: Select many comparison stars of similar brightness and color
Solve jointly for star magnitudes and per-frame zero-points (Honeycutt-style)
Identify and reject any comparison that is itself variable
Measure the target differentially against the cleaned ensemble

questions.explanation: You gather many suitable comparisons, self-calibrate them and the frames together, prune any that vary, then measure the target against the resulting low-noise, trustworthy reference.

lessons.label: Standard-System Transformation, Color Terms, and Detection Limits

sections.heading: From instrumental to standard magnitudes
sections.body: An instrumental magnitude is private to your telescope-filter-night. To compare with the literature or other observers you must transform onto a STANDARD photometric system — most commonly the Johnson–Cousins UBVRI system (Johnson & Morgan 1953; extended to R and I by Cousins in the 1970s). The transformation for the V band takes the form V = v + zₚ − k·X + c·(B−V), where v is your instrumental magnitude, zₚ is the zero-point (the offset that sets the flux scale), k is the atmospheric extinction coefficient, X is the airmass (≈ sec z, the path length through the atmosphere; X = 1 at the zenith), and the last term is the color term. You solve for zₚ, k, and c by observing fields of stars with precisely known standard magnitudes — the reference grids of Arlo Landolt (Landolt 1992, Astronomical Journal), equatorial fields of well-measured UBVRI standards that remain the workhorse calibrators for CCD photometry.

sections.heading: Why the color term exists
sections.body: The color term c·(B−V) corrects the fact that YOUR filter+detector passband is never identical to the standard system's. If your effective bandpass is slightly bluer or redder than the true Johnson V, then a blue star (small B−V) and a red star (large B−V) of the same true V will register different instrumental v — the mismatch depends on the star's spectral energy distribution, i.e., its color. The linear color term captures this to first order; c is typically small (a few hundredths to ~0.1) but ignoring it biases red and blue stars in OPPOSITE directions, which is fatal for a color-magnitude diagram. There is also a second-order extinction term (extinction that itself depends on color, since blue light is scattered more), usually a small k″·(B−V)·X correction that matters most in the blue U and B bands and at high airmass.

sections.heading: Detection limits and the CCD equation
sections.body: How faint can you go? The signal-to-noise of a stellar measurement is given by the CCD equation (Howell): SNR = N⋆ / √[ N⋆ + n_pix·(N_sky + N_dark + N_read²) ], where all terms are in electrons — N⋆ is the star's counts, N_sky the sky per pixel, N_dark the dark current per pixel, N_read the read noise per pixel, and n_pix the number of pixels in the aperture. For a BRIGHT star, N⋆ dominates the denominator and SNR → √N⋆ (photon-limited). For a FAINT star, the sky term n_pix·N_sky dominates and you are "sky-limited," so SNR grows only linearly with exposure time's square root and background matters enormously (Lesson 2). The magnitude error follows σ_mag ≈ 1.0857 / SNR (from 2.5/ln 10). The limiting magnitude is conventionally quoted at SNR = 5 (σ ≈ 0.22 mag) or SNR = 3; pushing to millimagnitude precision (σ = 0.001) requires SNR ≈ 1,086 — nearly a million detected electrons — which is why high-precision time-series demands bright targets, big apertures, or many stacked frames.

lessons.workedExample: You calibrate against a Landolt field and solve V = v + zₚ − k·X + c·(B−V) with zₚ = 21.30, k = 0.18 mag/airmass, and c = 0.04. Your program star has instrumental v = −8.35, sits at airmass X = 1.30, and (from a companion B-band frame) has B−V = 0.65. Then V = −8.35 + 21.30 − (0.18 × 1.30) + (0.04 × 0.65) = −8.35 + 21.30 − 0.234 + 0.026 = 12.74. Note the color term shifted the answer by only +0.026 mag here, but a red giant with B−V = 1.5 would get +0.060 while a hot blue star with B−V = 0.0 gets 0.000 — a 60-mmag spread that would smear a color-magnitude diagram if ignored. Now check whether you can even reach millimag on this star: with N⋆ = 400,000 e⁻ in a photon-limited regime, SNR ≈ √400,000 = 632, so σ_mag ≈ 1.0857/632 = 0.0017 = 1.7 mmag. To hit 1 mmag you would need SNR ≈ 1,086, i.e., N⋆ ≈ 1.18 million e⁻ — roughly 3× longer integration or 3 co-added frames.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "how did you calibrate to a standard system, and how faint could you go?" to test whether a student's numbers are comparable to anyone else's and whether they know their own error budget. The strong answer names the transformation and its color term ("I used Landolt standards to solve for the zero-point, extinction, and a 0.04 color term, without which my red and blue stars would be biased oppositely") and states a limiting magnitude with its SNR basis ("SNR = 5, so σ ≈ 0.2 mag, at V ≈ 19"). A student who reports magnitudes with no standardization and no stated detection limit cannot say whether a faint "detection" is real or noise.

questions.prompt: In the transformation V = v + z_p − k·X + c·(B−V), what does the color term c·(B−V) correct for?

options.text: The star moving across the sky during the exposure
The mismatch between your instrumental passband and the standard system’s, which biases stars by their color
The read noise of the detector
The distance to the star

explanations.a: Tracking errors are unrelated; the color term is about bandpass shape, not motion.
explanations.b: Correct — because your filter+detector passband differs slightly from the standard V, stars of different colors register differently, and c·(B−V) removes that color-dependent bias to first order.
explanations.c: Read noise enters the SNR/error budget, not the color term of the transformation.
explanations.d: Distance affects apparent brightness but is not what the color term corrects; the term corrects passband mismatch versus stellar color.

questions.prompt: For a FAINT star whose measurement is dominated by the background, the SNR is best described as:

options.text: Photon-limited, so SNR ≈ √N⋆
Sky-limited, so the sky term n_pix·N_sky dominates the noise and the background must be minimized/subtracted carefully
Independent of the sky background entirely
Limited only by the color term

explanations.a: Photon-limited (SNR ≈ √N⋆) describes a BRIGHT star, where the star’s own counts dominate the denominator — not a faint one.
explanations.b: Correct — for faint stars the n_pix·N_sky term dominates the CCD-equation denominator, so precision hinges on small apertures and accurate sky subtraction.
explanations.c: A faint star’s noise is dominated BY the sky, so it is anything but independent of the background.
explanations.d: The color term is a calibration correction, not a noise source in the SNR equation.

questions.prompt: A star yields a photon-limited N⋆ = 10,000 e⁻ (sky, dark, read noise negligible). What is its approximate magnitude error?

options.text: ≈ 1.1 mag

explanations.b: This uses SNR = 10 (√100), but N⋆ = 10,000 gives SNR = 100, ten times better.
explanations.c: This corresponds to SNR ≈ 1; SNR here is 100, giving ~0.011 mag.
explanations.d: 0.001 mag needs SNR ≈ 1,086 (over a million electrons), far more than 10,000 e⁻ provides.

questions.prompt: Match each photometric-calibration term to what it represents.

right.text: Offset setting the overall flux/magnitude scale
Magnitudes of dimming per unit airmass from the atmosphere
Atmospheric path length (≈ sec z; = 1 at the zenith)
Correction for passband mismatch that depends on stellar color

questions.explanation: z_p sets the flux scale; k is the extinction in magnitudes per airmass; X is the airmass (path length, sec z, =1 at zenith); the color term corrects for the difference between your bandpass and the standard system as a function of the star’s color.

units.label: The Time Domain: Variability and Transients

lessons.label: Building an Honest Light Curve: Barycentric Time, Flux, and Error Bars

sections.heading: The x-axis is a trap: put time on the barycenter
sections.body: A light curve is brightness versus time, and the time axis is where beginners quietly ruin their data. If you tag each measurement with the clock at your telescope, you are timing photons as they arrive at a platform that is itself hurtling around the Sun at ~30 km/s. Over a year, Earth moves across a ~2 AU baseline, so the light-travel time from a fixed star changes as the geometry shifts. Astronomers therefore convert observed times to the BARYCENTRIC JULIAN DATE — the time the same wavefront would have reached the Solar System barycenter, a fixed point. The correction is a projection of Earth's position onto the line to the target, and it ranges up to ±499 seconds (one-way light time across 1 AU is 8.32 minutes), a full ~16.6-minute swing over a year. A period measured against uncorrected clocks smears by this much; for a transit forecast years ahead it is the difference between catching the event and pointing at a quiet star. The modern convention (Eastman, Siegel & Agol 2010) is BJD_TDB — barycentric time expressed in Barycentric Dynamical Time (TDB), a uniform scale free of the leap seconds that make UTC jump by a second unpredictably.

sections.heading: Flux, magnitudes, and why differential photometry survives clouds
sections.body: The y-axis is a brightness, but which one? Raw counts from a detector drift with airmass, seeing, and thin cloud. The robust move is DIFFERENTIAL (relative) photometry: divide your target's counts by the summed counts of several steady comparison stars in the same frame. Clouds dim target and comparisons together, so the ratio holds steady — the target is measured in units of the comparisons, not in absolute flux. Results are reported either as normalized relative flux (out-of-transit set to 1.000) or in magnitudes, where the logarithmic scale means Δm = −2.5 log₁₀(F/F₀) and a 1% flux dip is about 0.011 mag. A clean light curve is normalized (baseline flattened to unity), detrended against airmass and any instrumental ramp, and phase-preserving — you must not let a detrending polynomial eat the very variability you are hunting.

sections.heading: Error bars are a claim, and photons set the floor
sections.body: An error bar is a promise about how much a point would jump if you re-took it, and the irreducible floor is PHOTON SHOT NOISE: photon arrivals are Poisson, so a measurement of N detected photons carries an uncertainty of √N, giving a signal-to-noise ratio of N/√N = √N. Collect a million photons and S/N ≈ 1000, a relative precision of 0.1% — 1 millimagnitude. To reach the tens-of-ppm needed for an Earth-sized transit you need billions of photons and a stable detector, which is why Kepler and TESS went to space to escape the atmosphere. Real error bars add read noise, sky background, scintillation, and systematic (correlated, "red") noise on top of the shot-noise floor. Under-reporting errors manufactures fake discoveries; over-reporting buries real ones. An honest light curve states its noise budget rather than drawing decorative bars.

lessons.workedExample: A student observes a bright star and, in a 60-second exposure, collects 4.0×10⁶ detected photons in the aperture. The shot-noise S/N is √(4.0×10⁶) = 2000, so the per-point relative precision is 1/2000 = 5×10⁻⁴, i.e. 0.5 mmag (σ_m ≈ 1.0857/(S/N) = 0.00054 mag). That is comfortably enough to see a hot Jupiter's ~1% (10 mmag) dip but nowhere near an Earth's ~84 ppm. Separately, the target sits near the ecliptic, and the observation is made when Earth is offset ~1 AU along the line of sight; the BJD correction is close to its 499 s maximum. If the student had left times on the observatory clock and folded three months of data, cycles taken near opposite ends of Earth's orbit would be misaligned by up to ~8 minutes — enough to blur a sharp 3-hour transit ingress into mush. Correcting to BJD_TDB first is not pedantry; it is what makes the fold sharp.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "what is on your axes, exactly?" because the answer separates students who plotted numbers from students who built a measurement. The two classic tells are the time system and the error bars: a student who says "times are BJD_TDB, corrected to the barycenter" has thought about light-travel geometry, and one who says "the error bars are the photon shot noise, √N, plus read and sky terms" is stating a falsifiable noise budget rather than decorating the plot. If a claimed detection is smaller than the honest per-point scatter divided by √(number of points), a judge will (rightly) doubt it.

questions.prompt: Why convert observed times to Barycentric Julian Date (BJD) before analyzing a long-baseline light curve?

options.text: Because the star physically moves, changing its true period night to night
Because Earth's orbital motion changes the light-travel time to the target by up to ±499 s over a year, smearing periods and event times
Because UTC runs faster than telescope clocks
Because magnitudes must be converted to flux first

explanations.a: The star's intrinsic period does not change; it is the geometry between the moving Earth and the target that shifts arrival times.
explanations.b: Correct — one-way light time across 1 AU is 8.32 min, so as Earth orbits, the arrival time at the telescope shifts by up to ±499 s; BJD projects times to the fixed barycenter to remove this.
explanations.c: UTC vs telescope clock is a separate (small) issue; the barycentric correction is about light-travel geometry, and the preferred scale is TDB precisely to avoid UTC leap seconds.
explanations.d: Time correction and flux/magnitude choice are independent; barycentric timing is needed regardless of the brightness unit.

questions.prompt: A photometric aperture collects 1.0×10⁶ detected photons. What is the shot-noise-limited signal-to-noise ratio and relative precision?

options.text: S/N = 10⁶; precision 10⁻⁶
S/N = 1000; precision ~0.1% (1 mmag)
S/N = 500; precision 0.2%
Cannot be determined without the exposure time

explanations.a: That would require noise of 1 photon; Poisson noise is √N = 1000, not 1, so S/N is 1000.
explanations.b: Correct — for Poisson photon statistics, noise = √N = √(10⁶) = 1000, so S/N = N/√N = 1000 and relative precision = 1/1000 = 0.1% ≈ 1 mmag.
explanations.c: S/N = √N = 1000 here; 500 does not follow from N = 10⁶.
explanations.d: The shot-noise S/N depends only on the number of collected photons, √N; exposure time matters only insofar as it set N.

questions.prompt: Match each light-curve ingredient to what it does.

right.text: Refers each time to the Solar System barycenter on a uniform (leap-second-free) scale
Divides target counts by comparison-star counts so clouds/airmass cancel
The irreducible Poisson noise floor set by photon counting statistics
Rescales out-of-event flux to one so dips are read as fractional depths

questions.explanation: BJD_TDB fixes the time axis to the barycenter on a uniform scale; differential photometry cancels common-mode atmospheric losses using comparison stars; shot noise (√N) is the Poisson floor; normalization sets the baseline to unity so a transit reads directly as its fractional depth.

questions.prompt: Why did Earth-sized transit detection (dips of ~100 ppm) require space missions like Kepler rather than ground telescopes?

options.text: Space is closer to the target stars
The atmosphere adds scintillation and correlated noise, and reaching tens-of-ppm precision requires the stable, high-photon-count conditions only space provides
Ground telescopes cannot measure time accurately
Transits do not occur for stars visible from the ground

explanations.a: Being in orbit does not meaningfully reduce the light-years to the star; the gain is photometric stability, not distance.
explanations.b: Correct — atmospheric scintillation and airmass-correlated systematics dominate ground light curves at the sub-mmag level, so the ~100 ppm floor for an Earth transit needs above-atmosphere stability and long, uninterrupted photon integration.
explanations.c: Ground observatories time perfectly well with GPS/atomic clocks; timing is not the limitation.
explanations.d: Transits happen for any suitably aligned system regardless of where it is observed; the barrier is noise, not geometry.

lessons.label: A Zoo of Variable Stars: Pulsators, Eclipsers, Rotators, and Cataclysmics

sections.heading: Pulsators: stars that ring like a bell
sections.body: The most famous variables are INTRINSIC pulsators — stars whose whole envelope rhythmically expands and contracts, driven by the κ (kappa) mechanism, in which a partially ionized helium layer acts as a valve: when compressed it becomes more opaque, traps heat, and pushes back out. Stars enter this instability when they cross the near-vertical INSTABILITY STRIP on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. CLASSICAL CEPHEIDS are luminous yellow supergiants with periods of ~1–100 days; Henrietta Leavitt, studying Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, published the PERIOD–LUMINOSITY relation in 1908 and quantitatively in 1912 — brighter Cepheids pulsate more slowly — which became the backbone of the extragalactic distance ladder. RR LYRAE stars are older, lower-mass horizontal-branch pulsators with short ~0.2–1.0 day periods and a nearly fixed absolute magnitude M_V ≈ +0.6, making them standard candles for the Galactic halo and globular clusters. MIRA variables are pulsating red giants with ~100–1000 day periods and amplitudes of several magnitudes; δ Scuti stars pulse in hours.

sections.heading: Eclipsers: geometry, not physics
sections.body: ECLIPSING BINARIES are EXTRINSIC variables — each star shines steadily, but their mutual orbit is edge-on enough that they periodically block one another. Their light curves split into three classical morphologies. ALGOL-type (EA) systems, named for β Persei, show flat baselines punctuated by two distinct dips (a deep primary eclipse when the hotter star is hidden, a shallow secondary). β LYRAE-type (EB) systems are close, tidally distorted stars whose brightness varies continuously and smoothly, so even the "out of eclipse" light changes. W UMa-type (EW) are contact binaries sharing an envelope, with near-equal minima and constant variation. Eclipsing binaries are astrophysical gold: because the dips constrain the geometry, a detached eclipsing binary with radial velocities yields both stars' masses and radii to a few percent — the most direct stellar masses we have, independent of models.

sections.heading: Rotators and cataclysmics: spots and explosions
sections.body: ROTATIONAL variables carry surface features — cool magnetic STARSPOTS — that modulate brightness at the rotation period as they wheel in and out of view (BY Draconis and spotted RS CVn systems); the amplitude tracks spot coverage, and this is how Kepler and TESS measure rotation periods for thousands of stars, a key input to gyrochronology (dating stars by spin-down). CATACLYSMIC VARIABLES are close binaries in which a white dwarf accretes hydrogen-rich gas from a low-mass companion via an accretion disk. DWARF NOVAE (e.g., U Geminorum, SS Cygni) brighten by 2–6 magnitudes in recurring days-to-months outbursts when the disk undergoes a thermal instability. Classical NOVAE erupt by 8–12 magnitudes when accreted hydrogen on the white dwarf surface reaches thermonuclear runaway — the star is not destroyed and can recur. These sit on the same evolutionary track that, at the extreme, produces Type Ia supernovae (Lesson 6).

lessons.workedExample: An RR Lyrae star in a Galactic globular cluster is measured at mean apparent magnitude V = 15.6, and (after correcting for interstellar reddening) its known standard-candle absolute magnitude is M_V ≈ +0.6. The distance modulus is m − M = 15.6 − 0.6 = 15.0. Inverting m − M = 5 log₁₀(d/10 pc) gives log₁₀(d/10) = 15.0/5 = 3.0, so d/10 = 10³ and d = 10,000 pc = 10 kpc. That single ~0.5-day light curve, once classified as RR Lyrae, delivers a 10-kpc distance to the cluster — the same standard-candle logic Leavitt's Cepheids provide for other galaxies, just tuned to older, fainter pulsators. Misclassifying the star (say, calling a Type II Cepheid a classical Cepheid) is exactly the error that, at the population level, once put extragalactic distances off by a factor of ~2 until Walter Baade sorted the two populations out in 1952.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe classification because the analysis you may legitimately run depends entirely on what kind of variable you have. Calling every dip a "transit," or treating an eclipsing binary as a planet, is a headline failure mode — a V-shaped, alternating-depth light curve screams grazing eclipsing binary, not planet. A student who can say "the two unequal minima and flat baseline make this an Algol-type eclipsing binary, so the depth ratio is a temperature ratio, not (Rp/Rs)²" demonstrates they matched method to phenomenon rather than forcing one favorite tool onto everything.

questions.prompt: Match each variable-star class to its defining mechanism or signature.

right.text: Pulsating supergiant obeying a period–luminosity relation; extragalactic distance indicator
Short-period horizontal-branch pulsator with M_V ≈ +0.6; halo/globular-cluster standard candle
Two unequal dips on a flat baseline as two steady stars eclipse each other
White dwarf accreting from a companion; recurring outbursts from a disk instability

questions.explanation: Classical Cepheids follow Leavitt's period–luminosity law; RR Lyrae are near-fixed-luminosity standard candles; Algol-type systems show two unequal eclipse dips on a flat baseline; dwarf-nova cataclysmics are accreting white-dwarf binaries whose disk instability drives recurring outbursts.

questions.prompt: What physically drives the pulsation of a Cepheid or RR Lyrae star?

options.text: A companion star tugging the envelope tidally
The κ (kappa) mechanism: a partially ionized helium layer that traps heat when compressed, acting as a valve
Starspots rotating in and out of view
Thermonuclear runaway on the stellar surface

explanations.a: Pulsators are intrinsic single-star variables; the driving is internal, not from a companion.
explanations.b: Correct — in the instability strip, a He⁺⁺ ionization zone becomes more opaque when compressed, dams up radiation, and pushes the envelope out, then leaks heat and lets it fall back: a self-sustaining valve (the κ mechanism).
explanations.c: Spot modulation drives rotational variables, not the radial pulsation of Cepheids/RR Lyrae.
explanations.d: Surface thermonuclear runaway describes novae, not the smooth pulsation of instability-strip stars.

questions.prompt: Walter Baade's 1952 revision of the distance scale corrected which mistake?

options.text: Confusing two distinct populations of pulsating stars (classical Cepheids vs. fainter Type II Cepheids/RR Lyrae), which had miscalibrated the period–luminosity zero point
Using magnitudes instead of flux
Failing to correct times to the barycenter
Assuming the universe was static

explanations.a: Correct — Baade showed there were two stellar populations with different period–luminosity relations; conflating them had made classical Cepheids appear fainter/closer, and untangling them roughly doubled the extragalactic distance scale.
explanations.b: The error was astrophysical misclassification of the calibrators, not a flux/magnitude bookkeeping choice.
explanations.c: Barycentric timing is a photometric-analysis concern, unrelated to Baade's population correction.
explanations.d: The static-universe question is Hubble's expansion story; Baade's fix was specifically about the Cepheid calibration.

questions.prompt: A detached eclipsing binary with measured radial velocities is astrophysically valuable mainly because it yields:

options.text: The chemical composition of the interstellar medium
Model-independent masses AND radii of both stars to a few percent
The exact age of the galaxy
Only the orbital period, nothing more

explanations.a: That is a spectroscopic/ISM measurement; eclipsing binaries constrain the stars themselves.
explanations.b: Correct — eclipse geometry (from the light curve) plus radial-velocity amplitudes together fix both stars' masses and radii directly, the gold standard for empirical stellar parameters.
explanations.c: A binary constrains its own stars, not a galaxy's absolute age.
explanations.d: The period is only the start; the whole point is that eclipse plus RV yields masses and radii.

lessons.label: Period-Finding: the Lomb–Scargle Periodogram and Phase Dispersion Minimization

sections.heading: Why a plain Fourier transform fails on real data
sections.body: A classical Fourier transform assumes evenly spaced samples. Real astronomical time series are gap-ridden — you observe at night, not through cloud, not when the target is below the horizon — so the sampling is wildly uneven, and a naive FFT is undefined. The LOMB–SCARGLE PERIODOGRAM solves this by reframing period-finding as least-squares fitting: at each trial frequency, fit a sinusoid to the data and record how much variance it explains as "power." Nicholas Lomb (1976) and Jeffrey Scargle (1982) worked out the exact statistical normalization so that the power spectrum of pure noise has a known distribution, letting you assign a FALSE-ALARM PROBABILITY to any peak. The GENERALIZED Lomb–Scargle (Zechmeister & Kürster 2009) adds a floating mean and weights points by their error bars, which matters when your baseline is not perfectly flat — the version most modern pipelines actually use.

sections.heading: Building and reading the periodogram
sections.body: You compute power on a grid of trial frequencies from roughly 1/T (one cycle over the whole baseline T) up to a maximum near the pseudo-Nyquist limit set by your typical sampling. The tallest peak that clears the false-alarm threshold is your candidate frequency; the period is P = 1/f. Two cautions are non-negotiable. First, Lomb–Scargle fits SINUSOIDS, so a sharply non-sinusoidal signal (an eclipse, a spiky RR Lyrae) spreads its power into harmonics at 2f, 3f, … and the fundamental peak can be weaker than a harmonic — you must check the harmonics before naming the period. Second, uneven sampling stamps ALIAS peaks into the periodogram (Lesson 5): the true peak is often flanked by spurious ones spaced by 1 cycle/day. The honest reader phase-folds on every strong peak and looks at which fold produces a coherent, physically sensible light curve.

sections.heading: PDM: a non-parametric alternative for weird shapes
sections.body: When the signal is decidedly non-sinusoidal — a boxy eclipse, a sawtooth pulsation — PHASE DISPERSION MINIMIZATION (Stellingwerf 1978) is often more sensitive because it assumes nothing about the shape. For each trial period you phase-fold the data, slice the phase axis into bins, and compute the statistic Θ = (variance WITHIN the phase bins) / (total variance of the data). At the true period, points that share a phase share a brightness, so the within-bin scatter collapses and Θ drops toward 0; at a wrong period the fold is scrambled and Θ ≈ 1. You therefore MINIMIZE Θ rather than maximize a power. PDM trades Lomb–Scargle's clean analytic false-alarm statistics for shape-agnostic robustness, so pipelines often run both and demand they agree before trusting a period.

lessons.workedExample: A student has 400 differential-photometry points on a suspected RR Lyrae spread over a 30-night baseline (T = 30 d), taken irregularly around weather. They compute a generalized Lomb–Scargle periodogram on a frequency grid from f_min = 1/30 = 0.033 cycles/day up to f_max = 5 cycles/day. The dominant peak, far above the 0.1% false-alarm level, sits at f = 1.89 cycles/day, giving a period P = 1/1.89 = 0.529 days — squarely in the RR Lyrae range. Because RR Lyrae light curves are sawtooth-shaped, the student sees a secondary bump at 2f = 3.78 cycles/day (the first harmonic) and, reassuringly, alias peaks at f ± 1 = 0.89 and 2.89 cycles/day. They confirm by phase-folding on P = 0.529 d, which yields a clean, single-valued sawtooth, and cross-check with PDM, whose Θ statistic hits its deepest minimum at the same 0.529-day period. Agreement across two independent methods is what promotes "a peak" to "a period."
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask how you found your period because "the software said so" hides the two ways period-finding goes wrong: reporting a harmonic or an alias instead of the true fundamental. A student who says "the Lomb–Scargle peak was at 0.529 days, I confirmed it wasn't the 1-cycle/day alias by folding, and PDM's Θ minimized at the same period" shows they understood that a periodogram peak is a hypothesis to be tested by folding, not an answer. That is exactly the discipline that separates a real variable-star period from a sampling artifact.

questions.prompt: Why is the Lomb–Scargle periodogram, rather than a standard FFT, the tool for most astronomical time series?

options.text: It is faster than an FFT
It handles unevenly sampled data by fitting sinusoids at each trial frequency via least squares, with a known noise distribution for false-alarm statistics
It works only on evenly sampled data, like the FFT
It measures brightness rather than period

explanations.a: Lomb–Scargle is generally slower than an FFT, not faster; speed is not its advantage.
explanations.b: Correct — real light curves have gaps, so an FFT is undefined; Lomb–Scargle reframes the problem as least-squares sinusoid fitting at each frequency and (Lomb 1976, Scargle 1982) has a known power distribution enabling false-alarm probabilities.
explanations.c: The whole point is that Lomb–Scargle does NOT require even sampling, unlike the FFT.
explanations.d: It produces a power-vs-frequency spectrum to find the period; it is not a brightness measurement.

questions.prompt: In Phase Dispersion Minimization, what happens to the statistic Θ at the TRUE period?

options.text: Θ is maximized (near 1) because within-bin scatter is largest
Θ is minimized (toward 0) because points at the same phase share the same brightness, collapsing within-bin scatter
Θ equals the period in days
Θ is undefined for non-sinusoidal signals

explanations.a: That describes a WRONG period, where the fold is scrambled and within-bin variance is high, giving Θ ≈ 1.
explanations.b: Correct — Θ is within-bin variance over total variance; at the true period the fold is coherent so within-bin scatter collapses and Θ drops toward 0, hence you MINIMIZE it.
explanations.c: Θ is a dimensionless variance ratio, not a period.
explanations.d: PDM is specifically strong for non-sinusoidal signals; it assumes no shape at all.

questions.prompt: A Lomb–Scargle periodogram of a sharply-eclipsing binary shows a strong peak at frequency 2f as well as at the true fundamental f. Why?

options.text: The binary actually has two different periods
Lomb–Scargle fits sinusoids, so a non-sinusoidal (boxy) signal spreads power into harmonics at 2f, 3f, …
It is a barycentric timing error
The comparison stars are variable

explanations.a: A single eclipsing period produces harmonic peaks; there is not a second physical period.
explanations.b: Correct — a boxy eclipse is far from a pure sine, so its Fourier content includes strong harmonics; Lomb–Scargle registers power at 2f, 3f, … and you must identify the true fundamental among them.
explanations.c: Timing errors smear peaks rather than create clean integer-multiple harmonics.
explanations.d: Variable comparison stars add noise/trends but do not systematically place power at exact multiples of the eclipse frequency.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a defensible period search.

items.text: Compute a generalized Lomb–Scargle periodogram over a sensible frequency grid
Identify peaks that clear the false-alarm threshold, noting harmonics and ±1 cycle/day aliases
Phase-fold the data on each candidate period and keep the one giving a coherent light curve
Cross-check the chosen period with an independent method (e.g., PDM) and require agreement

questions.explanation: Compute the periodogram, flag significant peaks while accounting for harmonics/aliases, fold on each candidate to see which yields a coherent curve, then confirm with an independent method like PDM before trusting the period.

lessons.label: Phase Folding and the Box-Least-Squares Transit Search

sections.heading: Phase folding: stacking cycles to beat the noise
sections.body: Once you have a candidate period P and a reference epoch t₀, you convert each timestamp to a PHASE: φ = ((t − t₀)/P) mod 1, a number from 0 to 1 marking where in the cycle the point falls. Plotting brightness against phase collapses every observed cycle onto a single canonical cycle — this is PHASE FOLDING. Its power is statistical: a transit only ~0.5% deep, invisible in any single noisy cycle, becomes obvious when hundreds of cycles are stacked, because coherent signal adds while independent noise averages down as 1/√N. Kepler folded four years of data — hundreds of orbits for a short-period planet — to pull Earth-sized transits out of the photon noise. A correct period produces a sharp, phase-aligned dip; a slightly wrong period smears the transit across phase into a shallow, widened trough — which is itself a sensitive diagnostic that your period is off.

sections.heading: BLS: matched-filtering for a box
sections.body: A transit is not a sine wave — it is close to a flat-bottomed BOX: the star sits at constant brightness, drops by depth δ for the transit duration, then returns. The BOX-LEAST-SQUARES algorithm (Kovács, Zucker & Mazeh 2002) is a matched filter for exactly this shape. It scans a grid of trial periods; for each, it folds the data and slides a two-level box (an "in-transit" low level and an "out-of-transit" high level) over all candidate epochs and durations, choosing the fit that minimizes the residual sum of squares. The output is a spectrum of SIGNAL DETECTION EFFICIENCY (SDE) versus period, and simultaneously the best-fit depth, duration, and epoch. Because BLS matches the true transit shape rather than a sinusoid, it is dramatically more sensitive to shallow transits than a plain Lomb–Scargle — it is the workhorse behind Kepler, K2, and TESS planet pipelines.

sections.heading: From a box to a planet — and the traps
sections.body: BLS hands you a depth δ, and depth is (Rp/Rs)² — the planet-to-star area ratio — so Rp/Rs = √δ, and multiplying by the independently known stellar radius gives the planet's physical radius. The transit duration and period further constrain the orbit. But a box fit is only a candidate, never a planet: eclipsing binaries, background blends, and starspot-crossing artifacts all mimic boxes. The standard vetting checks that the box has a flat bottom (not V-shaped, which flags a grazing binary), that ODD and EVEN transits have equal depth (unequal depths reveal a binary's two stars), and that there is no secondary eclipse at phase 0.5. Only a candidate that survives this gauntlet — ideally with a radial-velocity mass — graduates from "BLS box" to "planet."

lessons.workedExample: A student runs BLS on a TESS light curve and gets a strong SDE peak at P = 3.52 days with best-fit depth δ = 0.0121 (1.21%) and duration 2.1 hours. The radius ratio is Rp/Rs = √0.0121 = 0.11, so the planet is 11% of the star's radius. The host is a Sun-like star, R_s ≈ 1.0 R_☉ ≈ 696,000 km, giving Rp ≈ 0.11 × 696,000 ≈ 76,600 km ≈ 1.07 R_Jupiter — a hot Jupiter. Vetting: the folded transit shows a flat (not V-shaped) bottom, the odd and even transits match in depth to within the error bars, and there is no dip at phase 0.5. It survives, so the student reports it as a planet CANDIDATE and notes that a radial-velocity follow-up is needed to confirm a planetary (not brown-dwarf or stellar) mass — because BLS gives a radius, never a mass.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges press on the gap between "a box was detected" and "a planet was found," because that gap is where careful students are separated from credulous ones. The give-away answers are the vetting checks: flat-bottomed vs. V-shaped (planet vs. grazing binary), odd/even depth equality (single object vs. two stars), and absence of a secondary eclipse. A student who folded on the BLS period, showed those three checks passing, and then said "depth gives radius; I still need RV for the mass" has demonstrated they know both what BLS measures and what it cannot.

questions.prompt: How is the phase of an observation at time t computed, given period P and epoch t₀?

options.text: φ = (t − t₀) × P
φ = ((t − t₀)/P) mod 1
φ = t/t₀
φ = P/(t − t₀)

explanations.a: Multiplying by P has the wrong units and does not wrap into a 0–1 cycle fraction.
explanations.b: Correct — you divide the elapsed time by the period and take the fractional part, giving a phase from 0 to 1 that marks position within the cycle.
explanations.c: t/t₀ ignores the period entirely and is not a cycle fraction.
explanations.d: This inverts the relationship and does not yield a bounded 0–1 phase.

questions.prompt: BLS finds a transit with depth δ = 0.0025. What is the planet-to-star radius ratio?

options.text: Undetermined without radial velocities

explanations.a: That is the depth (area ratio) itself; the radius ratio is its square root.
explanations.b: Correct — depth = (Rp/Rs)², so Rp/Rs = √0.0025 = 0.05; the planet is 5% of the star's radius.
explanations.c: 0.5 would require depth = 0.25; √0.0025 is 0.05, not 0.5.
explanations.d: The radius ratio comes straight from depth; it is the MASS that needs radial velocities, not the radius ratio.

questions.prompt: Why is BLS more sensitive to shallow transits than a plain Lomb–Scargle periodogram?

options.text: It uses barycentric time and Lomb–Scargle does not
It matches the actual flat-bottomed box shape of a transit rather than a sinusoid, concentrating the signal instead of spreading it into harmonics
It requires fewer data points
It measures mass directly

explanations.a: Both can (and should) use barycentric time; that is not the source of BLS's edge.
explanations.b: Correct — BLS is a matched filter for the two-level box a transit actually produces, so it captures the signal coherently, whereas a sinusoidal fit leaks a boxy signal into weaker harmonics.
explanations.c: BLS does not need fewer points; its advantage is shape-matching, not data economy.
explanations.d: BLS returns depth (a radius ratio), never mass.

questions.prompt: Match each transit-vetting check to the false positive it rules out.

left.text: Equal odd- and even-numbered transit depths

right.text: Rejects a grazing eclipsing binary (which gives a V-shape)
Rejects a binary whose two stars alternate deep/shallow eclipses
Rejects a stellar companion producing a secondary eclipse
Confirms a planetary (not stellar/brown-dwarf) mass, which depth cannot give

questions.explanation: A flat bottom rules out a grazing binary's V-shape; equal odd/even depths rule out a two-star binary; no phase-0.5 dip rules out a secondary eclipse; and radial velocities supply the mass a transit depth can never provide.

lessons.label: Aliasing, the Window Function, and Sampling Irregular Time Series

sections.heading: Aliasing: when the sampling rhythm impersonates a signal
sections.body: Every time series is a true signal MULTIPLIED by a sampling pattern — the set of instants you actually observed. Any periodicity in that sampling pattern imprints itself on the periodogram, producing ALIASES: false peaks at frequencies f_alias = f_true ± n·f_sample for integer n. For ground-based astronomy the dominant sampling frequency is 1 cycle per day (you can only observe at night), so every real peak is flanked by twins spaced 1 cycle/day away, and a fainter set spaced 1 cycle/year from the annual observing window. The classic disaster is a true frequency and its daily alias both clearing the significance threshold; report the wrong one and your "period" is really a beat between the star and Earth's rotation. This is not a rare edge case — it is the single most common way a variable-star or exoplanet period is published wrong.

sections.heading: The spectral window function makes the aliases visible
sections.body: You do not have to guess where aliases will land — you can COMPUTE them. The SPECTRAL WINDOW FUNCTION is the periodogram of the sampling times alone (treating every observation as having brightness 1), and it maps out exactly which spurious frequencies your cadence manufactures. A true signal's periodogram is, in effect, the true spectrum CONVOLVED with this window function, so each real peak is reproduced at every offset where the window has a spike. Practically: compute the window function first, note its 1 cycle/day and 1 cycle/year spikes, and when a periodogram peak sits exactly one window-spike away from another peak, you know they are aliases of each other, not two real signals. Distinguishing the true peak among aliases usually comes down to which one phase-folds into a physically coherent, single-valued light curve.

sections.heading: Nyquist, undersampling, and irregular cadence
sections.body: For EVENLY sampled data at spacing Δt, the NYQUIST FREQUENCY f_Ny = 1/(2Δt) is the highest frequency you can recover; anything faster is aliased down below it and masquerades as a slower signal — you cannot tell a signal above Nyquist from its reflection. A signal sampled at exactly twice per cycle sits right at Nyquist; sample any coarser and you UNDERSAMPLE, folding real fast variability onto false slow variability. Irregular sampling complicates this — there is no single Nyquist frequency, and in fact good irregular ("random") cadence can suppress aliases and push the effective frequency ceiling higher than naive Δt suggests, which is why survey schedulers deliberately jitter and interleave visits. The defensive habit is universal: report the window function alongside the periodogram, and treat any peak near a window spike as guilty until phase-folding proves it innocent.

lessons.workedExample: A student observes a δ Scuti pulsator once per night (sampling frequency f_s = 1 cycle/day) and finds a strong periodogram peak at f = 0.28 cycles/day, suggesting P ≈ 3.6 days — oddly slow for a δ Scuti, which pulsate in hours. Suspicious, they compute the spectral window function and see the expected spike at 1 cycle/day. The candidate's DAILY ALIASES lie at 0.28 ± n·1 = 1.28, 2.28, 3.28, … cycles/day. Testing f = 2.28 cycles/day gives P = 1/2.28 = 0.44 days ≈ 10.5 hours — physically reasonable for a δ Scuti. Phase-folding on 0.44 d yields a clean sinusoidal pulse; folding on 3.6 d yields incoherent scatter. The nightly cadence had aliased a real ~10-hour pulsation down to a fake 3.6-day one. Had the student trusted the tallest peak, they would have published a period wrong by a factor of eight — a pure artifact of sampling once per rotation of the Earth.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "how do you know that's the real period and not an alias?" precisely because aliasing is the most common and most invisible failure in time-domain work — the wrong peak can be perfectly significant. A student who says "I computed the spectral window function, saw the 1 cycle/day spike, checked that my peak's neighbors were daily aliases, and confirmed the true period by which one phase-folds coherently" demonstrates they understand that sampling itself injects signal. Trusting the tallest peak without a window function is the tell of someone who does not.

questions.prompt: For ground-based nightly observations, aliases in the periodogram appear at which spacing from the true frequency?

options.text: Integer multiples of 1 cycle per hour
Integer multiples of 1 cycle per day (with a fainter 1 cycle/year set), i.e. f_true ± n·f_sample
At exactly half the true frequency
Aliases do not occur for periodic signals

explanations.a: The dominant ground cadence is once per night, so the alias spacing is 1 cycle/day, not per hour.
explanations.b: Correct — the sampling frequency of nightly data is 1 cycle/day, so aliases fall at f_true ± n·(1 cycle/day), with a secondary 1 cycle/year comb from the annual observing window.
explanations.c: Half the frequency is a harmonic/subharmonic issue, not the daily-alias spacing.
explanations.d: Aliases are exactly a periodic-signal phenomenon; uneven sampling makes them worse, not absent.

questions.prompt: What is the spectral window function, and why compute it?

options.text: The periodogram of the brightness values only, ignoring the times
The periodogram of the sampling TIMES alone; it reveals exactly which alias frequencies your cadence manufactures, since the true spectrum is convolved with it
A smoothing filter applied to the light curve
The Nyquist frequency of the data

explanations.a: It is built from the sampling times (each treated as amplitude 1), not from the brightness values.
