The community answer is "alert brokers" — automated systems such as ALeRCE, ANTARES, Fink, and Lasair that ingest the full alert stream, filter and classify it (often with machine learning), and forward the handful of interesting events to astronomers. The astronomer’s job shifts from taking the data to writing the filter that finds the needle.

sections.heading: Vera Rubin and the ten-year movie
sections.body: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, on Cerro Pachón in Chile, pushes this to an extreme. Its 8.4-meter Simonyi Survey Telescope feeds the largest digital camera ever built — a 3.2-gigapixel focal plane with a 9.6-square-degree field — and its Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will image the entire visible southern sky every three to four nights for ten years, releasing first science images in 2025. The result is effectively a decade-long time-lapse movie of the sky, and a flood of data: on the order of 20 terabytes and roughly 10 million transient alerts every single night. That volume makes automated brokering and machine classification not a convenience but a hard requirement — no plausible number of humans could eyeball ten million alerts a night — which sets up the central open debate of the next lesson: what happens to the human observer when the data outstrips human inspection entirely.

lessons.workedExample: Compare the survey firepower across three eras with a rough cadence-and-volume view. SDSS imaged a field essentially once, building a static catalog. ZTF, with its 47 deg² camera, covers the ~20,000 deg² of accessible sky about every 2 nights and emits of order 10⁵ alerts per night. Rubin/LSST, with a 9.6 deg² field on an 8.4-m telescope, revisits the whole southern sky every ~3–4 nights and emits about 10⁷ alerts per night — roughly a hundred times ZTF’s alert rate. If a single trained person could triage even one alert every 10 seconds nonstop, that is 8,640 alerts in a 24-hour day; clearing 10 million would require about 10,000,000 / 8,640 ≈ 1,160 people working every hour of every day. That impossibility is exactly why alert brokers and machine classifiers are mandatory infrastructure, not optional add-ons.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the survey firehose to test whether a student understands that data volume itself reshapes method. A strong answer connects three ideas: difference imaging is how change is detected, alerts are the data product, and brokers/ML are forced by a scale (≥10 million alerts/night for Rubin) that no human team could inspect. If your project pulled from ZTF or a broker feed, being able to explain where an "alert" comes from and why it was filtered by machine shows you understand the pipeline you drank from, rather than treating a transient catalog as if a person hand-picked it.

questions.prompt: How does a time-domain survey detect that something in the sky has changed?

options.text: By measuring the color of every object in a single image
By difference imaging: subtracting a deep reference image from a new one and inspecting the residual
By taking a spectrum of every star every night
By comparing photographic plates to CCD frames

explanations.a: Color from one image says nothing about change over time; it is a static measurement.
explanations.b: Correct — difference (subtraction) imaging removes the static sky by subtracting a reference; whatever is left in the residual is something that appeared, vanished, moved, or varied.
explanations.c: Taking a spectrum of every star nightly is infeasible and is not how transients are flagged; imaging then differencing is.
explanations.d: Modern time-domain surveys difference CCD images against CCD references; plates are not part of the nightly loop.

questions.prompt: Why are automated "alert brokers" a hard requirement for Vera Rubin/LSST rather than a convenience?

options.text: Because the telescope cannot store any images
Because LSST will emit on the order of 10 million alerts per night, far beyond any human team’s ability to inspect
Because brokers make the telescope point more accurately
Because human astronomers are not allowed to look at the data

explanations.a: Rubin stores enormous image volumes; the challenge is the alert rate, not an inability to store data.
explanations.b: Correct — at roughly 10 million alerts per night, no plausible number of people could triage the stream, so automated brokers that filter and classify are mandatory infrastructure.
explanations.c: Brokers process the alert stream downstream; they have nothing to do with telescope pointing accuracy.
explanations.d: Astronomers absolutely use the data — brokers exist to hand them the interesting fraction, not to exclude them.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of facility and description is correct?

options.text: ZTF: an 8.4-m telescope in Chile with a 3.2-gigapixel camera
Vera Rubin/LSST: an 8.4-m telescope on Cerro Pachón imaging the southern sky every ~3–4 nights for ten years
ZTF: a dedicated spectroscopic redshift survey of a third of the sky
Vera Rubin/LSST: a 1.2-m Schmidt telescope at Palomar

explanations.a: The 8.4-m telescope and 3.2-gigapixel camera describe Vera Rubin, not ZTF; ZTF is a 1.2-m Schmidt at Palomar.
explanations.b: Correct — Rubin’s 8.4-m Simonyi Survey Telescope on Cerro Pachón runs the 10-year LSST, revisiting the visible southern sky every few nights.
explanations.c: ZTF is an imaging time-domain survey, not a spectroscopic redshift survey; that description fits SDSS.
explanations.d: The 1.2-m Palomar Schmidt is ZTF; Rubin is the 8.4-m telescope in Chile.

questions.prompt: Order these surveys/facilities by increasing scale of nightly transient-alert output.

items.text: SDSS (chiefly a static imaging + redshift survey, ~2000)
ZTF (~10⁵ alerts per night, first light 2018)
Vera Rubin / LSST (~10⁷ alerts per night, first science 2025)

questions.explanation: SDSS was primarily a static survey with no large nightly alert stream; ZTF issues of order 100,000 alerts per night; Rubin/LSST will issue about 10 million per night — roughly a hundredfold jump over ZTF and the reason machine brokering is mandatory.

lessons.label: GW170817: LIGO, the Kilonova, and the Birth of Multi-Messenger Astronomy

sections.heading: 17 August 2017: two neutron stars and a chirp
sections.body: On 17 August 2017 the two LIGO detectors (in Hanford, Washington and Livingston, Louisiana) and the Virgo detector in Italy recorded GW170817, a gravitational-wave signal lasting roughly 100 seconds in the detectors’ sensitive band and sweeping up in frequency — the "chirp" of two neutron stars spiraling together and merging. The inferred component masses were about 1.1 to 1.6 solar masses each, squarely in the neutron-star range, with a total system mass near 2.7 M☉. That mass is the tell: each star sits close to the ~1.4 M☉ scale set by the Chandrasekhar mass (the electron-degeneracy limit for a white dwarf, and roughly the mass at which a stellar core collapses to a neutron star), and the pair is far too light to be black holes. The gravitational waves alone said "two neutron stars merged, about 40 megaparsecs away."

sections.heading: 1.7 seconds and 11 hours later: the electromagnetic sky answers
sections.body: What made GW170817 historic was that the merger was seen in light as well as gravity. Just 1.7 seconds after the merger time, NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor independently detected a short gamma-ray burst, GRB 170817A — direct evidence that neutron-star mergers are a source of short GRBs. About 11 hours later, optical astronomers (the Swope telescope team and others) pinpointed a new source of light in the galaxy NGC 4993, roughly 130 million light-years away: the kilonova, catalogued AT 2017gfo. Its spectrum reddened and faded over days exactly as models predicted for r-process nucleosynthesis — the rapid neutron capture that forges the heaviest elements. GW170817 is, in effect, direct evidence that neutron-star mergers manufacture gold, platinum, and other heavy elements and scatter them into space.

sections.heading: A standard siren and the birth of a field
sections.body: Because a gravitational-wave chirp encodes the absolute luminosity distance to its source directly from general relativity — no cosmic distance ladder needed — GW170817 acted as a "standard siren." Combine the GW distance with the recession velocity of the host galaxy NGC 4993 (its redshift) and Hubble’s law v = H0 d yields an independent measurement of the Hubble constant, H0 ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc, from a completely new method. More broadly, GW170817 is regarded as the founding event of multi-messenger astronomy: for the first time a single cosmic event was observed through two fundamentally different channels — gravitational waves and the full electromagnetic spectrum, with roughly 70 observatories following up — pinning down the source, its physics, and its distance in ways neither channel could alone.

lessons.workedExample: Treat GW170817 as a standard siren. The gravitational-wave signal gives a luminosity distance of about d ≈ 40 Mpc directly from general relativity, with no distance ladder. The host galaxy NGC 4993 has a measured recession velocity (after correcting its redshift for local peculiar motion) of roughly v ≈ 3,000 km/s. Hubble’s law then gives H0 = v / d = 3,000 km/s / 40 Mpc ≈ 75 km/s/Mpc — consistent, within its sizable uncertainty, with the more carefully quoted result of about 70 km/s/Mpc. The power of the method is that the distance came straight from the waveform physics, so this H0 estimate is genuinely independent of the Cepheid-and-supernova ladder and of the cosmic-microwave-background route — a fresh, third way to weigh the expansion of the universe.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges raise GW170817 to test whether a student understands what "multi-messenger" actually buys you: not just a cooler headline, but independent, cross-checking measurements of the same event. A strong answer names the three channels and their timing (gravitational waves, then a gamma-ray burst 1.7 s later, then an optical kilonova ~11 hours later), explains that the kilonova is r-process element factory caught in the act, and can sketch the standard-siren H0 measurement (GW distance + host redshift + Hubble’s law). That combination of history, physics, and a real number is exactly the depth a judge distinguishes from "gravitational waves are cool."

questions.prompt: Why does the ~2.7 M☉ total mass of the GW170817 system tell astronomers it was two neutron stars, not black holes?

options.text: Because black holes cannot emit gravitational waves
Because each component is near the ~1.4 M☉ (Chandrasekhar-scale) neutron-star range, far too light to be stellar black holes
Because neutron stars are always exactly 2.7 M☉
Because the signal lasted only 100 seconds

explanations.a: Merging black holes do emit gravitational waves — that is what LIGO first detected in 2015; emission is not the discriminator.
explanations.b: Correct — the inferred component masses (~1.1–1.6 M☉ each, near the ~1.4 M☉ Chandrasekhar scale) are typical of neutron stars and far below stellar-black-hole masses, so the system is a binary neutron star.
explanations.c: The ~2.7 M☉ is the total of two stars, not a fixed neutron-star mass; individual neutron stars are ~1.1–2 M☉.
explanations.d: Signal duration reflects the in-band inspiral, not directly whether the objects are neutron stars or black holes; the masses are the tell.

questions.prompt: What is the chief scientific significance of the AT 2017gfo kilonova seen after GW170817?

options.text: It proved the universe is not expanding
Its light matched r-process nucleosynthesis, giving direct evidence that neutron-star mergers forge heavy elements like gold and platinum
It was the first detected exoplanet
It showed neutron stars are made of dark matter

explanations.a: GW170817 in fact provided a new (standard-siren) measurement supporting cosmic expansion, not evidence against it.
explanations.b: Correct — the kilonova’s reddening, fading light matched models of r-process (rapid neutron capture) nucleosynthesis, direct evidence that neutron-star mergers manufacture the heaviest elements.
explanations.c: A kilonova is a merger transient, not an exoplanet; the two are unrelated.
explanations.d: The kilonova is powered by radioactive decay of freshly synthesized heavy nuclei, not by dark matter.

questions.prompt: Why can GW170817 measure the Hubble constant as a "standard siren" independent of the cosmic distance ladder?

options.text: Because the gravitational-wave chirp encodes the absolute distance directly from general relativity, which combined with the host’s redshift gives H0 via v = H0 d
Because the kilonova is a standard candle of known luminosity
Because gamma-ray bursts always occur at a fixed distance
Because the redshift alone gives the distance without any other input

explanations.a: Correct — the waveform yields the absolute luminosity distance with no ladder; pairing that distance with the host galaxy’s recession velocity in Hubble’s law v = H0 d gives an independent H0 (~70 km/s/Mpc).
explanations.b: The method does not rely on the kilonova being a standard candle; the distance comes from the gravitational waveform itself.
explanations.c: Gamma-ray bursts do not occur at any fixed distance; they span a huge range of distances.
explanations.d: Redshift gives velocity, not distance, on its own; you still need an independent distance (here from the gravitational waves) to get H0.

questions.prompt: Order the observational events of GW170817 by the time at which they were detected.

items.text: The ~100-second gravitational-wave chirp of the inspiral and merger
The short gamma-ray burst GRB 170817A, 1.7 s after merger
The optical kilonova AT 2017gfo, pinpointed in NGC 4993 ~11 hours later
Days-long fading of the kilonova matching r-process models

questions.explanation: The gravitational waves came first (the inspiral chirp), then the gamma-ray burst just 1.7 seconds after merger, then the optical kilonova located about 11 hours later, and finally the kilonova’s days-long reddening and fading that matched r-process nucleosynthesis.

lessons.label: Galaxy Zoo, Citizen Science, and the Data-Deluge Machine-Learning Debate

sections.heading: A million galaxies, too many for the experts
sections.body: By 2007, SDSS had imaged roughly a million galaxies — far more than a small team of astronomers could visually classify by shape (spiral, elliptical, merger, edge-on). Kevin Schawinski, then a graduate student, and Chris Lintott launched Galaxy Zoo in July 2007, putting SDSS galaxy images on a website and asking the public to classify them. The response was overwhelming: hundreds of thousands of volunteers delivered tens of millions of classifications in the first year, and because many people classified each galaxy, the "wisdom of the crowd" produced statistically robust morphologies. Citizen science also turned up genuine surprises that no target list contained — the Dutch schoolteacher Hanny van Arkel spotted the strange glowing cloud now called Hanny’s Voorwerp (2007), and volunteers identified the compact "green pea" galaxies — discoveries made precisely because unbiased human eyes were looking at everything.

sections.heading: The machine steps in
sections.body: What humans did for a million galaxies cannot scale to Vera Rubin/LSST’s ten million transient alerts per night. The natural answer is machine learning: convolutional neural networks now classify galaxy morphologies and transient light curves at least as accurately as humans on the common classes, and vastly faster, and they are the only tractable way to triage a firehose of that size. Galaxy Zoo itself evolved into a hybrid, using volunteer classifications as the labeled training set that teaches the neural networks, so citizen science partly became the engine that trains its own automated successor. On the well-populated, well-understood categories — obvious spirals and ellipticals, ordinary supernovae — the machines are genuinely excellent.

sections.heading: The open debate: is the observer being replaced?
sections.body: This sets up a live controversy. One camp argues that at LSST scale the human eyeball is simply obsolete: no crowd can inspect ten million nightly alerts, so classification must be automated end to end, and citizen science survives only as a labeling service for the models. The other camp counters that machine learning is powerful exactly where it is trained and weak exactly where it is not: a classifier trained on known classes tends to force a genuinely novel object into a familiar box, so the truly unexpected discovery — the anomaly, the thing no one built a label for — still slips past the machine and is caught by a curious human. Hanny’s Voorwerp is the standing example: it was found because a person looked at something odd, not because an algorithm was searching for it. The emerging synthesis is a division of labor — machines handle the overwhelming volume of routine classification, while humans (crowd and expert) are steered by the machine toward the anomalies and outliers it flags but cannot interpret — but exactly where to draw that line is unsettled and actively argued.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a machine classifier triaging a night of transient alerts. Suppose Rubin issues 10,000,000 alerts, of which only about 1,000 are real, interesting transients and the rest are asteroids, variable stars, and image artifacts. A classifier with 99% recall correctly flags 990 of the 1,000 real events — excellent — but its 1% miss rate drops 10 genuinely interesting events on the floor every night. If even one of those missed events is a novel class the model was never trained on (an anomaly it confidently mislabels as junk), a human scanning a machine-flagged "weird outlier" list is the only path to catching it. That is the quantitative heart of the debate: automation is mandatory for the volume, yet its confident errors on unfamiliar objects are exactly where human discovery still lives.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the citizen-science / machine-learning debate to see whether a student can hold a genuine controversy in view instead of picking a slogan. A strong answer states both the case for automation (ten million alerts a night cannot be eyeballed) and its real limitation (a classifier trained on known classes tends to mislabel a truly novel object, so anomalies still need a human), and ideally names a concrete discovery — Hanny’s Voorwerp — that came from a human noticing the unexpected. If your project used an ML classifier, being able to say what it is good at and where it would fail on something new is exactly the critical-thinking a judge wants to hear.

questions.prompt: What problem did Galaxy Zoo (launched 2007) originally set out to solve?

options.text: Building a larger telescope than SDSS
Visually classifying the ~1 million SDSS galaxies, far more than a small expert team could handle
Detecting gravitational waves
Measuring the Hubble constant with standard sirens

explanations.a: Galaxy Zoo was a classification project using existing SDSS images, not a telescope-building effort.
explanations.b: Correct — SDSS had imaged about a million galaxies, too many to classify by eye internally, so Galaxy Zoo enlisted the public to sort them by morphology.
explanations.c: Gravitational-wave detection is LIGO/Virgo’s domain, unrelated to Galaxy Zoo’s morphology task.
explanations.d: Standard-siren cosmology came from GW170817, not from citizen classification of galaxy shapes.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest argument that machine classification cannot fully replace the human observer?

options.text: Computers are slower than humans at classifying images
A classifier trained on known classes tends to force a truly novel object into a familiar category, so genuine anomalies still need a human to notice them
Neural networks cannot process astronomical images at all
Humans can inspect ten million alerts per night

explanations.a: Machines are far faster than humans; speed is an argument for automation, not against it.
explanations.b: Correct — machine learning is strong on trained classes but tends to mislabel genuinely unfamiliar objects, so the unexpected discovery (the anomaly) still relies on a curious human, as with Hanny’s Voorwerp.
explanations.c: Neural networks classify astronomical images very effectively; that is precisely why they dominate routine triage.
explanations.d: No human crowd can inspect ten million alerts a night — that is the case FOR automation, not against it.

questions.prompt: How did Galaxy Zoo’s human classifications end up supporting the machine-learning systems that partly succeed it?

options.text: They replaced neural networks entirely
They provided the labeled training set used to teach convolutional neural networks to classify galaxies
They were discarded once machines improved
They were used to build larger telescopes

explanations.a: Human classifications did not replace neural networks; they became the input that trains them.
explanations.b: Correct — the crowd’s labels became the training data that teaches CNNs, so citizen science partly became the engine that trains its own automated successor.
explanations.c: The classifications were not discarded; their lasting value is precisely as training labels.
explanations.d: Classifications are data labels, not hardware; they do not build telescopes.

questions.prompt: Match each discovery task to the approach best suited to it in the data-deluge era.

left.text: Triaging ten million routine transient alerts every night
Catching a genuinely novel object no label exists for
Producing the labeled examples that teach the classifier

right.text: Machine-learning classifier / alert broker
A curious human noticing the unexpected (e.g. Hanny’s Voorwerp)
Citizen-science crowd classifications

questions.explanation: Machines are mandatory for the sheer volume of routine classification; humans remain essential for catching genuinely novel anomalies the model cannot recognize (Hanny’s Voorwerp is the classic case); and citizen-science crowds supply the labeled training data that teaches the classifiers — the emerging division of labor rather than one side simply winning.

units.label: Advanced Methods and Designing a Time-Domain Project

lessons.label: Difference Imaging: the Image-Subtraction Engine Behind Modern Transient Surveys

sections.heading: The core idea: find what changed, not what is there
sections.body: Modern transient surveys — the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF, on-sky since 2018), Pan-STARRS, the Dark Energy Survey, and soon Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) — image the same patch of sky again and again and ask a single question: what changed since last time? A supernova, an asteroid, a microlensing event, or a flaring star is a needle in a haystack of millions of static stars and galaxies. The trick is DIFFERENCE IMAGING (also called image subtraction): take a deep, high-quality REFERENCE (or template) image built by stacking many past exposures, align it to a new SCIENCE image, and subtract. Everything that did not change cancels to near-zero; only sources that appeared, vanished, brightened, or moved survive as residuals. You then do photometry on the residual alone, which is why a supernova buried in the glare of its host galaxy — completely invisible in the raw frame — pops out cleanly in the difference image.

sections.heading: Why you cannot just subtract pixel-by-pixel
sections.body: Naive subtraction fails badly, for two reasons. First, PHOTOMETRIC SCALING: the two images were taken through different amounts of atmosphere and sky brightness, so a genuinely constant star has different counts in each. Second, and worse, the POINT-SPREAD FUNCTION (PSF) differs: atmospheric seeing blurs each exposure by a different amount, so the same star is a sharp 1.2-arcsecond blob one night and a fat 2.0-arcsecond blob the next. Subtract those two profiles and a perfectly constant star leaves a DIPOLE residual — a bright core ringed by a dark halo (or vice versa) — with leftover flux tens of percent of the original star. Do that across a whole field and you get millions of false "transients," each one just a seeing mismatch. Before subtracting you must first make the two PSFs identical.

sections.heading: Optimal image subtraction: convolve to a common PSF
sections.body: The field-standard solution is Alard & Lupton's Optimal Image Subtraction (1998): degrade the sharper image to match the blurrier one by convolving it with a small CONVOLUTION KERNEL, and solve for that kernel — plus a smooth photometric-scaling term — by least squares so the subtracted residual over all the static stars is minimized. Alard & Lupton wrote the kernel as a sum of fixed Gaussian-times-polynomial basis functions, making the fit linear; Bramich (2008) later showed you can solve for the kernel pixel values directly with no analytic basis. A newer statistically optimal method, ZOGY (Zackay, Ofek & Gal-Yam 2016), derives the properly noise-weighted difference and a matched-filter "score" image, and is used operationally by ZTF, with an implementation also available in the Rubin/LSST pipeline (whose baseline alert-production difference imaging is itself Alard & Lupton-based). Whatever the algorithm, the workflow is the same: align, PSF-match, scale, subtract, then detect and measure sources in the clean difference image.

lessons.workedExample: A student pulls two survey images of the same field. A bright, genuinely constant star has 10,000 counts at its peak. The reference frame has seeing FWHM 1.2 arcsec; the science frame was taken in poorer seeing, FWHM 1.9 arcsec, so the same star is spread wider and shallower. Subtracting the raw frames, the sharp reference core overshoots the broad science core: the residual is a dipole with a positive peak near +3,000 counts and a negative trough near -2,000 counts — about 30 percent of the star's flux, even though the star did not change at all. Run through the same field, that mismatch fabricates a "transient" on nearly every bright star. Now the student convolves the reference with a kernel that broadens its 1.2-arcsec PSF to match the 1.9-arcsec science PSF and rescales the flux, then subtracts: the residual on that same constant star collapses to under 1 percent (photon noise), while a true supernova — present in the science frame but absent from the reference — remains as a clean positive point source they can measure.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love to ask "how do you know your detection is real and not an artifact of the two images being different?" A student who says "I subtracted the pictures" but cannot explain PSF matching has probably reported seeing-mismatch dipoles as discoveries. The tell of real understanding is naming the PSF and photometric-scaling problems and describing the convolution-kernel fix — ideally citing Alard & Lupton or ZOGY. It signals the student knows a difference image measures CHANGE, and that the hard part is making everything except the change cancel.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of difference imaging in a transient survey?

options.text: To increase the resolution of a single exposure beyond the diffraction limit
To isolate sources that changed between a reference image and a new image by subtracting the two
To measure the parallax of nearby stars
To remove the color of stars so all objects look white

explanations.a: Difference imaging does not beat the diffraction limit; it degrades the sharper image on purpose to match the blurrier one before subtracting.
explanations.b: Correct — subtracting a stacked reference from a new science image cancels everything static and leaves only sources that appeared, vanished, brightened, or moved, so a supernova buried in its host galaxy becomes visible.
explanations.c: Parallax is measured from a star's apparent shift versus distant background over the year, not from image subtraction of transients.
explanations.d: Subtraction does not remove color; images are typically differenced within a single filter band, and color is preserved across bands.

questions.prompt: Why does naively subtracting two raw images of the same field produce false "transients" on constant stars?

options.text: Stars physically move too fast to line up between exposures
The two images have different PSFs (seeing) and photometric scaling, so a constant star leaves a dipole residual
CCD detectors cannot record the same star twice
The sky rotates, so no two images can ever be aligned

explanations.a: Ordinary stars do not move perceptibly between two nights; the residual comes from PSF and brightness mismatches, not stellar motion.
explanations.b: Correct — different seeing makes the same star a different width in each frame, and different sky/atmosphere makes it a different brightness, so raw subtraction of a constant star leaves a bright-plus-dark dipole that mimics a transient.
explanations.c: CCDs record the same star fine across exposures; the issue is matching the images before subtracting, not the detector.
explanations.d: Field rotation is corrected during alignment; the residual problem is PSF/scaling mismatch, which alignment alone does not fix.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an Alard & Lupton style optimal image-subtraction pipeline.

items.text: Align the science image to the reference (astrometric registration)
Solve for a convolution kernel + photometric scaling that matches the sharper image to the blurrier one
Convolve and subtract to produce the difference image
Detect and measure sources in the clean difference image

questions.explanation: You first register the frames to a common pixel grid, then solve (by least squares over the static stars) for the kernel and scaling that make the two PSFs and brightnesses identical, then apply that kernel and subtract to get the difference image, and finally run detection/photometry on the residuals — only sources that changed survive.

questions.prompt: Match each method or survey to what it is.

right.text: Optimal image subtraction using a basis-function kernel solved by least squares
Statistically optimal, noise-weighted difference image and matched-filter score
A wide-field time-domain survey generating hundreds of thousands of alerts per night
The small function convolved into the sharper image to match the blurrier image's PSF

questions.explanation: Alard & Lupton (1998) introduced optimal image subtraction with a least-squares basis-function kernel; ZOGY (Zackay, Ofek & Gal-Yam 2016) is the statistically optimal noise-weighted formulation used operationally by ZTF (and available as an implementation in the Rubin/LSST pipeline, whose baseline difference imaging is Alard & Lupton-based); ZTF is a wide-field transient survey producing enormous nightly alert streams; and the convolution kernel is the small function used to PSF-match the sharper image to the blurrier one before subtraction.

lessons.label: Detrending Space Photometry: Kepler/TESS Systematics, SAP vs PDCSAP, and Cotrending Basis Vectors

sections.heading: Why space photometry needs detrending at all
sections.body: NASA's Kepler mission (launched March 2009, PI William Borucki) and its successor TESS (launched April 2018) reach photometric precisions impossible from the ground — Kepler could detect brightness changes of tens of parts per million (ppm) — because they sit above the atmosphere and stare at the same field for long stretches. But "above the atmosphere" is not "noise-free." The spacecraft drifts and its pointing jitters; the optics breathe as the telescope warms and cools around its orbit; the field slowly shears across the detector through the year because of DIFFERENTIAL VELOCITY ABERRATION (the spacecraft's changing velocity relative to the stars); and individual CCD pixels have their own gain and sensitivity quirks. These INSTRUMENTAL SYSTEMATICS imprint slow trends and jumps on every light curve that can be far larger than the ~84 ppm dip an Earth-sized planet makes. Finding small transits means removing these trends without erasing the astrophysical signal you came for.

sections.heading: SAP vs PDCSAP: two flux columns, two different things
sections.body: Kepler and TESS data products give you two flux time series per target. SAP FLUX (Simple Aperture Photometry) is the raw sum of counts in the pixel aperture around the star — honest but riddled with systematics: you will see the flux ramp up or down by a fraction of a percent over a month, drift with the spacecraft's thermal cycle, and jump after data downlinks or pointing tweaks. PDCSAP FLUX (Pre-search Data Conditioning SAP) is the pipeline's systematics-corrected version, produced by the PDC module (Stumpe et al. 2012; Smith et al. 2012), and it is what most transit searches use because the instrumental trends are largely gone while real transits are preserved. The catch: PDC can occasionally over-correct and distort or suppress genuine long-timescale astrophysical variability (starspot modulation, long-period eclipses), so careful projects check SAP too.

sections.heading: Cotrending Basis Vectors: exploiting what all stars share
sections.body: The key insight behind the correction is that instrumental systematics are COMMON-MODE: pointing drift or a thermal ramp nudges thousands of stars on the same CCD in the same way at the same time, whereas a transit or a flare affects only one star. So the pipeline takes many quiet stars on a detector, extracts the shared trends (via a principal-component-like decomposition), and calls the resulting handful of common signals COTRENDING BASIS VECTORS (CBVs). Each target's light curve is then fit as a linear combination of these CBVs, and that fit is subtracted, removing the common instrumental part while leaving the star-specific signal. The danger is OVERFITTING: use too many CBVs (or too much weight) and the fit starts absorbing the star's real variability. This is why quality metrics like CDPP (Combined Differential Photometric Precision) are tracked — you want the flattest noise floor without eating your transits.

lessons.workedExample: A student downloads a Kepler light curve to look for an Earth-analog transit. The expected depth is fixed by geometry: transit depth = (Rp/Rs)^2 = (R_earth/R_sun)^2 = (6,371 km / 696,000 km)^2 = (0.00915)^2 ≈ 8.4×10^-5 ≈ 84 ppm. Looking at the SAP flux, the student sees the whole curve sloping downward by about 0.4 percent (4,000 ppm) over the 90-day quarter — differential velocity aberration slowly moving the star in the aperture — which utterly swamps an 84-ppm dip. Switching to PDCSAP flux, that slope and the post-downlink jumps are gone; the curve is flat to roughly its per-cadence noise. For a 12th-magnitude Kepler star the 6.5-hour CDPP noise is around 30 ppm, so a single Earth transit has signal-to-noise ≈ 84/30 ≈ 2.8 — too weak to trust alone. (Strictly, the per-transit SNR should be computed against the noise integrated over the full transit duration — a central Earth-analog transit lasts ~13 hours, not 6.5 — so this uses the 6.5-hr CDPP as an illustrative stand-in and slightly understates the noise-averaging benefit; the order-of-magnitude conclusion is unchanged.) Because an Earth-like orbit gives roughly one transit per year, the student folds the four transits from Kepler's ~4-year baseline, boosting SNR by √4 = 2 to ≈ 5.6 — right at the edge of a credible detection, which is exactly why Earth analogs were so hard and needed the full mission.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe "how did you know that dip was a planet and not the instrument?" because space-photometry projects live or die on detrending. A student who blindly used one flux column and never mentions systematics is vulnerable; one who explains SAP versus PDCSAP, names cotrending basis vectors as the common-mode correction, and warns that over-aggressive detrending can erase real variability shows they understand the measurement — not just that they downloaded a pretty light curve. Bonus credit for stating the expected transit depth from (Rp/Rs)^2 and comparing it to the noise floor.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between SAP flux and PDCSAP flux in Kepler/TESS data?

options.text: SAP is in magnitudes and PDCSAP is in flux units, but they are otherwise identical
SAP is the raw aperture-summed flux; PDCSAP is the same flux after the pipeline removes instrumental systematics
SAP is from the ground and PDCSAP is from space
PDCSAP is raw and SAP is the corrected version

explanations.a: Both are flux time series, not one in magnitudes; the difference is systematics correction, not units.
explanations.b: Correct — SAP (Simple Aperture Photometry) is the raw summed counts with all instrumental trends still in it, while PDCSAP is the Pre-search Data Conditioning version with common-mode systematics removed.
explanations.c: Both come from the same space telescope's data; neither is a ground measurement.
explanations.d: This is backwards — PDCSAP is the corrected product and SAP is the raw one.

questions.prompt: Cotrending Basis Vectors (CBVs) work because instrumental systematics are:

options.text: Common-mode — they affect many stars on the same detector the same way at the same time
Unique to each star, so they must be modeled one star at a time from scratch
Purely random noise with no time structure
Caused only by the target star's own starspots

explanations.a: Correct — pointing drift, thermal ramps, and aberration nudge thousands of stars identically, so shared trends extracted from many quiet stars (the CBVs) can be fit to and subtracted from any target.
explanations.b: The whole point is that the trends are shared, not unique; that shared structure is what lets a common set of basis vectors correct every target.
explanations.c: Systematics have strong time structure (slopes, thermal cycles, jumps); if they were pure random noise, CBVs could not capture and remove them.
explanations.d: Starspots are astrophysical and star-specific; CBVs target the instrumental common-mode signal, and over-fitting them can wrongly absorb real starspot variability.

questions.prompt: An Earth-sized planet transiting a Sun-like star produces a transit depth of about:

options.text: About 1% (10,000 ppm)
About 84 ppm
About 50% (the star half disappears)
About 1 ppm

explanations.a: ~1% is a HOT-JUPITER depth, since a Jupiter-radius planet gives (R_jup/R_sun)^2 ≈ 0.01; an Earth is far smaller.
explanations.b: Correct — depth = (R_earth/R_sun)^2 = (6,371/696,000)^2 ≈ 8.4×10^-5 ≈ 84 ppm, which is why Earth analogs demand tens-of-ppm precision.
explanations.c: A planet blocks only a tiny fraction of the stellar disk; even a Jupiter blocks ~1%, and Earth blocks under 0.01%.
explanations.d: 1 ppm is roughly 80× too small; the correct value from (R_earth/R_sun)^2 is about 84 ppm.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of over-aggressive detrending with too many CBVs?

options.text: It permanently damages the raw CCD data
The fit starts absorbing the star's real astrophysical variability, erasing genuine signal
It makes the light curve longer in time
It converts flux into magnitudes automatically

explanations.a: Detrending operates on the flux time series, not the archived raw pixels; the raw SAP data remain available.
explanations.b: Correct — with too many basis vectors the linear fit is flexible enough to soak up real starspot modulation, long-period eclipses, or shallow transits, removing signal you wanted to keep.
explanations.c: Detrending changes the flux values, not the time span of the observation.
explanations.d: Detrending does not change units; SAP and PDCSAP are both fluxes.

lessons.label: Machine Learning in the Pipeline: Real-Bogus Filtering and Automated Variable Classification

sections.heading: The alert deluge: why humans cannot keep up
sections.body: A modern survey like ZTF produces hundreds of thousands of candidate detections in a single night from its difference images, and Rubin/LSST will produce roughly ten million alerts per night. The overwhelming majority are BOGUS — not real astrophysical transients but artifacts: bad subtractions where a bright star left a dipole, cosmic-ray hits, satellite trails, CCD bleed and saturation spikes, ghosts and diffraction features around bright stars, and edge effects. Only a small fraction are REAL transients (supernovae, asteroids, variable-star peaks, flares). No team of humans can eyeball millions of candidate image stamps a night, so surveys front-load a machine-learning REAL-BOGUS classifier that scores each candidate 0-to-1 on how likely it is to be real, and only the high-scoring candidates flow downstream to follow-up.

sections.heading: From random forests to CNNs on image stamps
sections.body: Early real-bogus filters used engineered features fed to a RANDOM FOREST — Bloom et al. (2012) for the Palomar Transient Factory and Brink et al. (2013) built classifiers from measured properties of each candidate (shape, sharpness, distance to nearest source, how the subtraction looked). The current generation feeds the raw image stamps — the science, reference, and difference cutouts — directly into a CONVOLUTIONAL NEURAL NETWORK (CNN) that learns the visual signatures of real versus bogus on its own. ZTF's braai classifier (Duev et al. 2019) is a well-known example, reaching roughly 98 percent accuracy. A parallel problem is CLASSIFICATION of the real events: given a light curve, is this an RR Lyrae, a Cepheid, an eclipsing binary, a Type Ia supernova, or a flare? Richards et al. (2011) demonstrated machine-learned variable-star classification from light-curve features (period, amplitude, colors, shape), and brokers like ALeRCE now classify ZTF's stream in near-real time.

sections.heading: Why class imbalance makes "accuracy" a liar
sections.body: The statistic that matters is not raw accuracy but the trade-off between PRECISION (of the candidates I flagged real, what fraction truly are) and RECALL (of the truly real events, what fraction I caught). This is because the classes are wildly IMBALANCED — real transients might be under 1 percent of candidates — so a lazy classifier that labels EVERYTHING bogus scores over 99 percent "accuracy" while catching zero real events. Push recall too high (flag almost everything) and precision collapses, drowning astronomers in false positives that waste precious follow-up telescope time; push precision too high and you miss real discoveries. Where you set the decision threshold is a scientific choice: a supernova-cosmology program may accept more false positives to avoid missing a rare event, while an automated robotic follow-up with limited time demands high precision.

lessons.workedExample: A student evaluates a real-bogus classifier on one night: 1,000,000 candidates, of which 1 percent (10,000) are truly real transients and 990,000 are bogus. The classifier catches 95 percent of the real ones (recall 0.95 → 9,500 true positives) but has a 1 percent false-positive rate on bogus candidates (0.01 × 990,000 = 9,900 false positives). Its raw ACCURACY looks great: (9,500 true positives + 980,100 correctly rejected bogus) / 1,000,000 ≈ 99 percent. But PRECISION tells the real story: of the 9,500 + 9,900 = 19,400 candidates it flagged real, only 9,500 actually are — precision ≈ 49 percent. So even a "99 percent accurate" classifier hands astronomers a list that is half junk, purely because real events are rare. To cut false positives the student raises the score threshold, trading a little recall (maybe down to 0.90) for far better precision — the standard lever, and exactly the reasoning a judge wants to hear about imbalanced-class problems.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "how does your pipeline decide what's a real detection?" to see whether a student understands that classification is a statistical decision with costs on both sides, not a magic yes/no. A strong answer distinguishes precision from recall, explains why raw accuracy is misleading under heavy class imbalance (99 percent accuracy while missing everything), and frames the score threshold as a deliberate trade-off tuned to the science goal and the cost of follow-up time. Naming a real system (a random forest à la Bloom/Brink, or a CNN like ZTF's braai) grounds the answer in how surveys actually work.

questions.prompt: In a transient survey pipeline, what is a "real-bogus" classifier for?

options.text: Deciding which candidate detections are genuine transients versus artifacts of the imaging
Measuring the distance to each supernova
Calibrating the telescope's focus each night
Choosing which filter band to observe in

explanations.a: Correct — after difference imaging, most candidates are artifacts (bad subtractions, cosmic rays, satellite trails); the real-bogus classifier scores each on how likely it is genuine so only promising ones go to follow-up.
explanations.b: Distances come from redshifts or standard candles, not from a real-bogus filter, which only judges whether a detection is astrophysical at all.
explanations.c: Focus calibration is an instrument task; the classifier operates on candidate detections in software, not the optics.
explanations.d: Filter choice is a scheduling decision; the classifier acts after images are taken and differenced.

questions.prompt: Why is raw "accuracy" a misleading metric for a real-bogus classifier?

options.text: Because accuracy cannot be computed for images
Because the classes are heavily imbalanced, so labeling everything bogus can score over 99% while catching zero real events
Because accuracy always equals precision
Because neural networks cannot be evaluated numerically

explanations.a: Accuracy is perfectly computable for image classifiers; the issue is that it hides failure under class imbalance.
explanations.b: Correct — if real transients are under 1% of candidates, a classifier that calls everything bogus is >99% "accurate" yet useless, so precision and recall are the meaningful metrics.
explanations.c: Accuracy and precision are different quantities; they coincide only in special cases, not in general.
explanations.d: Neural networks are routinely evaluated with numerical metrics; the point is choosing the RIGHT metric, not that evaluation is impossible.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct meaning.

right.text: Of the candidates flagged real, the fraction that truly are real
Of the truly real events, the fraction the classifier caught
An artifact such as a bad subtraction, cosmic ray, or satellite trail — not a real transient
A neural network that learns real-vs-bogus directly from science/reference/difference image stamps

questions.explanation: Precision is the purity of the flagged-real set; recall is the completeness of catching truly real events; a bogus candidate is an imaging artifact rather than an astrophysical source; and a CNN like ZTF's braai (Duev et al. 2019) classifies candidates by learning directly from the image cutouts.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of a survey's automated candidate-handling pipeline.

items.text: Difference imaging flags millions of raw candidate detections
A real-bogus classifier scores each candidate and rejects likely artifacts
Surviving real candidates are classified by light-curve type (SN, RR Lyrae, etc.)
High-priority events are sent for telescope follow-up

questions.explanation: Difference imaging generates the flood of candidates, the real-bogus filter culls artifacts, a classifier then types the surviving real events by their light curves, and only the highest-priority events consume scarce follow-up telescope time.

lessons.label: Combining Surveys: a Multi-Epoch, Multi-Wavelength Study from Public Data

sections.heading: The archives are open — the science is in combining them
sections.body: You do not need your own telescope to do original astronomy. Enormous public archives already cover most of the sky at many wavelengths and epochs: Gaia (all-sky astrometry, parallaxes, and optical photometry — Data Release 3 in 2022 cataloged about 1.8 billion sources); SDSS (optical imaging and spectra); Pan-STARRS and ZTF (optical time-domain); 2MASS (near-infrared J, H, Ks); WISE (mid-infrared W1–W4); GALEX (ultraviolet). Each survey sees a different slice of the electromagnetic spectrum or a different moment in time. The original science comes from COMBINING them: cross-match a source across catalogs to assemble its SPECTRAL ENERGY DISTRIBUTION (SED — brightness versus wavelength), or stitch together many surveys' epochs to build a long-baseline light curve no single survey could.

sections.heading: Cross-matching: harder than it looks
sections.body: To combine catalogs you must decide that "this source here" and "that source there" are the SAME object. The basic tool is positional CROSS-MATCHING: pair sources whose sky coordinates agree within a small radius (often 1–3 arcsec, set by the surveys' astrometric precision and crowding). Two subtleties bite. First, PROPER MOTION: nearby stars move measurably across the sky over years, so a source's position in a 2003-era 2MASS catalog differs from its Gaia position unless you propagate coordinates to a common epoch using Gaia's measured proper motion. Second, PHOTOMETRIC SYSTEMS: surveys report brightness in different systems (AB versus Vega magnitudes) and zero points, so you must convert to a common system before comparing fluxes across bands — otherwise your SED has artificial jumps. Archive services like VizieR, MAST, and IRSA provide cross-match tools that handle much of this.

sections.heading: What the combination buys you
sections.body: Once matched, the payoff is real physics. Gaia's PARALLAX gives a geometric distance — d (parsecs) = 1 / p (arcseconds) — which converts apparent magnitude to absolute magnitude and pins the star on a color-magnitude diagram. Adding infrared points from 2MASS and WISE reveals dust: a young star or debris disk shows an INFRARED EXCESS, more mid-infrared flux than the stellar photosphere alone predicts, because circumstellar dust reradiates absorbed starlight. Adding time-domain epochs from ZTF and archival plates extends a variable star's baseline to catch long periods. This multi-survey approach is how many discoveries now happen — not with a new telescope, but by asking a question that only the combination of existing data can answer.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to characterize a candidate debris-disk star from public data. Gaia gives a parallax p = 5.0 milliarcsec = 0.0050 arcsec, so the distance is d = 1/p = 1/0.0050 = 200 parsecs. Gaia also gives apparent magnitude G ≈ 9.0; the absolute magnitude is M = m − 5·log10(d/10 pc) = 9.0 − 5·log10(20) = 9.0 − 5(1.301) = 9.0 − 6.505 ≈ 2.5, consistent with a main-sequence A/F star. The student cross-matches the position (propagating with Gaia's proper motion to the 2MASS epoch, within a 2-arcsec radius) and pulls 2MASS J, H, Ks and WISE W1–W4, converting all to a common flux system. Plotting the SED, the optical-through-near-IR points trace a stellar photosphere, but the WISE W3 (12 μm) and W4 (22 μm) points sit well ABOVE the photospheric extrapolation — an infrared excess. That excess is the signature of cool circumstellar dust reradiating starlight: a debris disk, identified entirely from three public catalogs with no new observations.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "where did your data come from, and how do you know two catalog entries are the same star?" because archival, multi-survey projects are only as good as the cross-match. A student who names the surveys, states the cross-match radius, and mentions the two traps — proper motion between epochs and differing photometric systems (AB vs Vega) — demonstrates they did real data work rather than eyeballing a table. Turning a Gaia parallax into a distance (d = 1/p) and reading an infrared excess off an SED shows the combination produced actual physics, which is the whole point of a public-data project.

questions.prompt: A star has a measured parallax of 5.0 milliarcseconds. What is its distance?

options.text: 5 parsecs
200 parsecs
0.2 parsecs
5000 parsecs

explanations.a: 5 pc would come from treating the 5 as arcseconds; but 5 mas = 0.005 arcsec, and distance is the reciprocal.
explanations.b: Correct — d (pc) = 1 / p (arcsec) = 1 / 0.0050 = 200 pc, using p = 5.0 mas = 0.0050 arcsec.
explanations.c: 0.2 pc would come from inverting 5 arcsec instead of 0.005 arcsec — off by the milliarcsecond conversion.
explanations.d: 5000 pc would require p = 0.2 mas; a 5 mas parallax corresponds to 200 pc, not 5000.

questions.prompt: Why must you account for proper motion when cross-matching a star between Gaia and an older survey like 2MASS?

options.text: Because the star changes color between surveys
Because nearby stars move measurably across the sky over years, so their catalog positions differ by epoch
Because Gaia and 2MASS use different constellations
Because proper motion changes a star's intrinsic brightness

explanations.a: A star's intrinsic color does not change between surveys; the cross-match problem is positional, driven by motion across the sky.
explanations.b: Correct — a nearby star's position shifts over the years between the 2MASS and Gaia epochs, so you must propagate coordinates to a common epoch (using Gaia proper motion) or a tight radius will miss the match.
explanations.c: Both surveys use the same sky and coordinate framework; constellations are irrelevant to cross-matching.
explanations.d: Proper motion is transverse angular motion; it does not change the star's luminosity.

questions.prompt: An SED built from optical (Gaia), near-IR (2MASS), and mid-IR (WISE) shows the WISE points sitting well above the stellar photosphere. This "infrared excess" indicates:

options.text: A calibration error that must be discarded
Cool circumstellar dust (e.g., a debris disk) reradiating absorbed starlight
The star is moving toward us (blueshift)
The star has no atmosphere

explanations.a: While calibration must always be checked, a consistent excess specifically in the mid-infrared is a known astrophysical signal, not automatically an error.
explanations.b: Correct — dust around the star absorbs starlight and reradiates it in the mid-infrared, producing more W3/W4 flux than the bare photosphere predicts; this is the classic debris-disk signature.
explanations.c: Blueshift is a wavelength shift from radial velocity, not a broadband excess of infrared flux.
explanations.d: An infrared excess reflects surrounding dust, not the presence or absence of a stellar atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Match each survey to the wavelength regime or data it primarily provides.

right.text: All-sky astrometry, parallaxes, and optical photometry
Near-infrared J, H, Ks photometry
Mid-infrared W1–W4 photometry (dust tracer)
Optical time-domain (repeated epochs / variability)

questions.explanation: Gaia delivers astrometry, parallaxes, and optical photometry; 2MASS covers the near-infrared (J, H, Ks); WISE covers the mid-infrared (W1–W4), ideal for detecting warm/cool dust; and ZTF provides repeated optical epochs for time-domain variability — combining them yields distances, SEDs, and long-baseline light curves.

lessons.label: Designing and Defending a Time-Domain / Photometry Science-Fair Project

sections.heading: A defensible question and a real control
sections.body: A strong time-domain project starts with a specific, testable question — "what is the period of variable star X?", "can I recover the transit of hot Jupiter Y with a backyard telescope?", "does source Z's brightness change over ZTF's baseline?" — not a vague "study the stars." The control that makes photometry trustworthy is DIFFERENTIAL PHOTOMETRY: you never measure a target's brightness in absolute terms from the ground (clouds, air mass, and transparency change minute to minute). Instead you measure the target RELATIVE to several nearby, constant COMPARISON STARS in the same frame. Any atmospheric dimming hits target and comparisons together and divides out, so a real dip in the target-to-comparison ratio is astrophysical. Choosing good comparisons — constant, similar brightness and color, in the same field — is the single most important design decision, and organizations like the AAVSO publish vetted comparison-star sequences for variable stars.

sections.heading: Systematics, uncertainty, and honest error bars
sections.body: Judges reward projects that treat noise and systematics head-on. Every measured point needs an UNCERTAINTY: photon (Poisson) noise scales as the square root of the counts, so signal-to-noise improves as √N with more photons or stacked frames, and you should also account for sky background, read noise, and scintillation. Beyond random noise, name your SYSTEMATICS: differential atmospheric extinction if a comparison star has a very different color, detector nonlinearity near saturation, a meridian flip that shifts the star on the chip, or imperfect flat-fielding. A project that plots error bars, states its noise floor, and reports what it did NOT control is far stronger than one with a suspiciously clean curve. The lessons of space-photometry detrending apply on the ground too: trends you do not model masquerade as signal.

sections.heading: The right statistics: finding and trusting a period
sections.body: For a periodic signal — a pulsating variable, an eclipsing binary, a rotating spotted star — the standard tool is the LOMB-SCARGLE periodogram (Lomb 1976; Scargle 1982), which finds periodicities in UNEVENLY sampled data, exactly the case for real observations interrupted by daylight and clouds. It returns power versus trial period; the peak is your candidate period, and you then PHASE-FOLD the light curve on that period to see if the data stack into a clean repeating shape. Crucially, you must ask whether the peak is significant — the FALSE-ALARM PROBABILITY estimates the chance that noise alone produced a peak that strong — and you must watch for ALIASING, spurious peaks at one-day and sidereal-day periods caused by the nightly observing gaps. A defended period is one folded, checked against a false-alarm threshold, and cross-checked against an independent survey when possible.

sections.heading: Reproducibility, provenance, and scope
sections.body: Finally, make the work reproducible and honestly scoped. Cite the archives and surveys you used (Gaia, ZTF, TESS, AAVSO) and their data releases, record your reduction steps, and keep the code and calibration frames. Match your claim to your instrument: a phone or DSLR and a small telescope can convincingly recover a deep hot-Jupiter transit (~1–2% dip) or a bright variable star's period, but not an 84-ppm Earth-analog transit — claiming the latter from backyard data is the fastest way to lose a judge's trust. The best projects state their limits explicitly, which paradoxically makes their positive result more believable.

lessons.workedExample: A student proposes to recover the transit of the hot Jupiter HD 189733 b with a small backyard telescope. First they check feasibility from geometry: with a planet radius Rp ≈ 1.13 R_jup and stellar radius Rs ≈ 0.76 R_sun, the predicted transit depth is (Rp/Rs)^2 = (1.13 × 71,492 km / (0.76 × 696,000 km))^2 = (80,786 / 528,960)^2 = (0.1527)^2 ≈ 0.0233 ≈ 2.3% ≈ 23,000 ppm — comfortably above a backyard setup's few-millimagnitude noise, so the project is realistic (unlike an 84-ppm Earth analog, which is not). They design the observation with three constant comparison stars of similar brightness in the same field for differential photometry, take calibration darks and flats, and plan to cover the ~1.8-hour transit plus baseline before and after. Each point carries a Poisson error bar; they watch for a meridian flip mid-run as a systematic. For a companion variable-star target observed over many nights, they run a Lomb-Scargle periodogram, find a peak near 0.55 days, phase-fold to confirm a clean repeating light curve, check the false-alarm probability, and note the one-day alias to rule out an observing-cadence artifact. The write-up cites AAVSO comparison sequences and states clearly what the instrument could and could not detect.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the capstone question: "walk me through your design — your control, your uncertainties, and how you know your result is real." A winning defense names differential photometry with vetted comparison stars as the control, shows honest error bars and identified systematics rather than a too-clean curve, uses the right statistic (Lomb-Scargle with a false-alarm check and phase-folding) for a period claim, and scopes the claim to the instrument — recovering a 2% hot-Jupiter transit, not an 84-ppm Earth. Judges reward a student who states the project's limits explicitly, because acknowledging what you cannot conclude is the strongest evidence you understand what you can.

questions.prompt: Why is differential photometry (measuring the target relative to comparison stars in the same frame) the key control in a ground-based photometry project?

options.text: It makes the target star physically brighter
Atmospheric dimming affects target and comparison stars together, so it divides out and leaves only real changes
It removes the need to calibrate the camera at all
It converts the data into a spectrum

explanations.a: Differential photometry changes nothing physical about the target; it is a measurement technique, not a way to brighten a star.
explanations.b: Correct — clouds, air mass, and transparency dim the target and nearby comparison stars by the same factor, so the target-to-comparison ratio cancels the atmosphere and isolates genuine astrophysical variability.
explanations.c: You still need darks and flats; differential photometry controls the atmosphere, not detector calibration.
explanations.d: Photometry measures brightness over time, not a spectrum; the comparison stars provide a reference, not spectral dispersion.

questions.prompt: A hot Jupiter (Rp ≈ 1.1 R_jup) transiting a Sun-like star gives a transit depth of roughly what — and is it recoverable with a small backyard telescope?

options.text: ~84 ppm; yes, easily recoverable from a backyard
~1–2% (10,000–20,000 ppm); yes, this is recoverable with careful differential photometry
~50%; the star nearly disappears
~1 ppm; only space telescopes can see it

explanations.a: 84 ppm is an EARTH-analog depth, which is NOT recoverable from a backyard; a hot Jupiter is far deeper.
explanations.b: Correct — (R_jup/R_sun)^2 ≈ 1%, and for a somewhat inflated hot Jupiter around a smaller star it reaches ~2%, well above backyard noise, so a small telescope with good differential photometry can recover it.
explanations.c: A planet blocks only a percent or two of the stellar disk, never half of it.
explanations.d: The depth is percent-level, not 1 ppm; hot-Jupiter transits are a classic amateur target, not space-only.

questions.prompt: Why is the Lomb-Scargle periodogram the right tool for finding a period in real observational data?

options.text: It requires perfectly evenly spaced data with no gaps
It handles UNEVENLY sampled data (interrupted by daylight and clouds), which real observations always have
It measures the star's distance
It only works on space-telescope data

explanations.a: The opposite is its strength — a plain FFT needs even sampling, whereas Lomb-Scargle was built precisely for uneven sampling.
explanations.b: Correct — Lomb & Scargle (1976, 1982) formulated a periodogram valid for irregularly sampled time series, which is exactly what ground-based observations produce because of nightly and weather gaps.
explanations.c: Period-finding gives a timescale of variability, not a distance; distance comes from parallax or standard candles.
explanations.d: It applies to any time series, ground or space; ground data, with its gaps, is where it is most needed.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of defending a claimed variable-star period.

items.text: Collect a differential light curve over many nights with comparison stars
Run a Lomb-Scargle periodogram to find the peak candidate period
Phase-fold the data on that period and check the false-alarm probability and aliases
Cross-check the period against an independent survey and report with uncertainty

questions.explanation: You first gather a clean differential light curve, then use Lomb-Scargle to identify the candidate period, then phase-fold and test whether the peak beats the false-alarm threshold (ruling out one-day aliases), and finally corroborate against an independent survey and quote an honest uncertainty — that full chain is what makes a period claim defensible.

questions.prompt: What most strengthens a judge's trust in a photometry project?

options.text: A perfectly smooth light curve with no error bars
Honest error bars, named systematics, and a claim scoped to what the instrument can actually detect
Claiming to have detected an Earth-analog transit from a backyard telescope
Reporting a result without citing the surveys or archives used

explanations.a: A suspiciously clean, error-bar-free curve reads as hidden processing or luck, not rigor; real data have scatter.
explanations.b: Correct — showing uncertainties, disclosing systematics you could not fully control, and matching the claim to the instrument's real sensitivity demonstrate genuine understanding and make the positive result credible.
explanations.c: An 84-ppm Earth-analog transit is far below backyard sensitivity; claiming it destroys credibility rather than building it.
explanations.d: Omitting data provenance makes the work unreproducible and untrustworthy; citing archives and releases is basic scientific practice.

units.label: Inside a Star: Structure and Hydrostatic Equilibrium

lessons.label: Hydrostatic Equilibrium: The Pressure-Gravity Balance That Holds a Star Up

sections.heading: A star is not falling in and not blowing apart
sections.body: A main-sequence star like the Sun has looked essentially the same for billions of years, which tells you something profound before you write a single equation: the inward pull of its own gravity and the outward push of its internal pressure are almost exactly balanced, everywhere, all the time. That balance is hydrostatic equilibrium. Consider a thin spherical shell of gas at radius r, thickness dr, with density ρ(r). Gravity pulls it inward with a force set by the mass m(r) enclosed below it; the gas pressure P is higher on the inside face of the shell than the outside, and that pressure difference pushes it outward. Setting the two equal for the shell gives the first structural equation of a star: dP/dr = −G·m(r)·ρ(r) / r². The minus sign is the whole physical story — pressure must DECREASE outward (dP/dr < 0), rising steadily as you go deeper, because deeper gas has to hold up more weight above it.

sections.heading: How much pressure? A crude integration gives a huge number
sections.body: You can estimate the central pressure without solving the full star. For a crude uniform-density sphere the equation integrates to a central pressure P_c = 3·G·M² / (8π·R⁴). Plugging in the Sun (M = 1.99×10³⁰ kg, R = 6.96×10⁸ m) gives P_c ≈ 1.3×10¹⁴ pascals — over a billion times Earth’s atmospheric pressure (10⁵ Pa). The real solar central pressure is even larger, about 2.5×10¹⁶ Pa, roughly 190× the uniform-sphere estimate, precisely because a real star’s mass is centrally concentrated rather than spread evenly. Either way the lesson is the same: to keep from collapsing, a star’s core must generate staggering pressures, and — via the ideal-gas law P = ρkT/(μ·m_H) — that pressure demands a staggering central temperature (about 1.5×10⁷ K in the Sun). Hydrostatic equilibrium is therefore the reason stellar cores are hot enough for nuclear fusion at all; the heat is not a lucky accident, it is a structural requirement of holding the star up.

sections.heading: Why the balance is stable, and who first wrote it down
sections.body: The equilibrium is self-correcting for an ordinary gas star. Squeeze the star slightly and its core heats and over-pressurizes, pushing back out; let it expand and it cools and under-pressurizes, letting gravity pull it back. This restoring behavior (rooted in the virial theorem of the next lessons) is why stars sit quietly on the main sequence instead of pulsing themselves apart. Jonathan Homer Lane published the first mathematical treatment of the Sun as a gaseous sphere in hydrostatic equilibrium in 1870, and Robert Emden’s 1907 book "Gaskugeln" developed the polytropic models (the Lane-Emden equation) that let astronomers solve idealized stellar structure by hand. Arthur Eddington synthesized these into the modern theory in "The Internal Constitution of the Stars" (1926), establishing hydrostatic equilibrium as the load-bearing assumption underneath essentially all of stellar physics.

lessons.workedExample: Estimate the Sun’s central pressure from hydrostatic equilibrium using the uniform-density formula P_c = 3·G·M² / (8π·R⁴). Numerator: 3 × (6.67×10⁻¹¹) × (1.99×10³⁰)² = 3 × 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 3.96×10⁶⁰ = 7.92×10⁵⁰. Denominator: 8π × (6.96×10⁸)⁴ = 25.13 × 2.35×10³⁵ = 5.90×10³⁶. So P_c ≈ 7.92×10⁵⁰ / 5.90×10³⁶ ≈ 1.3×10¹⁴ Pa. This is a floor: because the Sun’s mass is centrally concentrated, its true central pressure is about 2.5×10¹⁶ Pa (roughly 190× the estimate). Sanity check on temperature: setting P = ρkT/(μ·m_H) with the real central density ρ_c ≈ 1.5×10⁵ kg/m³, μ ≈ 0.6, and P_c ≈ 2.5×10¹⁶ Pa gives T_c = P_c·μ·m_H / (ρ_c·k) ≈ (2.5×10¹⁶ × 0.6 × 1.67×10⁻²⁷) / (1.5×10⁵ × 1.38×10⁻²³) ≈ 1.2×10⁷ K — right in the range needed for hydrogen fusion.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe hydrostatic equilibrium because it is the cleanest test of whether a student thinks of a star as a physical object or just a glowing dot. The tell of real understanding is being able to name the two competing terms (the inward weight ∝ G·m·ρ/r² versus the outward pressure gradient dP/dr) AND explain the minus sign — that pressure rises inward because deeper gas supports more overlying weight. A student who can then close the loop — "high pressure needs high temperature by the gas law, which is why cores are hot enough to fuse" — has understood that a star’s furnace is a structural consequence of not collapsing, not an add-on.

questions.prompt: The equation of hydrostatic equilibrium is dP/dr = −G·m(r)·ρ(r)/r². What does the minus sign tell you physically?

options.text: Pressure increases outward toward the star’s surface
Pressure decreases outward, i.e. it rises as you go deeper toward the core
Gravity points outward in a star
The star is losing mass over time

explanations.a: The opposite — a positive pressure gradient outward could not support the star; the minus sign forces pressure to fall outward.
explanations.b: Correct — dP/dr is negative, so pressure decreases with radius and therefore increases inward, because deeper gas must hold up more overlying weight.
explanations.c: Gravity points inward; the minus sign encodes that the inward gravity is balanced by an outward-pushing pressure gradient, not that gravity reverses.
explanations.d: The equation is about the static pressure structure at an instant, not mass loss.

questions.prompt: In hydrostatic equilibrium, which two effects are balanced within a spherical shell of stellar gas?

options.text: Radiation pressure and magnetic pressure only
The inward gravitational weight of the shell and the net outward force from the pressure gradient
The star’s rotation and its magnetic field
Nuclear fusion energy and the star’s luminosity

explanations.a: Radiation and magnetic pressure can contribute to the total pressure, but the fundamental balance is gravity against the total pressure gradient, not those two alone.
explanations.b: Correct — the pressure difference across the shell (the pressure gradient) provides an outward force that balances the inward gravitational pull set by the enclosed mass.
explanations.c: Rotation and magnetism are secondary; a non-rotating, unmagnetized star still obeys hydrostatic equilibrium.
explanations.d: Energy generation and transport are separate structural equations; hydrostatic equilibrium is a mechanical force balance, not an energy balance.

questions.prompt: A crude uniform-density estimate gives the Sun’s central pressure as about 1.3×10¹⁴ Pa, but the true value is roughly 2.5×10¹⁶ Pa. Why is the real value about 190× higher?

options.text: The Sun rotates, which adds pressure
The Sun’s mass is centrally concentrated rather than uniformly spread, so far more weight presses on the core
Magnetic fields dominate the central pressure
The uniform-density estimate used the wrong value of G

explanations.a: Solar rotation is far too slow to affect central pressure at the ~190× level.
explanations.b: Correct — real stars are strongly centrally concentrated, piling more mass near the center, which raises the pressure needed to support it well above the uniform-density estimate.
explanations.c: Magnetic pressure is negligible compared with gas pressure in the solar interior.
explanations.d: G is a fixed constant; the discrepancy comes from the density profile, not a wrong constant.

questions.prompt: Match each historical figure to their contribution to stellar structure theory.

right.text: First mathematical treatment of the Sun as a gaseous sphere in hydrostatic equilibrium
Developed polytropic gas-sphere models (the Lane-Emden equation) in the book "Gaskugeln"
Synthesized modern stellar-structure theory in "The Internal Constitution of the Stars"

questions.explanation: Lane (1870) first modeled the Sun as a self-gravitating gas sphere in equilibrium; Emden’s 1907 "Gaskugeln" developed the polytropic Lane-Emden models solvable by hand; Eddington’s 1926 "The Internal Constitution of the Stars" unified these into the modern theory that still frames the field.

lessons.label: The Four Equations of Stellar Structure and How They Close

sections.heading: Four coupled differential equations
sections.body: A spherical, non-rotating, non-magnetic star in equilibrium is described by four first-order differential equations in the radius r, each expressing a conservation law or a balance. (1) Mass continuity: dm/dr = 4π·r²·ρ — the mass enclosed grows as you add shells of density ρ. (2) Hydrostatic equilibrium: dP/dr = −G·m·ρ/r² — the mechanical balance from Lesson 1. (3) Energy generation: dL/dr = 4π·r²·ρ·ε, where ε is the nuclear energy released per kilogram per second, so the luminosity flowing outward accumulates from every shell that is fusing. (4) Energy transport, which sets the temperature gradient. In a radiative zone it reads dT/dr = −3κρL / (16π·a·c·r²·T³), where κ is the opacity; in a convective zone the gradient is set instead by the (roughly adiabatic) rising and sinking of gas parcels. These four link the four structural variables m(r), P(r), L(r), and T(r).

sections.heading: Three constitutive relations close the system
sections.body: Four equations for four running variables are not enough by themselves, because P, ε, and κ all depend on the local physics of the gas. They are supplied by three constitutive (or "material") relations that describe the stellar material: an equation of state P = P(ρ, T, composition) — for a normal star the ideal-gas law plus radiation pressure; an opacity law κ = κ(ρ, T, composition) — how strongly the gas blocks radiation; and an energy-generation law ε = ε(ρ, T, composition) — how fast nuclear reactions run. With these plugged in, the four differential equations become a closed, solvable system. This is why composition matters so much: change the hydrogen, helium, and metal fractions and you change the equation of state, the opacity, and the fusion rate all at once, which is exactly why stars evolve as they burn their fuel and alter their own composition.

sections.heading: Boundary conditions, the Vogt-Russell idea, and how they’re solved
sections.body: The system needs four boundary conditions: at the center (r = 0) both the enclosed mass and luminosity vanish (m = 0, L = 0), and at the surface the pressure and temperature drop to near-zero (essentially, P and T → the thin-atmosphere values). Given a star’s total mass and its composition profile, the solution is essentially unique — the heuristic Vogt-Russell "theorem" states that the mass and chemical composition of a star determine its radius, luminosity, and internal structure. Because the equations are stiff and coupled (central and surface conditions constrain opposite ends), they resisted hand solution beyond polytropes until the computer era. The Henyey relaxation method, introduced by Louis Henyey and collaborators around 1959, solves all the equations simultaneously by iterating a trial model toward consistency, and remains the backbone of modern stellar-evolution codes such as MESA.

lessons.workedExample: Use the mass-continuity equation to check the Sun’s mean density, then contrast it with the center. Mean density is just total mass over volume: ρ̄ = M / (4/3 · π·R³) = 1.99×10³⁰ / (4.19 × (6.96×10⁸)³) = 1.99×10³⁰ / (4.19 × 3.37×10²⁶) = 1.99×10³⁰ / 1.41×10²⁷ ≈ 1.41×10³ kg/m³ (1.4 g/cm³ — a bit denser than water). But integrating the full four-equation model gives a central density near 1.5×10⁵ kg/m³ (150 g/cm³, ~13× lead), over 100× the mean. That gap is the quantitative signature of the central concentration that also drove up the central pressure in Lesson 1: mass continuity ties the density profile directly to how the enclosed mass m(r) climbs with radius, and a centrally-peaked ρ makes m(r) rise steeply near the core and flatten in the tenuous outer envelope.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use "what are the equations of stellar structure?" as a depth check because a strong student can not only list the four (mass continuity, hydrostatic equilibrium, energy generation, energy transport) but explain that they are not self-contained — that the equation of state, opacity, and energy-generation rate must be supplied to close them. The most persuasive answer connects this to composition: because those three material relations all depend on chemical makeup, a star that fuses its hydrogen changes its own opacity, pressure, and burning rate, which is the mechanism behind stellar evolution. That link between "the closing relations" and "why stars evolve" is what separates memorization from understanding.

questions.prompt: Order these four structural relations by the quantity whose radial derivative they give, from the most purely geometric/mechanical to energy transport: mass continuity, hydrostatic equilibrium, energy generation, energy transport.

items.text: Mass continuity: dm/dr = 4πr²ρ
Hydrostatic equilibrium: dP/dr = −Gmρ/r²
Energy generation: dL/dr = 4πr²ρε
Energy transport: dT/dr (radiative or convective)

questions.explanation: The canonical ordering runs dm/dr (pure geometry of accumulating mass), then dP/dr (mechanical force balance), then dL/dr (where energy is produced), then dT/dr (how that energy is carried out) — the standard sequence in which the four equations are presented and integrated.

questions.prompt: Match each of the four structural equations to what it physically expresses.

right.text: How enclosed mass accumulates with radius
Mechanical balance of gravity and pressure gradient
How luminosity builds from nuclear energy release ε
The temperature gradient needed to carry the luminosity by radiative diffusion
