You pull Kepler/TESS light curves from MAST (the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes), and the Python package Lightkurve downloads, detrends, and phase-folds them for you in a few lines.

lessons.workedExample: You pick a Gaia DR3 star with parallax p = 10.0 milliarcseconds (mas) and apparent magnitude G = 9.00, and you want it on an HR diagram. Distance from parallax: d (parsecs) = 1 / p (arcseconds) = 1 / 0.0100 = 100 pc. Absolute magnitude from the distance modulus m − M = 5·log10(d) − 5: M_G = G − (5·log10(100) − 5) = 9.00 − (5·2 − 5) = 9.00 − 5 = 4.00. So this star sits near M_G ≈ +4, and if its BP–RP color is about +0.8 it lands squarely on the main sequence — a Sun-like G dwarf. Cross-match it to APOGEE and you might read Teff ≈ 5700 K, log g ≈ 4.4 (a dwarf, confirming the main-sequence placement), [Fe/H] ≈ 0.0. That single star, built from two free public archives, is a complete, defensible data point — distance, luminosity, temperature, and composition, each traceable to a measurement.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "where did your data come from, and could someone reproduce it?" because a defensible project rests on public, citable data rather than a hand-wave. Naming the actual archive and quantity — "Gaia DR3 parallaxes from the Gaia Archive via ADQL," "APOGEE Teff/log g/[Fe/H] from SDSS," "a Kepler light curve from MAST loaded with Lightkurve" — signals you know the difference between what each mission can and cannot tell you (Gaia gives distance and color but not composition; APOGEE gives composition but not a time series). A student who says "I got it off a website" has not shown they understand the provenance a judge is probing for.

questions.prompt: Which single measurement is Gaia's defining contribution that lets you place a field star on an HR diagram?

options.text: High-resolution chemical abundances of ~20 elements
Trigonometric parallax (hence distance) plus multi-band photometry
A four-year continuous light curve of each star
Radial velocity from the kappa mechanism

explanations.a: Detailed element-by-element abundances are APOGEE's specialty, not Gaia's core deliverable.
explanations.b: Correct — Gaia's parallaxes give distance (needed to turn apparent into absolute magnitude), and its G/BP/RP photometry gives brightness and color, which together are exactly the two axes of an observational HR diagram.
explanations.c: Continuous multi-year light curves are Kepler's hallmark; Gaia samples each star only sparsely over its scanning cycle.
explanations.d: The kappa mechanism drives pulsation; it is not a Gaia measurement, and radial velocity is not what places a star on an HR diagram.

questions.prompt: A star has a Gaia parallax of 5.0 mas. What is its distance?

options.text: 5 pc
50 pc
200 pc
500 pc

explanations.a: 5 pc would require a parallax of 200 mas — a very nearby star; 5.0 mas is much smaller.
explanations.b: 50 pc corresponds to a 20 mas parallax, not 5.0 mas.
explanations.c: Correct — d (pc) = 1 / p (arcsec) = 1 / 0.0050 = 200 pc. A smaller parallax means a larger distance.
explanations.d: 500 pc would correspond to a 2.0 mas parallax; at 5.0 mas the star is closer than that.

questions.prompt: Match each survey to the kind of data it primarily provides.

right.text: Parallax distance + multi-band colors
Infrared spectra → Teff, log g, [Fe/H], element abundances
High-cadence light curves (brightness vs. time)

questions.explanation: Gaia's astrometry yields parallax distances and G/BP/RP photometry; APOGEE's near-infrared spectra yield stellar parameters and detailed abundances; Kepler and TESS yield time-series light curves used for transits, variables, and asteroseismology.

questions.prompt: Why does APOGEE observe in the near-infrared (H-band) rather than in optical light?

options.text: Infrared light travels faster than optical light, so spectra arrive sooner
Infrared penetrates interstellar dust better, reaching red giants deep in the dusty Galactic plane
Stars emit no optical light, only infrared
Infrared spectra require no wavelength calibration

explanations.a: All light travels at the same speed in vacuum; wavelength does not change arrival time.
explanations.b: Correct — dust extinction is far weaker in the infrared than in the optical, so H-band spectroscopy can reach the red giants embedded in the dusty disk that optical surveys cannot see through.
explanations.c: Stars emit across the spectrum; cool giants peak toward the red/infrared but still radiate optically.
explanations.d: Infrared spectra still require careful wavelength and telluric calibration; that is not the reason for the band choice.

lessons.label: Building a Cluster Color-Magnitude Diagram and Fitting an Isochrone Age

sections.heading: Why a cluster is a natural laboratory
sections.body: A star cluster is the closest thing astronomy has to a controlled experiment. The stars in an open or globular cluster formed together from one gas cloud, so to good approximation they share the same age, the same distance, and the same initial chemical composition. That means the only thing that differs star-to-star is mass. When you plot a cluster on a color-magnitude diagram (CMD) — the observational HR diagram, absolute magnitude versus color — you are looking at a single-age population sorted by mass. This is what makes a cluster CMD an age clock: for a field star you cannot separate age, distance, and composition, but a cluster fixes distance and composition so the shape of the diagram encodes age alone.

sections.heading: The main-sequence turnoff is the hand of the clock
sections.body: Massive stars are more luminous and burn their hydrogen far faster, so they leave the main sequence first. As a cluster ages, the top of its main sequence "peels away" from the top down: the point where stars are just now exhausting core hydrogen and bending toward the giant branch is the main-sequence turnoff. Its brightness (and the mass of the star there) is the age indicator — a bright, blue turnoff means a young cluster whose massive stars are still shining, while a faint, red turnoff means an old cluster in which only low-mass stars survive on the main sequence. Main-sequence lifetime scales steeply with mass, roughly t ≈ 10 Gyr · (M/M_sun)^(−2.5), because luminosity rises much faster than mass (L ∝ M^~3.5) while fuel supply rises only linearly with mass.

sections.heading: Fitting an isochrone: distance, reddening, metallicity, then age
sections.body: An isochrone (Greek for "same time") is a theoretical curve showing where stars of a single age but a range of masses lie on the CMD, computed from stellar-evolution models (grids like PARSEC, MIST, or Dartmouth). Fitting one to a cluster is a four-step registration: (1) shift vertically by the distance modulus m − M to line up brightnesses, (2) shift diagonally to remove reddening/extinction from intervening dust (redder and fainter along the reddening vector), (3) pick the isochrone metallicity to match the cluster's known [Fe/H], and (4) then slide through ages until the model turnoff overlaps the observed turnoff. The age of the best-matching isochrone is the cluster age. Real benchmarks anchor your intuition: the Pleiades turnoff gives ≈100–125 Myr, the Hyades ≈625–650 Myr, the old open cluster M67 ≈4 Gyr, and globular clusters ≈12–13 Gyr — the last a genuine lower bound on the age of the Universe.

lessons.workedExample: You download Gaia photometry for an open cluster, correct for its distance modulus and a small reddening, and find the main-sequence turnoff sits at a stellar mass of about 1.5 M_sun (read off by matching the turnoff color/magnitude to model masses). Estimate the age directly from the turnoff mass: t ≈ 10 Gyr · (M/M_sun)^(−2.5) = 10 Gyr · (1.5)^(−2.5). Since 1.5^2.5 = 1.5^2 · 1.5^0.5 = 2.25 · 1.225 ≈ 2.76, the age ≈ 10 / 2.76 ≈ 3.6 Gyr. That places the cluster in the same regime as M67 (~4 Gyr) — an old open cluster. To defend it you would then overlay a 3.6-Gyr, solar-metallicity isochrone and show the turnoff, subgiant branch, and red-giant clump all fall on the model, and you would report an age uncertainty driven mainly by how sharply you can locate the turnoff and by the assumed distance and reddening.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges press on cluster ages because the CMD is where a student can either demonstrate real understanding or reveal that they plotted points without knowing what the shape means. The tell is whether you can point to the turnoff and explain that its position — not the color of the whole diagram — carries the age, and that you had to fix distance, reddening, and metallicity before the age readout is meaningful. A student who says "I matched an isochrone by eye and my turnoff-mass age agrees with the literature within my error bars" is defensible; one who reports a five-significant-figure age with no distance or reddening discussion is not.

questions.prompt: What makes a star cluster uniquely useful for measuring an age from a CMD?

options.text: Its stars all have exactly the same mass
Its stars share one age, distance, and composition, so the CMD shape reflects age alone
Clusters contain no dust, so reddening is never a concern
All clusters are exactly the same distance from Earth

explanations.a: The stars span a wide range of masses — that spread is precisely what draws out the main sequence and turnoff.
explanations.b: Correct — a common age, distance, and composition means mass is the only major variable left, so the diagram's morphology (especially the turnoff) encodes the cluster's age.
explanations.c: Many clusters do lie behind dust; reddening must still be estimated and removed before fitting.
explanations.d: Clusters span an enormous range of distances; each cluster's distance modulus must be determined individually.

questions.prompt: A cluster's main-sequence turnoff is at ~1.0 M_sun. Using t ≈ 10 Gyr · (M/M_sun)^(−2.5), roughly how old is it, and is it young or old?

options.text: ~0.1 Gyr — young
~1 Gyr — intermediate
~10 Gyr — old
~100 Gyr — older than the Universe

explanations.a: 0.1 Gyr would require a much more massive turnoff (~6 M_sun), a bright blue turnoff typical of a young cluster.
explanations.b: ~1 Gyr corresponds to a turnoff near ~2.5 M_sun, not 1.0 M_sun.
explanations.c: Correct — for M = 1.0 M_sun the formula gives t ≈ 10 · (1.0)^(−2.5) = 10 Gyr, an old cluster where only Sun-like and lower-mass stars remain on the main sequence.
explanations.d: 100 Gyr exceeds the age of the Universe (~13.8 Gyr) and would require an implausible sub-solar turnoff mass; the formula gives 10 Gyr here.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of fitting an isochrone to a cluster CMD to read off an age.

items.text: Shift the isochrone vertically by the distance modulus m − M
Apply the reddening/extinction correction along the reddening vector
Select the isochrone metallicity to match the cluster's [Fe/H]
Slide through model ages until the turnoff overlaps the data

questions.explanation: You first register brightness (distance modulus) and color (reddening), then fix composition (metallicity) so you are comparing to the right model family, and only then read the age off the isochrone whose turnoff matches — because age is the last free parameter once distance, reddening, and metallicity are pinned.

questions.prompt: Globular cluster ages of ~12–13 Gyr are scientifically important mainly because they:

options.text: Prove the Universe is exactly 13 Gyr old to high precision
Set an independent lower bound on the age of the Universe
Show that globular clusters are younger than open clusters
Demonstrate that all stars have the same lifetime

explanations.a: The turnoff age is a lower bound with real uncertainty, not an exact universal age; the cosmological age comes from independent methods.
explanations.b: Correct — the oldest stellar populations we can date must be younger than the Universe, so ~12–13 Gyr globular ages provide an independent floor on the cosmic age that any cosmology must respect.
explanations.c: Globular clusters are among the oldest stellar systems known — far older than typical open clusters like the Pleiades.
explanations.d: Lifetimes vary enormously with mass (t ∝ M^−2.5); the turnoff method depends on exactly that difference.

lessons.label: Timing a Pulsating Variable and Placing It on the Instability Strip

sections.heading: What pulsates, and why: the kappa mechanism and the instability strip
sections.body: Some stars are variable not because a companion eclipses them but because the star itself physically swells and shrinks — a radial pulsation. The engine is the kappa (opacity) mechanism operating in a partial-ionization zone, usually the layer where helium is transitioning between singly and doubly ionized (He II). When the star compresses, that zone becomes more opaque, traps heat, builds pressure, and pushes the layers back out; when it expands it becomes transparent, releases heat, and the cycle repeats — a heat-engine "valve" that keeps the oscillation going. Stars only pulsate this way when the ionization zone sits at the right depth, which happens in a narrow, nearly vertical band on the HR diagram called the instability strip. Classical Cepheids, RR Lyrae stars, and delta Scuti stars all live in this strip; a star crosses it as it evolves, pulsates while inside, and falls silent when it leaves.

sections.heading: The period-luminosity relation: Leavitt's law
sections.body: The reason pulsating variables are worth a science-fair project is Henrietta Swan Leavitt's discovery. Studying Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud at Harvard, Leavitt found (published 1908, quantified in 1912) that a Cepheid's pulsation period correlates tightly with its luminosity — longer-period Cepheids are intrinsically brighter. Because all her Cepheids sat in the same cloud at effectively one distance, apparent brightness stood in for luminosity, revealing the period-luminosity (P–L) relation cleanly. This is the calibrated ruler behind the cosmic distance ladder: measure a Cepheid's period from its light curve, read off its true luminosity (absolute magnitude) from the P–L law, compare to apparent magnitude, and you have a distance. Classical Cepheids have periods of roughly 1–100 days; RR Lyrae stars pulse faster (0.2–1 day) and are near-standard candles themselves, sitting close to absolute magnitude M_V ≈ +0.6.

sections.heading: Measuring the period: phase folding
sections.body: The core measurement in this project is the period, and the standard technique is phase folding. You take the light curve (brightness vs. time), guess a trial period P, and compute each observation's phase = (time mod P) / P, a number from 0 to 1. Plotting brightness against phase, the wrong period smears the points into a cloud; the correct period collapses every cycle on top of every other, producing one clean, repeating pulsation shape. In practice you scan many trial periods with an algorithm — a Lomb–Scargle periodogram or a string-length/phase-dispersion minimization — and pick the period that produces the tightest folded curve (the sharpest periodogram peak). Once you have the period and a mean color/temperature, you can plot the star on the instability strip and check that its period, temperature, and luminosity are mutually consistent with a Cepheid or RR Lyrae identification.

lessons.workedExample: You fold a TESS light curve and find a clean classical-Cepheid pulsation with period P = 10.0 days. Use the Benedict et al. (2007) HST-parallax calibration of Leavitt's law, M_V = −2.43·(log P − 1) − 4.05. With log10(10.0) = 1, the (log P − 1) term is zero, so M_V = −4.05 — a very luminous star, as expected for a Cepheid. Suppose its extinction-corrected mean apparent magnitude is V = 14.00. The distance modulus is m − M = 14.00 − (−4.05) = 18.05, so distance d = 10^((18.05 + 5)/5) = 10^4.61 ≈ 41,000 pc ≈ 41 kpc — comparable to the distance of the Large Magellanic Cloud (whose distance modulus is ≈18.5). The chain is exactly Leavitt's: period → luminosity → distance, and every step is a number you can defend from your own light curve plus a published P–L calibration.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe pulsating-variable projects by asking "how do you know the period, and how do you know it is a Cepheid and not just noise?" The strong answer names phase folding and a periodogram — you did not eyeball a bump, you found the period that minimizes scatter across many cycles — and then explains why period + color place the star inside the instability strip. A student who can add "and I used Leavitt's period-luminosity relation to turn the period into a distance" is demonstrating the exact reasoning that underpins the cosmic distance ladder, which is far more defensible than reporting a period with no method and no physical identification.

questions.prompt: What physically drives the pulsation of a Cepheid or RR Lyrae star?

options.text: A close companion star periodically eclipsing it
The kappa (opacity) mechanism in a helium partial-ionization zone acting as a heat valve
Sunspots rotating in and out of view
A planet transiting across its disk

explanations.a: That describes an eclipsing binary, whose brightness dips come from geometry, not from the star changing size.
explanations.b: Correct — in the He II partial-ionization zone, opacity rises on compression, traps heat, and pushes the layers out, then falls on expansion; this valve keeps the radial pulsation self-sustaining while the star is in the instability strip.
explanations.c: Starspots cause low-amplitude, rotation-tied modulation, not the large regular radial pulsation of a Cepheid.
explanations.d: A transiting planet produces a small periodic dip from occultation, not a physical swelling and shrinking of the star.

questions.prompt: Leavitt's period-luminosity relation states that, for classical Cepheids:

options.text: Shorter-period Cepheids are more luminous
Longer-period Cepheids are more luminous
Period and luminosity are unrelated
All Cepheids have identical luminosity regardless of period

explanations.a: It is the reverse — brighter Cepheids pulsate more slowly (longer period).
explanations.b: Correct — Leavitt found that longer pulsation periods correspond to greater intrinsic luminosity, the relation that lets a measured period yield an absolute magnitude and thus a distance.
explanations.c: The whole value of Leavitt's discovery is precisely that period and luminosity are tightly related.
explanations.d: RR Lyrae stars are near-standard candles, but classical Cepheids span a wide luminosity range set by period.

questions.prompt: When you fold a light curve at a trial period, how do you recognize the correct period?

options.text: The folded points scatter into a shapeless cloud
The folded points collapse onto a single clean, repeating curve
The star's average brightness increases
The number of data points doubles

explanations.a: A shapeless cloud is the signature of a wrong trial period, which fails to align successive cycles.
explanations.b: Correct — at the true period every cycle overlays every other, so the phased data trace one tight, repeating pulsation shape; a periodogram flags this as the sharpest peak.
explanations.c: Folding does not change the star's brightness; it only rearranges observations by phase.
explanations.d: Folding rearranges the existing points in phase; it does not create new data.

questions.prompt: A Cepheid has P = 10 days and, via Leavitt's law, M_V = −4.05. Its extinction-corrected apparent magnitude is V = 14.0. What is its approximate distance?

explanations.a: 410 pc would need a distance modulus of ~8, but m − M = 14.0 − (−4.05) = 18.05, far larger.
explanations.b: 4,100 pc corresponds to a modulus of ~13, not the 18.05 implied here.
explanations.c: Correct — m − M = 18.05 gives d = 10^((18.05 + 5)/5) = 10^4.61 ≈ 41,000 pc, roughly the distance of the Large Magellanic Cloud.
explanations.d: 410,000 pc corresponds to a modulus of ~23, much larger than 18.05.

lessons.label: Confronting a Stellar Model with Data: Where Theory and Observation Diverge

sections.heading: Stellar models are physics you can falsify
sections.body: A modern stellar-evolution model — computed with an open code like MESA (Modules for Experiments in Stellar Astrophysics, Paxton et al. 2011) and packaged as isochrone grids such as MIST or PARSEC — takes a mass and composition and integrates the equations of stellar structure forward in time, predicting how luminosity, temperature, and radius evolve. That makes it falsifiable: it outputs specific numbers you can hold against a measurement. The whole history of stellar astrophysics is confrontations of this kind. Cecilia Payne's 1925 thesis compared spectral-line strengths to ionization theory and concluded stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, overturning the prevailing view that the Sun's composition matched Earth's. Hans Bethe's late-1930s work identified nuclear fusion as the energy source — the proton-proton chain with Charles Critchfield (1938) and the CNO cycle in his 1939 paper (Nobel Prize 1967), replacing guesswork about what powers stars with nuclear physics that models could then encode.

sections.heading: A hard limit that models must respect: the Chandrasekhar mass
sections.body: Not every prediction is a soft fit; some are sharp thresholds. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar showed (1930–31) that electron-degeneracy pressure can support a white dwarf only up to a maximum mass of about 1.4 solar masses — the Chandrasekhar limit (Nobel Prize 1983). Above it, degeneracy fails and the star collapses. This is a place where theory and observation must agree exactly: if you found a stable, non-rotating white dwarf of 1.6 M_sun, the theory would be falsified, not merely adjusted. Instead, observed white-dwarf masses cluster below 1.4 M_sun, and the limit underpins the use of Type Ia supernovae — a white dwarf pushed toward the Chandrasekhar mass — as standardizable cosmological candles. A good confrontation-style project uses exactly this logic: identify a model prediction sharp enough that data can genuinely rule it out.

sections.heading: Where models actually strain: the solar abundance problem
sections.body: The most instructive divergences are the ones still unresolved. The standard solar model was long a triumph — using the older Grevesse & Sauval (1998) solar abundances it predicted the depth of the Sun's convective envelope at R_cz ≈ 0.713 R_sun, matching the helioseismic measurement of 0.713 ± 0.001 R_sun almost perfectly, and the surface helium fraction likewise agreed. Then Asplund, Grevesse and collaborators (2009) redetermined solar abundances with 3D model atmospheres and found substantially less carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen — a ~30% lower metallicity. Rebuilt with these "low-Z" abundances, the standard solar model now predicts a shallower convection zone (R_cz ≈ 0.72–0.73 R_sun) and a lower surface helium, disagreeing with helioseismology at many standard deviations. This "solar abundance problem" has resisted resolution for over a decade: either the new abundances, the opacities, or some transport physics in the model is wrong. It is the cleanest modern example that a model matching data with one input can be broken by a better measurement of another — and that a specific, quantified discrepancy is how progress is made.

lessons.workedExample: Frame a confrontation as a hypothesis test. Take the standard solar model's prediction for the base of the convection zone as your model output, and helioseismology as your data. Data: R_cz = 0.713 ± 0.001 R_sun (inferred from inverting observed solar oscillation frequencies). Model A (older, higher-metallicity abundances): predicts 0.713 R_sun — the residual is 0.000 R_sun, about 0 sigma, so the model is consistent with the data. Model B (revised low-metallicity abundances): predicts ≈0.723 R_sun — the residual is 0.010 R_sun, which against a 0.001 uncertainty is about 10 sigma, a decisive disagreement. The correct scientific conclusion is not "the Sun is wrong" but "the low-Z model fails this specific test, implicating the abundances, opacities, or mixing physics" — a diagnosis that points to what to fix, which is exactly what a judge wants to see instead of a vague claim that a model "matches" or "doesn't match."
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges love confrontation projects because they force the student to treat theory as testable rather than sacred, and the failure mode is easy to spot: a student who says "my data agree with the model" without an error bar has not really tested anything. The defensible move is to state the model's specific numerical prediction, state the measurement with its uncertainty, and quantify the gap in units of sigma — then interpret it (consistent, or which physics is implicated). Naming a real precedent, whether the sharp Chandrasekhar limit or the open solar abundance problem, shows you understand that "the model diverges here, by this much, for these possible reasons" is the actual output of good science, not "the model is right/wrong."

questions.prompt: The Chandrasekhar limit (~1.4 M_sun) is the maximum mass for which:

options.text: A main-sequence star can fuse hydrogen
Electron-degeneracy pressure can support a white dwarf against collapse
A star can form from a molecular cloud
A Cepheid can remain in the instability strip

explanations.a: Hydrogen fusion occurs across a huge mass range on the main sequence and is not what the Chandrasekhar limit bounds.
explanations.b: Correct — Chandrasekhar showed electron-degeneracy pressure can support a white dwarf only up to ~1.4 M_sun; above that it collapses, which is why observed white dwarfs stay below the limit and Type Ia supernovae ignite near it.
explanations.c: Star formation spans a vast mass range and is unrelated to the degeneracy-pressure limit.
explanations.d: Instability-strip membership depends on temperature and evolutionary phase, not the Chandrasekhar mass.

questions.prompt: In the "solar abundance problem," what broke the previously excellent agreement between the standard solar model and helioseismology?

options.text: A revised, lower determination of the Sun's heavy-element abundances (Asplund et al. 2009)
The discovery that the Sun is not powered by fusion
A measurement that the Sun has no convection zone
Evidence that the Sun exceeds the Chandrasekhar mass

explanations.a: Correct — 3D-atmosphere abundance work (Asplund, Grevesse and collaborators, 2009) lowered solar C/N/O and total metallicity by roughly 30%, and the rebuilt model no longer matches the helioseismic convection-zone depth and surface helium.
explanations.b: Solar fusion (the pp chain and CNO cycle) is well established and confirmed by solar neutrinos; that is not what changed.
explanations.c: The Sun clearly has a convection zone; the dispute is over its predicted depth, not its existence.
explanations.d: The Chandrasekhar limit concerns white dwarfs; the Sun is a main-sequence star far below any such threshold.

questions.prompt: A helioseismic measurement gives R_cz = 0.713 ± 0.001 R_sun; a model predicts 0.723 R_sun. How should this be characterized?

options.text: A ~10-sigma discrepancy — the model fails this specific test
Perfect agreement within uncertainty
An untestable claim, since models cannot be compared to data
Proof that helioseismology is impossible

explanations.a: Correct — the residual is 0.010 R_sun against a 0.001 uncertainty, so ~10 sigma; the model is decisively inconsistent with the data on this observable, implicating its abundances/opacities/mixing.
explanations.b: A 0.010 gap is ten times the 0.001 uncertainty, the opposite of agreement.
explanations.c: This is exactly a case where a model prediction is quantitatively compared to a measurement — the essence of testability.
explanations.d: Helioseismology produced the very 0.713 ± 0.001 measurement being used; the disagreement is with the model, not the method.

questions.prompt: Match each landmark to its correct contribution and date.

right.text: Stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium
The pp chain and CNO cycle power stars
The ~1.4 M_sun white-dwarf mass limit

questions.explanation: Cecilia Payne's 1925 thesis showed stellar atmospheres are dominated by hydrogen and helium; Hans Bethe (1939, Nobel 1967) identified nuclear fusion (pp chain and CNO cycle) as the stellar energy source; Chandrasekhar (1930–31, Nobel 1983) derived the ~1.4 M_sun maximum mass for a white dwarf supported by electron degeneracy.

lessons.label: Designing a Defensible Stellar-Astrophysics Science-Fair Project

sections.heading: A defensible project = one falsifiable question + one measurement + an error budget
sections.body: The difference between a poster that survives judging and one that collapses is scope. A defensible stellar-astrophysics project poses one falsifiable question, answers it with one clearly-defined measurement on public data, and quantifies the uncertainty. "How do stars work?" is not a project; "What is the age of open cluster M67 from its Gaia main-sequence turnoff, and does it agree with the literature value of ~4 Gyr?" is. The winning structure is always the same: hypothesis, method (which archive, which pipeline, which model to compare against), result with an error bar, and an honest comparison to a published value. The best projects in this branch reuse the exact tools from the earlier lessons — a Gaia CMD age, a Cepheid or RR Lyrae period-luminosity distance, an exoplanet transit depth, or a model-versus-data confrontation — each of which is bounded enough to finish and rich enough to defend.

sections.heading: A menu of bounded, defensible projects
sections.body: Concrete options, each anchored to a formula you can defend: (1) Cluster age — build a Gaia CMD of an open cluster, fit an isochrone, report the turnoff age against the literature. (2) Cepheid/RR Lyrae distance — phase-fold a TESS or AAVSO light curve, measure the period, apply Leavitt's law to get a distance. (3) Exoplanet radius from a transit — the fractional dip in brightness during a transit is the transit depth = (Rp/Rs)^2, the planet-to-star area ratio; measuring the depth and knowing the star's radius yields the planet's radius. A Jupiter-sized planet (Rp ≈ 0.1 Rs) produces a depth of (0.1)^2 = 0.01, a 1% dip — comfortably detectable in Kepler data. (4) Model confrontation — compare an observed turnoff or a white-dwarf mass to a MESA/MIST prediction and quantify the residual. Each of these turns a general curiosity into a single number with an uncertainty.

sections.heading: Systematics: the things that quietly wreck a stellar result
sections.body: Judges reward students who name the systematic errors that lurk in stellar measurements, because those are what separate a real result from a lucky one. For a CMD age: distance-modulus error, interstellar reddening/extinction (unaccounted dust makes stars look fainter and redder, biasing the age), and photometric contamination from field stars or unresolved binaries. For a variable-star distance: extinction again, the P–L relation's calibration zero-point, and blending in a crowded field. For a transit: stellar limb darkening and blended eclipsing binaries, which mimic a planet and are the classic false positive. Distinguishing random error (which averages down with more strides, more frames, more nights) from systematic error (a bias that does not average away, like a wrong extinction correction) is the single most sophisticated thing you can show. State your dominant systematic, say how you bounded it, and compare your value to the literature — a result consistent within its stated uncertainty is defensible even if it is not the last word.

lessons.workedExample: You choose the transit project on a Kepler target. Folding the light curve, you measure a flat-bottomed periodic dip of depth 0.0100 (a 1.00% drop) with period 3.5 days. Read the planet size from the transit depth: depth = (Rp/Rs)^2, so Rp/Rs = sqrt(0.0100) = 0.100. If APOGEE/Gaia give the host star a radius Rs = 1.0 R_sun ≈ 7.0×10^5 km, then Rp = 0.100 × 7.0×10^5 km = 7.0×10^4 km ≈ 1.0 R_Jupiter (Jupiter is ~7.1×10^4 km) — a hot Jupiter. Your error budget: the depth uncertainty (photometric scatter, propagating as roughly half the fractional error into the radius since Rp ∝ sqrt(depth)), the stellar-radius uncertainty (which enters Rp linearly and often dominates), and the false-positive check that the dip is flat-bottomed and single, not the V-shaped, secondary-eclipse-bearing signature of a blended eclipsing binary. You then compare Rp to the literature value for that known planet — agreement within your error bar is exactly the defensible result a judge is looking for.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the lesson judges are really testing across the whole fair: can you scope a question, execute one clean measurement, and know what could be fooling you? The strongest students volunteer their dominant systematic before being asked — "reddening is my biggest source of bias in the cluster age, and here is how I bounded it" — and they report a result with an error bar next to a literature value rather than a bare number. A project that says "I measured a 1% transit, inferred a Jupiter-radius planet from depth = (Rp/Rs)^2, and it matches the cataloged value within my uncertainty, after ruling out an eclipsing-binary false positive" is doing real science; one that reports a planet radius with no depth-to-radius reasoning and no false-positive check is not.

questions.prompt: Which is a defensibly-scoped stellar science-fair question?

options.text: How does the entire life cycle of every kind of star work?
What is M67's age from its Gaia main-sequence turnoff, and does it match the literature ~4 Gyr?
Is astrophysics important?
What is the meaning of the Universe?

explanations.a: This is far too broad to answer with one measurement and has no falsifiable claim or error budget.
explanations.b: Correct — it names one falsifiable question, one measurement (the turnoff age from a Gaia CMD), a specific dataset, and a literature value to compare against, which is exactly the defensible structure.
explanations.c: This is an opinion prompt, not a measurable hypothesis with data and uncertainty.
explanations.d: This is philosophical, not a bounded empirical question answerable with public stellar data.

questions.prompt: A transiting planet produces a 1.0% dip (depth = 0.010). Using transit depth = (Rp/Rs)^2, what is Rp/Rs?

explanations.a: 0.010 is the depth itself, not the radius ratio; you must take the square root.
explanations.b: Correct — Rp/Rs = sqrt(depth) = sqrt(0.010) = 0.10, so the planet's radius is one-tenth the star's, a Jupiter-sized planet around a Sun-like star.
explanations.c: 0.32 = sqrt(0.10); that would correspond to a much deeper 10% transit, not 1%.
explanations.d: Rp/Rs = 1.0 would mean the planet is as large as the star and would block all its light, a 100% depth.

questions.prompt: Which is a SYSTEMATIC error (a bias that does not average away with more data) in a cluster CMD age?

options.text: Random photon-counting noise on each star's magnitude
An unaccounted interstellar reddening/extinction correction
Occasional cosmic-ray hits on single exposures
Shot-to-shot scatter in repeated brightness measurements

explanations.a: Photon noise is random; it averages down as you combine more measurements, so it is not a systematic.
explanations.b: Correct — a wrong (or omitted) extinction correction biases every star the same way (fainter and redder), shifting the inferred age in one direction no matter how much data you collect; that is the definition of a systematic error.
explanations.c: Cosmic rays are random, occasional artifacts removed by combining frames, not a persistent bias.
explanations.d: Shot-to-shot scatter is random measurement noise that averages down, unlike a systematic bias.

questions.prompt: Order the elements of a defensible project write-up as a judge expects to hear them.

items.text: State a falsifiable hypothesis / question
Describe the method: dataset, pipeline, model to compare against
Report the measured result with an error bar
Compare to the literature value and interpret systematics

questions.explanation: A defensible project runs hypothesis → method → result-with-uncertainty → comparison to a published value with systematics discussed; the error bar and the literature comparison at the end are what make the result honest and testable rather than a bare claim.

questions.prompt: Match each project type to the key relation or check it relies on.

right.text: Main-sequence turnoff + isochrone fit
Leavitt's period-luminosity relation
Transit depth = (Rp/Rs)^2, plus an eclipsing-binary false-positive check

questions.explanation: A cluster age comes from fitting an isochrone to the main-sequence turnoff; a pulsating-variable distance comes from measuring the period and applying Leavitt's period-luminosity law; an exoplanet radius comes from the transit depth = (Rp/Rs)^2 combined with the stellar radius, after ruling out a blended eclipsing binary.
